The input “table” is not a numerical data table in the usual sense but rather a two-part extract from the Table of Contents of the SOFiSTiK “GRAPHIC – Graphical Representation of Finite Elements and Beam Structures” manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146). It lists all major sections, subsections and their page references. Below is a detailed, field-level description suitable for ingestion into a RAG-style vector store:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Two related lists:  
     – High-level Chapters and Subsections (Chapters 1–4)  
     – Detailed Command Reference nested under Chapter 3 (“Input and Output Description”)  

2. Common Columns  
   Each row in both lists is described by three principal attributes:  
   • section_id (string)  
     – A hierarchical numeric code separated by dots, e.g. “2.13.4”, “3.42”, “4.1.3”  
     – Top-level chapters appear as “1”, “2”, “3”, “4” (sometimes with a page suffix like “1-1”)  
   • title (string)  
     – A short textual description of the section or command, e.g. “Load/Design Cases”, “BEAM – Beam Element Results”, “Size and Paper Size”  
     – In some cases includes hyphenated keywords or acronyms (e.g. “LOAD – Load Pictures”, “CTRL – General Control Parameters”)  
   • page_ref (string)  
     – The page or sheet number where the section begins, e.g. “2-53”, “3-144”, “4-25”  
     – Uses chapter-based numbering in the format “chapter-page” for chapters 1–4 and simple page numbers for the command list  

3. High-Level TOC (Chapters 1–4)  
   • Rows 1–9: front matter and legal disclaimers (e.g. copyright notice, company contact)  
   • Sections:  
     – 1 (Task Description) – page 1-1  
     – 2 (WINDOWS Version) with subitems 2.1 through 2.14; among them:  
       • 2.13 (Load/Design Cases & Representation, Layer, Numbering Selection, Database) spanning pages 2-1 to 2-64  
       • 2.14 (How Does One Receive Pictures Fast?) – page 2-65  
     – 3 (Input and Output Description) – page 3-1, followed by top-level pointers to Sections 3.41…3.48  
     – 4 (Description of the Output Lists) – page 4-1, with examples 4.1.1…4.1.4 (Frame and Girder, Plate, Shell, Volume Structures)  

4. Command Reference (Chapter 3.1–3.40)  
   • A flat list of 40 “input record” commands used to define drawings and results plotting.  
   • Examples include:  
     – 3.1 INPUT LANGUAGE – page 3-1  
     – 3.3 CTRL – General Control Parameters – page 3-6  
     – 3.5 SIZE – Scale and Paper Size – page 3-10  
     – 3.12 LEGO – Objects of the Legend – page 3-31  
     – 3.25 DEFO – Deformed Structure – page 3-70  
     – 3.36 LC – Selection of a Load Case – page 3-88  
     – 3.40 STRU – Representation of Structure Values – page 3-102  

5. Hierarchy and Semantic Tags  
   • Hierarchy Level = number of numeric components in section_id (e.g. “3” = level 1, “3.42” = level 2, “3.42.5” = level 3 if present)  
   • Tag fields could include: “Chapter”, “Section”, “Subsection”, “Command”  
   • Keywords extracted from titles (e.g. “Load”, “Node”, “Beam”, “Quad”, “Isolines”, “Cuts”, “Database”, “Colour”, “Legend”, “Viewport”)  

6. Suggested Vector-Store Schema  
   Field Name      | Type    | Description  
   ——————      | ————  | ————————  
   document_id     | string  | Unique ID for the manual (e.g. “GRAPHIC_SP2025_4”)  
   section_id      | string  | Hierarchical code (e.g. “2.13.4”)  
   title           | string  | Section title text  
   page_ref        | string  | Page or sheet reference  
   hierarchy_level | integer | Count of dot-delimited levels  
   parent_id       | string  | section_id of the immediate parent (null for top level)  
   keywords        | [string] | Tokenized keywords from title  

This description captures the table’s structure, each column’s semantics and data types, plus hierarchy and keyword tagging, making it ready for RAG-style indexing and retrieval.

 GRAPHIC is a graphical program for the finite element and framework analysis modules of SOFiSTiK with a CDBASE database (e.g. FEABENCH, TALPA, ASE, STAR2, MAXIMA, BE- MESS, AQB, DYNA, HASE or HYDRA). The program allows the representation of almost all information saved in the database. These ones are in particular:
 Structures: Elements and nodes with or without numbers
 Support conditions
 Elastic foundations
 Cross sections and cross section values
 Material values
 Local coordinate systems
 Results: Principal stresses or principal moments as well as normal
 stresses
 (for plane structures according to magnitude and direction)
 Nodal and element loads
 Reinforcements in areas (contour lines)
 Non–linear stresses, strains and crack widths
 Vectors of velocities
 Potential values
 Deformed structure
 Bending forms of structure
 Internal forces and deformations for frame and girder systems
 Influence lines Beam loads Beam stiffnesses Maximum stresses Reinforcements
 The graphical representation can occur according to the result type in different manner:
 – Single lines or arrows with defined (scaled) length
 – Numerical values
 – Designations
 – Line representations for frame and girder systems or for
 – Cuts in plane structures
 – Isolines
 – Hatch or fill patterns

An interactive surface (GMEN) exists for the operating WINDOWS systems.
 An arbitrary input file can be read, graphical modifications can occur and an input file can be output again with this interactive version. In this case the interactive processing can be omitted for a new calculation of a known system.
 The drawings are arranged into graphics, pictures and layers. Every layer contains drawing elements (vectors, lines, text,...). A picture can consist of one or several layers which can lie over each other. A graphics is divided in one or several pictures which are positioned side by side.
 The WINDOWS version allows the direct layout of a representation with an immediate check of the result. The parameters can be changed or a new drawing can be requested if a picture is not liked.
 Two variants of the representation of result types are possible with the program GRAPHIC:
 1. the Edit box
 2. the result tree
 The working with the result tree is suitable for the fast generation of the desired pictures with- out user–specific definitions. The processing with the Edit box is recommended, if specific definitions become desired or necessary.

GRAPHIC:

On the left side of this black workspace are two thin, vertically stacked panels with light-gray backgrounds, each enclosed in its own border. The top panel is labeled “Result types” and the bottom panel “Loadcases:”. At the top right corner of the workspace is another narrow panel titled “Layer”; this panel is also empty, indicating no layers or results have yet been defined.

Directly beneath the canvas area, spanning the full width of the window, is a console-style status pane with monospaced text reporting initialization messages:

The overall look evokes DOS-era engineering software with a graphical frontend: stark black drawing space, lightweight panels for managing layers and results, and a combined command/status area for diagnostic messages. The caption beneath the screenshot, “Figure 2.1: Screen at beginning,” implies this is the initial state of the SOFiSTiK graphics module before any data or models have been loaded.

The image is a screenshot of the “SOFiSTiK WinGraf” application running on Windows. It has been annotated with arrows and labels to illustrate the standard components of a RAG-style graphical window. From top to bottom, left to right, the key elements are as follows:

1. Windows Title Bar  
   • Text reads “SOFiSTiK WinGraf – \<New File\> [2]” on the left and the standard close/minimize/maximize buttons on the right.  
   • Serves to identify the application and the active document.

2. Menu Bar  
   • Directly beneath the title bar, with the usual menu headings: File, Edit, View, Select, Extras, Options, Help.  
   • Provides access to all commands, options and settings via pull-down menus.

3. Toolbar Buttons  
   • Immediately below the menu bar is a horizontal strip of icon buttons for quick access to common functions (open, save, zoom, pan, grid toggle, various drawing and analysis tools, etc.).  
   • The annotation arrow points to this “toolbar” region.

4. Tree Panes (Docked on the Left)  
   a) Result Tree  
     – A vertical pane labeled “Result types” at the top.  
     – Contains a collapsible tree of items, e.g. System values → Structure, Contour, Nodes, All elements, Area element, Boundaries; Loads; Results; Design; Deformed struct.  
     – Allows the user to select which result data to display.  
   b) Layer Tree  
     – A smaller pane above the graphic area, titled “Layer,” showing Page 1 → Picture 1 → 1: Contour.  
     – Controls visibility and organization of layers and individual picture frames.

5. Floating Slider Controls  
   • Two small, independent dialog windows placed over the main graphic area:  
     – “Text height” with a slider bar and an “Aa” preview button to adjust annotation font size.  
     – “Unit” with a slider and a unit-icon button to scale axis or unit markers.  
   • The arrows labeled “slider control text heights” and “slider control unit” point to these.

6. Graphic Area (Central Region)  
   • The main plotting area shows a dashed‐line contour of a rectangular frame, with coordinate ticks along the bottom axis (0.00, 5.00, 10.00) and a small XYZ triad at the lower left.  
   • Red triangular markers are scattered to indicate special points or warnings.  
   • Date and structure info are displayed in light text across the top of the drawing (e.g. “12.07-991 . 04.2002”).  
   • This region is where the user picks, zooms, pans or otherwise interacts with graphical results.  
   • A cursor (not shown here) would change shape—commonly to a pickbox—when the user hovers over points or lines that can be selected.

7. Dialogue Area (Lower Region)  
   • A text console along the bottom of the window, showing system messages and user commands.  
   • In this screenshot it reads:  
     “CDBase could not open file  
      Reading initialisation from file WINGRAF.DEF  
      Command:  
      CANCEL  
      Command:”  
   • Acts like a command‐line interface for inputting requests, viewing error messages and prompting.

8. Status Bar (Very Bottom)  
   • A thin strip at the very bottom displaying “Ready” at left and context info on the right: “Page 1 | Picture 1 | Layer 1 : Contour.”  
   • Provides live feedback on the current mode and selection.

Together, these areas—title bar, menu bar, toolbar, tree panes, floating controls, graphic area, dialogue area and status bar—constitute the full RAG‐style graphical user interface. Each section is explicitly annotated to teach users how to navigate and manipulate structural‐analysis graphics within the SOFiSTiK WinGraf environment.

 The dialogue area at the lower picture border corresponds to a normal text screen. The inputs of the user with the keyboard, error estimates and requests are represented here. In this case the lines are shifted upward.
 The position of the pointer is symbolized in the graphical window via the so–called cursor. The form of the cursor can change according to the task. A pickbox is represented fundamentally, if a point or a line should be picked.

Subsequently the process of the GRAPHIC initialization is shown. In this case all settings are defined for the next layer to be generated after the start of the program.
 • Fixed values defined in the program are set directly after the start of the program.
 • Then the environment variables (GRAFSIZE,...,GRAFD000...) are searched for in the sys- tem environment or the file SOFISTIK.DEF. This environment variables are set, if they are available.
 • Then a predefinition file WINGRAF.DEF is searched for. This file contains the predefinitions as inputs in the CADINP format. The file WINGRAF.DEF is searched for according to the following rules:
 – first in the local working directory
 – then in the SOFiSTiK path, in all directories which are defined in the SOFiSTiK environ- ment variable
 – then in the directory in which the program (WINGRAF.EXE) is
 – If there are still no search results, the environment variables are evaluated in the order of CDBASETMP and TEMP.
 The file WINGRAF.DEF is stored manually, not automatically. This file contains the definitions of the interactive buttons, which are saved with the help of the INTE records.
 Furthermore the most important defaults can be defined in this file for a new graphic (SIZE, SCHH, COLO ...). The size of the saved data can be defined with the command predefinitions of drawing in the menu options.

The image is a schematic diagram entitled “Figure 2.3: Cursor types.” It sits on top of a large, evenly spaced, two-dimensional snap grid composed of thin, dashed blue horizontal and vertical lines, with a small blue dot marking each grid intersection. Superimposed on this grid are five stylized cursor shapes—each labeled a, b, c, d or e—together illustrating the various ways a CAD‐style program can draw the pointing device on the screen in “mouse” mode. A small red triangular pointer icon (resembling a standard mouse cursor) appears twice in the bottom-left region and once in the centre of the larger window, serving as a reference “anchor” for some of the cursor shapes.

1. Cursor type a (target cross)  
   • Located near the top-left corner of the overall snap grid, just inside a large black-outline rectangle (described under d).  
   • Depicted by two very short, perpendicular black lines crossing at their midpoints, forming a small “plus” sign or target reticle.  
   • This cursor appears centered on the red pointer icon, showing where a precise pick would occur.

2. Cursor type b (crosshair)  
   • Placed roughly in the centre horizontally (just right of the big window) and slightly above the midline of the grid.  
   • Rendered as two infinitely long (i.e. spanning the entire grid) thin black lines—one vertical, one horizontal—intersecting at the current pointer location.  
   • Labeled with a small lowercase “b” at the intersection point.

3. Cursor type c (rubber-band line)  
   • To the right of the full-screen crosshair, appearing as a single thin black line segment drawn at an oblique angle.  
   • One end of the line tethers back to an implied fixed “start” point; the other end tracks the cursor, simulating a dynamic “rubber line” that stretches as you move the mouse.  
   • This illustrates the mode used when interactively defining new line segments or trimming existing ones.

4. Cursor type d (window or box selection)  
   • Shown in the upper-left quadrant: a large, unfilled rectangle drawn in bold black outline.  
   • Its opposing corners lie on the snap-grid, indicating the diagonal drag from a starting corner to the current cursor position.  
   • Inside that rectangle is a faint dashed rectangle and the small target cross (cursor a), suggesting that the user can dynamically resize the selection box.  
   • A lowercase “d” label sits just outside the rectangle on its right edge.

5. Cursor type e (pickbox)  
   • Located just below the red pointer icon in the bottom-left area of the grid.  
   • Depicted as a small, solid black square (the pickbox) surrounding the cursor position; its size defines the “snap radius” used for object-snap operations (e.g. point or endpoint snapping).  
   • Labeled with a lowercase “e” just to its right.

At the very bottom of the page, centered beneath the grid, is the caption “Figure 2.3: Cursor types,” tying the illustration back to the accompanying text. Overall, the diagram makes clear how the program switches between these five distinct on‐screen cursor representations—target cross, crosshair, rubber line, window rectangle and pickbox—depending on the active drawing or selection command.

If the left mouse button is pressed in the graphic area, the corresponding coordinates of the picture plane are returned to GRAPHIC. The program changes to the keyboard, if a key on the keyboard is pressed. If the ESC–key or the RETURN key are used, the keyboard mode is interrupted or ended. It is changed to the mouse.
 The cursor has a different look dependently on the commands:
 target cross intersection of two short lines
 (a)
 cross line intersection of two long lines
 (b)
 rubber line line between start point and the point to be chosen (e.g. for cutting (c) line definitions)
 window rectangle at the diagonal between start point and the point to be (d) chosen (e.g. for box and window definitions)
 pickbox small box whose size shows the snap radius for the object snap (e) (e.g. for point snap) If this representation type appears, the pro- gram is in the pick mode.

Interpretation in Context  
According to the accompanying documentation, this list is one way to switch the various trees (layer tree, load case tree, database tree) and slider controls on and off, just as one would toggle toolbars. When a toolbar name is checked, it remains docked beside the main GRAPHIC window; if the user holds CTRL (STRG) while dragging a toolbar item from this list, that toolbar will float freely rather than dock.

Visual Details  
• Checkmarks are small, solid black ticks placed immediately to the left of the first character of each selected toolbar’s name.  
• Unchecked items have an empty space where the checkmark would appear, aligning the text labels in a neat column.  
• Text alignment is left-justified with equal vertical spacing (roughly one line height) between each entry.  
• The figure caption at the bottom is centered horizontally and set in a slightly smaller font, indicating this is an excerpt from a printed or PDF manual.

Together, the menu and its checkmarks give the user a clear, at-a-glance overview of which toolbars/trees are active, and provide a mechanism for quickly enabling or disabling any of the fifty-odd UI panels available in the software.

At the very top is a thin title bar labeled Toolbars, beneath which lies a bordered rectangular area containing a vertically scrollable list of available toolbars. A narrow scrollbar on the right edge of this list indicates that more items exist above and below the visible window.

The third and fourth entries (“Default Views” and “Delete page/picture/layer”) are highlighted with a dark background and white text, indicating they are currently selected. All other entries appear in standard (unselected) black text on a light gray background. The list box uses simple horizontal separators and no icons, relying solely on text labels to identify each toolbar. 

Immediately below the list and slightly off-frame, the figure is captioned “Figure 2.5: List of the toolbars in the menu Options,” suggesting that this dialog appears when the user chooses the “Options” or “Command Options” menu and then selects “Toolbars.” In the broader context of the accompanying documentation, this dialog is one of two ways (the other being a right-mouse-click on the gray border adjacent to existing toolbars) to toggle visibility for various interface elements such as the layer tree, load-case tree, database tree, and slider control. According to that text, any toolbar enabled in this list will display a small checkmark (or “hooklet”) next to its name when shown on the main interface. The screenshot itself does not display these checkmarks, implying that this list is in an editing or selection mode.

Visually, the window’s aesthetics evoke an early 2000s Windows environment: flat gray backgrounds, minimal padding, and thin black borders. There are no additional buttons (e.g., OK, Cancel, Apply) shown in the capture, suggesting that they may exist below the visible region or that this list is part of a larger pane. The list supports multi-selection, as evidenced by the two adjacent entries highlighted simultaneously. A faint, unbroken line separates the final visible entry (“Layer”) from blank space, indicating where additional, unscrolled items would appear.

Overall, Figure 2.5 communicates how end users can customize which toolbars (and, by extension, which functional panels or “trees”) are available within the main GRAPHIC window. When combined with the rest of the UI – including the ability to drag trees out of or dock them into the graphical workspace (with or without the CTRL key pressed) – this dialog plays a central role in tailoring the software layout to the user’s workflow.

The trees (layer tree, load case tree and database tree as well as the slider control, except for the result tree) can be switched on like the toolbar buttons:
 1. A list of the toolbars / trees / slider controls appears with a right–mouse–click at the free grey border next to the toolbars. Switched on toolbars get a hooklet.
 2. in the menu options command options there is a list tool bars.
 The trees can be arranged also outside the GRAPHIC window. If the STRG or CTRL key is pressed during the shift, the tree is not docked (mostly) also in the nearness of the border.

Frequently numerical values are necessary. These values are input via the keyboard in GRAPHIC. In this case the request in the dialogue area can show the values proposed by the program in peaked clips (e.g. < 0>). If the user has the same opinion, then he confirms it with return. Otherwise one or more values can be input separately with comma. Two commas following immediately or missing values do not change the corresponding value. The request is repeated, if the values are no numbers or if too much numbers are input. Numerical values has to be closed with RETURN of the keyboard (and not with the mouse button RETURN).

Texts are expected via the keyboard. If a standard text is planned, it is shown in peaked clips. This text can be accepted with return, or a new text is input. The return key deletes the input text and escape interrupts the request. The text input is ended automatically, if the maximum number of the signs is reached. Also texts have to be closed with RETURN of the keyboard (and not with the mouse button RETURN). Frequently also numbers are necessary within the text inputs.

The cursor can be moved to an arbitrary position in the graphical window. The coordinates are delivered from the picture plane to GRAPHIC with a click of the left mouse button. The missing third coordinate results from the current representation specification.
 The coordinates can be input also via the keyboard separately with comma. In this case the coordinates can be outside of the screen. If no Z coordinate is defined, it is calculated from the equation of the picture plane and the available coordinates.
 GRAPHIC allows like the program AutoCAD also the definition of local screen coordinate sys- tems as well as polar or relative coordinates.
 The polar coordinates are input with a < between the first value (radius) and the second value (angle). The relative coordinates to the previous point are defined with a prepositioned @.

The menu File contains the basic commands for the file management. Some commands of
 this menu are available also as toolbar buttons. The commands are described subsequently:
 New
 The just processed data file is saved as SOFiSTiK metafile. Then this file can be considered, stimulated, printed with the program REPORT BROWSER. On the other hand other graphic formats (e.g. DXF) can be generated.
 The values used for the representation are written as a list in a LST–file. The name results from the current document or from the database name, if no document name exists yet. The output can be limited to the current layer or the picture or the graphics in a dialogue box. Else the values of all graphics are written. Then this file can be considered and printed with the program WINTED.
 The input which led to the values is recorded as a batch input (as for the GRA file) in the so generated LST file. The lists can be formed differently. However, there is always a reference number (in general the element number or the number set in an intern way) and at least one result value (1st value). Also a 2nd and a 3rd value (for the main reinforcement, the transverse reinforcement or for the support components in the X, Y and Z direction) is available for the representation of some components (e.g. area reinforcement or support components). The section value at the beam axis is printed in addition to the results at line elements. The global insertion point or the group number is printed also for some results.
 Occurred changes can be taken back command–wise and produced also again.

The image is a black-and-white line drawing of a rectangular prism rendered in simple perspective, overlaid with both the orthogonal-Cartesian axes and the corresponding cylindrical-coordinate construction.  The prism’s top face appears as a slanted quadrilateral; from its two front‐corner vertices thin vertical lines drop down to form the front‐face edges, and from its two rear‐corner vertices similar inclined edges recede into depth.  

• Axes  
  – The X-axis is indicated by a bold arrow emanating from the top‐right corner of the prism and pointing off to the right.  
  – The Y-axis is similarly shown by an arrow at the top‐left corner, pointing off to the left.  
  – The Z-axis is drawn as a vertical arrow extending downward from a point at the center of the prism’s top face.  

• Cylindrical-coordinate elements  
  – A radial line, labeled “r,” connects that same central top‐face point to the lower front-right corner of the prism.  This slanted line represents the distance from the Z-axis to the target point.  
  – The projection of this radial line onto the horizontal (top) face is indicated by drawing the same corner point joined by a faint line to the central top point; at their junction an arc marks off the included angle, labeled “φ,” between that projection and the X-axis direction.  
  – The vertical drop from the chosen point on the top face to the horizontal plane beneath gives the coordinate “z.”  

Together, these elements illustrate how a single point in three-dimensional space can be specified either by its Cartesian coordinates (x along the X-axis, y along the Y-axis, z down the Z-axis) or by cylindrical coordinates (r, φ, z), where r is the horizontal radius from the Z-axis, φ the azimuthal angle in the XY-plane measured from the X-direction, and z the vertical height.  

Below the drawing, the caption reads:  
“Figure 2.6: Orthogonal–Cartesian resp. cylindrical coordinates.”  

Context note (from accompanying text): cylindrical coordinates in the global system are entered as “r < φ, z,” using a “<” to separate radius and angle, and may be toggled between global (“g”) or local (“l”) coordinate modes, or entered relative to the last reference point by prefixing with “r” or “@.”

 The coordinate input is defined in the global coordinate system (X, Y, Z) as soon as the option global is active or the letter ” g ” is added in front of the coordinates.
 The coordinates are arranged in a local coordinate system if the option local is active or the coordinates are entered with a ” l ”in front of them. A rotated or a skew local coordinate system can be defined in the option OPTIONS⇒coordinate system ⇒define local system .
 Cylindrical coordinates can be used in the global system (user defined system) and polar coordinates in the local system (display plane). For the input of these coordinates a ” < ” instead of a ”,” (comma) has to be used between the first and second coordinate.
 r < φ, z
 The first value is the radius r, the second value is the angle φ and the third value is the height z.

content:
The image is a composite perspective view showing both the finite‐element representation of a curved two-span T-beam bridge deck and the corresponding sequence of beam‐section “cuts” generated by the SIR module. At the top of the image you see a gently arched slab or deck element, displayed in a teal-green color gradient with a fine black mesh overlay. This upper geometry is composed entirely of eccentrically placed quadrilateral area elements (QUAD elements) arranged along the curved axis of the bridge. The deck surface is slightly warped in the vertical direction (z-axis), and the mesh lines define the individual shell or slab finite elements. The shading shifts subtly from darker teal at the far end toward lighter turquoise closer to the viewer, suggesting either a thickness variation or simply lighting from above.

Beneath this shell mesh, the lower half of the image illustrates how the three-dimensional cuts have been extracted and converted into an equivalent beam system for internal-force evaluation. A thin yellow-gold wireframe envelope traces the overall footprint of the deck, indicating the section-window boundaries used for integration. Along the curved length of the bridge, regularly spaced green rectangular frames represent the local cross-section planes (“cuts”)—each one oriented perpendicular to the beam axis as defined by the user’s “line of vision.” At each cut, small green coordinate axes or reference markers may be faintly visible, showing the local y- and z-directions.

Superimposed on these section frames is a continuous bending‐moment diagram drawn as a smooth blue curved line that runs beneath the beams, dipping and rising in accordance with the computed moment values. At key locations this blue line is annotated in blue text with numeric values—for example “863.9” near one peak, “201.4” at a trough—indicating the integrated bending moments (most likely in kilonewton-meters). Above the section frames, red triangular arrow symbols point upward or downward, and adjacent to these are red numeric labels such as “–276.1,” “–1623,” and “–721.4,” which correspond to shear forces or axial forces at those cross sections.

All elements in the lower view sit in a three-dimensional space with slight perspective distortion: the far end of the bridge curves away and slightly downward, while the near end appears closer and slightly elevated in the viewport. The ground or reference plane is omitted for clarity, leaving only the mesh, the gold outline, the green section frames, and the overlaid force diagrams. The caption beneath reads “Figure 2.8: SIR Cuts at a Bridge,” indicating that this visualization is part of a workflow in which SIR extracts integrated beam forces from a shell‐element model, stores them in the SOFiSTiK database, and prepares them for further checks such as ultimate‐limit‐state design.

Overall, the image conveys the transition from a detailed finite-element shell model of a skewed T-beam bridge deck to an equivalent line‐element representation, complete with user-defined section windows, integrated shear and moment results, and annotated numeric outputs ready for downstream structural design.

The image is a screen–capture of the “Properties of external beam section of the next input” dialog in the GRAPHIC module of SOFiSTiK (Windows version). This dialog is used to define the geometric and orientation parameters for a single SIR (Section Integration Routine) cut through a three-dimensional shell or slab model. Its components are as follows:

1. Window Title
   • “Properties of external beam section of the next input” appears in the title bar, indicating that the user is about to specify the next SIR cut.

2. Kind of local direction
   • A drop-down labeled “The” shows the selected option “default (positive cut local z direction).”  
   • To its right, a non-editable field reads “goes along the line of vision.”  
   • Below, three read-only numeric boxes labeled “Vector in X”, “Y”, “Z” display the direction vector components:  
     – X = 0.000  
     – Y = 0.000  
     – Z = 1.000  
   These settings define the local 3-D orientation of the SIR cut reference axis.

3. Position of reference point along the cut-local Y axis
   • A descriptive label explains: “positive y direction = along the beam to the right side.”  
   • A drop-down set to “on the Middle (on point 0.5*(YMIN+YMAX))” with an adjacent read-only text “[50.00 %]” shows that the reference point in the local Y direction is placed at the midpoint of the Y-window.

4. Local Y coordinates of the active window of the section plane
   • Two editable fields labeled “YMIN” and “YMAX” allow entry of the Y-extent of the integration window:  
     – YMIN = –1.500 m  
     – YMAX = 1.500 m

5. Position of reference point along the cut-local Z axis
   • A label states: “positive z direction = positive line of vision.”  
   • A drop-down set to “on the Middle (on point 0.5*(ZMIN+ZMAX))” with “[50.00 %]” again indicates the midpoint reference for the Z axis.

6. Local Z coordinates of the active window of the section plane
   • Two editable boxes labeled “ZMIN” and “ZMAX”:  
     – ZMIN = –999.000 m  
     – ZMAX =  999.000 m  
   These extreme values typically allow the cut to pass through the entire thickness of planar elements (i.e. no truncation in Z).

7. Depth of the section box for the support reactions
   • Two small numeric fields labeled “XMIN” and “XMAX” specify the half-thickness or depth in the local X direction used to collect support reactions:  
     – XMIN = –0.001 m  
     – XMAX =  0.001 m

8. In group
   • A small text field labeled “in group” with the default value “0 (0…999)” lets the user assign the cut to a user-defined group number (useful for filtering or later batch operations).

9. Dialog buttons
   • OK — confirms and closes the dialog, saving these properties to memory.  
   • Cancel — closes the dialog without saving changes.  
   • (In some versions a Help button may also appear, though not visible here.)

10. Figure Caption
   • Below the dialog image (in the original document) is the caption “Figure 2.9: Properties of the next SIR cut,” tying the screenshot back to the user manual’s explanation of how to set up a single cut.

Overall, this dialog centralizes the definition of orientation, reference-point placement, active window dimensions, reaction-depth box, and grouping for a SIR cut. Once confirmed, these parameters are stored in the SOFiSTiK database and later used by the SIR program to integrate internal forces, generate equivalent beam cross-sections, and drive subsequent design checks in GRAPHIC or downstream modules (AQUA, AQB, WinAQUA, etc.).

content:
The image is a grayscale screenshot of a modal dialog box titled “Save the SIR sections in database.” It is taken from the GRAPHIC interface of SOFiSTiK, showing the final step in storing externally generated beam‐section cuts (from program SIR) back into the project database. Below the title bar the dialog is subdivided into four logical areas:

1. Summary and Warning Text  
   - A static text line reads “Found external beam sections from program SIR: 11,” indicating that eleven sections have been generated.  
   - Directly below is a warning paragraph: “With the SAVE command these external beam sections will overwritten; corresponding forces and design values will be deleted.”  
   - A final summary line in this block states “Number of defined external sections: 11.”  

2. Overwrite Options  
   - Two checkboxes are listed one under the other:  
     • “Overwrite the found sections in database with the newer ones” (checked)  
     • “Overwrite the SIR input file (.GSR)” (checked)  
   These options allow the user to replace previously stored section definitions and the input file on disk.

3. Control of the SIR Calculation (to be stored in the GSR file)  
   – A labeled group box (“Control of the SIR calculation (will stored in the GSR file)”) contains three further checkboxes, all initially unchecked:  
     • “Delete unused SIR-cross sections in the database”  
     • “Generate SREC cross sections, if it is possible”  
     • “Use of only one (the first) material number in the generated cross section”  
   These flags control post‐processing behavior: cleaning up unused sections, generating simplified rectangular sections (“SREC”) where possible, and coercing multi‐material sections to a single material.

4. Launching calculation of the saved sections?  
   – A second group box poses the question “Launching calculation of the saved sections?” and presents three mutually exclusive radio buttons:  
     ○ “No, no following action”  
     ○ “Not directly, only launch TEDDY with the SIR input”  
     ● “Yes, launch calculation with program SIR directly” (selected)  
   – Below the selected radio button are two indented checkboxes (both checked):  
     ◦ “Afterwards calculate the new cross sections with program A…” (the remainder of the text is truncated in the screenshot but implies AQUA or AQB)  
     ◦ “Put the reference axes to the Y- and Z- center of gravity (centroids)”  
   – A concluding line “Launch the calculation again.” appears immediately beneath these options.

At the bottom of the dialog, an “OK” button sits right-aligned, ready to confirm all settings and invoke the database update and optionally the SIR calculation. Outside and below the window, a small caption reads “Figure 2.12: Save SIR cut to database.”

Overall, the screenshot captures the final interactive step in GRAPHIC for persisting beam‐section cuts: it summarizes what will be saved, offers overwrite controls, additional calculation flags, and a choice of triggering the SIR solver or auxiliary processes immediately.

sections: 2.7.3 Three–Dimensional Cuts through a Structure (SIR Cuts)

content:
The illustration shows the cut-plane results of an SIR (Section Integration of a shell Resultant) operation through a two-dimensional tunnel shell model, displayed in the GRAPHIC environment of SOFiSTiK. What you see is essentially a plan view of a tunnel lining and its surrounding ground, discretized entirely with quadrilateral area (QUAD) finite elements. All element edges and mesh lines are drawn in a light yellow color, forming a rectangular outer boundary and an inner oval void that represents the tunnel opening.

Along the upper portion of the oval (the tunnel crown), a series of closely spaced SIR cuts has been generated. Each cut is defined by a local plane which intersects the shell elements; the sequence of cuts follows the curvature of the tunnel lining. At each cut location:

 • A small green arrow—originating on the shell surface and pointing outward—represents one component of the resultant beam forces obtained by integrating plate internal forces over the section window. These could be shear or axial force resultants, depending on the chosen local axis.  
 • Blue numeric labels are placed above or next to each green arrow. These numbers (for example “+22.47,” “+23.01,” etc.) show the magnitude of an integrated bending moment (or another specified force component) for each cut.  
 • At one central location just below the others, a red arrow and the red legend “–280.2” highlight a negative bending moment or force component of larger magnitude. This draws attention to a peak internal force that may govern design checks.  

The section window geometry—its local Y and Z extents—is implicitly defined by the dialog settings (for instance ZMIN = –1.5 m, ZMAX = +1.5 m for the effective girder width). The uniform spacing of cuts, and the fact that they conform to the curved geometry, indicates the “multiple SIR cuts via beam” option was used. The user has likely limited the maximum distance between successive cuts to capture the full curvature without over-cutting at the tunnel’s edges.

Surrounding the oval, the mesh extends into a rectangular soil domain, suggesting that ground–structure interaction might also be part of the analysis. The fine mesh near the tunnel lining and the coarser mesh farther away indicate graded refinement. No beam elements are used for the main girder here; instead, the shell elements provide a continuous area representation, and the SIR cuts extract equivalent beam results for design.

At the very top of the image one can also spot a few stray mesh lines that appear to represent boundary constraints or supports in the Z direction, but these are not the focus. The primary takeaway is that the snapshot visualizes how SIR integrates internal forces over user-defined section planes within a shell model, producing an equivalent girder system that can be used for ultimate limit state checks or cross-section design.

content:
The image is a modal dialog window, titled “Save the SIR sections in database,” set in a light‐gray Windows style. Its contents are organized into several logical blocks, each governing part of the workflow for saving and (optionally) recalculating beam‐section cuts generated by the SIR program:

1. Header information  
   - A static text line reads “Found external beam sections from program SIR: 120,” indicating how many sections have been generated.  
   - Directly beneath it is a warning: “With the SAVE command this external beam sections will overwritten. The corresponding forces and design values will be deleted.”  
   - A simple label restates “Number of defined external sections: 120.”

2. Overwrite options  
   - A checkbox labeled “Overwrite the found sections in database with the newer ones” is checked, meaning any previous sections in the database will be replaced.  
   - A second checkbox, “Overwrite the SIR input file (*.GSR),” is present but left unchecked, so the original SIR input file will remain intact.

3. Control of the SIR calculation (will stored in the GSR file)  
   Enclosed in a framed group box are three further checkboxes, all of which are checked:  
   • “Delete unused SIR-cross sections in the database” – unreferenced cuts will be purged.  
   • “Generate SREC cross sections, if it is possible” – instructs the system to create simplified rectangular cross-section definitions where applicable.  
   • “Use of only one (the first) material number in the generated cross section” – prevents multiple materials from contaminating a single cross section.

4. Launching calculation of the saved sections?  
   In another framed group, three radio buttons let the user choose the post-save action:  
   – “No, no following action” (not selected)  
   – “Not directly, only launch TEDDY with the SIR input” (not selected)  
   – “Yes, launch calculation with program SIR directly” (selected)  

   Below these are three additional checkboxes:  
   • “Afterwards calculate the new cross sections with program AQUA” (checked),  
   • “Put the reference axes to the Y- and Z- center of gravity” (checked),  
   • “Launch the calculation again” (unchecked).

At the bottom right corner sits an “OK” button (no Cancel button is shown in the cropped image), ready to confirm and execute the above settings. The figure is captioned “Figure 2.20: Save SIR cut to database.” This dialog is clearly part of the SOFiSTiK GRAPHIC interface, offering fine control over which beam‐section cuts are preserved, overwritten, or recalculated downstream by SIR (and optionally by AQUA) once the user confirms.

The cutting pattern lines at the membrane structures are defined with the commands of the submenu Cutting pattern. Therefrom the geodetic isolines are determined. The resultant cut- ting pattern areas are transmitted to the program TEXTILE. The menu Cutting pattern contains the following commands:
 it is possible to allocate BRIC cuts, which should be generated, to an own group num- ber. Thus BRIC cuts with different directions can get for example different group numbers. BRIC cuts can be also deleted via their group number (see Delete BRIC cuts).
 A straight BRIC cut or a BRIC cut as polygon can be generated via
 The start point and the end point of the line are input interactively with the mouse or via the keyboard. If the user wants to input the relative coordinates with the keyboard, a @ must be input at first as in AutoCAD. BRIC cuts with several segments (polygon) retain their direction. The direction of single cuts is aligned.
 The deletion of cuts can be done via
 The selection of BRIC cuts in the active groups is done via an input in the dialogue area. The input for each single cut is Y = Yes (deleting) or N = No (not deleting). The input for all cuts is A. The selection is accepted with ENTER and is canceled with ESC. If only the BRIC cuts of a specific group number are supposed to be selected, the group numbers of the remaining BRIC cuts have to be switched off via the Group definition .

Below is a focused description of the four attribute‐type input records shown in the table. In the WING/CADINP input language these records do not generate their own drawing; instead they establish parameters (“attributes”) that affect all subsequent plot commands until they are re-defined.  

1. CTRL  (Control Options)  
   • Purpose: Globally manages on/off switches and numeric settings used by downstream plotting routines.  
   • Fields:  
     – OPT  : Name of the control option (e.g. “GRID”, “AXES”, “FRAME”).  
     – VAL  : Primary value for the option (often “ON”/“OFF”, but may be numeric).  
     – V2   : Secondary or alternate setting (used when an option has two parameters).  
   • Behavior: When you input “CTRL OPT=…, VAL=…, V2=…”, the specified option is activated immediately, and remains in force for every subsequent drawing until an overriding CTRL record appears.  

2. DB  (Database Output Settings)  
   • Purpose: Selects information from the internal SOFiSTiK database to annotate or report on the plot.  
   • Fields:  
     – NO    : Numeric code of the database table or result type (load cases, material data, etc.).  
     – INIT  : Initialization flag (e.g. “YES” to start a fresh table block, “NO” to continue).  
     – TITL  : Text title or heading for the database printout.  
   • Behavior: A DB record causes the requested database information to be printed on the current sheet (as title block or table). Its settings persist until re-issued.  

3. SIZE  (Basic Page and Plot Scaling)  
   • Purpose: Defines the overall plotting window, paper size, aspect ratio, and scaling behavior. This record is typically sent once at the start of a drawing session (or whenever the page layout changes).  
   • Fields:  
     – TYPE : Page orientation or format (e.g. “LP” for landscape paper, “PN” for portrait).  
     – SC   : Overall scaling factor (unitless multiplier for all coordinates).  
     – W, H : Width and height of the plotting area.  
     – MARG : Margin size around the active plotting frame.  
     – FORM : Paper form or device code (e.g. “A4”, “A3”).  
     – HLEG : Height reserved for legends or footnotes.  
     – WLEG : Width reserved for legends.  
     – SCAL : Secondary scaling parameter (e.g. annotation scale).  
     – SPLI : Spacing between plot elements (line spacing).  
     – SLEG : Spacing allocated around legend boxes.  
   • Behavior: Once SIZE is set, all subsequent graphical and text elements abide by these dimensions and scale factors until re-specified by another SIZE record.  

4. SIZ2  (Extended Layout Parameters)  
   • Purpose: Provides more granular control over special layout offsets, clipping boundaries, and free‐area definitions. This refines what was started in the basic SIZE record.  
   • Fields:  
     – UMBR : Umbra or clipping zone size (the unprintable margin).  
     – DRUO, DRUR, DRUL : Offsets for drawing origin in the origin (O), right (R) and left (L) directions.  
     – LEGW : Additional width reserved specifically for legends beyond WLEG.  
     – FREE : Size of a “free area” where custom annotations can be added.  
     – FAKH : Height factor for footers or header bars.  
   • Behavior: These parameters modify only those aspects of the plot that require finer adjustments (e.g. shifting the entire drawing window to make room for side tables). SIZ2 stays in effect until changed by a subsequent SIZ2 record.  

Usage Notes:  
– Ordering: CTRL, DB, SIZE and SIZ2 are attribute records; they do not themselves produce a visible plot but configure subsequent drawing orders (STRU, LOAD, NODE, etc.).  
– Persistence: Once set, attribute values apply to all following drawings until overridden.  
– Flexibility: You may intersperse these attribute records freely among drawing commands. The system always applies the latest definitions to the next plot output.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the “input table” for the WING plotting module.  This table lists every valid CADINP record that you can feed into WING, classifying them by their role (drawing orders vs. attribute records) and explaining their purpose and interplay.  

1.  Overview  
    - WING reads a single block of CADINP input records terminated by END.  
    - Records fall into two categories:  
      a.  Drawing‐order records (trigger a new plot or overlay)  
      b.  Attribute records (modify parameters for subsequent drawings)  
    - Attributes take effect only on the next drawing command. If you interpose the keyword AND between drawing orders, the next plot is merged into the last one (AND is then reset).  

2.  Drawing Orders  
    These eight keywords each generate (or append to) a plot. Every plot inherits the most recently updated attributes.  
    •  STRU   – Full structural plot: elements, numbering, designations; can show deformed shapes, eigenmodes, stress‐peak areas.  
    •  LOAD   – Loads in vector form, line loads (beams), or area‐block loads (QUAD elements).  
    •  NODE   – Nodal results (displacements, reactions, boundary forces) as vectors or numeric labels.  
    •  QUAD   – Field plot on quadrilateral elements: scalar (e.g. bending moment), vector (shear), tensor (principal stresses), or numeric/fill‐pattern displays.  
    •  BEAM   – Line diagrams for frame/girder systems (e.g. bending‐moment diagrams) with numeric designations.  
    •  ISOL   – Isolines drawn on QUAD elements.  
    •  SECT   – Results along user‐defined cuts through the structure.  
    •  BRIC   – Results on volume (brick) elements.  

3.  Attribute Records  
    All other entries in the table configure line styles, colors, text, grouping and other per‐plot parameters. Once set, they persist until redefined. Common attribute categories include:  

    A.  Color/Fill/Pattern  
       – COLB  : Color block index  
       – GRAFFARB, GRAFFILL (from SOFISTIK.DEF) to set default colors/fills  
       – PA21–PA27 : Custom pattern definitions  

    B.  Text & Designations  
       – T     : Text command (font, size, string)  
       – TITL  : Plot title  
       – DESI  : Element or node designations  
       – HEAD  : Header line (language‐sensitive, via GRAFKOPF)  

    C.  Geometry & Positioning  
       – MOVE, DRAW : Common drawing attributes  
       – X, (and implicitly Y,Z via DISX, DISY, DISZ) for text/element offsets  
       – LENG, WIDE : Symbol length and line width  
       – LMAX, LMIN : Clipping or symbol‐size parameters  
       – DIST : Marker spacing  

    D.  Selection & Grouping  
       – SELE  : Node/element selection filter  
       – GRP   : Assign to group for collective styling or visibility  

    E.  Load & Case Control  
       – LC    : Load‐case number specification (duplicated entry in table)  
       – LOAD  : See drawing‐orders above (but can also appear as attribute in rare contexts)  

    F.  Material & Section Properties  
       – MAT, NMAT : Material assignment (original and “new”)  
       – SECT : Draw section cuts/results  
       – ENO   : Element number override or reference  
       – REF   : External reference tag for plots  

    G.  Scaling & Factors  
       – FAC1, FAC2, FAC3 : Scaling factors for vector‐plot components  
       – DIF1, DIF2, DIF3 : Differentiation factors or component offsets  

    H.  Arrows & Directions  
       – ARRO  : Arrowhead style  
       – DIRE  : Vector direction override  
       – KIND, KIN2, KIN3 : Symbol or vector kind codes (arrow, circle, etc.)  

4.  Environment‐Level Defaults  
    WING also honors system environment parameters defined in SOFISTIK.DEF under “[SOFiSTiK]”. Each begins with GRAF plus the record name. Examples:  
    •  GRAFKOPF  – Default HEAD record (e.g. “KOPF” for German or “HEAD” for English)  
    •  GRAFSTEU  – Switch default‐control (e.g. “CTRL DEF VARI”) instead of WINGRAF.DEF  
    •  GRAFSIZE  – Paper and margin settings (e.g. “SIZE 0 LP MARG NO”)  
    •  GRAFD000 … GRAFDZZZ – Up to thousands of expanded default CADINP records that pre‐populate every WING input session.  

5.  Special Records (from the general “Basics” manual)  
    – UNIT  : User‐specific unit definitions  
    – PAGE  : Page‐control (orientation, numbering)  
    – END   : Terminates the WING input block  

6.  Sequence Rules  
    – Records may appear in any order.  
    – Attribute records only affect the drawings issued after their appearance.  
    – When you need a deformed‐and‐undeformed superposed plot, use:  
         STRU ; AND ; DEFO … ; STRU  

This table therefore serves as the definitive catalog of every CADINP keyword that WING can process—distinguishing which commands actually produce plots and which merely set up attributes for those plots.

This description covers the “master list” of CADINP/WING input records as shown in the continuation table. It is organized to support a RAG-style vector store by identifying each record’s role, grouping, and behavior.

1. Overall Structure  
- WING processes one input block (terminated by END).  
- Records are read sequentially; most are attribute updates and take effect on the next drawing command.  
- A small set are “drawing orders” that actually generate plots.  

2. Drawing‐Order Records  
These commands trigger a new drawing (or, with AND, are overlaid on the current drawing). They query a specific load case or system result from the database.  
• STRU – Structural plot of geometry, numbering, systems, deformed shapes, eigenmodes or stress fields.  
• LOAD – Plot of applied loads (vectors, line loads, area blocks).  
• NODE – Node‐based results (displacements, reactions) as vectors or numeric labels.  
• QUAD – Element results on quadrilaterals: scalar, vector, tensor, numeric or filled patterns.  
• BEAM – Line plots for frame/girder bending moments, shear forces, etc., with labels.  
• ISOL – Isolines over QUAD elements.  
• SECT – Cut‐through results along arbitrary sections.  
• BRIC – Volume‐element results (e.g. stresses in solids).  

3. Combining Drawings  
• The keyword AND placed between two drawing orders causes the second plot to be overlaid onto the first.  
• After use, AND resets automatically.  
• Example sequence to show both undeformed and deformed shapes in one view:  
  STRU ; AND ; DEFO ... ; STRU  

4. Attribute Records  
All other records in the table are considered attribute records—they set graphics parameters, text, formatting, or data‐filtering options, but do not by themselves produce a plot. Examples include:  
• TEXT, DRAW, MOVE – common positioning, text and drawing attributes.  
• MAT, DESI, TITL – material or designation filters, plot titles.  
• FAC1/FAC2/FAC3 – scaling factors for different result types.  
• DIF1/DIF2/DIF3, DIRE – specialized difference or direction parameters.  
• CUT/CUTP – define section planes or cutting parameters.  
• REF, ENO, X – reference offsets, element/node numbers, coordinate axes.  

5. SOFiSTiK Environment Defaults  
• WING reads optional environment parameters from SOFISTIK.DEF under section “[SOFiSTiK]”.  
• Names are eight characters, start with “GRAF” + record name, value is a full CADINP line.  
• Standard default keys: GRAFKOPF (language), GRAFSTEU (control defaults), GRAFSIZE (paper size), GRAFSCHR (font), GRAFFARB (colors), GRAFFILL (fills).  
• Example: GRAFKOPF=HEAD sets English prompts; GRAFSIZE=SIZE 0 LP MARG NO sets default paper to A4.  

6. Extended Defaults via GRAFDnnn  
• User may define a sequence of up to 36×36×36 expanded defaults: GRAFD000, GRAFD001 … GRAFD00A … GRAFDZZZ.  
• Each value is any valid CADINP line (e.g. PAGE, GRP).  
• This mechanism streamlines repetitive startup commands.  

7. Units  
• Base units are partly determined by WING.  
• Custom unit settings via the UNIT record (see “Basics” manual).

The table in question is the CADINP “record‐to‐items” reference used by the SOFiSTiK WING module. It lists every input keyword (the “Record” column) and, for each, the permitted parameter names or fields (“Items” column).  In practice this table drives how WING parses attribute and drawing orders: almost every record is an attribute‐setting record whose values take effect on the next drawing order.  

General structure  
• Two columns:  
  – Record: the CADINP keyword you type (e.g. FILL, SELE, VIEW, MOVE, DRAW, etc.)  
  – Items: the named parameters you may supply on that record line (e.g. X, Y, TYPE, LC, AXIS, RED, BLUE, and so forth)  

• Attribute vs. drawing records  
  – Attribute records (most of those listed) merely update settings: color fills (FILL), selection filters (SELE/SEL/GRP/BOX), visibility (VISI), deformation scale (DEFO), view and projection (VIEW, PERS), annotation and text (TEXT, POST), line‐drawing style (DRAW), geometric moves (MOVE), and other display modifiers.  
  – Drawing orders (not shown in this excerpt but called STRU, LOAD, NODE, QUAD, BEAM, ISOL, SECT, BRIC) actually emit graphics using the currently defined attributes.  

Key records and their items  

1. FILL  
   • Controls how quadrilateral and area fills are drawn:  
     – TYPE, FROM/TO (value range), INC, NUMB (number of levels), MODE, EDGE  
     – Color components and indices: INTE, COLO, INDX, RED, GREE, BLUE  
     – Light and dark shading parameters: LIGH, LIPX/LIPY/LIPZ, DARK, BRIG, DMOD  

2. SELE, SEL, GRP, BOX  
   • SELE: high‐level filter for load‐cases, groups or views (NO, GRP, BOX, SICH, PERS, VIEW, DEFO, SEL, ALTE, TITL)  
   • GRP: selects structural groups (NO, OPTI, ETYP, GDIV, TO, INC, DOMA, LC)  
   • BOX: clamps drawing extents or selects by bounding‐box (XMIN/YMIN/ZMIN, XMAX/YMAX/ZMAX, TYPE, VXCM, VYCM, KREF, OPER, BGRP)  
   • SEL: detailed item‐by‐item selection (ETYP, TYPE, VAL1–3, TOL, REF, MODE, OPER, SGRP, TITL)  

3. VIEW & PERS  
   • VIEW: defines camera or projection direction (TYPE, X, Y, Z, AXIS, ROTA)  
   • PERS: perspective parameters (A, BX, BY, BZ, ANGL)  

4. VISI & DEFO  
   • VISI: visibility thresholds (HIDD, DMAX, DMIN, DREL)  
   • DEFO: deformation‐scale settings for plotting displaced shapes (TYPE, FAC, LC, T, EXPO, SMOV)  

5. MOVE & DRAW  
   • MOVE: geometric translation or offset for subsequent drawing primitives (X, Y, Z, REF, UNIT, A, SCHH, FACW, MARG, C, CB, ALIG, SET, BOX, GRNO, DTYP, DISZ, DIST, DASH, PICT, SBOX, ADJU)  
   • DRAW: primitive line or symbol plotting (X, Y, Z, REF, UNIT, C, DTYP, GRP, MNO, HINT, DIST)  

6. TEXT, POST, NIVE, CURV  
   • TEXT: free‐form annotation (parameters not fully shown but generally include font, size, position, content, orientation)  
   • POST: post‐processing annotation (TITL)  
   • NIVE: contour‐level titles or numbering (TITL)  
   • CURV: curve plotting options (NO, F, DX, H)  

7. AXIS, DSIR, CUTP  
   • AXIS: axis‐label definitions (TITL)  
   • DSIR: directional vector or slice‐plane (NO, NX/NY/NZ, XMIN–ZMAX, SNO, LDIR)  
   • CUTP: cutting‐plane specification (CUT, GRP, SELE, LC)  

Usage notes  
• You may chain multiple attribute records in any order; they remain active until overridden.  
• To merge content into the same drawing, insert the AND record between drawing orders (e.g. STRU; AND; DEFO …; STRU).  
• Default attribute records can also be set via environment variables GRAF* in SOFISTIK.DEF.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the “input table” for WING (the CADINP‐based plotting front‐end in SOFiSTiK). It covers the two main record categories (drawing orders vs. attribute records), their general behavior, the special “AND”/“DSGN” logic, the environment-file overrides, and a breakdown of the individual record names.

1.  OVERALL STRUCTURE  
 •  WING reads a single input block (terminated by END).  
 •  Records fall into two classes:  
  –  Drawing Orders: issue a new plot (or add to an existing one via AND).  
  –  Attributes: modify parameters (line styles, text settings, colors, etc.) that only take effect on the next drawing order.  
 •  The special keyword DSGN can be used as a TYPE in a drawing order – it updates attributes without producing geometry.  
 •  If you place “AND” between two drawing orders, the second is layered into the first drawing; after use, AND resets to OFF.  
 •  Record ordering is completely free; attributes always apply to subsequent drawings until overwritten.  

2.  DRAWING ORDERS  
 These commands request a plot of specific result types. When invoked, they use the attributes last defined.  
 •  STRU – full structural view (elements, numbering, deformed shape, eigenmodes, stress contours)  
 •  LOAD – loads as vectors, line loads or area‐block loads  
 •  NODE – nodal results (displacements, reactions) as vectors or labels  
 •  QUAD – field of a scalar, vector or tensor on quadrilateral elements (with optional numeric labels or fill patterns)  
 •  BEAM – line‐plot of frame/girder results (e.g. bending moment diagrams)  
 •  ISOL – isolines for QUAD elements  
 •  SECT – cut‐section result plots  
 •  BRIC – results on volume (brick) elements  

3.  ENVIRONMENT / DEFAULTS  
 WING can draw default records from two sources:  
 •  SOFISTIK.DEF, in the “[SOFiSTiK]” section, via parameters named GRAFxxxx (e.g. GRAFKOPF, GRAFFARB). Each holds a complete CADINP line.  
 •  The system SET file via GRAFSTEU to force “CTRL DEF VARI,” preventing WING from reading its own default file.  
 Common environment parameters:  
  –  GRAFKOPF – plot‐header text language (“KOPF”=German, “HEAD”=English)  
  –  GRAFSIZE – default page size/margins  
  –  GRAFSCHR – font settings  
  –  GRAFFARB – default color settings  
  –  GRAFFILL – default fill patterns  
  –  Additional GRAFDnnn variables (nnn = 000…ZZZ) for arbitrary extra defaults  

4.  CONTROL RECORDS  
 These are defined in the general manual (“Basics”) and finalize or structure the input:  
 •  HEAD – plot header definition  
 •  UNIT – unit‐system override  
 •  PAGE – page setup  
 •  END – end of WING input  

5.  ATTRIBUTE RECORDS  
 Each of the following codes names one CADINP‐style attribute record. They configure line styles, text, symbols, reference values, scales, array fills, etc. Effects take place on the next drawing order (or when DSGN is used).  

 General styling:  
 •  C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C13 – line‐type, width, layer, symbol and text attributes  
 •  C15 … C37 – extended parameter slots for user‐defined purposes (often coordinate offsets or special switches)  
 •  COLB – background color  
 •  CUT, CUTP – define section/cutting planes  
 •  GRP – group assignment  
 •  SELE – selection filters  
 •  LC – load‐case selection  

 Annotation & labeling:  
 •  NO – numbering format  
 •  T – general text attributes  
 •  DESI – element/designation text  
 •  MAT – material labels  
 •  TITL – plot title  

 Scaling & reference:  
 •  FAC1, FAC2, FAC3 – vector scaling factors  
 •  DIF1, DIF2, DIF3 – differential scaling factors  
 •  DIRE – direction vector for glyphs or text  
 •  NMAT – new material index override  
 •  REF – reference value for normalized plots  
 •  X – user‐defined scale factor  

 Graphics object types:  
 •  KIND, KIN2, KIN3 – primary and secondary object “kinds” (e.g. arrowheads, marker types)  
 •  TYPE, DTYP – subtype or drawing‐type switches  
 •  DSGN – (special) design‐only mode (attributes set without geometry)  

 Geometric controls:  
 •  LENG – line‐length override for vectors  
 •  WIDE – pen width override  
 •  LMAX, LMIN – maximum/minimum line lengths  
 •  DIST – distance parameter for repetitive symbols  
 •  DISX, DISY, DISZ – displacements for symbol offsets  
 •  LFRB, EXCE – frame‐bar lettering/exaggeration switches  

 Fill & pattern:  
 •  TABS – tabular fill specification  
 •  ADD, ARRO – arrow‐drawing attributes  
 •  DOUB – double‐line toggle  
 •  PA21 … PA27 – pattern‐fill definitions (hatch angles, spacing, etc.)  

 Other parameters:  
 •  CUTP – alternative cut‐plane parameters (if differentiating from CUT)  
 •  PA2x range – multi‐slot pattern definitions for advanced hatch control  
 •  Additional codes (ENO, REF, etc.) tie into element selection or labeling logic.  

6.  WORK-FLOW NOTES  
 •  Start by setting global attributes (HEAD, PAGE, UNIT, plus any C‐records or GRAF defaults).  
 •  Issue a drawing order (e.g. STRU); it reads the attributes just set.  
 •  To overlay results in a single view, interpose AND between drawing orders:  
  STR U ; AND ; LOAD … ; NODE … ; STRU  
 •  Reset or tweak attributes any time; new settings apply only at the next drawing command or when TYPE=DSGN is used.

The input table defines three parameters (OPT, VAL and V2) used to control graphic‐related batch or interactive processing. Each row describes the parameter’s purpose, permissible values, its “unit” or value type, and its default setting. Below is a structured, column-by-column and row-by-row breakdown suitable for indexing in a RAG vector store.

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The parameter name: OPT, VAL or V2.  
   • Description  
     – A human-readable summary of what the parameter controls and, for OPT, a list of its allowable literals along with their meanings.  
   • Unit  
     – The expected data type or format. For OPT this is “LIT/—” (literal keywords). For VAL and V2 it is “*” (any user-supplied value).  
   • Default  
     – The built-in fallback when the user does not specify an override.  

2. Row: OPT  
   • Purpose  
     OPT selects one of ten configuration options that adjust how graphics are generated.  
   • Allowed Literals  
     – NOHE: “Number of HEAD line” – specifies the line at which to continue inserting HEAD records without deleting earlier ones.  
     – GSTR: “Default of the structure” – controls the drawing of base structural lines. Sub-options are:  
        • DEFA (use result‐type default)  
        • NO (no structure)  
        • CONT (contour only)  
        • FULL (full structure)  
        • MESH (lines and points)  
        • AX (axis only)  
        – Support for delayed or per-layer assignment via STRU commands.  
     – DEF: “Level of defaults” – selects the initialization profile at the start of each batch run. Sub-values:  
        • WING (built-in GRAPHIC defaults)  
        • VARI (WING plus user‐defined vars)  
        • WDEF (also read WINGRAF.DEF)  
        • — (retain current values, for interactive use)  
     – EMPT: “Blank‐sheet behavior” – how to handle missing data. Choices: OFF, NO, ZERO, YES.  
     – MEAS: “Measurability” – two-dimensional vs. three-dimensional projection. Values: 2D, 3D, OFF.  
     – AXIS: “Axis representation” – full vs. hint vs. current. Values: FULL, CURR, — (always hint), OFF.  
     – CUT: “Area‐element cuts” – use or discard precomputed database cuts. Values: DEL, NO, YES, REPL, SAVE.  
     – WARN: “Warnings switch” – suppress or limit warning calls. Controlled via VAL and V2.  
     – REPR: “Representation correction” – auto-correct invalid display modes. Values: OFF, NO, YES, MEAS.  
     – EDGE: “Edge‐direction uniting” – whether to merge opposite spring directions. Values: NO, YES, FULL.  
   • Unit  
     – LIT/— (selection from the list above).  
   • Default  
     – 0 for NOHE; DEFA for GSTR; WDEF for DEF; NO for EMPT; 3D for MEAS; DEFA for AXIS; YES for CUT; – for WARN; YES for REPR; YES for EDGE.  

3. Row: VAL  
   • Purpose  
     VAL provides the numeric or string argument corresponding to the OPT literal. For example, if OPT=NOHE, VAL is the line number; if OPT=WARN, VAL is the warning number.  
   • Unit  
     – * (free format).  
   • Default  
     – ! (required unless OPT implies its own default).  

4. Row: V2  
   • Purpose  
     V2 supplies a secondary value when an OPT literal needs two parameters—most commonly for setting the maximum number of warning calls (with OPT=WARN).  
   • Unit  
     – * (free format).  
   • Default  
     – – (no second value expected by default).  

Summary  
This table lets a user precisely configure graphic‐generation behavior by (1) picking a keyword (OPT), (2) supplying a primary argument (VAL) and (3) optionally a secondary argument (V2). Each OPT literal activates a distinct subgroup of parameters—ranging from structural drawing defaults (GSTR) and sheet initialization (DEF) to warning limits (WARN) and area cuts (CUT). The “Unit” column tells parsers how to validate inputs, and the “Default” column supplies fallback values for interactive or batch modes.
