content:
The table defines a collection of numeric settings that control the size and line‐width of various spring, support, hinge and kinematic‐constraint symbols in the graphic output of the software.  Each row has four fields:

• Item – a short mnemonic code used by the program  
• Description – English name of the symbol or dimension being controlled  
• Unit – the measurement unit ( “cm” for an absolute length, “–” for a dimensionless scale factor)  
• Default – the initial value assigned at startup (often expressed relative to a base symbol height, HS, or another parameter)

All of these “Item” values are loaded on first initialization and remain in force until the user explicitly enters a new value.  For additional background on symbol heights (SCHH, SCH2), grid placement (GRID), color tables (COLO, COLB) and element “LEGO” settings, see the referenced records (SCH3, HSPD) and COL2.

1. Basic Spring Symbols  
   WSPS (–)  
     • Width factor for the common spring symbol, default = 0.6 × SCHH HS  
   SPSC (cm)  
     • Maximum length of any spring‐symbol segment in the view, default = HS / 3.0  

2. Support Spring Symbols  
   HSPU (cm)  
     • Absolute size (height) of the support‐spring symbol, default = HS  
   WSPU (–)  
     • Width factor for support spring symbol (relative to HSPU), default = 0.6  

3. Beam‐Hinge Symbols  
   HBEH (cm)  
     • Size (height) of the beam‐hinge graphic, default = HS  
   WBEH (–)  
     • Width factor for beam‐hinge symbol relative to HBEH, default = 1.0  

4. Support Symbols  
   HSUP (cm)  
     • Base size of support symbols, default = HS  
   WSUP (–)  
     • Width factor for support symbols relative to HSUP, default = 1.0  

5. Coupling Spring Symbols  
   HSPC (cm)  
     • Height of the coupling spring symbol, default = HS  
   WSPC (–)  
     • Width factor for coupling spring symbol relative to HSPC, default = 0.6  

6. Torsional Spring Symbols  
   HSPM (cm)  
     • Size of support‐torsional spring symbol, default = HS × 1.5  
   HSPT (cm)  
     • Size of coupling‐torsional spring symbol, default = HS × 1.5  

7. Kinematic Constraints Symbols  
   HCPS (cm)  
     • Size of support‐kinematic‐constraints symbol, default = HS  
   HCPC (cm)  
     • Size of node coupling symbol, default = HS × 0.1  

8. External Beam‐Section Symbols  
   HSIR (cm)  
     • Size of external beam‐section symbol, default = 0.12  
   WSIR (–)  
     • Width factor relative to HSIR, default = 0.5  

9. Boundary‐Support/Torsion Symbols  
   HSBS (cm)  
     • Size of boundary‐support spring symbol, default = HS × 0.7  
   WSBS (–)  
     • Width factor relative to HSBS, default = 0.6  
   HSBM (cm)  
     • Size of boundary‐moment spring symbol, default = HS  
   WSBM (–)  
     • Width factor relative to HSBM, default = 0.6  

10. Constraint‐Direction Symbols  
   HCPD (cm)  
     • Height of the kinematic constraint‐direction symbol (points toward the 2nd node), default = HS  
   WCPD (–)  
     • Width factor relative to HCPD, default = 0.5  
   HSPD (cm)  
     • Size of the coupling‐spring direction symbol (dir. to 2nd node), default = HS × 1.7  

Usage Notes  
– If you need finer control of text placement or to avoid overlapping annotations, consult the GRID record: it defines “grid areas” (SIZP, SIZC), offsets (DP), principal direction (DIRE) and shift‐rules for QUAD/BRIC reinforcement text (VMH, VMQ, VM3).  
– Should more than one value fall in the same grid cell, the GRID TYPE setting governs whether you see the minimum, maximum or another aggregate (MINW, MAXW, AMIN, AMAX).  
– All symbol‐size defaults refer back to HS (the standard symbol height from SCHH); changing HS will proportionally adjust most of these items unless you override them explicitly.

The input table defines the “GRID” record, which controls how result values from quadrilateral (QUAD) and brick (BRIC) elements are mapped onto a regular text‐grid for postprocessing (display, reinforcement‐shift rules, etc.).  Each row in the table specifies one parameter of the GRID block, along with its meaning, units, default value and behavior.  Below is a structured breakdown:

1. General Notes  
   • This GRID definition ties into several other records (see SCHH, SCH2, SIZE, LEGO, COLO, COLB, COL2 for symbol sizing, color, line weight, etc.).  Further symbol details (e.g. coupling‐spring‐direction arrows, SCH3, HSPD) are in COL2.  
   • Presettings remain in force until explicitly overridden by a new GRID input.  
   • GRID only takes effect if “TYPE” ≠ NO.  When TYPE=NO the grid is effectively switched off.

2. Column Headings  
   – Item: mnemonic for the parameter  
   – Description: what the parameter controls  
   – Unit: physical units (m = meters, dimensionless, etc.)  
   – Default: startup value if omitted  
   – TYPE: allowable modes or keyword values

3. Parameter Details  

 A. TYPE (grid‐evaluation mode)  
   • NO: Grid logic disabled. No values are collected.  
   • MINW: In each grid cell, the minimum of all found values is chosen.  
   • MAXW: Maximum value in the cell.  
   • AMAX: Absolut maximum (largest magnitude).  
   • AMIN: Absolut minimum.  

 B. SIZP (grid cell size, principal direction)  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: –7.0 (negative indicates factor of text height SCHH H6)  
   • Behavior: Defines the spacing of the grid in its principal (DIRE) direction.  A positive value is taken literally; negative values are scaled by the text‐height factor.  

 C. SIZC (cell size, transverse direction)  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: (implicitly same rule as SIZP)  
   • Behavior: Spacing perpendicular to the principal direction.  

 D. DP (initial displacement)  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: –(distance DC to system zero point)  
   • Behavior: Shifts the entire grid origin by DP in both principal and transverse directions.  For plane systems (slabs) it may be positioned at a non‐zero value; otherwise default is zero.  

 E. DIRE (grid principal orientation)  
   • TYPE values:  
       – DEFA: Align with first data‐value’s direction  
       – X: Align with local element x‐axis  
       – CURR: Use the normal vector from the previous VIEW command  
   • Default: DEFA  

 F. VMH, VMQ, VM3 (shift‐rule offsets for QUAD reinforcement layers)  
   • Unit: m  
   • Default: 0 for each  
   • Behavior: After the grid has been established, these offsets shift the text or vector labels for reinforcement layers 1 (VMH), 2 (VMQ) and 3 (VM3).  

4. Result‐Value Mapping and Overlap Rules  
   • All QUAD/BRIC result values that have text (DTXT) or vector (DVEC) representations will be binned into grid cells if GRID is active.  
   • If multiple results fall into the same cell, the chosen output depends on the TYPE setting (MINW, MAXW, etc.).  
   • The automatic text‐overlap check (SCHH REVI) remains enabled; labels that would overlap are suppressed or shifted according to that rule.  

5. Treatment of Partially Cut Elements  
   • A “grid element” is generated whenever a QUAD/BRIC element is intersected by the grid lines—even if only marginally.  
   • With a separate MPNT control, you can require that only those grid elements whose centroids lie within the parent QUAD/BRIC envelope be used.  

6. Persistence  
   • Once defined, GRID parameters persist through subsequent analyses until a new GRID record is read.  
   • Changing any GRID parameter requires re‐issuing the GRID block in full.  

Overall, this table provides a comprehensive mechanism to overlay a structured grid on finite-element results, choose which scalar or vector value to represent in each cell, adjust cell sizing and orientation, offset text or vectors to avoid clashes, and filter out unwanted partial elements.

The input table is part of the SCH3‐type record that defines default symbol sizes and width‐factors for a number of graphical elements in the post‐processing display (coupling springs, design‐element sections, storey‐level symbols).  These defaults are established at the first initialization and remain in effect until explicitly reentered.  Cross-references: SCHH (global text-height control), SCH2 (text attributes such as color or font), SIZE (numeric precision), LEGO (graphical legend), COLO / COLB (color tables) and COL2 (further explanations of symbol conventions).  

Table Structure  
• Columns  
  – Item:  A short parameter code.  
  – Description:  Explains which symbol or factor the parameter controls.  
  – Unit:  The physical or dimensionless unit for the parameter value.  
  – Default:  The preset value applied on first initialization.  

• Rows (five parameters)  

1. WSPD  
   – Description: Width of the coupling‐spring‐direction symbol, expressed as a multiplicative factor of the symbol height HSPD.  In other words, if HSPD controls the symbol’s vertical size, WSPD scales its horizontal stroke width.  
   – Unit: dimensionless (—)  
   – Default: 0.50  

2. HDSL  
   – Description: Absolute size (height) of the symbol used to represent a design‐element section.  This governs how large the cross‐section symbol will appear.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.10  

3. WDSL  
   – Description: Width of the design‐element section symbol as a factor of its own height (HDSL).  This allows the symbol to keep a consistent aspect ratio while scaling.  
   – Unit: dimensionless (—)  
   – Default: 1.50  

4. HSCM  
   – Description: Text height of the “center of mass” symbol for each storey level.  This parameter defines the size at which mass‐centroid markers are drawn.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.25  

5. HSCR  
   – Description: Text height of the “center of rigidity” symbol for each storey level.  Analogous to HSCM, but for rigidity‐centroid markers.  
   – Unit: cm  
   – Default: 0.25  

Additional Context  
• HSPD (not shown above) itself is the base text height for coupling spring symbols; WSPD multiplies off that value.  Further details on coupling‐spring symbol conventions (e.g. direction arrow to the second node) appear in the COL2 record.  
• All “factor” parameters (WSPD, WDSL) are unitless scale factors; the “size” parameters (HDSL, HSCM, HSCR) are specified in centimeters.  
• These parameter settings apply globally to all QUAD and BRIC element results when rendered with vector (“DVEC”) or text‐based (“DTXT”) representations.  They will only change if reentered via SCH3.  
• If you switch on the text grid (with GRID TYPE input), these symbol sizes interact with the grid area sizing (SIZP, SIZC, etc.) and may be subject to overlap tests (SCHH REVI) when multiple values fall in the same grid cell.

This input block defines the GRID record, which controls how results from QUAD and BRIC finite-element elements are collected, aggregated and displayed on a regular text grid, and how reinforcement layers are shifted. It should be read together with related records (SCHH, SCH2, SIZE, LEGO, COLO, COLB, SCH3, HSPD) and the color definitions in COL2. The preset values apply at first initialization and remain in force until explicitly changed.

1. Purpose  
   • Establish a 2-D grid over the model for placing text or vector result values.  
   • Aggregate multiple values falling in the same grid cell according to a chosen rule.  
   • Control local displacements (offsets) for printing reinforcement layers (QUAD reinforcements).

2. Columns / Fields  
   – Item: parameter name  
   – Description: what it controls  
   – Unit: physical or internal unit  
   – Default: initial value  
   – TYPE: classification or selection of aggregation rule (for the TYPE field only)

3. Key Parameters  
   • TYPE  
     · LT / NO: grid switched off (no aggregation)  
     · MINW / MAXW: minimum or maximum of all values in a cell  
     · AMAX / AMIN: absolute maximum/minimum (magnitude)  
   • SIZP (m)  
     · Principal grid spacing along the DIRE direction  
     · Default = –7.0; if negative, SIZP = factor × SCHH H6 text height  
   • SIZC (m)  
     · Transverse grid spacing; must satisfy SIZP < 0 criterion when using text-height factor  
   • DP (m)  
     · Initial displacement from the global origin or system zero point  
     · For plane systems (slabs), grid is positioned; otherwise DP = 0  
   • DIRE  
     · Principal grid orientation selector  
     · DEFA: direction of the first value encountered  
     · X: local x-direction of the element  
     · CURR: normal vector from previous VIEW input

4. Shift-Rule Offsets for QUAD Reinforcements  
   • VMH (m): offset for 1st (principal) layer; default 0  
   • VMQ (m): offset for 2nd (transverse) layer; default 0  
   • VM3 (m): offset for 3rd layer; default 0  

5. Aggregation and Display Logic  
   • When GRID TYPE is active, all result values (text or vector) from QUAD/BRIC elements (via REPR DTXT or DVEC) are mapped into grid cells.  
   • If more than one value falls into the same cell, the final printed value is chosen according to the TYPE rule.  
   • The SCHH REVI record still applies to prevent overlapping text.

6. Grid-Element Creation  
   • A grid cell is created whenever it is intersected (even partially) by a QUAD or BRIC element.  
   • Cells that lie entirely or mostly outside the model envelope can be excluded via the MPNT control: only cells whose centers lie inside the enveloping volume are retained.

See record COL2 for additional symbol shapes and color explanations, and SCH3/HSPD for coupling-spring and spacing symbols. This GRID record ensures that numerical output is organized in a clear, adjustable mesh overlay for post-processing and graphic annotation.

The table shown is part of the GRID input record, which controls how text‐ or vector‐based results from QUAD and BRIC finite‐element elements are grouped into rectangular “grid areas” for display and output. Each row in this table defines one optional parameter (Item) that refines which grid elements are generated or printed, how they are coloured and filtered, and what tolerances are allowed when associating an element’s result with a grid area. Columns are:

• Item: The keyword used on the GRID input line.  
• Description: What the parameter does, including any sub-options.  
• Unit: The physical unit or data type. “LIT” denotes a literal enumeration.  
• Default: The value assumed if the item is not entered explicitly.

1. TOLA (unit: °; default: 15)  
   – Angular tolerance of an element’s normal vector relative to the grid plane. If the angle between an element’s surface normal and the GRID plane exceeds TOLA, that element’s result will not be associated with—or cut into—a grid area. Typical default is 15°.

2. TOLZ (unit: %/m; default: –5.0)  
   – Maximum offset distance of an element from the grid plane.  
     • If TOLZ < 0: treated as a percentage of the overall system size (absolute value).  
     • If TOLZ > 0: treated as an absolute distance in meters.  
   – Elements lying farther than this distance are ignored. The default –5.0 means ±5% of the system’s bounding dimension.

3. LINE (unit: —; default: 9003)  
   – Colour key for drawing the frame around each grid cell. The code must refer to the colour lookup defined in the COLO record. No unit applies; you simply supply the integer colour index.

4. GRP (unit: LIT; default: YES)  
   – Additional criterion: whether the element’s group number must match before its result is placed into a grid cell.  
     • NO: ignore group number—any element in the relevant spatial area contributes.  
     • YES: only elements belonging to the current group selection are considered.

5. MPNT (unit: LIT; default: FULL)  
   – Controls whether grid elements that are only marginally cut by an element (and thus may lie outside the true model region) are kept or discarded.  
     • FULL: Perform a midpoint check; delete cells whose centroids fall outside their parent QUAD/BRIC envelope, but carry forward any “important” result values so nothing is silently lost.  
     • YES: Delete out-of-envelope cells; no special forwarding—important values may be lost.  
     • NO: Do not perform any midpoint check—every cut piece generates a grid cell regardless of where its centroid lies.

How these parameters work in context:
– All QUAD/BRIC results with DTXT or DVEC representation are sliced into grid cells when GRID TYPE is activated.  
– If multiple element results fall into the same cell, the final printed value is chosen according to GRID TYPE (e.g. MINW, MAXW, AMIN, AMAX, SIZP).  
– The SCHH REVI record (text‐overlap test) remains active, preventing overlapping labels even when the grid is on.  
– See also related GRID inputs: SIZP (grid-cell size), DP (origin offset), DIRE (grid orientation), VMH/VMQ/VM3 (layer offsets), and the records SCHH, SCH2, SIZE, LEGO, COLO, COLB for full display control.

See also: SCHH, SCH2, SIZE, LEGO, COLO, COLB

The input is a comprehensive parameter table for positioning and styling various “legend” objects in a graphics or CAD output (for use in a RAG vector store).  It is organized into four main columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and one header field (“TYPE”) that selects which block of defaults applies.  The seven supported legend‐object types (TYPE) are:
  • FSKL Fill‐pattern legend  
  • PLEG Picture legend  
  • SCAL Picture dimensional lines  
  • SC  Picture scale  
  • COOR Coordinate cross  
  • TWIS Distortion factors  
  • PAGE Page numbering  

Across all types, the following “common properties” (items) can be set:
  • X – horizontal insertion point: >0 in cm, <0 as % of picture width, DEFA=default, ON/OFF/DEFA switching.  
  • Y – vertical insertion point: >0 in cm, <0 as % of picture height, same activation flags.  
  • SIZW – object width, in % of picture area.  
  • SIZH – object height, in % of picture area.  
  • MAXW, MAXH – maximal width/height in cm.  
  • SCHH – text height in cm.  
  • FACW – text‐height factor (unitless).  
  • EDGE – margin around object in cm.  
  • COL – text colour code (e.g. 1001).  
  • ORIG – anchor point (“LEFT”, etc.) for displaced objects.  
  • ND – number of decimal digits (integer).  

In addition, each TYPE may define up to eight “PAR” parameters for advanced behavior (orientation, overwrite rules, text spacing, symbol size, etc.).  Below is a summary of default settings by TYPE:

1. Fill‐pattern legend (TYPE=FSKL)  
   • X=1.0 % (left border), Y=5.0 % (top), SIZW=8.0 %, SIZH=90 %  
   • MAXW=1.5 cm, MAXH=20 cm, SCHH=0.18 cm, FACW=0.7, EDGE=0.1 cm, COL=1001  
   • PAR1…PAR8 control placement side (LEFT, RIGH, UPPE, etc.), over-write rules, text-distance factors, min/max colour‐bar widths, text angle.

2. Picture legend (TYPE=PLEG)  
   • X=0.2 cm, Y=0.2 cm, SIZW=100 % of picture, MAXW=18 cm, SCHH=H1, FACW=0.8, EDGE=0.1 cm, COL=1001  
   • PAR1..PAR3 toggle writing of result line, selection line, displaced‐structure line  
   • PAR4 = line‐spacing factor (0.5), PAR5 = symbol‐size factor (–5. default → 5× text height, clipped 0.2–1.5 cm)

3. Picture dimensional lines (TYPE=SCAL)  
   • Always drawn along bottom and right border: SIZW,SIZH=100 %, ND=2  
   • SCHH=0.85·H1 or H5, FACW=0.7  
   • PAR1 = unit system, PAR2 = max number of ticks per axis

4. Picture scale (TYPE=SC)  
   • Within legend at right, or within picture at left of coordinate axes  
   • SIZW/SIZH/MAXW/MAXH = text‐dependent, SCHH=H1, FACW=0.85, EDGE=0.1 cm, COL=1001, ORIG=LEFT, ND=2  

5. Coordinate cross (TYPE=COOR)  
   • SIZW=SIZH=MAXW=MAXH=1.0 cm, SCHH=H1, FACW=0.85, EDGE=0.1 cm, COL=1001, ORIG=LEFT, ND=2  

6. Distortion factors (TYPE=TWIS)  
   • Same as picture‐scale defaults for positioning and styling, ND=2  

7. Page numbering (TYPE=PAGE)  
   • Uses only X to toggle ON/OFF page‐number display  

All these controls let users fine‐tune size, placement, text style, and overlap behavior of legends and scales so they do not obscure each other and remain legible. See also SIZE and SIZ2 for related sizing parameters.

The input consists of two related tables that together define the schema for “legend objects” in a plotting or drawing system. The first (large) table enumerates the full set of parameters available for any legend object, grouped by “TYPE” of object. The second (small) table lists a handful of general‐purpose items (COLB, COLE, ORIG, ND, PAR1…PAR8) that apply across types.

1. Common Columns  
   • Item – the 2– to 5–character keyword you use in input.  
   • Description – a brief explanation of what the item controls.  
   • Unit – the expected unit or data type (cm, %, –, LIT for literal text, etc.).  
   • Default – the value assumed if you do not override it.

2. Legend Object Types (TYPE)  
   The “TYPE” column lets you choose one of seven built‐in legend object kinds:  
   • FSKL – fill-pattern legend (colour scales, hatch scales, etc.)  
   • PLEG – picture legend (symbols, page numbers, etc.)  
   • SCAL – picture dimensional lines (axis/grid scales)  
   • SC   – picture scale (textual scale bar)  
   • COOR – coordinate cross (little axes in legend)  
   • TWIS – distortion factors (text blocks describing scale distortion)  
   • PAGE – page numbering (simply on/off via X)

3. Universal Geometry/Text Parameters  
   These items exist for every TYPE, controlling position, size, typography, and colour:  
   • X, Y           – insertion point relative to picture area.  
       • > 0 ⇒ absolute cm from left / top; < 0 ⇒ percentage of picture width / height  
   • SIZW, SIZH     – width/height of the object, expressed as % of picture area  
   • MAXW, MAXH     – maximum width/height in cm (caps the % values)  
   • SCHH           – text height in cm  
   • FACW           – scale factor for text height (multiplier of SCHH)  
   • EDGE           – extra border around the object in cm  
   • COL            – text colour index (integer code, e.g. 1001)

4. Defaults by TYPE  
   For each TYPE, the table then lists the default values of X, Y, SIZW, SIZH, MAXW, MAXH, SCHH, FACW, EDGE, COLE (edge‐colour) plus certain additional parameters (ND, ORIG, PAR1…PAR8). Highlights:  
   • FSKL (fill pattern)  
       – X = 1 % (left border), Y = 5 %, SIZW = 8 %, SIZH = 90 %, MAXW = 1.5 cm, MAXH = 20 cm, SCHH = 0.18 cm, FACW = 0.7, EDGE = 0.1 cm, COLE = 1001  
       – PAR1…PAR8 control placement around the picture (LEFT, RIGH, UPPE, LOWE), label distances, widths, and text angles.  
   • PLEG (picture legend)  
       – X = 0.2 cm, Y = 0.2 cm, SIZW = 100 %, MAXW = 18 cm, SCHH = SCHH H1 (header text height), FACW = 0.8, EDGE = 0.1 cm, COLE = 1001  
       – PAR1…PAR3 toggle writing of result, selection, and displaced‐structure lines; PAR4 controls line spacing; PAR5 sets symbol sizes.  
   • SCAL (dimensional lines)  
       – Always fixed at bottom/right of picture; SCHH = 0.85·SCHH H1 or SCHH H5; FACW = 0.7; ND = 2; PAR1 selects unit system; PAR2 caps number of tick values.  
   • SC (picture scale)  
       – Placed within legend at right or within picture at left of axes; sizing depends on text; SCHH = H1; FACW = 0.85; EDGE = 0.1 cm; COLE = 1001; ND = 2.  
   • COOR (coordinate cross)  
       – SIZW/SIZH = 1 cm; MAXW/MAXH = 1 cm; SCHH = H1; FACW = 0.85; EDGE = 0.1 cm; ND = 2.  
   • TWIS (distortion factors)  
       – Similar placement to SC; SCHH = 0.85·H1; FACW = 0.85; EDGE = 0.1 cm; ND = 2.  
   • PAGE (page numbering)  
       – Only X is meaningful (switch legend on/off).

5. General-Purpose Items (Second Table)  
   These items are referenced by all types whenever fine-grained control is needed:  
   • COLB – background colour index (default –101)  
   • COLE – edge colour (default inherits “*” from the TYPE default)  
   • ORIG – writing origin/direction if object is displaced:  
       – LEFT (text left-justified), MIDD (centered), RIGH (text right-justified)  
       – Unit type: LIT (literal code), default ‘*’  
   • ND   – number of decimals after the decimal point for numeric text (unit – or LIT)  
   • PAR1…PAR8 – reserved for TYPE-specific sub-parameters (see FSKL, PLEG, etc.).

Any parameters you omit will fall back to the TYPE’s documented defaults. This modular design allows you to place multiple legend objects independently, customize their geometry, and ensure they never overwrite one another.

The table under consideration defines a small “palette” input block that users employ to collect and apply a consistent set of color, fill-pattern and isoline settings in downstream graphical or reporting routines.  It lists six items (NUMB, COLO, FILL, VAL, ISOL, TITL), describes how each one works, specifies its data type/unit, and gives a default behavior.  Together these fields allow the user to name a palette, select it by number or title, and control whether its stored color and pattern definitions are loaded or updated.

1.  NUMB  
   • Description: an integer identifier for a palette.  It may be used directly or indirectly:  
      – If NUMB is omitted but TITL (the palette name) is supplied, the system looks up the number that corresponds to that name.  
      – A positive value (> 0) refers to a palette defined earlier within the same input block.  
      – A negative value (< 0) refers to a palette pre-defined outside of the current block (for example, in a file such as WINGRAF.DEF).  
      – If neither NUMB nor TITL is provided, the “last selected” palette is assumed.  
   • Unit/Type: none (integer index)  
   • Default: none

2.  COLO  
   • Description: controls the application of colors for text, line work and marker symbols.  It aggregates settings from three underlying records (COLO, COL2, COLB).  Three flags are available:  
      – PUT instructs the system to update the stored palette entries with the current COLO definitions.  
      – NO suppresses the use of any stored colors (i.e. makes the palette “inactive” for color).  
      – YES enables the use of the stored color entries.  
   • Unit/Type: LIT (literal switch)  
   • Default: YES

3.  FILL  
   • Description: governs fill patterns and fill-color usage, via the record FILL.  Two flags:  
      – NO means “do not apply any fill pattern or color from the palette.”  
      – YES means “apply the palette’s fill settings.”  
   • Unit/Type: LIT  
   • Default: YES

4.  VAL  
   • Description: pertains to contour or “fill‐value” definitions associated with FILL.  If a palette includes a set of data‐value thresholds (e.g. for shading intervals), VAL=YES applies those thresholds and associated colors; VAL=NO disables them.  
   • Unit/Type: LIT  
   • Default: YES

5.  ISOL  
   • Description: controls whether isolines (contour lines) that accompany a filled contour plot are drawn using the palette’s definitions.  As with VAL, YES applies pre-defined isoline settings; NO omits them.  
   • Unit/Type: LIT  
   • Default: YES

6.  TITL  
   • Description: a short text name for the palette.  If you do not supply NUMB, the system will look for this name among previously defined palettes.  If the name is new, it assigns the next unused reference number automatically.  If neither NUMB nor TITL is given, the most recent palette remains in force.  
   • Unit/Type: LIT  
   • Default: none

Operational notes:  
– A new palette is “defined” (i.e. its color, fill, value and isoline tables are stored) either when its reference number was not yet used or when you explicitly call COLO PUT.  
– When COLO PUT is invoked, the palette’s color entries are always overwritten.  The existing fill patterns (FILL), fill‐value breakpoints (VAL) and isoline definitions (ISOL) are overwritten only if their corresponding flags are set to YES.  
– In normal use, setting COLO=YES, FILL=YES, VAL=YES and ISOL=YES will cause the entire stored palette (colors, patterns and isolines) to be applied, replacing any ad hoc values that had been input earlier in the same run.  
– By toggling individual flags to NO, you can selectively suppress color, pattern or contour values while leaving other aspects of the palette in place.

 A palette can summarize all inputs for colours and/or fill patterns, so that a change is easier and clearer within the input (for example for differentiation of a deformed and a undeformed structure)

If TITL is not defined, the last reference number +1 is given to this palette. The last selected palette is used, if neither NO or TITL is input.
 The palette is defined with the actual values, if it is not available yet (the reference number is not defined up to now) or COLO PUT is input. The saved values for FILL, VAL and ISOL already available in a palette are overwritten, if YES is set. COLO is updated always.
 Using this palette the values for COLO, FILL, VAL or ISOL which are indicated with YES are set. That means all previous inputs for these records are overwritten.

The table is a catalogue of “C-codes” used by the SOFiSTiK plotting routines to assign colours, line-types and pen widths to specific graphical entities (elements, edges, results, annotations, etc.).  Each row defines one code (C1, C2, … C22) by giving  
• the code name (Item),  
• a brief Description of what it controls,  
• an optional Unit (most are simple indices; only C1 uses “–/LIT” to denote line attributes), and  
• a Default four-digit index which encodes both colour and line style.  

Below is a structured breakdown:

1.  C1 – Legend / Plotting Control  
    • MONO: force all colours to 0 (background)  
    • STAN: reset all line‐type attributes to the program default  
    • COLO: restore the default colour palette (keeping line styles)  
    • PENW: use pen widths instead of colours (for electrostatic or ink plotters)  
    • ALL: set all C-codes to behave like C2  
    • ALLC: match only the colour‐index of C2  
    • ALLW: match only the width‐index of C2  
    • ALLK: match only the kind (line‐style) of C2  
    Default = 1001  

2.  C2 – Element numbers (3001)  
    Labels the numbering of finite elements.

3.  C3 – Node numbers (2001)  
    Labels the numbering of nodes.

4.  C4 – Zero-crossing results & cutting-pattern corners (8001)  
    Highlights locations where results ≲ 0 or corner points of cutting patterns.

5.  C5 – Free inner edges (5006)  
    Edges of elements not constrained or supported.

6.  C6 – Simply supported inner element edges (7001)  
    Inner edges with simple supports (no moment restraint).

7.  C7 – Inner edges with fixed moment, free displacements (7402)  
    Partially fixed inner element edges.

8.  C8 – Fully fixed inner element edges (7401)  
    Inner edges with both moment and displacement restraints.

9.  C9 – Design elements (10001)  
    Elements flagged for design checks.

10. C10 – Kinematic constraints (6004)  
    Internal constraint definitions used in mechanisms or linkages.

11. C11 – Cable elements (3001)  
    Tension‐only bar or cable members.

12. C12 – Beam elements (3301)  
    Standard frame or beam members.

13. C13 – Positive results (4001)  
    Only display tensile (positive) stress or moment extremal values.

14. C14 – Negative results (2001)  
    Only display compressive (negative) stress or moment extremal values.

15. C15 – Free inner edges that are group boundaries (5007)  
    Edges separating groups by material, element number, crack-presence or local‐axis orientation.

16. C16 – Boundary elements (7001)  
    Elements forming the external boundary.

17. C17 – Contour lines of 2D cutting-pattern areas (6005)  
    Lines demarcating contour levels in slab‐cut layouts.

18. C18 – Contour lines of the untensioned 2D cutting pattern (3001)  
    Similar to C17 but for untensioned patterns.

19. C19 – Structure lines of 2D cutting-pattern areas (9006)  
    Underlying grid or pattern structure.

20. C20 – Cutted elements (9006)  
    Elements that have been “cut” or trimmed in a pattern.

21. C21 – Kinematic constraints for supports  
    Special constraint plots at support locations. (no default index)

22. C22 – Kinematic constraints between nodes  
    Constraint relations between nodal pairs. (no default index)

The four-digit default indices follow the scheme “xBCC” or “BCxx” where the leading digit encodes colour (0=delete, 1=black/white, 2=red, 3=green, etc.) and the last two digits encode line style (01=continuous, 02=medium dashed, 03=medium dotted, … 10=far dot-dashed). A nonzero “b” multiplier (xb01, xb02…) doubles a line’s thickness by rendering it as a close parallel pair. The table therefore provides a complete, ready-to-use mapping from structural‐analysis entities to their default graphical presentation.

content:
The excerpted table is part of the SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual and defines a series of graphic‐plotting parameters (denoted C-codes) that control color, line type, line width, and placement of various result objects in a FEM‐postprocessing drawing. It is intended to guide the user in specifying how structural elements, result envelopes, supports, group boundaries, tendons, etc. are rendered in plots (on screen or printer) via the COLO command and related settings. Below is a structured description of the table and its context:

1. Table Structure  
   • Column “COLO” (also referred to as C-codes): Identifiers (C20, C21, C22, …, C26) that the user assigns within a COLO statement.  
   • Column “Default Value”: Often shown as “−” (no default) or a numerical code.  
   • Column “Description”: A brief phrase explaining which feature or result the code controls.

2. Defined Codes in This Excerpt  
   • C20 – “Cutted elements”  
   • C21 – “Kinematic constraints for supports”  
   • C22 – “Kinematic constraints between nodes”  
   • C10 – “Section contour”  
   • C13, C14 – Envelope results filtering only stresses of a specific sign (e.g. tensile only or compressive only). C14 must be set to –1 for “only tensile” representations.  
   • C15 – Group boundaries: drawn whenever adjoining elements differ by group number, material number, have cracks, differing local directions, or when more than two elements meet.  
   • C25, C26 – Tendon results placement:  
       – If C25 ≥ 0, results are drawn at the eccentric tendon location.  
       – If C25 < 0 and C26 ≥ 0, results are placed along the tendon’s lane in the QUAD element’s node plane.

3. Envelope Example  
   To generate a My-moment envelope from stored load cases 51 (maximum My) and 52 (minimum My), two COLO statements are given:  
     • LC 51; COLO C13 1001 C14 –1  → beam My, only positive extremes  
     • LC 52; COLO C13 –1   C14 1001 → beam My, only negative extremes

4. Color & Line-Type Coding Scheme  
   Any COLO code takes a four-digit integer of the form abcd:  
     • Thousands digit (a) selects color palette:  
         0xxx = delete (background)  
         1xxx = black or white  
         2xxx = red  
         3xxx = green  
         …  
         14xxx = dark cyan  
     • Last two digits or embedded patterns select line style:  
         xb01 = continuous  
         xb02 = medium dashed  
         xb03 = medium dotted  
         xb04 = medium dot–dashed  
         xb05 = close dashed  
         xb06 = close dotted  
         xb07 = close dot–dashed  
         xb08 = far dashed  
         xb09 = far dotted  
         xb10 = far dot–dashed  
     • “b” is a width factor: 0 = single line; >0 = double line with spacing = 1.4·b.

5. Global Color/Line Overrides  
   • COLO MONO: forces all indices into monochrome (index 1) while preserving line types.  
   • COLO COLO: reverts to user‐defined colors after MONO.  
   • COLO STAN: resets colors and line types to SOFiSTiK defaults.

6. Pen-Width Control for Plotters  
   Instead of colors, pens 1–3 can be assigned line‐thickness values (C2, C3, C5, C7, C10, C15 with C1, C4, C6, C8, C13, C14 with C11, C12) via COLO PENW:  
     • Pen 1 = 0.25 mm  
     • Pen 2 = 0.35 mm  
     • Pen 3 = 0.50 mm  

7. Meta-File Storage and Palette Application  
   Only the four-digit indices are stored in the generated PLB metafile. The actual RGB or printer color is mapped by a palette at display/print time. The values listed above reflect the default palette.

See also related table entries and commands: PALE, COL2, COLB, SCH3, FILL, and the continuation of this table on the next page.

content:
The table shown is a fragment of the SOFiSTiK “COLO” (colour and line‐type) parameter list.  Each row defines one of the user‐selectable colour/line‐type indices (C23 through C40) that the program will apply when generating graphical output (metafiles, plots, diagrams).  All entries share the same four‐column format:  

  •  Item:   The parameter name (C23–C40)  
  •  Description:  A brief English label of the graphical element controlled by that parameter  
  •  Unit:   Always “–” for these graphical parameters (no physical units)  
  •  Default:  The default four- or five-digit index value the program assigns if the user does not override it  

Here is a concise walkthrough of each parameter in the table:

1.  C23 – External beams (program SIR)  
      Default index: 12001  
      Controls the line colour/ style used to draw external beam elements imported from the SIR module.

2.  C24 – Fill colour of the external beam sections (program SIR)  
      Default index: 14241  
      Defines the interior hatch or solid‐fill colour used inside the section contours of SIR external beams.

3.  C25 – Tendons of the QUAD elements  
      Default index: 27001  
      Selects the colour/line‐type for prestressing tendons in QUAD plate elements.  
      Note: If you add +16000 to this index, the tendon will appear only during the structural‐representation phase (and not in section plots).

4.  C26 – Lane of the tendon in the QUAD element plane  
      Default index: –2001  
      Assigns the colour/line‐type for the “lane” or offset line where tendon forces are projected in the QUAD element’s mid-plane.

5.  C27 – Boundary support springs  
      Default index: 7001  
      Colour/line‐type for support‐spring symbols drawn at pinned or spring‐supported boundary nodes.

6.  C28 – Boundary moment springs  
      Default index: 7001  
      Colour/line‐type for rotational springs (moment springs) at supports.

7.  C29 – Thrust line  
      Default index: 11004  
      Colour/line‐type for the graphical representation of the thrust line (resultant line of compressive force) in masonry or arch analyses.

8.  C30 – Nodal sequences  
      Default index: –10019  
      Colour/line‐type for numbering or connecting node‐sequence markers.

9.  C31 – Beam tendon  
      Default index: 27001  
      Same as C25 but for beam‐element tendons (rather than QUAD plate tendons).  
      +16000 again limits display to the structural‐representation phase only.

10. C32 – Piercing points of tendon in cross‐section contour  
      Default index: 11004  
      Colour/line‐type for the locations where tendons intersect a section cut.

11. C33 – Numbers of structural elements  
      Default index: 1001  
      Colour/line‐type used when drawing element‐number labels.

12. C34 – HASE pile start point  
      Default index: 14001  
      Colour/line‐type for marking the toe (start) of a HASE (pile‐cap) element.

13. C35 – HASE pile length  
      Default index: 14001  
      Colour/line‐type for the pile length indicator in HASE plots.

14. C36 – Direction of kinematic constraints  
      Default index: C10  
      Rather than a numeric index, it references the C10 parameter (which itself encodes a particular colour/line‐type).

15. C37 – Direction of the resultant  
      Default index: C4  
      This points to parameter C4 for its colour/line settings (used to draw arrows indicating resultant forces).

16. C38 – Fill colour of sections of design elements  
      Default index: 10241  
      Interior fill (hatch or solid) used inside section contours for design‐stage elements.

17. C39 – Tendons of design elements  
      Default index: 27001  
      Line‐type for tendons in “design” elements (as opposed to geometry/model elements).  
      +16000 again toggles on‐only‐in‐structure‐view mode.

18. C40 – Piercing points of tendons of design elements in cross‐section contour  
      Default index: 11004  
      Colour/line‐type for tendon‐intersection markers in design‐element section cuts.

Additional notes (from the general COLO manual “Basics”):  
•  Each index is a four-digit code of the form xbbb or xb0y, where the first digit (0–14) selects a base colour (0 = delete/background, 1 = black/white, 2 = red, etc.), “b” controls line width (0 = single, >0 = double‐line with 1.4 × b spacing), and the last two digits select line style (b01 = continuous, b02 = medium dashed, … b10 = far dot‐dashed).  
•  Negative values suppress the element in certain views.  
•  The +16000 flag on tendon parameters forces display only during the overall structure plot, not in section detail.  
•  Parameters C36 and C37 may refer to other C-codes rather than raw numbers, allowing hierarchical reuse of line/colour settings.  
•  Users can override these defaults interactively or with COLO commands (COLO MONO, COLO COLO, COLO STAN, COLO PENW).

The input table “C1 … C28” defines a standardized set of drawing‐ and output‐markers used by SOFiSTiK’s graphic modules (GIRD, FRAM, SPAC, etc.). Its four columns specify:

 1. Item  
    − A code label (“C1”, “C2”, … “C28”) identifying a particular element type, edge, symbol or text group in the model output.  

 2. Description  
    − A concise English phrase describing what is drawn when that code is active. Entries include group identifiers (C1), node markers (C4), support symbols (C5), various contour‐element edges (C7 – C10), element‐type lines (C11 – C15), special geometric features (beam hinges C18, cutting pattern lines C17/C19, sections through plane elements C16), and text or warning labels (C20).  

 3. Unit  
    − Always shown as “–” because these codes do not carry a physical unit; they merely reference graphic attributes.  

 4. Default  
    − A numeric key (positive or negative) or reference to another C-code. This key points to a color, pen thickness, line type or symbol definition stored in the COLO record (or COLB/COL2/COL3 in certain contexts). A negative value means “do not draw,” e.g. default “–2005” for C4 suppresses node‐symbol drawing unless explicitly overridden.  

Key patterns in the Default column:  
• Codes 2001 / 3001 / 4001 / 5001 / 6001 / 7001 / 7401 / 7402 etc. map to standard pen, color and line‐type combinations. For example:  
 – C1 “Group numbers” → default COLO code 4001  
 – C2 “Material numbers or referenced lines/points” → 5001  
 – C3 “Cross section numbers” → 6001  

• Element‐type lines (C11–C15, C18) share the same default 3001 or 4001, grouping mesh lines, trusses, springs, pipes, and hinges under a consistent pen/color.  

• Contour edges use distinct defaults to differentiate boundary conditions:  
 – C7 “Free contour element edges” → 5002  
 – C8 “Simply supported edges” → 7001  
 – C9 “Edges with fixed M and free displacements” → 7402  
 – C10 “Fully fixed edges” → 7401  

• Support symbols (C5) default to code 2071. Sub-categories C21–C24 inherit C5; specialized spring-support symbols (C25–C28) reference C13.  

• Text for design errors (C20) and zero‐lines for HYDRA volumes (C6) both default to 2001.  

How it ties into the broader SOFiSTiK system:  
  – COLO (and COL2/.) holds the pen thickness, color and line‐style definitions keyed by these numeric codes.  
  – SCH3 allows control of symbol sizes (HSUP, WSUP for supports; WSPS, SPSC for springs; HBEH, WBEH for hinges).  
  – PALE and FILL rely on these code definitions to apply area fills or shading between structural lines.  
  – Negative defaults suppress drawing until specifically enabled by the user.  

In practice, when a drawing record refers to “marker set C12,” the system looks up row C12 (“Truss elements”) and applies its default graphic attributes (COLO code = 3001) unless overridden. This table thus centralizes the mapping from structural‐model concepts (groups, nodes, edges, supports, element types) to their visual representations in all SOFiSTiK output formats.

This table fragment is part of the SOFiSTiK graphics‐and‐text (SCH) family of records used to control how structural elements are drawn in RAG‐vector outputs. It defines two sub‐records of the “COL2” record (which itself links to related records PALE, COLO, COLB, SCH3, and FILL) that govern the depiction of interior structure lines and positive edge volumes. Below is a structured breakdown of its contents and related drawing rules:

1. Table “COL2” Sub-records  
   • C29 – Inner lines of structure areas  
     – linetype: “–” (a placeholder indicating no default line type; see COLO for actual styles)  
     – colour code: 2019  
     – purpose: When a structural area (plate, surface, etc.) is filled or hatched, C29 controls the drawing of its internal grid or outline lines.  
   • C30 – Structural volumes, edges of positive structural areas  
     – linetype: “–”  
     – colour code: 3001  
     – purpose: Governs the visibility of edges when volume (solid) elements are rendered positively (solid regions rather than cuts).

2. Colour and Line–type Reference  
   – Detailed colour definitions and line‐type patterns reside in the general SOFiSTiK manual “Basics” or in the COLO record.  
   – Negative line types (e.g. –1) suppress drawing of those elements, even if a valid colour is assigned.

3. Support Symbols (Record C5)  
   The standard markers for support points can be overridden or extended via numerical codes:  
   – 0: no symbol  
   – 1: point ●  
   – 2: plus +  
   – 3: star *  
   – 4: circle ○  
   – 5: cross ×  
   Extended display options:  
   – 71: auto-select 2D (GIRD, FRAM) or 3D (SPAC) symbol style  
   – 72: force 3D symbol  
   – 73: force 2D symbol  
   – 74: arrows (single arrow = support, double arrow = fixed moment)  
   – 75: text label flush-left  
   – 76: text label flush-right  
   Alignment modifiers:  
   – +0: symbols radiate outward from support, text axial  
   – +10: symbols point along positive global axes, text above  
   – +20: symbols point along negative global axes, text below  
   • Symbol size is set via SCH3 items HSUP (height) and WSUP (width).

4. Springs (Record C13)  
   – Drawn as zigzag lines in the view plane.  
   – Peak height HS is defined in SCHH; peak width WSPS is defined in SCH3.  
   – SPSC (in SCH3) can raise the number of zigzag peaks beyond the default three, up to ten for long springs.

5. Beam Hinges (Record C18)  
   – Always shown as a lozenge (♦) pointing toward the hinge location.  
   – Size is controlled by SCH3 items HBEH (height) and WBEH (width).

Notes:  
• All colour and linetype selections reference the master COLO table; changes there will automatically propagate to COL2-defined sub‐records.  
• The “See also” cross‐references (PALE, COLO, COLB, SCH3, FILL) guide the user toward related fill patterns, colour lists, column definitions, general SCH settings, and fill‐style parameters, ensuring consistent graphical output across all RAG vector store records.

The table shown below is part of SOFiSTiK’s graphical‐output configuration. It defines seven “C‐records” (C31 through C37) that specify how various structural entities are drawn in plan or section views. Each record associates a particular type of object or graphical detail with a line‐type/colour code or a reference to another record. In combination with the general COLO (colour/line‐type) table and other SCH3 settings, these items control the appearance of volumes, edges, symbols and markers in the post‐processing graphics.  

1. Column headings  
   • Item: the C‐record number.  
   • Description: which graphical entity or structural feature the record represents.  
   • Unit: always “–” here, indicating a dimensionless code.  
   • Default: the default COLO entry (or record reference) used if no other code is supplied.  

2. Records in detail  
   C31  
     – Description: Edges of “negative structural areas.” These are the outlines of cut‐out or subtracted volume regions (for example, openings, recesses or material removals).  
     – Default code: 12005. In COLO this code picks a specific colour and line‐type combination for rendering negative‐area edges.  

   C32  
     – Description: Column dimensions, column heads and splays. This covers the drawn outline of columns, typically including capital enlargements or head treatments where columns meet beams or slabs.  
     – Default code: 13017.  

   C33  
     – Description: Edges of positive QUAD areas. QUAD elements often represent panel‐type surface loads or simplified surface meshes; this code governs how their boundaries are traced.  
     – Default code: 4001.  

   C34  
     – Description: Edges of negative QUAD areas. Similar to C31 but specifically for QUAD‐type (shell) elements that have cut‐outs or omissions.  
     – Default code: 13005.  

   C35  
     – Description: Direction of spring elements. Springs (C13‐type supports) can have orientation arrows or zig‐zag symbols to show stiffness direction.  
     – Default: refers back to record C13, which in turn holds its own COLO code plus marker type/size parameters (HS, WSPS, SPSC).  

   C36  
     – Description: Center of mass for each storey level. This marker shows the centroid of the storey’s mass distribution in plan.  
     – Default code: 6257.  

   C37  
     – Description: Center of rigidity for each storey level. This marker indicates the stiffness‐centroid location, useful in seismic or lateral‐load design.  
     – Default code: 10257.  

3. How these records fit into the overall graphic setup  
   • Colour/line‐type definitions reside in COLO or a similar table. A given code (e.g. 12005) expands into a specific line width, colour index and dash pattern.  
   • Negative line‐type values (e.g. –1) suppress drawing of those elements.  
   • Marker shapes (point, plus, star, circle, cross) and more specialized symbols (dimensional arrows, text labels, 2D/3D support icons, spring zigzags, beam‐hinge lozenges) are configured via SCH3 (items HSUP, WSUP, HS, WSPS, HBEH, WBEH, etc.).  
   • These seven records (C31…C37) extend the basic support and element markers with additional structural‐analysis‐specific decorations: outlines of volumes and panels, directional arrows for springs, and storey‐level centroids.  

By editing the Default codes or overriding them in your input deck, you can readily customize the visibility and styling of these features without touching the core plotting routines. This modular approach keeps the graphics engine flexible, while still driven by a concise set of C‐record parameters.

 The springs C13 are represented as a zigzag line in their view with the item HS in the record SCHH and the item WSPS in the record SCH3. A maximum value for the peak distance can be input with SPSC in the record SCH3 in order to get more than the three standard peaks for very long springs. In this case up to 10 peaks are possible.
 Beam hinges C18 are represented always as a lozenge with the peak to the hinge. The size is controlled with the items HBEH and WBEH in the record SCH3.

This input table defines ten configurable “colour‐by” items (C1, C2, C3, C4, C5, C6, C13, C14, C20, C21) that instruct the plotting routine which sets of entities or result types should receive a coloured background fill. Each row consists of:

 • Item  
   – A unique code (C1, C2, … C21) identifying one of the predefined colouring modes.  
 • Description  
   – A brief textual label explaining what the code selects:  
     • C1: group numbers  
     • C2: element numbers or numbers of referenced structural lines or points  
     • C3: node numbers  
     • C4: results near 0 or equal to 0  
     • C5: material numbers  
     • C6: cross-section numbers  
     • C13: positive results  
     • C14: negative results  
     • C20: text for design errors  
     • C21: numbers of structural elements  
 • Unit  
   – In this context no physical units apply (marked “–”).  
 • Default  
   – The default fill-colour index, here “–101” for every item, indicates “no fill.” Any negative fill index suppresses colouring unless overridden.

Key usage notes (see also records PALE, COLO, COL2, SCHH, SCH2):

1. Colouring applies to the text background area rather than the text itself.  
2. A nonnegative fill code is interpreted as  
     fill_colour_code = colour_number × 1000 + fill_index  
   • colour_number (0…14) references the palette entry defined in COLO/PALE/​COL2.  
   • fill_index specifies the fill style:  
     – 101 = solid coloured fill  
     – 201…210 = patterns of increasing intensity  
     – 301…331 = hatch styles  
   • To request a translucent fill, add 32 to the fill_index (for example, 101 + 32 = 133 yields a semi-transparent solid).  
3. A negative fill_index (e.g. –101) disables filling altogether.  
4. The spatial extent of the fill area is governed by SCH2 subfields BACX, BACY, BMIN, BMAX, which establish the rectangular bounds around each plotted element or text label. The background area is not cleared before drawing, so overlapping fills accumulate unless explicitly removed.

By mapping one of the C-codes to a nonnegative fill colour code, users can highlight specific groups of elements, ranges of result values, structural regions or error messages in graphical output. This mechanism integrates with the broader PLB plotting system—COLB triggers the fill, COLO/​COL2 define the colour ramps, SCHH handles hatch settings, and SCH2 lays out the geometry of the background rectangles.

See also: PALE, COLO, COL2, SCHH, SCH2
 COLB
 The text background area can be coloured unlike the actual text. For this the areas get a fill colour. No filling occurs with a negative fill colour (e.g. -101). The size of the background area is controlled by using the items BACX, BACY, BMIN and BMAX in the record SCH2.
 The fill colour is defined with colour·1000+fill index. In this case the colour and the fill index have the following meaning:
 colour colour number (0...14, description see record COLO)
 fill index Type of the filling
 101 coloured
 201....210 pattern with different intensity
 301....331 hatches
 Transparently filling areas are created if the fill index is increased by 32. The area is not deleted before drawing.

Below is a field-by-field description of the “FILL” input table, which drives area-filling and isoline patterns in the RAG vector store.  Use this schema as a reference for automated ingestion or for building a UI for interactive editing.

1.  NAME: TYPE  
    •  Purpose: selects the overall fill‐pattern scheme or (when numeric) designates an individual fill step to override.  
    •  Data type: literal keyword or integer (1–255), also “ABOV”/“BELO” for ranges above / below the defined steps.  
    •  Predefined literals (when resetting the pattern):  
       –  COLO, PATT, HATC, RGB, RGBL, RGBD, MONO, BLUS, MBLU, MGRE, MRED, VRGB, VRGL, VRGD, ANI, RGB2, RPAT, RHAT, RTRP, VRTR, R2TR  
    •  Behavior:  
       –  First record’s TYPE chooses the fill family.  
       –  Subsequent numeric TYPE records override individual steps (incrementing the step counter automatically).  

2.  NAME: FROM  
    •  Purpose: lower boundary of the data‐value interval for this fill or isoline.  
    •  Type: real number.  
    •  Default: database minimum (if unspecified on the first record).  

3.  NAME: TO  
    •  Purpose: upper boundary of the data‐value interval.  
    •  Type: real number.  
    •  Default: database maximum (if unspecified on the first record).  

4.  NAME: INC  
    •  Purpose: either a fixed tolerance for the step or the spacing between isolines / fill transitions.  
    •  Type: real.  
    •  Behavior: used only if NUMB is zero or when automatic step insertion is requested.  

5.  NAME: NUMB  
    •  Purpose: number of fill steps (intervals) to generate between FROM and TO.  
    •  Type: integer ≥ 0.  
    •  Notes: when zero, the table falls back on default “base points” for that pattern family.  

6.  NAME: MODE  
    •  Purpose: adjusts how the fill‐step definitions are interpreted or altered.  
    •  Possible values (combineable):  
       –  T: translucent pattern  
       –  A: absolute numeric values (no normalization)  
       –  U / N: explicit reversal or “no reversal” of step sequence  
       –  0: ignore zero line  
       –  EDGE, OFF, ON: edge‐only / full fill / edge‐only fill  
       –  INTE, NO, YES: when inserting/deleting steps, adapt intermediate points or recompute them  
       –  INSE: insert a new range  
       –  DELE: delete an existing range  
       –  NFIX: fix this range as a control point (no further auto‐interpolation)  
       –  TEXT / NTXT: always or never draw the value label  

7.  NAME: COLI  
    •  Purpose: for indexed / palette fills, selects one of 0…14.  
    •  Type: integer (negative values suppress the step).  
    •  Default: “–” (use built-in inherited color)  
    •  Note: for any RGB-based family, COLI is forced to 15 and can be omitted.

8.  NAME: INDX  
    •  Purpose: identifies the sub-pattern or hatch index within the chosen family.  
    •  Type: integer (depends on TYPE; see the COLOB / COLB record for full mapping).

9.  NAME: RED, GREE, BLUE  
    •  Purpose: override individual RGB channels (0.0…1.0) for this step.  
    •  Type: real.  
    •  Behavior: negative values trigger interpolation from neighbors; (0,0,0)=black, (1,1,1)=white; equal channels produce gray.

Additional notes and context:
•  DMOD (not a table column but a companion parameter) controls automatic increment strategies (e.g. DEFA, RDEF, DDEF, LMAT, LG_1…LG_4, INK/DINK, MSIK/DMSK, SINK/DSIN, SING/DSIG).  
•  If NUMB>0, the table computes uniform steps; if NUMB=0, default “base points” apply unless explicitly overridden by individual step records.  
•  Interpolation: any gaps in FROM–TO sequences are interpolated automatically, unless flagged with NFIX.  
•  Shading (LIGH, DARK, BRIG, LIPX/Y/Z) and advanced lighting options (POIN, DIFF, DPOI, BDIF…) are handled separately but respect the color assignments from FILL.  
•  ABOV and BELO records allow styling of out-of-range values above the highest step or below the lowest.  

Use this structure to parse, validate, or generate FILL records programmatically in your RAG vector‐store workflows.

The table defines seven key parameters for controlling how filled areas (especially RGB‐based fills and isolines) are rendered, shaded and stepped.  It is typically used in conjunction with fill‐pattern definitions (see also PALE, COLO, ISOL) to fine‐tune the appearance of contours, color gradations or hatch patterns in a graphical output.  Each row lists an input “Item,” its role (“Description”), the unit of measure, and the system “Default” if the user does not supply a value.

1.  DMOD (Increment control)  
    •  Purpose: selects the method by which the interval size (INC) or tolerance for successive fill steps is computed and rounded.  
    •  Unit: literal (LIT)  
    •  Default: ‘*’ (i.e. uses the result‐type default)  
    •  Common literals:  
       – DEFA: follow result‐type default rules  
       – RDEF: as DEFA, but always round INC  
       – DDEF: as DEFA, but never round INC  
       – LMAT: variable increments (e.g. reinforcement mats)  
       – LG_1…LG_4: logarithmic series of increasing bases  
       – INK / DINK: engineering (“1,2,5,10,…”) or direct increments  
       – MSIK / DMSK: read actual database values, adjust INK/DINK  
       – SINK / DSIN: fixed single‐step increments  
       – SING / DSIG: repeat a single area step to cover all values  
    By choosing DMOD, you control the number, spacing and numeric rounding of your contour or fill boundaries.

2.  LIGH (Light control)  
    •  Purpose: enables and configures lighting effects on RGB‐filled areas (not used for monochrome or pattern fills).  
    •  Unit: LIT  
    •  Default: DEFA  
    •  Options:  
       – OFF: no lighting  
       – DEFA: light on with default‐computed intensity  
       – BELO: darker shading on underside of QUAD/BRIC elements  
       – DIFF: simple diffuse illumination  
       – POIN: single‐point light source  
       – DPOI: point light with distance‐based falloff  
       – BDIF: DIFF + BELO combination  
       – BPOI: POIN + BELO  
       – BDPO: DPOI + BELO  

3.  LIPX (Light X coordinate or direction)  
    •  Purpose: defines the x‐component of the light vector or location of a point light.  
    •  Unit: meters (m) or literal (LIT)  
    •  Default: SCRE  
    •  Special literal:  
       – SCRE: interpret (LIPX,LIPY) as screen‐relative reference (bit‐mask in LIPY, see below)

4.  LIPY (Light Y coordinate or direction / screen‐point selector)  
    •  Purpose: y‐component of the light vector or, when LIPX=SCRE, an encoded screen‐point position.  
    •  Unit: m or no‐unit  
    •  Default: 16  
    •  If LIPX=SCRE, LIPY is a bitmask:  
       0 = centre, +1 left, +2 right, +4 top, +8 bottom, +16 front, +32 behind.

5.  LIPZ (Light Z coordinate or direction / additional distance)  
    •  Purpose: z‐component of the light vector or, in SCRE mode, an extra distance along the viewing axis.  
    •  Unit: m or no‐unit  
    •  Default: –0.2  
    •  Interpretation:  
       – >0: absolute distance in meters  
       – <0: fraction of the overall system (bounding box) size

6.  DARK (Factor of dim-out)  
    •  Purpose: controls how much darker regions turned away from the light become (shadow strength).  
    •  Unit: LIT or no‐unit  
    •  Default: A57  
    •  Range: 0 (no darkening) to 255 (full black).  
    •  Special ‘A’ prefix: scales the dim‐out by the number of fill colors to avoid incorrect color isolation.

7.  BRIG (Factor of booster light)  
    •  Purpose: adjusts how much brighter regions facing the light become (highlight strength).  
    •  Unit: no‐unit  
    •  Default: 115  
    •  Range: 0 (no extra brightness) to 255 (maximum boost).

Together, these parameters let you precisely govern the numerical spacing of contours (via DMOD), enable or disable and configure nuanced lighting effects (LIGH), position the light source in space or relative to the screen (LIPX/Y/Z), and set how strongly shadow and highlight are applied (DARK, BRIG) when rendering color‐filled or isoline charts.

See also: PALE, COLO, ISOL

 A default number of base points exists for each fill type, to define the sequence of fill colours. These base points were not used if NUMB is set to 0. Then is it possible to define owner base points, without influence of the defaulted ones.
 If the default values or colours for individual fill steps should be modified, this can be achieved by using the subsequent records. TYPE is here the number of the fill step (maximum 255). The number of the fill steps is increased around 1 without an input for TYPE. The literals ABOV and
 BELO can be input for change of the colour definitions of the value ranges above the last step or below the first step.
 FROM and TO define the value range of a fill step. Irregular fill distributions can be achieved with that. Single FROM – TO areas should be input in the ascending sequence of the fill steps (from the smallest to the largest value). Intermediate values which were not defined are interpolated. The properties of a fill steps can be changed with an input of a literal for MODE. In this case the following literals have the meaning:
 INSE Insertion of a value range FROM–TO
 DELE Deletion of a value range FROM–TO
 NFIX Deletion of the markers of a value range. The marked value ranges are the supporting points in the case of an automatic interpolation of inter- mediate values. Then they are not changed any more automatically (e.g. areas which were input with INSE)

DELE Deletion of a value range FROM–TO. NFIX Deletion of the markers of a value range. The marked value ranges are the supporting points in the case of an automatic interpolation of inter- mediate values. Then they are not changed any more automatically (e.g. areas which were input with INSE).
 TEXT Description of these isolines always
 NTXT Description of these isolines never
 The colour which should be used can be defined independently from the input for the value range of a fill step (FROM, TO, MODE).
 In this case the colour index which should be used is defined in the record COLO (0...14, ex- planation of the single values see in the record COLO). No input of a colour index is necessary for RGB colours (is always 15). A negative colour index does not represented this colour step.
 The type of the area filling is defined with INDX (it is described in the record COLB).
 Inputs for the colour combination (values from 0.0 to 1.0) can be defined with RED, GREE and BLUE in the case of the RGB colours. The RGB value is set according to its default, if a negative input occurs for one of the three values. Then the RGB value is interpolated. One gets a black representation, if all three values are defined with 0.0. An input of all three values with 1.0 gives a white representation. If all three values are of the same size, that shows a grey step.
 Additionally the RGB colours can be printed more brightly or more darkly in dependence on the area orientation (item LIGH).
 The undersides of the QUAD elements (in positive local z direction) and the inner sides of BRIC surfaces are printed more darkly about the dimension of DARK with LIGH BELO. Inputs for LIPX, LIPY and LIPZ are not used here.
 The areas turned to the light are printed more brightly about the sum of DARK+BRIG using the dimension DARK with LIGH DIFF. This depends on the size of the angle between the unit light direction and the area normal direction. The areas which are turned away the light are printed more darkly about the dimension DARK.
 LIGH POIN acts as LIGH DIFF. However, the distance between the areas and the light point is considered additionally: The areas with the smallest distances to the light point are the brightest ones. The respective light direction is determined from the direction of the area centre of gravity to the light point.

The areas which are turned away the light are printed more darkly about the dimension DARK.. LIGH POIN acts as LIGH DIFF. However, the distance between the areas and the light point is considered additionally: The areas with the smallest distances to the light point are the brightest ones. The respective light direction is determined from the direction of the area centre of gravity to the light point..
 LIGH DPOI acts similar as POIN. While the whole element area is illuminated uniformly, at
 DPOI, however, the light shines at the element area in dependence on the distance.
 LIGH BDIF acts as LIGH DIFF, however, only the dimension of the black–out or the flare is different: QUAD undersides or BRIC inner sides become more darkly at the shadow side about the dimension DARK. At the light side they become more brightly about the dimension DARK beginning at DARK. QUAD top sides and BRIC outer sides are not changed at the shadow side, and they are printed more brightly about the dimension BRIG at the light side.
 LIGH BPOI or BDPO act as LIGH BDIF, however, with additional properties which are de- scribed at POIN or DPOI.
 The default LIGH DEFA is for the isoareas BELO, for QUAD and BRIC load area POIN.
 If the literal A is defined at the item DARK, The number of the fill colours is considered for black–out and flare. The dimension is reduced for many colours in order to prevent not correct colour representations.
 The light direction results from the input at LIPX, LIPY and LPIZ. The light point is defined in the system coordinate with an input of a number at LIPX. For LIGH DIFF and BDIF the uniform light direction results from the direction of the light point to the system origin.
 The light points which depends on the respective box of the current system section with ref- erence to the screen are defined with the input of the literal SCRE at LIPX. The uniform light direction results from the direction of the light point to the box centre for LIGH DIFF and BDIF. For the definition of light points the input for LIPY is used as bit pattern as follows:
 0 centre
 +1 left screen border
 +2 right screen border
 +4 upper screen border

The light points which depends on the respective box of the current system section with ref- erence to the screen are defined with the input of the literal SCRE at LIPX. The uniform light direction results from the direction of the light point to the box centre for LIGH DIFF and BDIF. For the definition of light points the input for LIPY is used as bit pattern as follows:. 0 centre. +1 left screen border. +2 right screen border. +4 upper screen border.
 +8 lower screen border
 +16 in front
 +32 behind
 For the definition of the light point in centre, above, in front LIPY 20 (=0+4+16) has to be input.
 For a larger cone of light an additional distance (in light direction) can be input with LIPZ. Negative values are used as a factor of the largest box side and positive values as a distance in m.

The table defines the syntax and semantics of the SELE command’s input records (parameters) that control how “selections” of structural elements are created, stored and recalled. It consists of four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and nine parameter rows (NUMB, GRP, BOX, VISI, PERS, VIEW, DEFO, SEL, ALTE). Below is a structured breakdown.

1. Purpose and Context  
• SELE collects, names or numbers a set of structure‐elements for later operations (viewing, hiding, deforming, grouping, etc.).  
• A selection can be:  
  – Defined explicitly by a reference number (NUMB) or a name (TITL).  
  – Automatically created from the “current settings” of BOX, GRP, VISI, PERS, VIEW, DEFO, SEL.  
  – Updated (via PUT or PUTG) or overwritten when READ back into memory.  
• Alternation (ALTE) flips visibility logic: selected items become invisible and vice versa.

2. Columns  
• Item: Parameter name.  
• Description: Meaning of each parameter, acceptable values and side‐effects.  
• Unit: Data type (all are literal or N/A).  
• Default: Value assumed if the parameter is omitted.

3. Detailed Parameters

A. NUMB (Number of the selection)  
 ­ Unit: – (not applicable)  
 ­ Default: – (no number)  
 ­ Description:  
   • “–” : Search for a selection by its name (TITL).  
   • 0   : Use the “current” unnamed settings or apply ALTE without an explicit selection.  
   • nr  : Use selection number nr. If nr doesn’t exist yet, create it using the current BOX/GRP/... settings.  
   • If neither NUMB nor TITL is given, the command reuses the “last chosen” selection.

B. GRP (Group selection, record GRP)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values:  
   • PUT  – Update the stored selection to match the current group flags.  
   • PUTG – Update selection but ignore grouping subdivision.  
   • NO   – Do not apply group‐based filtering.  
   • YES  – Apply the group‐based filter.

C. BOX (Box‐based filtering, record BOX)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle use of bounding‐box selection.

D. VISI (Visibility record VISI)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle element‐visibility filtering.

E. PERS (Perspective record PERS)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle whether perspective‐distance is used in the selection.

F. VIEW (Line of vision record VIEW)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle inclusion by view‐frustum or camera constraint.

G. DEFO (Deformed‐structure record DEFO)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle selection of deformed mesh positions.

H. SEL (Single‐selection record SEL)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: YES  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – toggle whether only a single element may be selected.

I. ALTE (Alternation of the selection)  
 ­ Unit: LIT  
 ­ Default: NO  
 ­ Values: NO/YES – if YES, invert the selection: marked items become hidden and unmarked become shown.

4. Workflow Notes  
• To store a new selection, first define BOX, GRP, VISI, PERS, VIEW and DEFO as needed, then call SELE with PUT/PUTG or with a fresh NO/TITL reference.  
• Reading back a saved selection (NUMB or TITL) restores all records flagged YES, overwriting interim inputs.  
• Omitting PUT or PUTG leaves existing stored selections intact.  
• ALTE works in tandem with GRP/BOX flags to produce a complementary set.

Below is a structured breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG-enabled vector store:

1. Table Structure  
   - Columns:  
     • Parameter (leftmost column, always “SELE” in this excerpt)  
     • Sub-field name (e.g. NO, WIND, CROS)  
     • Sub-field value or state description  
     • Short natural-language explanation  

2. Rows in the Extracted Fragment  
   • SELE–NO  
     – Value: (no alternate word)  
     – Description: “does not alternate”  
     – Interpretation: If NO is specified, the selection will not use the alternate view mechanism.  
   • SELE–WIND  
     – Value: “Only completely switched off elements”  
     – Description: Wind-down flag hides only elements that have been fully deactivated.  
   • SELE–CROS  
     – Value: “Also the cut elements of the selection”  
     – Description: Cut‐away parts of the geometry are included in the current selection.  

3. Key Behavioral Rules (from the accompanying text)  
   a. Selection Composition  
      – SELE aggregates inputs from BOX, GRP, VIEW, PERS, VISI, DEFO.  
      – Changes to underlying records immediately propagate to any SELE unless saved.  
   b. Defining an Instance  
      – Via NO: use an explicit reference number.  
      – Via TITL: use a named selection; if TITL exists, program finds its NO.  
      – If neither NO nor TITL is provided, selection reuses the last active one.  
      – If TITL is new, assigns the next available reference number.  
   c. Saving vs. Updating  
      – A new SELE is auto‐created when first naming or using PUT/PUTG, requiring BOX, GRP, VIEW, etc., to be pre-defined.  
      – On SELE-save, any flags set to YES overwrite stored BOX, VISI, DEFO, PERS, VIEW in that selection.  
      – PUT updates GRP only; it does not alter current on-screen settings.  
      – PUTG acts similarly but within grouped contexts.  
   d. RESTORATION (Reading SELE)  
      – When reading a saved SELE, any record flags marked YES will be restored, overwriting prior inputs for those record types.  
   e. Alternate Visibility (ALTE)  
      – Toggles visibility: selected elements (via GRP or BOX) become hidden; non-selected ones become visible.  

4. Continuation Notice  
   – The table concludes with “Table continued on next page,” indicating additional parameters and rules may follow.

content:
The table you’ve provided defines a single input parameter for the “SELE” (selection) routine. Below is a comprehensive description suitable for indexing in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store. It explicitly links TITL to related commands and contextual behavior.

1. Parameter Name  
   • Identifier: TITL  
   • Role: Name of the selection  

2. Data Type and Format  
   • Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   • Expected Content: Any textual label or identifier that describes the selection group. May include letters, digits, spaces, and punctuation, subject to system naming rules.  

3. Default Behavior  
   • Default Value: “–” (no name)  
   • If neither TITL nor an explicit reference number (NO) is supplied when invoking SELE, the program will:  
     – Search existing selections for the first available TITL and automatically assign it’s reference number to the new selection.  
     – If no existing TITL is defined, it generates a new reference number by taking the last used selection index and adding one.  
     – Use the last chosen selection by reference if no naming information is provided.  

4. Interaction with SELE and Related Records  
   • SELE command uses TITL to group and reference structure elements (see also GRP, BOX, VIEW, PERS, VISI, DEFO).  
   • When you save a selection (via GRP PUT or PUTG), the routine will auto-define the selection with its current settings—provided TITL is present or generated.  
   • Stored settings for BOX, VISI, DEFO, PERS and VIEW within an existing selection are overwritten only if the user explicitly inputs YES. GRP settings update when PUT is issued; no automatic updates occur otherwise.  
   • Reading a saved selection applies all subsettings marked YES, overwriting previous runtime inputs.  

5. Naming Conventions and Best Practices  
   • Keep TITL concise yet descriptive (e.g. “Wings_Left”, “Door_Cuts”).  
   • Avoid special characters that might conflict with file systems or downstream parsers.  
   • If you intend to alternate visibility (ALTE), use a consistent naming scheme so that “invert” or “alt” suffixes remain clear. Alternating a selection hides GRP/BOX-selected elements and shows the remainder.  

6. Example Usage  
   • Define a new selection called “CutEdges”:  
     SELE TITL = “CutEdges” GRP … VIEW … PUT  
   • Load an existing selection by name without specifying NO:  
     SELE TITL = “CutEdges”  

7. Related References  
   • GRP: group-based element specification  
   • BOX: bounding-box selection  
   • VIEW: viewpoint or camera settings  
   • PERS: perspective projection flag  
   • VISI/DEFO: visibility and default attributes  

By capturing all of the above metadata—identifier, type, default logic, interdependencies, usage examples and cross-references—you ensure the vector store can deliver accurate, context-rich responses whenever a user or system agent queries the term “TITL.”

 SELE
 NO
 does not alternate
 WIND Only completely switched off elements
 CROS Also the cut elements of the selection
 The selection can summarize all inputs for the choice and the view of structure elements. Thus a change within the input (for example for a differentiation of various parts of the structure) can occur more easily and more clearly.
 The selection can be defined via a reference number NO or via its name TITL. If NO is not input, the program searches for an available selection TITL and set the corresponding reference number. The selection gets the last reference number+1, if TITL is not defined. The last chosen selection is used, if neither NO nor TITL is defined.
 The selection is defined automatically with its current settings, if it is not available yet or GRP PUT or PUTG is input. That is, the records BOX, GRP, VIEW and so on must be defined before. The stored settings for BOX, VISI, DEFO, PERS and VIEW which are already in an available selection are overwritten, if YES is input. GRP is updated if PUT is input. The current settings are not changed during the saving of SELE.
 All settings for GRP, BOX, VISI, DEFO, PERS and VIEW which are indicated with YES are set during the reading of the selection. In this case all previous inputs for these records are overwritten.
 The selection can be alternated with the input for ALTE. In this case all elements which are selected with GRP or BOX are invisible. The not selected elements are visible.
