The table you are seeing defines the fields of the “GRP” input record, which controls which element‐groups (and associated annotations) will be drawn in a graphic‐output module.  Every record has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and each Item may accept one or more literal keywords.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown:

1.  NUMB   (Unit “– / LIT”, Default “–”)  
    This switch turns on various numbering or annotation features.  You supply one or more of the literals below:  
    •  no – print group‐, element‐, material‐ or cross‐section numbers (as determined by the current GDIV)  
    •  NODE – show all free (unconnected) nodes  
    •  ENOD – make deleted nodes visible (structural‐lines only)  
    •  EDGE – draw all nodal connectivity sequences  
    •  ADDI – label all additional elements (axes suppressed)  
    •  SBOX – show all ADDI elements (axes and cuts suppressed) lying outside the structural BOX  
    •  BSEC – mark all cutting areas through volume elements  
    •  QSEC – mark all cutting lines through plane elements  
    •  BNOD – label BRIC‐element inner nodes  
    •  GLAZ – outline the entire BRIC surface, including back faces  

    In addition you may label various geometry‐axes and placement markers:  
    •  AUSR, AUNS, ASTR, ALAN, AGEO, ASEC, ATEN, AINT, AXIS, SBXA, PLAC  

2.  OPTI   (Unit “LIT”, Default “YES”)  
    A simple on/off flag for the group:  
    •  NO – do not draw this group at all  
    •  YES – include this group in the output  

3.  ETYP   (Unit “LIT”, Default “all”)  
    Select by element‐type rather than by numeric group.  You may supply one or more of:  
    •  BEAM, SPRI, BOUN, TRUS, CABL, TUBE (line elements)  
    •  QUAD, BRIC (plane/volume)  
    •  DSLN, GLN, GAR, GVO (structural lines/areas/volumes)  
    •  KINE (kinematic constraints)  
    •  SIR (external beam‐sections), FIXL (fixed cutting pattern), CUT (cut pattern)  
    •  ADDI (additional element types), LINE, AREA, TEXT, POST, NIVE, CURV, NODE, QSEC, BSEC  

4.  GDIV   (Unit “LT”, Default from database, usually 1000)  
    Defines the divisor for converting an element’s full ID into its group number via  
      group = int(element-number / GDIV).  
    •  NO = specify a custom divisor in this record (integer 0…999)  
    •  DEFA = use the database’s default value  
    (“TO” and “INC” are now obsolete)  

5.  DOMA   (Unit “– / LT”, Default “DEFA”)  
    Restrict drawing to a single domain or domain set.  By default (“DEFA”) all domains appear.

6.  LC     (Unit “– / LT”, Default “YES”)  
    When load‐case results are requested, this field toggles between:  
    •  NO = suppress all load‐case diagrams  
    •  YES = plot the load case whose index you provide in the accompanying LC record  

—  
Usage notes:  
•  On the very first GRP record you typically deactivate all existing groups; subsequent GRP records re‐activate only those you name here.  The legend will list each activated group or element type.  
•  If you redefine GDIV away from the database default, be careful when reading node‐based records (ISOL, SECT, NODE) so that the old and new divisors remain an integer ratio.  (Dynamic groups, where GDIV=0, cannot be changed.)  
•  To avoid ambiguity between NUMB‐literals and secondary‐group names (SGRP), you may need to use OPTI with OFFL/YESL modifiers.  
•  For BRIC volumes you can further refine surface‐drawing with OPTI flags IGNO, NO, YES, VGRP or FULL, and—even in lateral view—show internal axes by using SBXA FULL.

This table documents the “GRP” record, which controls how groups of elements (and additional graphical primitives) are represented in the RAG‐based viewer.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, followed by behavioral notes and special options:

1. Record Name  
   • GRP – enables or disables group representation.  
   • Active flag: YES means the record is in effect.

2. Element‐Type Filter (ETYP)  
   If specified, only the listed types will be drawn.  Multiple types can be combined.  Valid codes are:
   • BEAM – beam elements  
   • SPRI – springs  
   • BOUN – boundary elements  
   • TRUS – trusses  
   • CABL – cables  
   • TUBE – tubes  
   • QUAD – plane (shell) elements  
   • BRIC – solids (brick elements)  
   • KINE – kinematic constraints  
   • SIR – external beam sections  
   • DSLN – design elements  
   • GLN – structural lines  
   • GAR – structural areas  
   • GVO – structural volumes  
   • NODE – nodes  
   • QSEC/BSEC – cutting lines/areas  
   • CUT – cutting pattern  
   • FIXL – fixed cutting pattern  
   • ADDI – all additional element types  
   • LINE, AREA, TEXT, POST, NIVE, CURV – auxiliary graphics (lines, areas, text, position markers, level symbols, geometry axes)

3. Group Divisor (GDIV)  
   Defines how the integer group-number is computed from an element’s ID:  
   • NO – no divisor applied (use the raw group number)  
   • DEFA – use the database default (normally 1 000)  
   • TO, INC – obsolete  
   Unit: integer 0…999.  Changing GDIV requires care if node-based values (e.g. load or temperature at NODE) are also used; dynamic groups (GDIV=0) cannot be altered.

4. Domain Number (DOMA)  
   • Specifies a domain to which the record applies  
   • “DEFA” means “all domains”

5. Load‐Case Selection (LC)  
   • NO – do not use any load case  
   • YES – apply the load case index given in field LC (as defined by record LC)  
   This is interpreted by the ASE analysis program.

Behavioral Notes and Special Options  
• By default, all groups and types are drawn.  If you enter the first GRP record, all structural groups are initially switched off; you then explicitly reactivate the desired groups or types.  The active groups will appear in the on‐screen legend.  Secondary groups (SGRP) may also be defined.  
• Element group = integer part of (element number ÷ GDIV).  If you redefine GDIV, ensure the old and new divisors are integer multiples so that node‐value references (ISOL, SECT, NODE records) remain consistent.  
• Specifying ETYP alone restricts the display strictly to those element types, regardless of group membership.  
• BRIC‐surface visualization options (use in combination with “GRP GLAZ” or as an OPTI field):  
   – IGNO – do not draw any BRIC faces  
   – NO – draw only visible (front) faces  
   – YES – draw all faces  
   – VGRP – draw all group surfaces (for load plots)  
   – FULL – render full brick mesh (including internal edges), not just surfaces  
• To show structural axes in a lateral view, use the “SBXA FULL” option in conjunction with the GRP record.  
• Table continues on next page.

The table defines the parameters of the BOX record, which controls how a 3-D “ashlar-shaped” window is extracted from a larger model, how it is filtered, combined, and finally placed on the drawing sheet.  Each line in the table gives (1) the keyword (Item), (2) what it means (Description), (3) the measurement unit (Unit) and (4) its default value (Default).  In practice BOX is often used together with record GRP (group selection), or with SELE/SEL and VISI for more advanced selection and visibility control.

1. XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN  
   • Description:  
     – If given as numbers, they specify the minimum X, Y or Z coordinate of the window in the model’s world coordinates (“ashlar-shaped” means that the window faces are aligned with coordinate planes).  
     – Alternatively, you can give a reference to an element type plus an element number or range.  In that case the minimum window coordinate is computed from the envelope of all referenced elements.  Possible element types include: record GRP items, ETYP, GPT (structural points), QTEN (quad tendons), BTEN (beam tendons), DTEN (design-element tendons).  
   • Unit: m (meters) or LIT (literal reference when used as element reference)  
   • Default: * (asterisk means “not defined”)

2. XMAX, YMAX, ZMAX  
   • Description:  
     – Mirror of XMIN, YMIN, ZMIN: maximum coordinates of the window.  If referenced by element IDs or group numbers, the envelope of those elements defines the upper bound.  
   • Unit: m / —  
   • Default: *  

3. TYP  
   • Description: Type of element filtering inside the BOX.  It determines which elements (and thus which nodes) are considered “visible” inside the window.  The literal values are:  
     – LIMI: All nodes are activated, regardless of position.  
     – WIND: Only elements completely contained in the box are used (all their nodes lie within).  
     – CROS: Partial cut: elements with at least one node inside the box are included.  
     – BWIN: Same as WIND but the window is first rotated according to the current VIEW/PERS settings (X-axis to the right, Y-axis upward).  
     – BCRO: Same as CROS but in the rotated coordinate system.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: WIND  

4. VXCM, VYCM  
   • Description: Horizontal (VXCM) and vertical (VYCM) displacement of the selected box in the final picture.  Values are relative shifts: positive moves right/up, negative moves left/down.  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 0, 0  

5. KREF  
   • Description: A reference node chosen so that it always appears at the same sheet location (even when deformations are applied via DEFO).  By assigning a “literal” position code to KREF you can “snap” the structure to one of nine positions on the sheet (center, edges, corners).  VXCM/VYCM then act as offsets from that base position.  
   • Unit: —  
   • Default: –  

6. OPER  
   • Description: When combining up to eight partial BOX definitions you control how they merge with this linkage operator.  The order of combination is: first all partial boxes sharing the same group number are combined in input order; then the resulting box‐groups are combined in turn, using the operator of the first partial box in each group.  Possible values:  
     – NO: Ignore this partial box entirely.  
     – AND: Intersect – only nodes active in all combined boxes remain.  
     – OR: Union – all nodes active in any of the combined boxes are kept.  
     – –AND: Inverse AND – nodes activated by the partial box are deactivated, and vice versa.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: UND (German “AND”)

How BOX interacts with other records (context):  
• If YMIN is given as ALL, the numbers for defining X/Y/Z ranges are ignored; BOX simply spans all elements of the chosen type.  
• Kinematic constraints are only drawn if all nodes for that constraint belong to visible elements when TYPE is WIND; only one visible node is needed if TYPE is CROS.  
• Additional graphical elements placed in world coordinates (“MOVE … UNIT WC”) are clipped to the final BOX—unless you disable clipping with “MOVE … SBOX OFF.”  
• For skewed or rotated views you can store multiple partial BOX definitions (with their own VIEW, PERS, VISI, DEFO settings) and blend them using BWIN or BCRO. This lets you create composite windows that follow different orientations.  
• BOX and GRP can be used together to flexibly select subsets of elements by group, by geometry, or by attribute.

sections: 3.20 BOX – Window of an Overall System

content:
Below is a structured, detailed description of the BOX record and its input table. Wherever relevant, cross-references to SELE, GRP, SEL and VISI are noted.

1. Purpose of BOX  
   • Defines a drawing “window” within the overall model space. Anything outside this window will not be displayed.  
   • If the specified BOX coordinates are undefined or exceed real system limits, they default to the full system extents.

2. Defining the BOX  
   • Two methods:  
     – Explicit coordinates: supply XMIN, YMIN, XMAX, YMAX directly.  
     – Reference-based: specify an element type and a list of element numbers; BOX is then the envelope of those elements.  
   • Supported element types (ETYP) for reference:  
     – record GRP item ETYP  
     – GPT   (structural points)  
     – QTEN  (quad tendons)  
     – BTEN  (beam tendons)  
     – DTEN  (design-element tendons)

3. Numbering Modes (item YMIN)  
   • NO   — no element numbers used  
   • INR  — internal, consecutively counted elements  
   • GR   — group numbers (see GRP)  
   • ALL  — all elements of the chosen type  
   If YMIN ≠ ALL, you must also supply ZMIN, XMAX, YMAX in the form “from to increment.” Default: from=1, to=from, increment=1.

4. Drawing Rules  
   • Kinematic constraints are shown only when all involved nodes belong to visible elements (TYPE WIND). If TYPE CROS is defined, only one visible node is required.  
   • “MOVE … UNIT WC” elements (e.g. additional lines in world coordinates) are clipped to the BOX bounds. This clipping can be disabled with “MOVE … SBOX OFF.”

5. Partial BOXes and Linking (OPER)  
   • You may define up to 8 partial BOXes, each with its own input settings.  
   • All partial BOXes sharing the same group number (item GRP) are first merged in input order.  
   • The resulting BOX groups are then linked together; the link operator is taken from the first partial BOX in each group.  

6. View Settings Snapshot  
   • Each partial BOX “freezes” the current VIEW, PERS, VISI and DEFO settings.  
   • This allows you to blend differently oriented (skewed) views using types BWIN or BCRO.  
   • You may also switch to a completely different VIEW record for the final presentation.  

7. Interaction with GRP, SELE, SEL, VISI  
   • BOX can be used in tandem with GRP to select element groups for windowing.  
   • See SELE/SEL for element selection criteria and VISI for visibility filtering details.

8. Placement on the Sheet  
   • By default, GRAPHIC centers the selected BOX in the viewport.  
   • Offsets can be applied with VXCM (horizontal) and VYCM (vertical):  
     – Positive VXCM → shift to the right  
     – Positive VYCM → shift upward  
   • KREF allows you to anchor a specific node to a fixed sheet position. When KREF is a literal, you can pin the structure to any sheet edge:  
     Layout of KREF codes:  
       +2  +3  +4  
       –1   0  +1  
       –4  –3  –2  
   • VXCM/VYCM then define the offset from that anchor toward the picture center.

Notes: • Use “BOX …” whenever you need focused detail on a subset of your model.  
       • Combine BOX with GRP, SELE and VISI for powerful, precise control over what appears in your drawing.

content:
The table you’ve provided defines a single input parameter for the BOX record—namely BGRP. In the context of “BOX” in this system, you can define up to five “partial” view‐windows (or sub‐boxes) that later get combined into a final drawing window. BGRP is the field that controls how those partial boxes are grouped and subsequently linked. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and how BGRP fits into the larger BOX mechanism.  

1. Item  
   • Name: BGRP  
   • Role: Identifies the group number of the current partial box (sub‐window definition).  

2. Description  
   • Full text: “Group number of the partial box (1…5)”  
   • What it means:  
     – When you issue BOX commands multiple times, each invocation can define its own sub‐region of the model to display (“partial box”).  
     – BGRP assigns that invocation to one of up to five distinct groups, allowing finer control over which sub‐windows are combined first.  

3. Unit  
   • “—” (no physical unit)  
   • Reason: BGRP is an integer index, not a dimensional quantity.  

4. Default  
   • Value: 1  
   • Interpretation:  
     – If you omit BGRP in your BOX record, the system assumes you are defining partial box group #1.  
     – All un‐tagged (default) BOX entries will be treated as members of group 1 until you explicitly change BGRP.  

How BGRP interacts with other BOX parameters and system behavior  
---------------------------------------------------------------  
• Grouping and Linkage (OPER):  
  – Partial boxes with the same BGRP value are merged in the order they appear in the input stream.  
  – After each group’s sub‐boxes are combined, the system then links those group envelopes together to form the overall BOX.  
  – The operator (union, intersection, etc.) used for combining across different BGRP groups is taken from the first partial box of the first group.  

• Maximum of 8 Partial Boxes (across all groups):  
  – You may issue up to eight BOX records in total. These can be spread arbitrarily among the five BGRP values.  
  – This lets you stitch together complex viewing regions by combining multiple simpler boxes.  

• Synchronicity with Other Records:  
  – When you store a partial box (via BOX with BGRP), the system snapshots the current settings of VIEW / PERS / VISI / DEFO.  
  – Later, when the final combined BOX is activated, you can optionally choose which VIEW/PERS/VISI settings apply.  
  – BGRP ensures that each snapshot stays associated with its own sub‐box.  

• Practical Usage Example:  
  1. BOX, BGRP=1, XMIN=…, YMIN=…, XMAX=…, YMAX=…  
  2. BOX, BGRP=1, XMIN=…, YMIN=…, XMAX=…, YMAX=…  
     → These two records define two adjacent sub‐regions that get merged as group #1.  
  3. BOX, BGRP=2, XMIN=…, YMIN=…, XMAX=…, YMAX=…, OPER=‘INTERSECT’  
     → This defines a second group. Once its single sub‐box is set, the system will intersect group #1 envelope with group #2 envelope (using group #2’s OPER setting if desired).  

Why you need BGRP  
-----------------  
Without BGRP you can only define one continuous BOX or force all sub‐boxes into a single sequence. By varying BGRP you gain the ability to modularize the view‐definition process, snapshot different camera/view settings per sub‐region, and then blend those sub‐regions according to logical group operators. In short, BGRP is the key to organizing and linking partial view‐windows when creating complex composite views of your model.

 The selected box is placed in the centre of the picture with GRAPHIC. Using VXCM and VYCM it is possible to move this insertion point relatively (positive values upward or to the right-hand side, negative values downward or to the left-hand side).  ’+2’ ’+3’ ’+4’
 ’-1’ ’0’ ’+1’

content:
The screenshot shows part of the SEL‐record specification for a finite-element post–processing system.  In particular, it documents one input field (ETYP) in a table of “input items” that the user can supply to the SEL record.  Below is a structured, detailed description of that table and its role in the overall selection machinery:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: The name of the input parameter (here “ETYP”).  
     – Description: A human-readable explanation of what the parameter does or what values it can take.  
     – Unit: The data type or unit expected (here “LIT” meaning a literal string).  
     – Default: The default value if the user omits this entry (shown as “–”, meaning “nothing specified,” which in practice equates to “select all elements”).  

2. Purpose of the ETYP Item  
   • ETYP stands for “element type.”  
   • It lets the user restrict the selection to one or more classes of elements in the model (beams, springs, planes, volumes, nodes, cutting lines/texts, etc.).  
   • If ETYP is not given, SEL processes all elements by default.  

3. Legal Values for ETYP (Unit = LIT)  
   The table lists every valid keyword you can give to ETYP, each identifying a different element group.  Below is a condensed enumeration (keyword followed by its meaning):  
   – –  : all elements  
   – BEAM: Beam elements  
   – SPRI: Spring elements  
   – BOUN: Boundary elements  
   – TRUS: Truss elements  
   – CABL: Cable elements  
   – TUBE: Tube elements  
   – QUAD: Plane elements  
   – BRIC: Volume elements  
   – KINE: Kinematic constraints  
   – EDGE: Nodal sequences  
   – SIR : External beam sections  
   – DSLN: Design elements  
   – QTEN: QUAD tendons  
   – BTEN: Beam tendons  
   – GVO : Structural volumes  
   – GAR : Structural areas  
   – GLN : Structural lines  
   – GPT : Structural points  
   – NODE: Nodes  
   – QSEC: Cutting lines  
   – BSEC: Cutting areas  
   – CUT : Cutting pattern  
   – FIXL: Fixed cutting pattern  
   – ADDI: All additional element types  
   – LINE: Additional lines  
   – AREA: Additional areas  
   – TEXT: Additional texts  
   – POST: Position markers  
   – NIVE: Level symbols  
   – CURV: Geometry axes  

4. Interaction with Other SEL Options  
   • A plain SEL record de-activates all elements initially; you then “turn on” the ones you list.  
   • Multiple ETYP keywords can be combined in one SEL record to select several types at once.  
   • You may also invert the selection:  
     – SEL ETYP … TYPE EXCE will switch on all element types except those named.  
   • MODE B appended to SEL ETYP instructs the system to only include those elements whose nodes have been selected by other criteria.  

5. Further Selection Features (for full context)  
   • SEL supports up to 100 separate selection records.  
   • Selections can be logically grouped (SGRP) and combined with Boolean operators (OPER = “AND” or “OR”).  
   • The SEL record may be used in concert with BOX (spatial filtering) and GRP (group-based filtering) for highly complex queries.  

In summary, this table is your master list of element‐type keywords for the SEL record.  By supplying one or more of these LIT values under the ETYP column, you control exactly which elements (beams, volumes, nodes, cutting lines, texts, etc.) are included in your post-processing or graphical output.

The “SEL” table governs how individual model elements are picked for further processing or output. It is part of a family of selection records (see also SELE, BOX, GRP) and lets you build very flexible filters based on element type, numeric attributes, directions, text matches, tolerances and reference copying.  

1.  Table Structure  
    •  Columns  
      –  TYPE: what attribute or element‐type you’re testing (e.g. NO, MAT, CROS, LENG, DIRX/Y/Z, NODE, TEND, etc.)  
      –  VAL1, VAL2, VAL3: numeric or vector values defining search criteria  
      –  TOL: tolerance (numeric or angular)  
      –  REF: a reference element ID from which VAL1–3 (or TOL) may be inherited  
      –  MODE: up to four flags modifying matching logic (case‐sensitivity, whole‐word, direction sign, Boolean behavior)  
    •  Default behavior  
      –  On first use, all existing model elements are deactivated, then the SEL record(s) switch on only those matching your criteria.  
      –  An empty SEL record resets to “no selection,” i.e. all elements again pass through.  

2.  Filtering by TYPE  
    •  TYPE = ETYP  
      –  Only elements of the specified element‐type are switched on.  
      –  To invert, use “ETYP … EXCE” to select all except the listed type(s).  
      –  If MODE contains “B,” then even excluded types are only turned on if they share nodes with selected elements.  
    •  Numeric or text‐based TYPEs  
      –  NO, MAT, CROS, LENG, GLN, GAR, GVO, TEND, NODE, T: treat VAL1–3 as search values or ranges.  
      –  If only VAL1 is set, look for equality (±TOL if given).  
      –  If VAL1 & VAL2 are set, select elements whose attribute lies within [VAL1…VAL2].  
      –  If VAL1, VAL2 & VAL3 are set, perform an incremental search from VAL1 to VAL2 in steps of VAL3.  
      –  TOL defines the allowable deviation (numeric or, for directions, angular in degrees).  
      –  REF allows you to copy VAL1–3 (and optionally TOL) from a previously defined element.  

3.  Directional TYPEs (DIRX, DIRY, DIRZ)  
    •  VAL1–3 represent a global direction vector; TOL the angular tolerance.  
    •  MODE flags “P” or “N” restrict to positive or negative components along that axis (default is both).  

4.  Text‐based matching  
    •  For MAT, CROS, GLN, GAR, GVO, TEND: you may supply a title string in VAL1 (and VAL2/3 unused).  
    •  MODE flags:  
      –  C: case‐sensitive match (default is case‐insensitive)  
      –  W: whole‐word match only (default allows substrings)  

5.  Advanced grouping and logic  
    •  Up to 100 SEL records can be defined in a single job.  
    •  Use SGRP to partition SEL records into groups of your own choosing.  
    •  Within each group, records combine with OPER (default “OR”).  
    •  Between groups, the default logical connector is OPER “AND.”  
    •  SEL, BOX and GRP records can be used concurrently—BOX for geometric bounding, GRP for user‐defined groups, and SEL for attribute‐based filtering.  

In sum, the SEL table is a highly parameterized filter mechanism. By combining TYPE, numeric or vector VALs, tolerances, reference copying, text flags and Boolean logic, you can pinpoint exactly the elements you need for reporting, plotting or exporting.

The table defines the input record SEL, which is used to pick out (“select”) finite‐element entities for further processing.  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and seven primary items (rows).  Below is a detailed description of each item and how SEL works in context with BOX and GRP.  

1.  Item = TYPE  
   •  Description: Specifies the kind of selection to perform.  It drives which elements are switched on (active) or off (inactive).  
   •  Allowed values (LIT):  
     –  “–” : All elements of a given element type ETYP.  
     –  EXCE : All elements except those of type ETYP.  
     –  NO : Explicit element numbers.  
     –  MAT : Materials, for QUAD and BRIC elements.  
     –  CROS : Cross‐section IDs for BEAM, TRUS, CABL, TUBE, SIR.  
     –  LENG : Element or edge lengths (multiple ETYPs).  
     –  DIRX, DIRY, DIRZ : Local coordinate directions x, y, z (many ETYPs).  
     –  GLN : Structural line numbers (BEAM, TRUS, CABL, BOUN).  
     –  GAR : Structural area numbers (QUAD).  
     –  GVO : Structural volume numbers (BRIC).  
     –  TEND : Tendons (BEAM, QUAD).  
     –  NODE : Node numbers.  
     –  T : Thickness (QUAD).  
   •  Unit: LIT (literal).  
   •  Default: none.  

2.  Item = VAL1, VAL2, VAL3  
   •  Description: Numeric inputs whose meaning depends on TYPE.  They can be:  
     – A single value (VAL1 only).  
     – A range (VAL1 to VAL2).  
     – A sequence (VAL1 start, VAL2 end, VAL3 increment).  
     – For DIRX/DIRY/DIRZ: Components of a global direction vector.  
   •  Unit: same unit as TYPE (e.g. meters, degrees, IDs).  
   •  Default: none.  

3.  Item = TOL  
   •  Description: Tolerance for matching numeric criteria.  
     – If > 0: absolute tolerance in the TYPE’s unit.  
     – If < 0: percentage tolerance relative to VAL2–VAL1.  
   •  Unit: same as TYPE.  
   •  Default: none.  

4.  Item = REF  
   •  Description: Reference element number from which VAL1, VAL2, VAL3 may be derived (not used for TYPE NO).  
   •  Unit: —  
   •  Default: —  

5.  Item = MODE  
   •  Description: Special selection flags (up to 4 characters), interpreted per TYPE:  
     – For MAT, CROS, GLN, GAR, GVO: Search by title string (TITL).  
         •  C: Case sensitive (default is case‐insensitive).  
         •  W: Whole‐word match (default is substring).  
     – For DIRX/DIRY/DIRZ: Direction qualifiers:  
         •  P: Only positive direction (default is all).  
         •  N: Only negative direction (default is all).  
   •  Unit: LIT.  
   •  Default: none.  

SEL usage notes and interaction with BOX and GRP:  
 •  On the very first SEL record, all structure elements are deactivated.  Subsequent SEL records then activate only those matching the criteria.  
 •  An empty SEL record (no inputs) turns selection OFF, reverting to the default “all on” behavior.  
 •  Specifying only ETYP in SEL activates only those element types.  Adding EXCE does the inverse.  If MODE = B is added, only elements which also have selected nodes remain on.  
 •  Up to 100 SEL records can define individual selections.  
 •  Records may be grouped via SGRP.  Within each group, criteria are combined with OPER (default OR).  Groups themselves combine with OPER (default AND).  
 •  SEL, BOX, and GRP may be used together to refine selections by geometric region (BOX) or logical grouping (GRP).

The input table defines the record layout and field semantics for the “SEL” (select) command, which controls how individual finite‐element model entities are turned on or off for further processing (for example, in a RAG-based vector store).  It also points out how SEL interacts with the companion records BOX and GRP, and summarizes special selection modes that depend on the TYPE field.

1. General Remarks  
• By default, all “structure” elements are processed; additional elements (LINE, TEXT, QSEC) require explicit SEL records.  
• The very first SEL record you input deactivates everything (a “clear” operation). Subsequent SEL records build or modify the active set.  
• An empty SEL record (no values specified) switches selection back off (i.e., it halts any further selection filtering).  
• A maximum of 100 SEL records can be defined individually. If you need logical grouping you combine selections with SGRP (sub-group) and then specify the logical operator (OPER) within and between groups (default OPER is OR, and GROUP default operator is AND).

2. Field-by-Field Description  
SEL – literal keyword denoting the record type.  
CURV/Geometry Axes/Item – these text labels indicate optional headings or notes in the document but do not correspond to input fields; they distinguish when SEL is being used to select curves, geometry axes, or other items.  
TYPE – the attribute on which to filter.  Common choices include:  
 • NO (element number)  
 • MAT (material ID)  
 • CROS (cross-section ID)  
 • LENG, GLN, GAR, GVO, TEND (various length, angle or geometry measures)  
 • NODE (node number)  
 • T (thickness)  
 • DIRX, DIRY, DIRZ (global direction tests)  
VAL1, VAL2, VAL3 – up to three numeric inputs whose meaning depends on TYPE:  
 • Single‐value search: only VAL1 defined → exact match (within tolerance).  
 • Range search: VAL1 and VAL2 → search for values in [VAL1 … VAL2].  
 • Incremental search: VAL1, VAL2, VAL3 → start=VAL1, stop=VAL2, increment=VAL3.  
 • For directional types (DIRX/Y/Z): VAL1–3 are the vector components, tested within an angular tolerance.  
TOL – tolerance value, interpreted according to TYPE:  
 • Numeric types: absolute tolerance around VAL1 (or range endpoints).  
 • Directional types: angular tolerance in degrees.  
 • Text‐based types (MAT, CROS, GLN, GAR, GVO) ignore TOL.  
REF – reference element number.  Except for TYPE=NO, VAL1–3 may be pulled automatically from the attribute values of element REF (handy for relative or copy‐based selection).  
MODE – up to four characters modifying matching behavior. Common flags:  
 • C (case sensitive) vs. default case-insensitive for textual titles.  
 • W (whole‐word match) vs. substring default.  
 • P or N (for DIRX/Y/Z) to limit only to positive or negative direction components.  
 • A (anchor search) in some implementations.

3. Special Selection Modes Depending on TYPE  
• For TYPE=MAT, CROS, GLN, GAR, GVO: if a textual title (TITL) is supplied, MODE picks up case or whole‐word rules.  
• For DIRX/Y/Z: MODE “P” limits to positive projections along the axis, “N” to negative, default (neither) allows both.

4. Interaction with BOX and GRP  
• BOX (bounding‐box based selection) and GRP (group‐based set definitions) may be interleaved with SEL records.  
• Within a GRP, you can combine multiple SELs by OPER (AND/OR), then combine groups by a higher‐level OPER.  
• This layered logic gives full flexibility to build complex selection sets without resorting to external scripting.

In practice, you begin by clearing the active set with a bare “SEL” or “SEL NO 0” record, then add or subtract subsets by specifying TYPE plus VAL/TOL/REF/MODE, using negative logic (EXCE) if needed, grouping with SGRP, and finally combining with BOX or GRP to achieve the precise filter for post-processing in your RAG vector store.

The table in question defines three key input fields used to govern “partial selections” when invoking the SEL record (selection), and it is designed to work in concert with related records BOX and GRP.  Each field controls how subsets of elements (nodes, lines, text, cross‐sections, etc.) are combined, grouped or designated by title.  Below is a detailed breakdown of the table structure and each parameter:

1. Table Layout  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the name of the input field.  
     – Description: textual explanation of the field’s effect and options.  
     – Unit: the data type or unit (LIT = literal string, “–” = not applicable).  
     – Default: the value assumed if the field is omitted.  

2. Fields  

  A. OPER (Linkage Operator for Partial Selections)  
     • Unit: LIT  
     • Default: “*” (all elements)  
     • Purpose: defines the logical combination (“linkage”) of multiple partial selections when more than one selection record or group is active.  
     • Valid Values and Effects:  
       – NO  
         · “Does not use this partial selection.”  
         · Any elements activated by this particular partial selection are ignored in the final set.  
       – AND  
         · “Does use only the elements which are activated in the combined partial selections.”  
         · Only those elements common to every partial selection involved are retained.  
       – OR  
         · “Does use all elements which are activated in one or more of the combined partial selections.”  
         · Union of all individual selections.  
       – –AND (minus-AND)  
         · “As AND, however, all elements are activated (the elements activated with the partial selection are deactivated).”  
         · Inverts the result of a standard AND: selects everything except the intersection.  
       – –OR (minus-OR)  
         · “As OR, however, with the inverted elements.”  
         · Selects everything except the union.  

  B. SGRP (Group Number of the Partial Selection)  
     • Unit: –  
     • Default: 1  
     • Purpose: assigns each partial selection to one of up to 32 groups (1…32).  
     • Behavior:  
       – Within a group, multiple partial‐selection records are combined by their OPER setting (default OPER = OR).  
       – Different groups themselves are combined via OPER (default = AND for the first group, as if each group’s result is AND’ed with the next).  
       – Using SGRP you can build complex logical structures by grouping and linking selections hierarchically.  

  C. TITL (Selection via Title or Designation)  
     • Unit: LIT  
     • Default: “–” (none)  
     • Purpose: restricts the selection by matching an element’s title or designation string.  
     • Applicable only for certain types:  
       – TYPE MAT, CROS, GLN, GAR, GVO  
       – ETYP GPT, GLN, GAR, GVO  
     • Matching Modes (in MODE field of SEL):  
       – C: case‐sensitive (default is case‐insensitive)  
       – W: whole‐word only (default allows substrings)  
       – The title to match is supplied in this TITL field.  

3. Context & Cross-References  
   • These inputs augment the primary SEL record, where items such as TYPE, VAL1/2/3, TOL, REF and MODE define numeric and geometric filtering.  
   • The BOX record can further restrict selections to elements inside or outside a specified geometric box.  
   • The GRP record sets up grouping rules that may mirror or complement SGRP usage.  
   • Up to 100 total selection records (across SEL, BOX, GRP) may be combined for highly customized filtering.  

In practice, you would use OPER to define how this particular SEL invocation merges with others, SGRP to assign it to a logical subgroup, and TITL to narrow the scope by matching element titles—together enabling precise, multi-stage selection strategies.

Below is a structured, human‐readable description of the VIEW input table. It explains each column, the valid keywords (items), and the semantic role of their associated fields. Use this summary when ingesting VIEW records into a RAG‐style vector store.

1. Overall Purpose  
   • VIEW defines a parallel (or optionally perspective) projection of a 3D model onto the drawing sheet.  
   • It controls the observer’s position, the line of vision, axonometric angles, axis-scale reductions, or a full 3×3 transformation matrix.  
   • Defaults may be chosen automatically based on model extents or overridden by explicit keywords.  

2. Table Columns  
   • Item   
     – The literal keyword to appear in the VIEW command (e.g. STAN, DIRE, ANGL, SCAL, TRAN, DEFA, etc.)  
   • TYPE  
     – Classifies how the subsequent numeric or reference fields are interpreted.  
   • X, Y, Z  
     – Numeric entries whose meaning depends on TYPE. They may form a 3-vector (direction or point), three angles, scale factors, or matrix elements.  
   • AXIS  
     – Specifies which coordinate axis is aligned toward the bottom of the picture (for STAN, DIRE, SCAL) or which matrix row/column is being set (for TRAN).  

3. Primary VIEW Modes  
   1. STAN (standpoint)  
      • TYPE = STAN  
      • X, Y, Z = coordinates of a far‐away observer position “in front” of the origin.  
      • AXIS = which axis (POSX, NEGX, POSY, NEGY, POSZ, NEGZ) points downward on the page.  
      • Effect: A parallel projection looking toward the origin from (X,Y,Z).  
   2. DIRE (direction)  
      • TYPE = DIRE  
      • X, Y, Z = components of the line-of-sight vector from the origin.  
      • AXIS = same set of axis-orientation literals as STAN.  
      • Effect: Observer at infinity looking along the direction (X,Y,Z).  
   3. ANGL (axonometry angles)  
      • TYPE = ANGL  
      • X, Y, Z = rotation angles (degrees) of each model axis relative to horizontal.  
      • AXIS is not used.  
      • Warning: Certain angle combinations degenerate into edge-on or ambiguous views.  
   4. SCAL (scale reduction)  
      • TYPE = SCAL  
      • X, Y, Z = axis reduction factors (can be two or three values). Positive means axis points away from viewer; negative toward.  
      • AXIS = same axis-orientation literals.  
      • If only two values are given, they are normalized (largest = 1) and the third is computed by quadratic normalization.  
   5. TRAN (transformation)  
      • TYPE = TRAN  
      • X, Y, Z = values to directly populate one row or column of the 3×3 transformation matrix.  
      • AXIS = selects which matrix line (POSX/NEGX for row 1, POSY/NEGY for row 2, others for row 3) and which column to fill.  
   6. DEFA (default)  
      • TYPE = DEFA  
      • No X, Y, Z required.  
      • AXIS = selects one of a set of predefined dead-load or geometric orientations (EG3, –EG3, EGX, –EGX, EGY, –EGY, EGZ, –EGZ, EGXY, EGXZ, EGYZ, YZ, ZX, XY, –ZY, –XZ, –YX, ZY, XZ, YX, –YZ, –ZX, –XY).  
      • Effect: Automatically position observer according to the smallest model extent, place the largest axis to the right, z-axis downward.  

4. Axis-Orientation Literals  
   After specifying STAN, DIRE or SCAL, you must pick exactly one of:  
   • POSX, POSY, POSZ  → positive X, Y or Z axis points down the page  
   • NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ  → negative X, Y or Z axis points down the page  

5. Special Keywords  
   • ALTE  
     – TYPE = ALTE  
     – Rotates the chosen view by 180° about the view direction.  
   • QUAD, BEAM, DSLN, GLN, GAR, ...  
     – Reference entities (area, beam, line, etc.) for which an element-local transform may override the global VIEW.  

Usage Notes  
• STAN and DIRE define parallel projections; PERS controls perspective separately.  
• ANGL and SCAL can be combined, but beware of degenerate axis alignments.  
• TRAN gives full freedom but requires careful row/column bookkeeping.  
• DEFA is the simplest—let the system pick a “nice” default view.

Below is a breakdown of the “VIEW” input-table, which drives the parallel or perspective projection in GRAPHIC.  It lists each parameter (Item), what it does, its allowed values/units, and its default when omitted.  (See also SELE, PERS.)

1. Table structure  
   • Item – the parameter name you supply on the VIEW command.  
   • Description – what that parameter controls.  
   • Unit – physical units, if applicable.  
   • Default – the value assumed if you do not specify this parameter.  

2. Core parameters (Item)  
   A. TYPE  
     – Description: selects the kind of viewing definition.  Must be one of:  
       • STAN – “standard” point-of-view; observer at (X,Y,Z) looks toward the origin.  
       • DIRE – parallel line of vision; the vector (X,Y,Z) is the view direction from origin.  
       • ANGL – axonometric angles; X, Y, Z are rotations (in degrees) of each axis relative to the horizontal.  
       • SCAL – axis scale‐factors; the relative reductions along X:Y:Z (condensed or stretched diagrams).  
       • TRAN – direct input of the 3×3 transformation matrix; you must then specify individual matrix lines via the AXIS item.  
       • DEFA – resets to the default view, chosen automatically from model extents and dead-load direction.  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: DEFA  

   B. X, Y, Z  
     – Description: their meaning depends on TYPE:  
       • For STAN or DIRE, these are spatial coordinates of the “look point” or direction vector.  
       • For ANGL, they are rotation angles in degrees around the X, Y and Z axes.  
       • For SCAL, they are the numerical scale factors (can be positive or negative to indicate “away from” or “toward” the observer).  
       – Unit:  
         • STAN/DIRE: model length units  
         • ANGL: degree  
         • SCAL: dimensionless ratio  
       – Default: 0 for ANGL; 1:1:1 for SCAL  

   C. AXIS  
     – Description: for STAN, DIRE or SCAL types, defines which coordinate axis is drawn “downwards” on the sheet.  Choose one of:  
       • POSX, POSY, POSZ – positive X, Y or Z axis points down.  
       • NEGX, NEGY, NEGZ – negative X, Y or Z axis points down.  
     – Unit: n/a  
     – Default: POSZ  

3. Matrix override (when TYPE=TRAN)  
   – You may enter each of the three matrix rows directly.  Specify AXIS=POSX or NEGX for the first row, POSY/NEGY for the second, or one of the other AXIS literals for the third.  The X, Y, Z fields then fill or modify that row of the 3×3 transformation matrix.

4. Additional rotation  
   Item: ROTA  
     – Description: an extra image rotation in the sheet-plane, applied after all other transforms.  Positive values rotate clockwise.  
     – Unit: degree  
     – Default: 0°  

5. Usage notes  
   • If you supply only two SCAL values, GRAPHIC normalizes them to the larger one and computes the third by quadratic normalization, allowing quick shorthand (e.g. “X 1 Y 4” ⇒ Z = √(1²+4²) to maintain equal-length axes in 3D).  
   • ANGL inputs must avoid “degenerate” cases (two axes vertical or parallel to the projection plane), which yield ambiguous or collapsed views.  
   • DEFA inspects your model’s bounding-box extents: the smallest-extent axis becomes the view direction, the largest-extent axis is drawn to the right, and Z is downwards if the structure is significantly 3D.

This table gives you full control over how GRAPHIC constructs the projection and orientation of your structural drawings, whether you need standard orthogonal views, custom axonometries, scaled condensations or even perspectively distorted projections.

The table summarizes the parameters of the “A” (perspective) record, which is used—together with SELE and VIEW—to switch between parallel, central‐perspective and cylindrical projections in the graphics kernel. Each row of the table corresponds to one field in the record; columns give the mnemonic, its meaning, the expected unit, and its default value.

1. A  (Set perspective)  
   • Description: Controls whether and how a perspective projection is applied.  
     – value: a positive real number (distance A) giving the observer’s distance from the focal point.  
     – OFF: disables all perspective; use pure parallel projection.  
     – ON: re-enable perspective using the last stored distance and angle.  
     – INFI: infinite observer distance → pure parallel projection (same as OFF, but preserves the “perspective on” flag).  
   • Unit: LIT/m (length‐unit per metre; effectively a dimensionless scale factor when LIT=m).  
   • Default: “!” (this special code forces an error or user prompt if A is not explicitly set on first use).

2. BX, BY, BZ  (Coordinates of the focal point)  
   • Description: three real numbers specifying the position of the focal point in model coordinates. The focal point lies on the optical plane and defines the origin of the central‐perspective optical axis. It may also be used to set the “depth of focus” reference for a parallel projection (making it exact in one plane).  
   • Units: m (metres in model space).  
   • Defaults: 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 (all three default to the model‐space origin).

3. ANGL  (Visual angle for perspective)  
   • Description: defines the field of view (half‐angle between the optical axis and the edge rays) when perspective is on. Only points whose direction from the observer makes an angle ≤ ANGL with the axis will be projected; others are effectively clipped or sent to infinity.  
   • Numeric mode: a real number between 0 and π/2 (radians) or its equivalent in length units per metre (LIT/–).  
   • Keyword modes: use one of the following to invoke non‐standard projections in lieu of numeric half‐angle:  
     – CYL  : cylindrical projection (optical plane is the developed surface of a vertical‐axis cylinder of radius A; observer stands at the cylinder axis)  
     – CYLD : developed cylinder view (same as CYL, but “unwrapped” into a planar layout)  
     – SPH  : spherical projection (optical plane = sphere)  
     – SPHD : developed spherical view (unwrapped sphere)  
   • Default: 99  (numeric sentinel prompting the system to treat ANGL as “not yet set” and issue an error if perspective is used without adjustment).

How it all fits together:  
– To request a central perspective, set A to a finite positive value, place the focal point via BX/BY/BZ, and choose ANGL either as a real half‐angle or one of the CYL/SPH keywords for specialized map‐like projections.  
– To revert to parallel projection, either set A=INFI (or A=OFF) or choose ANGL=0.  
– All three coordinates and angle must be consistent with the VIEW record, which defines the observer’s line of sight direction.

Therefore it is suitable for a three-dimensional representation including all results without limit. However, a projection, the central perspective, is wanted sometimes, which is more adequate to the human eye.  1. Central Perspective
 The central perspective is defined with a observer standpoint (camera) in a finite area, a projection centre in the optical plane (focal point) and a visual angle.
 The horizontal and vertical position of the observer due to his standpoint in the infinity is irrel- evant for the parallel projection. On the other hand the observer moves to a finite distance to the object for a perspective representation. Therefore not only his distance but also his relative position to the object are important. The line of vision was defined in record VIEW.
 The focal point is the point which lies both in the optical plane and in the optical axis of the illustration. The focal point can be used also for the depth of focus of a parallel projection. The illustration is length- and angle-precise in the focal point.
 The observer is the point at the optical axis with a distance A from the focal point. The vector focal point to observer point has the absolute value A and the direction defined with the record VIEW.
 The observer can see principally only the things in his line of vision in case of the per- spective representation. A visual angle must be introduced because the points which are exactly next to the observer are projected to the infinity. The observer can see only points which lie to the optical axis within a tangential angle which is smaller than ANGL. The following table describes values for ANGL in the comparison to the lens focal length of a miniature camera:
 0.643 correspond to 28 mm (wide angle)

A visual angle must be introduced because the points which are exactly next to the observer are projected to the infinity. The observer can see only points which lie to the optical axis within a tangential angle which is smaller than ANGL. The following table describes values for ANGL in the comparison to the lens focal length of a miniature camera:. 0.643 correspond to 28 mm (wide angle).
 0.360 correspond to 50 mm (normal)
 0.144 correspond to 125 mm (tele)
 2. Cylinder Projection
 One can receive a very special illustration if the literal CYL is defined for ANGL. Then the optical plane is the developed view of a cylinder with a vertical axis which contains the focal point at the cylinder surface. The radius of the cylinder is A. Thus the observer stands at the axis of the cylinder.
 It can result in smaller inaccuracies in the representation of hidden lines, because this illustra- tion is not length-precise and all lines are drawn, however, as straight parts.

Below is a structured, item-by-item description of the table you provided. It is written so that each table entry (Item) is clearly defined, its parameters and defaults are explained, and the relationship to the surrounding VISI documentation is noted. 

1. Overall Table Structure  
   • Four main parameter blocks are defined: HIDD, DMAX, DMIN and DREL.  
   • Columns in the table:  
     – Item: the keyword used in input or command files.  
     – Description: explanation of the parameter and its sub-options.  
     – Unit: the data type or measurement unit expected.  
     – Default: the built-in value when the user does not override it.  

2. HIDD – Omission of Hidden Lines  
   • Purpose: Controls whether hidden edges or lines are drawn in three-dimensional representations (both perspective and parallel). By default hidden lines are included (“NO”). In the VISI context, selecting HIDD=NO corresponds to “HIDDEN NO” in the VISI manual, meaning all lines (even those behind surfaces) appear.  
   • Sub-options (literal values – LIT):  
     – NO   : do not omit hidden lines (default).  
     – NODE : use the “node-dependent” method (fastest).  The algorithm checks visibility on a per-node basis, drawing only those elements whose nodes are visible. It cannot handle partial occlusion of edges.  
     – LINE : use the “line-dependent” or classical hidden-line method.  Edges are tested individually, leading to more accurate visibility handling, but still limited by its lack of area-based occlusion checks.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: NO  

3. DMAX – Depth of Focus, Maximum  
   • Purpose: Sets an upper distance cut-off (farthest depth) relative to the optical plane. Anything behind the DMAX plane will be clipped (not displayed).  
   • Special literal: OFF – disables the maximum depth limit (no clipping on the far side).  
   • Unit: meters (m) – the distance is measured along the viewing direction.  
   • Default value: “–” (meaning the user must explicitly set it if desired; otherwise DMAX remains at its default internal value of +1.0E12 from the VISI documentation).  

4. DMIN – Depth of Focus, Minimum  
   • Purpose: Sets a lower distance cut-off (closest depth) relative to the optical plane. Anything in front of the DMIN plane (toward the observer) will be clipped.  
   • Special literal: OFF – disables the minimum depth limit (no clipping near the observer).  
   • Unit: meters (m)  
   • Default value: “–” (internally defaulted in VISI to the negative of the observer’s distance from the projection point for perspective views, or –1.0E12 for parallel projections).  

5. DREL – Input of Depth Mode  
   • Purpose: Determines whether the numerical values for DMIN/DMAX are taken as absolute scene coordinates, or as values relative to the current observer’s position (the optical plane).  
   • Sub-options (literal values – LIT):  
     – YES  : interpret DMIN/DMAX distances relative to the observer’s stand-point (recommended default).  
     – NO   : interpret DMIN/DMAX as absolute coordinates in the model’s reference system.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal keyword)  
   • Default: YES  

Additional Context from VISI Documentation  
• “See also: SELE, GRP, BOX” – these keywords in VISI control selection filters, grouping of elements, and bounding-box clipping respectively, and can be combined with HIDD/DMIN/DMAX to refine rendering.  
• The VISI system allows two principal hidden-line methods (NODE vs. LINE) with different accuracy/performance trade-offs.  
• By adjusting DMIN and DMAX (and choosing DREL=YES or NO), users can create sectional cut-views or focus on particular depth ranges in both perspective and parallel projections.

The image is a schematic side-view illustrating how the “depth of focus” (or viewing frustum limits) is defined in a simple one-dimensional sense along the optical axis.  It is labeled “Figure 3.10: Depth of the focus” at the bottom.

1. Observer symbol  
   • On the far left there is a stylized “observer” icon—an arrowhead or triangular eye-shape pointing to the right—indicating the viewer’s eye or camera position.  

2. Line of sight  
   • A horizontal dashed line (– – –) extends from the observer toward the right.  This represents the center line of sight or the optical axis.  

3. DMIN plane  
   • Partway between the observer and the optical plane stands a vertical dashed line, labeled “DMIN.”  
   • An arrow immediately to the right of the “DMIN” label points back toward the observer, indicating that negative DMIN values lie in front of the optical plane (i.e., between the viewer and that plane).  

4. Visible area  
   • The region between the DMIN plane (left dashed line) and the optical plane (right solid line) is annotated “Visible area.”  Only geometry whose nodal points fall within this interval will be rendered or displayed.  

5. Optical plane  
   • A solid vertical line on the right is labeled “Optical.”  It represents the plane of focus or the reference plane in the projection.  
   • Immediately above this line is a small “+” sign; above that, a short vertical tick.  These denote positive depth values behind the optical plane.  
   • Symmetrically below the optical plane’s intersection with the sight line is another short tick (and, just below, a small “⊕” circle marking the exact intersection point).  

6. Depth sign conventions  
   • To the right of the optical plane, depths are positive (“+”), meaning behind the plane, out into the scene.  
   • Between the observer and the optical plane, depths are negative (“–”), in front of the focus plane.  
   • By default, DMAX (the far‐clipping limit) is +1·E12 and DMIN (the near‐clipping limit) is set to the negative of the observer–plane distance in perspective mode (–1·E12 in parallel mode), though the user may override both.  

Context (from accompanying text):  
• Hidden‐line removal in 3D plots can be controlled either by the “1st NODE” approach (fast but coarse) or the “2nd LINE” classical edge‐based method (more precise but slower).  
• Limiting DMIN and DMAX restricts which portions of the 3D model are actually rendered, slicing away geometry in front of DMIN or beyond DMAX.  

See also references in the manual: SELE, GRP, BOX, VISI for related selection, grouping, box‐clipping, and visibility controls.

See also: SELE, GRP, BOX
 VISI
 All lines are represented normally including hidden lines which lie behind a QUAD or BRIC area in a three–dimensional representation (HIDD NO). An exception is the BRIC surface. It omits all BRIC areas which lie behind the observer.
 However, it is possible not to draw parts of the system for all representations, also for perspec- tive or parallel projections. For this two variants are possible.
 The representation of hidden lines can be prevented in case of three–dimensional plots. For this purpose two methods whose CPU time increases for the refined representation possibilities are available.
 1st NODE
 The method examines all nodes, whether they are covered from areas. Then only these elements or their results are drawn whose nodes are visible. This method is very fast. However, it can not realize partial not visible or hidden lines.
 2nd LINE
 This method is the classical hidden–line method. It can not distinguish, whether an element area is covered, because it works edge related. Therefore the results are represented in all elements which are visible according to the first method.
 2nd Depth of the focus
 The represented area behind (DMAX) and in front of the optical plane (DMIN) can be limited in the direction of the observer for all representations. The default for DMAX is +1.E12.
 The default for DMIN is equal to the negative distance of the observer from the picture point for perspective representation. In the case of parallel projection it is -1.E12.
 The user can define the values DMIN and DMAX arbitrarily (even behind the observer). How- ever, the positive values refer always to the area behind the optical plane and the negative values refer to the area in front of it.

Below is a consolidated description of the DEFO input table (used by the STRU record to control deformed‐structure output). It explains each field, its valid keywords or numeric ranges, default behavior and units, and how DEFO interacts with other records.

1. DEFO record purpose  
   • When you issue DEFO, all subsequent drawing records (for example STRU) use the deformed geometry rather than the undeformed model.  
   • The new node coordinates are computed by adding a scaled “offset‐for‐shift” to the original coordinates.  
   • No drawing is produced if you only issue DEFO; you must follow it with a drawing record such as STRU.

2. Field definitions  
   a) TYPE (select exactly one):  
     – NO: do not display any deformation (turns off prior DEFO)  
     – YES: use nodal displacements of the load case specified by LC  
     – lc–no (integer): use nodal displacements of load case number lc–no  
     – POT: use HYDRA potential values (instead of z‐coordinate)  
     – FREE: generate free‐surface through BRIC elements (creates holes where surface intersects BRIC)  
     – FRGL: same as FREE, but displace only surface nodes by their potential peaks  
     – MXX, MYY, MZZ, VXX, VYY, NXX, NXY, etc.: add local‐z‐axis internal moments (M…), shear forces (V…) or membrane forces (N…) at each node; STRU then draws contour areas  

   b) GAR / GARB:  
     – Project and display the QUAD structural area defined by the last FAKV area selection  
     – GAR uses a simple projection; GARB builds a bounding box around the area  
     – A negative FAKV value overrides SEL/BOX and selects only elements in that area  

   c) GVO / GVOB:  
     – 3D view of the BRIC structural volume defined by FAKV  
     – GVO uses direct element selection; GVOB builds a bounding box  
     – Negative FAKV behaves like a standalone SEL  

   d) FAKV (real):  
     – Magnification factor for TYPE=YES, POT, MXX…, GAR/GVO, etc.  
     – Default (“DEFA”) = 1/10 of the maximum structure length  
     – Can be set explicitly or by the keyword DEFA  

   e) LC (integer or CURR):  
     – If numeric, selects that load case for deformation or potential  
     – If CURR, uses the current load case as last defined by LC in a prior record  

   f) T (real or CURR):  
     – Time‐step for dynamic or hydraulic free‐surface plots  
     – CURR picks up the current time step from the last LC record  

3. Units and defaults  
   • Displacements, potentials, forces etc. are plotted in model length units; time (T) in seconds.  
   • Default for TYPE is NO (no deformation).  
   • Default FAKV = DEFA = 0.1 × structure length.  
   • CURR for LC or T follows this resolution order:  
     1) DEFO‐specified load case  
     2) Current load/result case  
     3) Load case from group controls  

4. How the “offset‐for‐shift” is generated  
   1) Deformed shape (displacements or eigen‐mode): nodal offsets = input TYPE × computed displacement  
   2) Potential surfaces (HYDRA): z = potential; FREE/FRGL displace only surface nodes  
   3) Internal forces/moments: nodal offsets = TYPE value × force or moment  

5. Interaction notes  
   • A DEFO NO resets to undeformed display.  
   • Always follow DEFO with a drawing command (e.g., STRU).  
   • DEFO GAR/GVO override any prior SEL or BOX definitions.  
   • System‐movement cases (SMOV) can be added by specifying SMOV in place of TYPE; these use the incremental system‐movement load case.  

By configuring DEFO with the appropriate TYPE, FAKV, LC and T, you control how and which result fields are visualized in subsequent STRU contour and deformed‐shape plots.

The table below defines two optional keywords you can use with the DEFO record to control secondary effects on your deformed‐structure plots.  In each case the columns mean:

• Item  
  – The keyword you supply in your DEFO card.  
• Description  
  – A brief summary of what that keyword does and, where relevant, the legal values you can specify.  
• Unit  
  – The physical units or dimension of the input.  A dash (–) means “unitless.”  
• Default  
  – The value assumed if you omit this keyword from your DEFO entry.

  
1) EXPO  
   • Description  
     – “Explosion factor” for two purposes:  
       a) When you draw two‐dimensional cutting patterns via STRU (e.g. using NUME ZS2…), EXPO separates cut pieces by a uniform gap.  This makes it easier to view individual fragments of a plate or shell pattern.  
       b) When you display bore profiles or drilling paths, EXPO introduces spacing between adjacent bore lines.  
     – You supply a nonnegative scalar; the code multiplies all in‐plane distances (or cut‐piece offsets) by this factor.  
   • Unit  
     – None (–).  It is a pure magnification/gap factor.  
   • Default  
     – 0.0.  With EXPO = 0 the pieces or lines remain exactly in their original positions (no “explosion” gap).  

   Usage note:  A small positive EXPO (for example 0.1 or 0.2) can greatly improve readability on dense pattern plots.  Larger values will exaggerate the gaps and may distort your sense of overall geometry.  

2) SMOV  
   • Description  
     – Controls “system movement” loading (for example, incremental launching of a bridge deck or other staged‐construction sequence).  The nodal coordinates of your deformed mesh are shifted by the displacements from one of three sources:  
       – NO  
         Do not show any system‐movement case.  Only the standard DEFO displacements (if any) will be applied.  
       – CURR  
         Take the displacements from the current load case.  “Current” here follows the priority rules for LC:  
         1) the load case you explicitly assigned to DEFO (if any),  
         2) the active load case or result set,  
         3) any group‐control load case in effect.  
       – > 0  
         A positive integer referring to a specific system‐movement load case number.  The code reads the nodal displacements from that numbered LC and adds them to the node coordinates.  
   • Unit  
     – None (–).  You either name a literal (NO or CURR) or supply an integer.  
   • Default  
     – “*” (an asterisk).  This tells the program to fall back to CURR behavior (i.e. use the current load case) unless you override it.  

   Usage note:  When simulating staged erection or incremental launching, it is often essential to combine both the ordinary deformation load case (e.g. wind, dead load) with the system‐movement case.  By specifying SMOV you automatically superimpose those staged‐displacements on top of your regular DEFO visualization.  

See also the STRU record (structure plot) to control the graphical output of both cut‐piece layouts (using EXPO) and plate‐force areas or moment contours.

 DEFO

DEFO GAR and a negative FAKV set a single selection like SEL including all QUAD elements belonging to this area. DEFO GARB creates a surrounding BOX. Inputs for SEL and BOX, defined before DEFO, will overwritten.
 With the input DEFO GVO or GVOB it is possible to define a 3D view of a structural volume defined via FAKV. A positive input of FAKV is not changed the current selection defined with SEL and BOX. DEFO GVO and a negative FAKV set a single selection like SEL including all BRIC elements belonging to this volume. DEFO GVOB creates a surrounding BOX. Inputs for SEL and BOX, defined before DEFO, will overwritten.

Then the displacements of this load case are added to the node coordinates. When using CURR the current load case is determined by this following order:. 1st Load case of deformed structure.
