See also: MOVE, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE, CURV, AXIS
 The user can produce own texts or lines at any position in the drawing additionally to the output generated by the program. The records MOVE, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE and CURV as well as AXIS are used for this purpose.
 These additional elements are stored with their group number, so that they do not have to be repeated continuously. They can be activated or deactivated via their group numbers. The number of the additional outputs is not limited.
 All additional elements can be deactivated (NO) or activated (FULL) summary with an input GRP ADDI. The default (YES) activates in each case the additional elements of the active groups.
 BRIC sections can be deactivated with an input GRP BSEC NO (= default) and activated with an input GRP BSEC YES.
 All outputs defined with MOVE, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE, CURV or AXIS are repeated in all drawings until a new input of these records occurs. The properties of the additional element defined via DTYP in record MOVE can be changed. The first MOVE record after a drawing deletes the additional elements of the current group (defined at last). This can be prevented with an input of the literal NDEL at X in the record MOVE. The additional elements of a type can be deleted explicitly with DEL. A MOVE record without further items (that means "MOVE ") deletes all additional outputs of the groups switched on with GRP record.
 All additional elements are switched off at the beginning. The additional outputs are activated with an input YES or FULL for ADDI in the record GRUP or through an input of an additional element (MOVE, DRAW...).

The screenshot you provided is the parameter‐table for a “MOVE” (or positioning) command in a CAD/drafting environment.  It defines how text or other auxiliary elements are placed, in which coordinate system, with what orientation and size, and with a set of keywords for special behaviors (deleting or importing existing elements, cutting patterns, etc.).  Below is a structured, row-by-row description of that table, plus a summary of the related “BOX/ON/GRNO/DTYP…” and “ADJU” contexts which your extra text references.

1. Table Columns  
   • Item – the parameter name you supply to MOVE.  
   • Description – what it controls.  
   • Unit – allowed units, or type of input.  
   • Default – value assumed if you omit the parameter.

2. Core Parameters (Rows)

  • X  
    – Coordinates of the insertion (start) point along the X-axis.  
    – Special keywords in place of a number:  
       · DEL  – delete all existing additional elements of the type given in DTYP.  
       · NDEL – do not delete those elements.  
       · IMPO – import cutting‐pattern lines stored in the database.  
    – Unit: LIT (logical unit in drawing), cm or % of picture area.  
    – Default: “*” – no default; you must supply it.

  • Y  
    – Y-coordinate of the same insertion point.  
    – Unit: m, cm or % of picture area.  
    – Default: 0

  • Z  
    – Z-coordinate (useful in 3D or plan/elevation contexts).  
    – Unit: m, cm or %.  
    – Default: 0

  • REF  
    – Specifies an alternate origin node number for the (X,Y,Z) coordinates.  
    – Unit: none.  
    – Default: “–” (no reference node).

  • UNIT  
    – Selects the coordinate system in which X,Y,Z are interpreted.  
    – Options (all under a “LIT” type):  
       · WC  – world (system) coordinates  
       · CM  – inner-window drawing coords in cm (X to right, Y up, origin at lower left)  
       · IN  – same as CM but in inches  
       · PL  – plan view clipped or lifted at BOX limits (e.g. axes grid), else like WC  
       · PLF – plan clipped at BOX only (e.g. main bridge axis), else like WC  
       · PR  – drawing coords in percent of picture area (directions as CM)  
       · PRWC – percent of selection box in system coords  
       · PRB – percent of selection box in picture coords  
    – Default: WC

  • A  
    – Angle to rotate text relative to the horizontal.  
    – Unit: degree  
    – Default: 0°

  • SCHH  
    – Height (size) of the text.  
    – Unit: cm  
    – Default: 0.16 cm

  • FACW  
    – Width factor for text (stretches or compresses horizontally).  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: 0.7

3. Related “BOX / ON / GRNO / DTYP…” Context  
   Before you call MOVE you can set additional flags via separate keywords:  
   – BOX / ON  – constrain text insertion to the system box boundaries, or override it.  
   – GRNO  – assign a group number to new elements.  
   – DTYP – type of auxiliary element you’re adding; values include LINE, AREA, QSEC (cutting line through plane), BSEC (cutting through volumes), CUT (pattern line), FIXL (fixed cut), TEXT, POST (positioning symbol), NIVE (level symbol), CURV (geometry axis), SIR (external-beam section), DIML (dimension lines), AXIS (system axis).  

   Placements read from database via PXLA (center lane), PSEC (secondary axis), DISZ (distance for multiline TEXT).

4. “ADJU” Table for Cutting-Line Adjustment  
   The ADJU parameter governs how cutting lines (plane elements) are adjusted or coupled:  
   – DEFA – default local X-direction; polygonal cuts follow SERI, single cuts GLOB  
   – SERI – couple all cuts together  
   – SEPA – break polygonal cuts into individual lines  
   – GLOB – align cuts to a global direction  
   – NO – no adjustment; point‐order defines direction  
   – POLY – only polygonal cuts coupled; single remain independent  
   – SING – only single cuts aligned globally  
   – CONN, CSRI, CGLB, CNO, CPOL, CSNG  – like the above but allow end-to-end connection  
   – +X…–Z or +GX…–GZ or +EX…–EZ  – force a specific axis (local, global, or single-cut)  

Summary  
This table is the heart of the MOVE command: you feed in a starting point (X,Y,Z), optionally reference an existing node, choose your coordinate frame, then set text orientation and sizing.  Combined with the BOX/ON/GRNO/DTYP and ADJU controls, you gain fine‐grained management over deletion/import of existing elements, cutting‐pattern placement, and the coupling or separation of those cuts.

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
Below is a structured, narrative description of the two related parameter tables that control how additional graphic elements (text, cutting lines, axes, etc.) are moved or adjusted in a CAD-style drawing environment. This summary is suitable for indexing in a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) vector store.

1. TABLE CONTEXT  
   • Command Group: MOVE (used in DRAW routines when placing or shifting additional elements such as TEXT, POST symbols, NIVE levels or AXIS lines).  
   • Related Modules: Information, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE, AXIS.  

2. PRIMARY PARAMETERS (Columns: Item, Description, Unit, Default)  

   A) BOX  
     – Describes the maximum allowable offset of a text insertion point from the boundary of its system box.  
     – Unit: can be specified in centimeters (positive values) or as a percentage of the picture area (zero or negative values).  
     – Default: OFF.  

   B) OFF  
     – When BOX = OFF, the text insertion point will be clipped to the system box; no extra offset is applied.  
     – Behavior:  
       • If BOX > 0, that is the offset in cm.  
       • If BOX ≤ 0, the absolute value is interpreted as % of the drawing area.  

   C) GRNO  
     – Group number to which the additional element is assigned.  
     – Unit: none (“–”).  
     – Default: 0.  

   D) DTYP (“Type of the additional element”)  
     – Unit: LT (list type).  
     – Default: “–” denoting “all element types.”  
     – Enumerated types:  
       • LINE: simple lines  
       • AREA: filled or hatched regions  
       • QSEC: cutting line through planar elements  
       • BSEC: cutting area through volume elements  
       • CUT: generic cutting-pattern line  
       • FIXL: fixed cutting-pattern line  
       • TEXT: any additional text labels  
       • POST: positioning symbol  
       • NIVE: level-level symbol  
       • CURV: geometry axis  
       • SIR: external beam sections  
       • DIML: dimensional lines  
       • AXIS: system axis  
     – Axis-specific options (read from database): AXST, AXLA, AXGE, ASEC, AXTE, AINT, SOFIMSHC, AXUN  
     – Placement codes (from database): PXLA, PSEC  

   E) DISZ  
     – Distance for multiline TEXT objects.  
     – Unit: none (scalar).  
     – Default: 1.3.  
     – Constraint: must be > 0; always checked regardless of UNIT.  

3. ADJUSTMENT OF CUTTING LINES (ADJU Table)  

   Purpose: govern how cutting-pattern lines through planar elements are coupled, oriented, and connected.  
   Unit: none. Default: DEFA.  

   A) Modes of coupling and orientation  
     • DEFA: default local X-direction; cuts are not connected.  
     • SERI: polygonal cuts are chained together.  
     • SEPA: polygonal cuts are separated into individual segments.  
     • GLOB: all cuts are aligned to a global reference direction.  
     • NO: cuts follow the input point sequence; no global or coupling adjustment.  
     • POLY: only polygonal cuts are paired; single cuts left unchanged.  
     • SING: only single cuts are aligned globally; polygonal cuts unchanged.  

   B) “Connected” variants  
     These options mirror DEFA, SERI, GLOB, NO, POLY and SING but allow geometry to be connected end-to-end: CONN, CSRI, CGLB, CNO, CPOL, CSNG.  

   C) Explicit global directions  
     • +X … –Z: explicit local axes directions  
     • +GX … –GZ: explicit global axes directions  
     • +EX … –EZ: explicit single-cut global directions  

In combination, these parameters let users finely control where and how labels, axes and cutting patterns appear and align in complex technical drawings.

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
The input table defines four user‐configurable items that control the appearance and placement of “additional elements” (such as text labels, symbols, level marks, dimensional lines, etc.) in a CAD or vector‐drawing environment.  Each row lists:

 • Item: the parameter name  
 • Description: what it does (with rules for positive, zero or negative values where applicable)  
 • Unit: the measurement unit or data type  
 • Default: the value used if the user does not override it  

Below is a detailed walk-through of each parameter:

1. MARG (Unit: cm Default: 0.0)  
   Governs the “margin” or overall size factor for various additional elements.  Its meaning changes depending on the element type:  
   – TEXT:  
     • MARG > 0: absolute distance (in cm) between the text and any reference boundary.  
     • MARG ≤ 0: interpreted as percentage of the “picture area”; negative values disable automatic bounding-box clipping.  
   – POST (positioning symbols) & ACHS (axis symbols):  
     • MARG > 0: overall symbol size becomes MARG cm.  
     • MARG ≤ 0: symbol size = (2 × |MARG|) + text length.  
     • MARG ≤ –100: also enforces a cap on text length, computed as –MARG/100 characters.  
   – NIVE (level marks):  
     • MARG > 0: absolute symbol size in cm.  
     • MARG ≤ 0: symbol size is derived from the current text height.  
   – DIML (dimensional lines):  
     • MARG > 0: offset distance around the text in cm.  
     • MARG < 0: offset = |MARG| × text height.  
   – “Placement” symbols (generic point markers):  
     • MARG > 0: symbol diameter or brush size = MARG cm.  
     • MARG ≤ 0: symbol size = 2 × text height.  

2. C (Unit: – Default: 1001)  
   Defines the colour index used for the additional element’s foreground (text, lines, symbol outlines, etc.).  The actual colour is looked up in a palette or database under index 1001 by default.

3. CB (Unit: – Default: 101)  
   Defines the background‐fill colour index for any element that supports a background (e.g. text halos or filled symbols).  Defaults to index 101.

4. ALIG (Unit: LIT (literal) Default: DEFA)  
   Controls horizontal alignment of text at its insertion point.  Possible literal values:  
   – RIGH: right‐justified  
   – MIDD: centred  
   – LEFT: left‐justified  
   – DEFA: use the system’s default, which is determined by the current DTYP (element type) setting  

5. SET (Unit: LIT Default: ‘*’)  
   Determines which point on a multi‐point entity (e.g. polyline, spline) is used as the “text insertion point.”  The options are:  
   – PBEG: at the beginning (the MOVE point)  
   – PEND: at the end (the DRAW point)  
   – PBE : both beginning and end  
   – PMID: at the geometric middle  

See also the related settings under INFORMATION (global text parameters), DRAW (primitive shapes), TEXT (font and height), POST (positioning symbols), NIVE (level symbols), and AXIS (axis definitions), which together allow complete customization of annotation graphics in the vector‐drawing environment.

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
The input is a two-part parameter table that governs how auxiliary graphics and text are placed, grouped and adjusted in a RAG‐based vector store.  It is organized into five columns—MOVE (logical section), Item (parameter name), Description, Unit, Default—and includes a “continued on next page” note.  Below is a structured walkthrough of each parameter and its valid values:

1. Section “MOVE = BOX/GROUP/TEXT”:  
   • BOX  
     – Description: Defines the maximum allowable offset of any text insertion point from the boundary of the system box (which is itself defined via a GRP/BOX command).  
     – Unit: cm when positive, % of picture area when zero or negative.  
     – Default: ON (meaning text insertion is clipped to the system box).  

   • GRNO  
     – Description: Group number to which the additional element belongs.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: 0  

   • DTYP  
     – Description: Type code of the additional drawing element. Whenever a new element is inserted, this code determines its kind.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: LT (all element types)  
     – Valid values:  
       · LINE – additional line  
       · AREA – additional filled area  
       · QSEC – cutting line through plane elements  
       · BSEC – cutting area through volume elements  
       · CUT – cutting-pattern line  
       · FIXL – fixed cutting-pattern line  
       · TEXT – additional text label  
       · POST – positioning symbol  
       · NIVE – level symbol  
       · CURV – geometry axis  
       · SIR – external beam section  
       · DIML – dimensional line  
       · AXIS – system axis  
     – Further axis codes (read from database): AXST (structural axis), AXLA (bridge center lane), AXGE (additional bridge lane), ASEC (secondary axis), AXTE (tendon geometry), AINT (internal SOFIMSHC axis), AXUN (general axis)  
     – Placement codes (from DB): PXLA (central lane), PSEC (secondary axis)  

   • DISZ  
     – Description: Vertical or radial distance between lines in a multiline TEXT element.  
     – Unit: none (actual value is in drawing units)  
     – Default: 1.3  
     – Constraint: must be > 0.0, applies regardless of Unit setting.  

2. Section “MOVE = ADJU (Adjustment of cutting lines)”:  
   • ADJU  
     – Description: Defines how cutting lines through plane elements are oriented, grouped or connected.  
     – Unit: none  
     – Default: DEFA (cuts are not connected; local X direction defined by input order)  
     – Primary modes:  
       · DEFA – default local X-direction; no interconnection  
       · SERI – polygonal cuts are chained together  
       · GLOB – single cuts oriented to a global axis  
       · SEPA – polygonal cuts split into individual segments  
       · NO – cuts follow point-entry order, no adjustment  
       · POLY – only polygonal cuts are chained  
       · SING – only single cuts follow global orientation  
     – Connector variants (suffix “C…”): CONN, CSRI, CGLB, CNO, CPOL, CSNG; same behavior as primary modes but allow geometric connection between successive cuts.  
     – Explicit global-direction codes: +X…–Z (matches DEFA axes), +GX…–GZ (matches GLOB), +EX…–EZ (matches SING).  

See also related tables on INFORMATION, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE and AXIS. This specification ensures consistent placement, styling and logical grouping of supplemental graphics and annotations in the vector‐based drawing environment.

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
The input table is a configuration reference for “additional elements” and the adjustment of “cutting lines” in a CAD-style system. It is organized into two main blocks—general element parameters and cutting-line adjustment parameters—each with four columns:

 1. Item  
 2. Description  
 3. Unit  
 4. Default  

Below is a structured walkthrough of its contents and how you would interpret it when building a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) vector store schema.

1. General Element Parameters  
   • BOX  
     – Description: Maximum allowed distance of the text insertion point from the outer boundary of the group or system box (defined by GRP/BOX).  
     – Unit: cm (if >0) or % of picture area (if ≤0)  
     – Default: ON (insertion point is clipped to the box)  
   • GRNO  
     – Description: Group number to which this additional element belongs  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: 0  
   • DTYP  
     – Description: Type of additional element. Enumerations include:  
         · LINE – simple line  
         · AREA – planar region  
         · QSEC – sectional cut through planar elements  
         · BSEC – cutting area through volumetric elements  
         · CUT – pattern line for cutting  
         · FIXL – fixed cutting-pattern line  
         · TEXT – textual annotation  
         · POST – positioning symbol  
         · NIVE – level symbol  
         · CURV – geometric axis  
         · SIR – external beam section  
         · DIML – dimension line  
         · AXIS – system axis  
     – Unit: –  
     – Default: LT (all element types)  
   • Axis Reading (from database)  
     – AXST – structural axis  
     – AXLA – central bridge lane  
     – AXGE – additional bridge lane  
     – ASEC – secondary axis  
     – AXTE – tendon geometry  
     – AINT – internal SOFIM-SHC axis  
     – AXUN – general axis  
   • Placements (from database)  
     – PXLA – at central lane of bridge  
     – PSEC – at secondary axis  
   • DISZ  
     – Description: Distance between multiline text lines (for TEXT elements)  
     – Unit: cm  
     – Default: 1.3 (>0 always enforced)

2. Cutting-Line Adjustment (ADJU)  
   This parameter determines how “cuts” (QSEC/BSEC/CUT/FIXL) are oriented and whether they are grouped. Columns: Item (always “ADJU”), Description, Unit (–), Default (DEFA). The possible enumerations fall into two conceptual layers:

   A. Base Modes  
     • DEFA: Local X-direction; polygonal cuts unconnected; single cuts global  
     • SERI: Polygonal cuts grouped (“coupled”); single cuts global  
     • SEPA: Polygonal cuts separated into single cuts  
     • GLOB: All cuts follow a global direction  
     • NO: Use input-order direction, no adjustment  
     • POLY: Only polygonal cuts grouped; singles unchanged  
     • SING: Only single cuts global; polygons unchanged  

   B. “Connected” Variants  
     Same as above but allowing adjacent cuts to connect:  
     • CONN, CSRI, CGLB, CNO, CPOL, CSNG  

   C. Explicit Global Directions  
     • +X…–Z: Corresponds to DEFA with fixed local axes  
     • +GX…–GZ: Corresponds to GLOB with global axes  
     • +EX…–EZ: Corresponds to SING with explicit global axes  

   – Unit: –  
   – Default: DEFA  

3. Cross-References (“See also”)  
   The table header refers to related modules or commands: INFORMATION, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE, AXIS, MOVE. These imply that the additional-element parameters interact with element-drawing routines, text insertion, level markers, axis geometry, and move operations.

How to index for a RAG store  
• Treat each Item as a distinct document or vector entry.  
• Index fields: “Item,” “Description,” “Unit,” “Default,” plus enumerated value lists.  
• Tag cross-references (“See also”) for navigation.  
• Normalize the enumerations (e.g. DTYP=“LINE”, “AREA”, …) into separate metadata arrays.  
• Expose range constraints (DISZ>0) and unit-switch logic (BOX uses cm or %).

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
The table you’ve provided defines a set of drawing‐ and annotation-related parameters (items), each with a textual description, an associated unit of measure, and a default value. It is keyed off the “Item” column, which you can think of as a short mnemonic. The remaining columns explain in more detail what each item does, how to control or interpret its values, and what baseline setting (“Default”) the system uses if you do not override it.

1. Overall Structure  
   •  Columns  
      – Item: A short code identifying the parameter.  
      – Description: Explains what the parameter controls, often including sub-cases or keyword settings.  
      – Unit: The unit of measure (if any) or a placeholder (–) when unitless.  
      – Default: The value assumed when you do not explicitly set the parameter.  

   •  “See also” context: This table is part of a larger annotation/drawing feature set, cross-referenced by modules such as Information, DRAW, TEXT, POST, NIVE, AXIS and MOVE.

2. Dimensional-line Parameters  
   • DIST  
     – “Distance of dimensional lines (DIML) to the measured line.”  
     – Positive values (cm) place the dim-line to the right; negative to the left.  
     – Unit = cm; Default = 0.6  

   • DASH  
     – “Size of dash at the dimensional lines (DIML).”  
     – >0: absolute dash length in cm;  
       <0: treated as a multiplier of the text height (refers to +MARG).  
     – Unit = –/cm; Default = 0.4  

3. Text-insertion and Visibility Controls  
   • PICT  
     – “Maximum distance of the text insertion point from the picture boundaries.”  
     – =0: text shown only if fully inside the picture.  
       ON: any text point outside is snapped to the picture boundary.  
       >0: explicit distance in cm.  
       ≤0: interpreted as percentage of picture area.  
       OFF: no boundary checks; insertion points remain unchanged.  
     – Unit = cm/%; Default = 0.2  

   • SBOX  
     – “Check for visibility inside the structural box.”  
     – OFF: skip visibility check entirely.  
       ON or “0.0”: same as default—clip to the box.  
       ≤0.0: check only elements whose UNIT = WC.  
       >0.0: always enforce box clipping, regardless of UNIT.  
     – Unit = m/–; Default = 0.0  

4. Grouping, Types, and Placements  
   • GRNO  
     – “Group number to which the additional element appertains.”  
     – Integer index allowing you to group supplementary drawing objects.  
     – Unit = –; Default = 0  

   • DTYP  
     – “Type of the additional element.” Enumerated codes:  
       All: LT (all types), LINE (polyline), AREA (filled area), QSEC (plane cut‐line),  
       BSEC (volume cut‐area), CUT (pattern line), FIXL (fixed pattern line), TEXT,  
       POST (position symbol), NIVE (level symbol), CURV (geometry axis), SIR  
       (external beam section), DIML (dimensional lines), AXIS (system axis).  
     – “Placements reading from database” further specialize AXIS into:  
       AXST (structural), AXLA (central bridge lane), AXGE (additional lane),  
       ASEC (secondary axis), AXTE (tendon geometry), AINT (internal SOFIMSHC),  
       AXUN (general axis).  
       PXLA and PSEC denote placement at central or secondary bridge axis.  
     – Unit = –; Default = LT (all types)  

5. Text Spacing  
   • DISZ  
     – “Distance of multiline texts (TEXT).”  
     – Must be >0.0; always enforced, regardless of UNIT.  
     – Unit = –; Default = 1.3  

6. Cutting-line Adjustment  
   • ADJU  
     – “Adjustment of cutting lines through plane elements.” Determines how polygonal and single‐point cuts are grouped, oriented, or left independent.  
     – Default: DEFA (“Definition of local X direction”), which:  
       • Leaves cuts unconnected by default.  
       • Treats polygonal chains as SERI (series-coupled) and single cuts as GLOB (global direction).  
     – Other keywords let you choose:  
       • SERI: couple polygonal cuts only.  
       • SEPA: break polygonal cuts into individual cuts.  
       • GLOB: apply a uniform global orientation.  
       • NO: keep the input point order.  
       • POLY, SING: couple only polygonal or single cuts.  
       • CONN, CSRI, CGLB, CNO, CPOL, CSNG: same behaviors as above but allow connectivity between cut segments.  
       • +X…–Z: force the local‐axis direction from DEFA.  
       • +GX…–GZ: force the global direction axes from GLOB.  
       • +EX…–EZ: force the global direction axes from SING.  
     – Unit = –; Default = DEFA  

In practice, you would load these parameter definitions into your RAG or vector-store schema so that a drawing/annotation engine or UI can present users with tooltips, valid ranges (e.g. “>0 for cm”), and drop-down lists of keywords (e.g. ADJU’s options). Each row becomes a single document or structured entry, keyed by “Item,” and enriched with semantic tags (e.g. UNIT: “length,” CATEGORY: “text insertion,” “cutting line”).

sections: 3.27 MOVE – Starting Point and Properties of Additional Elements

content:
The input table is organized into two main sections, each sharing the same four-column structure and defining a palette of parameters used in a vector-based annotation or drafting system.  Every parameter (“Item”) has an associated Description, Unit of measure (if any), and a Default setting.  What follows is a detailed breakdown of each section and its entries.

1. Common Columns  
   • Item  
     – The keyword or code used to reference a particular setting.  
   • Description  
     – A brief explanation of what the setting controls.  
   • Unit  
     – The physical or logical unit in which the parameter is expressed (e.g., cm, %, none).  
   • Default  
     – The out‐of‐the‐box value applied when no user override is provided.

2. Section 1: MOVE (Text Insertion & Additional Elements)  
   This section controls how text and auxiliary graphic elements are positioned and classified.

   A. BOX  
     • Description: “Maximum distance of the text insertion point from the boundary of the system box defined via GRP/BOX.”  
     • Unit: cm or % of the picture area.  
     • Default: ON (i.e. text insertion is clipped to the system box boundaries; negative or zero means use % scaling).

   B. GRNO (Group Number)  
     • Description: Associates an additional element with a group ID (0 means no group).  
     • Unit: none, Default: –.

   C. DTYP (Type of the Additional Element)  
     • Description: Selects the category of annotation or graphic addition.  
     • Unit: none, Default: LT (all element types).  
     • Valid Values:  
       – LINE: Additional line  
       – AREA: Additional area  
       – QSEC: Cutting line through planar elements  
       – BSEC: Cutting area through volumetric elements  
       – CUT: Cutting pattern line  
       – FIXL: Fixed cutting pattern line  
       – TEXT: Additional text  
       – POST: Positioning symbol  
       – NIVE: Level symbol  
       – CURV: Geometry axis  
       – SIR: External beam sections  
       – DIML: Dimensional lines  
       – AXIS: System axis

   D. AXIS (System Axis)  
     • Description: Reads axis definitions from the database.  
     • Unit: none, Default: AXST (structural axis).  
     • Examples of axis types:  
       – AXLA: Central lane of bridge  
       – AXGE: Additional lane of bridge  
       – ASEC: Secondary axis  
       – AXTE: Tendon geometry  
       – AINT: Internal SOFIMSHC axis  
       – AXUN: General axis

   E. Placements from Database  
     • PXLA: at Central lane of bridge  
     • PSEC: at Secondary axis

   F. DISZ (Distance of multiline texts)  
     • Description: Space between text lines for TEXT type.  
     • Unit: unspecified (could be cm).  
     • Default: 1.3 (>0.0 always enforced).

3. Section 2: ADJU (Adjustment of Cutting Lines)  
   This section configures how cutting lines—used in sectioning or pattern generation—are aligned, coupled, and globally oriented.

   A. General  
     • Description: “Adjustment of cutting lines through plane elements.”  
     • Unit: none, Default: DEFA (local X direction).  
     • Note: Always checked, regardless of UNIT.

   B. Core Modes (mutually exclusive base behaviors)  
     1. DEFA  – Default: cuts are not connected; local X-direction basis.  
     2. SERI  – Polygonal cuts are coupled; single cuts adopt global direction.  
     3. SEPA  – Polygonal cuts are separated and saved individually.  
     4. GLOB  – All cuts are aligned to a single global direction.  
     5. NO    – No adjustment; direction follows point input order.  
     6. POLY  – Only polygonal cuts are coupled; single cuts unadjusted.  
     7. SING  – Only single cuts are aligned globally; polygonal cuts unadjusted.

   C. “Connected” Variants  
     • CONN  : Like DEFA but polygon segments may connect.  
     • CSRI  : Like SERI but cuts may connect.  
     • CGLB  : Like GLOB with possible connections.  
     • CNO   : Like NO with possible connections.  
     • CPOL  : Like POLY with possible connections.  
     • CSNG  : Like SING with possible connections.

   D. Explicit Direction Overrides  
     • +X … –Z    : Apply DEFA logic but locked to local axis X, Y, or Z (positive or negative).  
     • +GX … –GZ  : Apply GLOB logic but locked to global axis G-X, G-Y, or G-Z.  
     • +EX … –EZ  : Apply SING logic but locked to local axis X, Y, or Z.

4. Continuation  
   • The table indicates that additional rows or context appear on the following page, suggesting further parameter definitions or continuation of ADJU variants.

Together, these definitions allow fine-grained control over text layout, annotation grouping, axis references, and the behavior of sectional or cutting patterns in a CAD or drawing application.

content:
The table defines the syntax and semantics of a generic “DRAW” record used to place additional graphical elements (lines, areas, cutting lines, projections, etc.) into a drawing or section.  It is organized into four columns:

 1.  Item  
    – the keyword or parameter name you must supply.  

 2.  Description  
    – a concise explanation of the meaning or role of that parameter.  

 3.  Unit  
    – the expected data type or unit for that field.  Often “m/cm/%” for coordinates, “LIT” for a literal enumeration, or “–” when unitless.  

 4.  Default  
    – the value assumed if you omit that field.  

Below is a row‐by‐row breakdown:

1.  X  
    •  Description: X‐coordinate of the next point in the element you’re drawing.  
    •  Unit: m/cm/% (you choose meters, centimetres or percent).  
    •  Default: 0  

2.  Y  
    •  As for X, but the Y‐coordinate.  
    •  Unit: m/cm/%  
    •  Default: 0  

3.  Z  
    •  As for X, but the Z‐coordinate (in 3D drawings).  
    •  Unit: m/cm/%  
    •  Default: 0  

4.  REF  
    •  The node number that serves as the origin for the (X,Y,Z) you supply. In other words, coordinates are measured relative to the node you specify here.  
    •  Unit: – (an integer index)  
    •  Default: –  

5.  UNIT  
    •  Selects which coordinate system your X/Y/Z refer to. It is an enumerated literal (LIT).  
    •  Possible values:  
       – WC : system (world) coordinates  
       – CM : drawing coordinates of the inner window in cm  
              (X rightward, Y upward, zero at lower‐left)  
       – PR : same as CM but in percent of picture area  
       – PL : like WC, but projected along the current VIEW direction (useful for axis grids)  
       – PLF: like WC but clipped at the BOX limits (e.g. main bridge axis)  
       – Preceding R (RWC, RCM, RPR, RPL) refers to the previous point.  
    •  Default: WC  

6.  C  
    •  Colour index, line‐type or fill‐pattern for the element.  
    •  Unit: – (integer or “*”)  
    •  Default: *  (use the current or inherited style)  

7.  DTYP  
    •  Type of additional graphic element you are drawing.  It is a literal (LIT).  
    •  Default: –  (must usually be supplied)  
    •  Sub-values:  
       – LINE : a simple (poly)line  
       – AREA : a filled polygonal area  
       – QSEC : cutting line through existing area elements; “effect plane is the current line of vision”  
       – XX   : projection onto global X axis  
       – YY   : projection onto global Y axis  
       – ZZ   : projection onto global Z axis  

Once you select DTYP, you supply as many successive DRAW records (with X,Y,Z, etc.) as needed to define the vertices of that entity.  For LINE or AREA you trace the polygon; for QSEC you define the intersection (cutting) curve in the current view; for XX/YY/ZZ you generate a projection line along the respective global axis.  

Notes on context from related commands:  
•  “BSEC, BXX, BYY, BZZ” define full “cutting areas” through volume elements for global‐axis sections.  
•  “CUT, CXX, CYY, CZZ” define short geodetic isolines (“cutting patterns”) on area structures.  
•  “SIR, SXX, SYY, SZZ” are used by the external SIR program for beam‐section views, specifying local vs. global axis directions.  
•  Group and Material flags (FIRS, NO) control which elements participate in a cut.  
•  HINT and cm/LT parameters allow you to draw auxiliary guide lines or dimension hints of specified length.  

This table equips the user to place auxiliary graphics—lines, filled areas, cutting‐plane traces or projections—into an engineering drawing, fully parameterized by coordinates, reference nodes, styles, and element types.

The input table defines how different “cuts,” “sections,” and “projection” operations are specified in a structural‐drawing or post‐processing environment.  Its primary columns are:

  • DTYP (Item)  
    – A code that selects one of several drawing or cutting operations.  
  • GRP (Group filter)  
    – An integer ≥ 0, or keyword NO or FIRS, limiting the operation to elements in a particular group.  
  • MNO (Material filter)  
    – An integer ≥ 0, or keyword NO or FIRS, limiting the operation to elements of a particular material.  
  • Description  
    – A human‐readable summary of the geometric or filtering action.  
  • Unit  
    – Measurement unit (e.g. cm/LT for hint‐line length).  
  • Default  
    – The default value if none is provided explicitly.

Below is a detailed breakdown of each DTYP code, its semantics and default filter behavior:

1. BSEC  
   • “Cutting area through volume elements”  
   • Projects results in the current view plane (effect plane = line of vision).  
   • Use ISOL or SECT records to query the cut‐surface results.

2. BXX, BYY, BZZ  
   • “Projection in global X, Y or Z” respectively for a cutting area.  
   • The cutting plane is orthogonal to the chosen global axis.  
   • Same record attachment (ISOL or SECT) as BSEC.

3. CUT  
   • “Cutting pattern line through plane elements”  
   • Defines a geodetic isoline (shortest path across the structure).  
   • Results are not volumetric areas but isoline traces.

4. CXX, CYY, CZZ  
   • “Fixed cutting pattern line” in global X, Y or Z.  
   • The cut geometry remains unchanged if view orientation changes.

5. FIXC  
   • Alias for CXX/CYY/CZZ style: “Fixed cutting pattern, view‐independent.”

6. ZXX, ZYY, ZZZ  
   • “External section along a continuous beam” in global X, Y or Z.  
   • Specifically used by the external‐section module (program SIR).

7. SIR  
   • “Section for program SIR” with local axis direction aligned to current view.  
   • Requires downstream SIR processing to generate section results.

8. SXX, SYY, SZZ  
   • “Local section” in global X, Y or Z direction for SIR.  
   • Local y/z axes orientation is defined by the chosen axis.

Filter columns (GRP, MNO) accept three forms:  
  • A non‐negative integer n ≥ 0  
    – Apply the operation only to elements in group/material number n.  
  • FIRS  
    – Apply only to the group/material of the first element encountered.  
  • NO  
    – Ignore group/material; apply to all active elements.

9. HINT  
   • “Hint lines” drawn at the start and end points of cuts.  
   • Unit: cm/LT. Default = NO (full drawing line).  
   • If ≥ 0, draws a hint‐line segment of the specified length.

Additional notes on usage:  
– A “cutting area” is defined by BSEC/BXX/BYY/BZZ; you attach ISOL or SECT records to visualize internal results on that plane.  
– A “cut” (linear intersection) uses DEFA, PICT, XX, YY or ZZ (older synonyms of BSEC/BXX/BYY/BZZ) together with SECT for result output. Cuts may consist of multiple DRAW segments; multi‐segment polygons preserve their direction orientation.  
– A “cutting pattern” (geodetic isoline) is defined via CUT/CXX/CYY/CZZ and yields the shortest possible path along the area structure.  
– An “external beam section” for SIR uses SIR/SXX/SYY/SZZ and can include arbitrary DRAW records; DTYP controls local‐axis orientation in 3D.  
– Additional planar areas (DTYP = AREA) are filled when Colour C ≠ 0, with fill types encoded via:  
    • COLO (solid colour), PATT (pattern), HATC (hatch), or explicit RGB codes.  
    • Negative indices (–1…–255) select entries from the current fill table.

The table is a specification of the “DRAW” input record for defining cuts, projections and related graphical elements in a 3-D structural model (especially when used in conjunction with SECT, ISOL or SIR).  Each row in the table corresponds to one allowable setting of the DTYP field or to one of the auxiliary parameters (group, material, hints).  Below is a field-by-field breakdown and an explanation of how these settings control the way sections, projections and isolines are generated.  

1. Fields and Their Purpose  
   - DRAW:    The name of the input record.  
   - ZZ:      (Placeholder column header – in the live system this is the sub‐identifier for each record line.)  
   - Projection in global Z / global X / global Y / through volume elements / local direction:  These labels describe the geometric behavior associated with each DTYP code.  
   - Item (DTYP):  Specifies the type of cut/projection/isoline or external section.  Valid codes are grouped into five categories:  
       • Cutting area through volume elements:  
           – BSEC   : dynamic cutting plane at current view line  
           – BXX, BYY, BZZ : projection of volume‐element intersections onto global X, Y or Z  
       • Cutting pattern (geodetic isoline):  
           – CUT    : shortest path (geodetic) through the volume  
           – CXX, CYY, CZZ : same as CUT but locked to global X, Y or Z direction  
           – FIXC   : fixed cutting pattern (remains unchanged on view change)  
       • External beam section for SIR program:  
           – SIR    : external section along a beam, visualized in SIR  
           – SXX, SYY, SZZ : like SIR but directed along global X, Y or Z axis  
   - GRP (Group constraint):  
       – NO ≥0 : The cut/projection affects only elements belonging to this group number.  
       – FIRS   : The cut uses the group of the first element it encounters.  
       – NO     : All active element groups are processed.  
   - MNO (Material constraint):  
       – NO ≥0 : The cut/projection affects only elements of this material number.  
       – FIRS   : The cut uses the material of the first element it encounters.  
       – NO     : Material is ignored; all elements are processed.  
   - Description:  A free‐text field reiterating what the code does; it is for user reference.  
   - Unit:        Specifies the measurement units for any numeric argument (e.g. cm or generic “length unit” (LT)).  
   - Default / Value constraints:  
       • Many settings default to 0 or “NO,” meaning “no restriction” or “no hint.”  
       • HINT code: draws small guideline segments at the start and end points; requires a length ≥0 (in cm or LT).  
       • YES/NO toggles: YES produces a full drawing line; NO produces only hint lines.  

2. How It Works in Practice  
   - To define a full‐volume slice (an area cut), specify DTYP = BSEC (or BXX/BYY/BZZ).  You may then invoke ISOL or SECT to display results on that plane.  
   - For a 2-D cut through the structure, use DTYP = DEFA, PICT, XX, YY or ZZ together with subsequent DRAW records to trace the cut path.  Each segment aligns with the chosen global or local direction.  
   - To draw a “geodetic isoline” (shortest path) on the structure’s surface, use DTYP in the CUT family (CUT, CXX, CYY, CZZ).  
   - External beam sections for the SIR post‐processor are created by selecting SIR or its axis-aligned variants.  The local y–z axes of the beam are oriented according to DTYP.  
   - An additional filled area can be inserted via DTYP = AREA plus a nonzero colour code.  The colour field accepts either:  
       • Predefined colour steps: index·1000+101  
       • Fill patterns: index·1000+201+density  
       • Hatch patterns: index·1000+300+hatch-index  
       • True RGB: 100000 + R + 256·G + 256²·B  
       • Negative indices (-1…-255) to reference the current fill table  

3. Usage Notes  
   - You may supply as many DRAW records as needed: one for each segment of a polygonal cut or multiple isolines.  
   - Group and material filters let you isolate certain element subsets without modifying the model.  
   - Hints are purely graphical aids; they do not influence the numerical results.  

In sum, this table documents every permissible DTYP setting for shaping and visualizing cuts, patterns and sections in 3-D structural analyses.  By combining the DTYP code with group/material filters and optional hint lengths, users gain fine-grained control over what is displayed and how.

   • Default: the value assumed when the user does not specify an explicit setting.

2. Parameter: DIST  
   – Purpose  
     • DIST defines the maximum offset distance from the nominal cut- or projection-line, measured along the selected projection axis.  
     • It is used when the UNIT setting is “PL” (projection line units), i.e. you want to limit how far the drawing routine extends geometry or results on either side of the reference line.

   – Allowed Values  
     1. DEFA (the literal keyword “DEFA”)  
        • Interpreted as “no limit.”  
        • The cutting or projection routine will extend indefinitely (or as far as model geometry exists) along both sides of the reference line.  
     2. Any positive real number (> 0)  
        • That number becomes the maximum distance in BOTH the positive and negative directions along the projection axis.  
        • Example: DIST = 5 means extend 5 units “forwards” and 5 units “backwards.”  
     3. Any negative real number (< 0)  
        • The absolute value of that number becomes the maximum in the POSITIVE direction only.  
        • The negative-side limit is fixed at zero (i.e. no backward extension).  
        • Example: DIST = –3 means extend 3 units in the positive direction only.

   – Unit  
     • m/LT  
       – “m” denotes meters if absolute world units are used.  
       – “LT” indicates “length unit,” i.e. the current model’s generic length unit (could be mm, inch, etc., depending on global settings).

   – Default  
     • DEFA  
       – If DIST is omitted, the system assumes “no limit” and will project or cut through the entire model extent in both directions.

3. Operational Context and Related Settings  
   – When you define a cutting area through volume elements (via DTYP=BSEC, BXX, BYY or BZZ), DIST controls how far beyond the central reference line the cut-through is drawn.  
   – In SECT commands (DTYP=DEFA, PICT, XX, YY, or ZZ), DIST similarly limits section-view extent.  
   – For polygonal cuts (“cuts with several segments”), DIST is applied along each segment’s local projection direction.  
   – No other table rows here—this is a single-parameter attribute table. Future tables for other DTYP values (CUT, CXX, …) or for “AREA” fill patterns will follow the same column format.

4. Example Usages  
   • To cut a cross-section 2 m on either side of the reference line:  
       SECT … DIST=2  
   • To show only the forward half of a projection up to 8 units:  
       POST … UNIT=PL DIST=-8  
   • To display an unlimited projection:  
       AXIS … DIST=DEFA

Below is a structured, detailed description of the four input parameters used by the CURV routine when drawing geometry axes (as defined by GEOS or ELLA) in a plot. Each parameter appears as a table entry with its name (“Item”), its functional role (“Description”), the measurement unit (“Unit”), and the preset setting applied if the user does not override it (“Default”).

1. NO  
   • Description: Specifies which axis number is to be drawn. In many CAD or plotting contexts, multiple axes or alignments can be defined; NO tells CURV which of these pre-defined axes to render on the current drawing.  
   • Unit: Not applicable (—). This is an integer index rather than a physical measure.  
   • Default: 1. If the user omits NO, CURV will draw the first (primary) axis by default.

2. F  
   • Description: Controls the line type used when plotting the axis geometry. Line types often correspond to solid, dashed, dotted, or custom‐dash patterns in the plotting library or CAD environment. By changing F, users can visually distinguish reference axes, centerlines, or alternate alignments.  
   • Unit: Not applicable (—). F is an enumerated code for line styles rather than a dimensional quantity.  
   • Default: 3. This default code typically maps to a predefined dash pattern or style that the system designer has chosen for axis depiction.

3. DX  
   • Description: Defines the interval between successive plotted points along the axis. CURV internally samples the axis curve at regular intervals (DX) to produce a polyline or series of marker points for display. A smaller DX yields a smoother, more finely segmented representation; a larger DX gives a coarser, faster‐rendering curve.  
   • Unit: meters (m). Reflects real‐world distances along the alignment.  
   • Default: 1. When unspecified, points are plotted every 1 m.

4. H  
   • Description: Sets the text height for station labels along the axis. As CURV renders chainage or station annotations (e.g., “+00.000”, “+50.000”), H determines the font size so that labels remain legible relative to the drawing scale.  
   • Unit: centimeters (cm). This allows text size to scale consistently with plotted elements.  
   • Default: “–” (no default). If the user does not supply a value, CURV leaves the station text height unchanged from the environment’s current text size, or else prompts the operator to specify H before rendering.

Contextual Note: CURV is typically invoked after defining a roadway or pipeline alignment via GEOS or ELLA. Along with plotting the centerline geometry, CURV reads these four parameters to control which axis is drawn, how it appears, how densely it is sampled, and how its station labels are formatted.      • You can supply a rotation angle (inclination) or size override via MOVE.  
     • If you omit MOVE, the default text size and orientation apply.  
   – The DRAW record is then typically invoked to render the geometric elements (circles, lines) surrounding the TITL text.

4. Database and Layer Consistency  
   – Each AXIS entry belongs to a single database (referenced by the DB record).  
   – The same drawing conventions (circles, text placement, line style) must be applied in every layer of that database.  
   – Mixing different TITL inputs or drawing styles across layers is not allowed.

5. Cross-References  
   – See also “Information”: for metadata about the axis beyond its label, such as creation date or author.  
   – See “MOVE”: for positioning commands that affect TITL text orientation, size, or insertion point.  
   – See “DRAW”: for the actual rendering sequence that uses both MOVE and TITL to place the axis label in the graphic.

In summary, this table entry defines how to supply and format the textual label of an axis in your vector drawing system. “TITL” is mandatory if you wish to visually annotate the axis; it must be an eight-bit character string, will not default to any value, and its appearance is controlled by the accompanying MOVE/DRAW commands within the same database record.

See also: Information, MOVE, DRAW
 AXIS
 The designation placed in the same line (analog HEAD lines) is written in a circle at both sides in the last position defined with the records MOVE or DRAW. A possible inclination of the text or a different character size must be input with the record MOVE.
 The axis are referred always to their corresponding database (DB record). They are always drawn in the same manner in all layers of this database. Different inputs in different layers are not possible.

The table shown defines the items available in the DSIR record, which is used to alter or specify the properties of a section point on a continuous beam (as generated by MOVE/DRAW).  Each row corresponds to one input parameter (“Item”), gives a brief text “Description,” the physical or logical “Unit,” and the “Default” value if that item is omitted.  DSIR may be applied immediately after a DRAW/MOVE point to change its section‐related parameters or to set up defaults for the next point.

1.  NO  
 – Description: Section number.  
 – Unit: none  
 – Default: 1  
 – Notes: Identifies which section type (from SECT definitions in the corresponding database layer) is used at this beam point.

2.  NX, NY, NZ  
 – Description: Components of the section’s local normal vector.  
 – Unit: none  
 – Default: NX = 1, NY = 0, NZ = 0  
 – Notes: If all three are omitted, the program computes the section’s local x-axis automatically from the beam direction.  Otherwise you may orient the section plane arbitrarily.

3.  XMIN, XMAX  
 – Description: Depth limits of the “section box” used to collect support reactions.  
 – Unit: meters (m)  
 – Default: XMIN = –0.001 m, XMAX = +0.001 m  
 – Notes: These small offsets create a thin slab around the section plane for reaction integration.

4.  YMIN, YMAX  
 – Description: Local y-coordinate window extents of the active section plane (relative to the section’s origin).  
 – Unit: meters (m)  
 – Default: YMIN = –999 m, YMAX = +999 m  
 – Notes: Generally set wide enough to include the entire cross section.

5.  ZMIN, ZMAX  
 – Description: Local z-coordinate window extents of the active section plane (relative to the section’s origin).  
 – Unit: meters (m)  
 – Default: ZMIN = –999 m, ZMAX = +999 m  
 – Notes: As with Y-limits, defines the slice of the section plane to be considered.

6.  SNO  
 – Description: Cross-section number.  
 – Unit: none  
 – Default: 1  
 – Notes: Selects which cross‐sectional geometry (from a library of section shapes) is assigned here.

7.  LDIR  
 – Description: Kind of local direction, i.e. the section’s “line of vision” orientation.  
 – Unit: literal (LIT)  
 – Default: DEFA  
 – Allowed values and effects:  
  • DEFA  – default behavior: if the section is a disc or framework, Y is used; otherwise Z is used.  
  • Y     – force positive local y as the view direction.  
  • –Y    – force negative local y as view direction.  
  • Z     – force positive local z as view direction.  
  • –Z    – force negative local z as view direction.  
 – Notes: This determines whether the section’s local y–z plane is “facing” the viewer along +Y, –Y, +Z or –Z in the current VIEW orientation.

Contextual Summary  
• The continuous‐beam geometry is seeded by a MOVE record at XS = 0.0; each subsequent DRAW extends it and automatically updates the station coordinate XS based on the distance between points.  
• At each beam point, DSIR may override section number, orientation, bounding‐box, or cross‐section selection.  
• The local y/z axes of each section are aligned with the active VIEW’s line of sight; you can explicitly force them via LDIR.  
• If you do not supply NX/NY/NZ, the program computes a local x-axis tangent to the beam, averaging at kinks.  
• Sections are always linked to their defining database (DB record) and must be defined uniformly in that layer. Different section inputs in different layers are not supported.

See also: Information, MOVE, DRAW
 DSIR
 –Z
 negative local z direction
 The beginning of the continuous beam with the ordinate XS=0.0 is generated with the record MOVE. All following records DRAW define the polygon points of the continuous beam. Here the beam ordinate XS is calculated automatically from the distance between the points. These points are the reference points of the section (in the program SIR record SECT items XM, YM, ZM). The local y/z direction of the section corresponds to the current line of vision which was defined in the record VIEW. The kind of the local direction is selectable with the item LDIR ( default: Y if it is a disc or framework ; otherwise Z ). With the record DSIR the properties of the last defined point are changed or the properties of the next point are defined. The local x direction is generated from the continuous beam direction, if the items NX, NY or NZ are not input. Then an average X direction is calculated at the breaks of the continuous beam.
 The SIR sections are referred always to their corresponding database (DB record). They are defined in the same manner in all layers of this database. Different inputs in different layers are not possible.

The table defines four parameters (CUT, GRP, SELE, LC) that govern how cutting‐pattern areas are generated, filtered and applied in the system. Each parameter appears as a row with four fields—Item name, Description (including valid literal values), Unit and Default setting. Below is a detailed breakdown:

1. CUT  
   – Purpose: Switches on or off the use of previously defined cutting‐pattern lines when computing pattern areas.  
   – Possible Values (LIT):  
     • YES  – incorporate all defined cutting lines into the pattern computation.  
     • NO   – ignore any cutting lines that were either imported via MOVE IMPO or created with MOVE/DRAW commands.  
   – Unit: Literal flag (LIT)  
   – Default: YES  

   Contextual Note: When set to YES, the algorithm will respect any preexisting pattern lines—ideal for incremental refinements. If NO, the system rebuilds patterns from scratch, discarding any user‐drawn or database‐imported lines.

2. GRP  
   – Purpose: Determines whether group‐limit boundaries influence the generation of additional cutting lines.  
   – Possible Values (LIT):  
     • YES  – tile the cutting pattern according to group membership; group boundaries spawn extra cut lines at their limits.  
     • NO   – ignore group limits; cutting lines do not respect group‐defined partitions.  
   – Unit: Literal flag (LIT)  
   – Default: NO  

   Contextual Note: Enabling group consideration (YES) is useful when structural elements are organized into logical or geometric groups whose interfaces must be cut.

3. SELE  
   – Purpose: Controls whether only currently selected/visible QUAD elements are used in the cutting‐pattern calculation.  
   – Possible Values (LIT):  
     • YES  – restrict processing to the set of QUAD elements presently visible on‐screen (i.e. those not hidden by BOX or GRP).  
     • NO   – use every QUAD element loaded in the system database, including those currently hidden or deselected.  
   – Unit: Literal flag (LIT)  
   – Default: NO  

   Contextual Note: When you want to focus the cutter on a subset of the model, SELE=YES confines patterns to visible geometry only. Otherwise, the full model is considered even if parts are hidden.

4. LC  
   – Purpose: Specifies an optional stress‐load case against which the cutting pattern is calculated. This is relevant when the deformed structural geometry has no associated load case defined.  
   – Possible Values: Any load‐case identifier (no literal unit)  
   – Unit: “–” (not a literal flag)  
   – Default: DEFO LC  

   Contextual Note: If the deformed structure already has a prescribed load case, that case is used. Otherwise the user can explicitly supply one here—often a “DEFAULT LC” which governs stress‐based pattern generation.

Additional Context from Upstream Processing (for reference):  
• At CUTP=0 (unstressed initial state), the system generates cutting‐pattern areas by analyzing geometry discontinuities (thickness jumps, T‐shapes, material limits) and stores them via the record “STRU CUT FILL YES.” Older pattern definitions are purged upon regeneration.  
• The final numbering and ordering of pattern areas derive from the QUAD element indices: by arranging the first QUAD numbers judiciously, users can influence the sequence in which patterns are output or filled.

In combination, these four parameters let users toggle preexisting cut lines, include or exclude grouping boundaries, limit geometry scope to the current selection, and define stress‐based load cases—thereby providing fine‐grained control over the automatic creation and management of cutting‐pattern areas.

See also: Information, MOVE, DRAW
 CUTP
 0
 Unstressed initial state
 Cutting pattern areas are generated with consideration of the material limits, the sudden thick- ness changes and the areas which have a T–shape. They are saved in the database. Old saved cutting pattern areas are deleted here. The generated areas can represented with the record STRU CUT FILL YES.
 Cutting pattern areas are sorted via the numbering of QUAD elements. So the cutting pattern area numbering can be influenced through a clever arrangement of the first QUAD element numbers in the original system, ie one per cutting pattern.

The table under review defines the input parameters available for the “LC” command (Load Case) in a FE-post-processing context.  It is laid out in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and each row corresponds to a distinct input keyword that controls which results are extracted from the database and how they are filtered or combined.  Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure and semantics:

1.  Overall Structure  
    •  Columns  
       –  Item: the keyword to be specified on the LC record.  
       –  Description: a concise explanation of what the keyword does and any special sub-options or behaviors.  
       –  Unit: the units or syntax expected (often “–/LIT” meaning no physical unit, literal input).  
       –  Default: the value assumed when the keyword is omitted.  
    •  Context  
       –  Many results in the database are stored against a load case or design case number.  Specifying or changing the LC inputs affects subsequent result queries for beams, areas, volumes, reinforcements, etc.  
       –  Some post-processors (AQUA, AQB, BEMESS, TALPA/ASE) produce multiple sub-results (stress points, time steps, material laws, composite materials).  LC with its associated items selects among these.

2.  Row-by-Row Description  
    1.  NO  
        •  Purpose: selects which load case’s results to display.  
        •  Semantics:  
          –  A non-negative integer (≥ 0) directly chooses that case.  
          –  A negative integer (< 0) references the Nth entry in an internal case list.  
          –  Predefined literals:  
            •  DEFA = use first case from list (same as FIRS)  
            •  FIRS = first load case  
            •  LAST = last load case  
            •  NEXT / PREV = navigate relative to current case  
            •  NAME / FIND = search by title string (with or without warning)  
        •  Unit: –/LIT  
        •  Default: DEFA (i.e. FIRS)  
    2.  T  
        •  Purpose: time value for transient (time-history or ECHO STEP) results from programs such as HYDRA.  
        •  Semantics: behaves exactly like NO (choose among stored time levels instead of load cases).  If T falls between two stored steps, results are interpolated linearly.  
        •  Unit: sec/LIT  
        •  Default: LAST (latest stored time)  
    3.  DESI  
        •  Purpose: selects a design case rather than a pure load case.  Typically used to fetch design stresses or reinforcement results from BEMESS or beam stresses from AQB that are stored per design load case.  
        •  Semantics: identical input rules as NO (including NAME, FIND).  
        •  Unit: –/LIT  
        •  Default: DEFA  
    4.  MAT  
        •  Purpose: selects which material (in a composite element) to report.  Also accepts special literals for stress-point programs (e.g. AQUA’s FAC1/2/3).  
        •  Semantics:  
          –  If omitted, the first material encountered is used.  
          –  Special suffixes allow aggregation across all sub-materials:  
             _MID = average value  
             _MAX = maximum  
             _MIN = minimum  
             _AMX = absolute maximum  
             _AMN = absolute minimum  
             _LST = last value  
             _SUM = sum (only for beam bond force)  
          –  Only materials of the same type/class are used if a reference material (item REF) is also specified.  
        •  Unit: –/LIT  
        •  Default: DEFA  

3.  Cross-References and Extended Options  
    •  NMAT: analogous to MAT but for selecting a particular nonlinear material law (e.g. outputs from TALPA/ASE).  
    •  DIRE: choose among directional components (X_ or 1, Y_ or 2, Z_ or 3, XY, XZ, YZ, XYZ).  
    •  DIF1/2/3: compute differences relative to specified limit values—useful in fatigue or code-check workflows.  
    •  KIND: compares two load/design cases (e.g. KIND DIF, KIND TMAX, KIND TMIN) and generates combined results or envelopes.  
    •  REF: restricts multi-material aggregations to those matching a reference material.  

4.  How to Use in a RAG Vector Store  
    When ingesting this table into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store, each row becomes a distinct knowledge chunk.  Key metadata:  
    •  “Item” → primary key, query handle.  
    •  “Description” → full passage for semantic retrieval.  
    •  “Unit” and “Default” → attributes for filtering or prompt-building.  
    •  Cross-refs (NMAT, DIRE, KIND, etc.) can be linked as “See also” pointers.  

This granular mapping ensures that, at query time, a user or downstream application can retrieve exactly the parameter definition they need (for example, “What does MAT _AMX do?”) and see both the conceptual description and default behavior in one place.

sections: 3.36 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
Below is a structured description of the “LC”-type input table and its core fields. This definition is intended for use in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setup or any vector-store indexing of documentation on post-processing parameters for structural analysis programs (AQUA, AQB, TALPA/ASE, HYDRA, BEMESS, etc.).

1. Table Purpose  
   – Defines a single “LC” record that drives selection, scaling, differencing, direction filtering, and material-law choices when plotting or exporting results.  
   – Applies to beam results (AQUA, AQB), area stresses, composite/nonlinear materials, time histories, and design versus service load states.

2. Core Columns (Items)  
   • FAC1, FAC2, FAC3  
     • Multiplicative factors on the numerical results in up to three directions.  
     • Default = 1.0.  
   • DIF1, DIF2, DIF3  
     • Threshold or comparison differences for each direction (e.g. to flag exceedances).  
     • Default = 0.0 (no differencing).  
   • DIRE  
     • Selection of which directional components to display:  
       – X_/1, Y_/2, Z_/3 (single axes)  
       – XY, XZ, YZ (axis pairs)  
       – XYZ or ALL (all three).  
   • NMAT  
     • Picks a specific nonlinear material law when multiple laws (TALPA/ASE) are stored under the same load case.  
     • If omitted, the first found law is used.  
   • REF  
     • Filters composite-beam output to only materials matching a reference classification (same type).  
     • When omitted, all materials of the same classification are included (unless other selection suffixes below are used).  
   • Description  
     • Free-text note to identify the record’s purpose (e.g. “service load deflections,” “ultimate shear envelope”).

3. Material-Selection Suffixes (attached to MAT or _MID)  
   • _MID  – average value across materials  
   • _MAX  – maximum value  
   • _MIN  – minimum value  
   • _AMX  – absolute maximum  
   • _AMN  – absolute minimum  
   • _LST  – last (chronologically) recorded value  
   • _SUM  – sum (used for beam bond forces)  
   – These suffixes override a single MAT selection and operate on all materials or on those filtered by REF.

4. Load-Case and Design-Case Interaction  
   – An LC record may reference either a load case (LC) or a design case (DESI).  
   – A single record governs retrieval of all results tied to that case (including reinforcement checks from BEMESS).  
   – HYDRA transient results are all stored under one case—use parameter T to interpolate between time steps.

5. Enumerated Concrete/Material Laws  
   – A long list of codes (e.g. EC_C, ECLC, DN_B, OE_B, SA_C, BS_C, AI_C, JI_C, GB_C, … NZPC, CSLC, etc.) covers a variety of national standards, lightweight, prestress, no-tension, high-strength, ductile-fibre, etc.  
   – These codes populate MAT or NMAT fields to select the correct stress–strain behavior.

6. Additional Features  
   • Safety factors can be applied post-query; chosen factors are recorded in the plot legend.  
   • DIF1–3 may also be used to compute “exceedance quantities” and will likewise appear in the legend.  
   • KIND (not a table column but an additional record qualifier) enables arithmetic comparisons (MAX, MIN, DIF, TMAX, TMIN) between two LC records—useful for envelopes or difference plots.  
   • Examples in the manual show envelope creation across a range of cases and difference of design- versus service-state reinforcement.

By indexing each of these fields and their permissible values into your vector store, RAG agents can accurately parse user requests (“show me max positive beam moment for LC 200 in X direction with EC2 concrete”) and translate them into the appropriate LC table record.

sections: 3.36 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
This table defines the syntax and semantic roles of the “LC” (Load-Case) input record in the AQUA family of programs (AQUA, AQB, BEMESS, HYDRA, TALPA/ASE), and the related fields used to extract, filter or post-process load-case–based results. It is meant as a grab-and-go reference for constructing queries against a RAG-backed vector store.

1. Key Columns  
• Item  
  – “LC” or “LC DESI” to select a load case or design case.  
  – Accepts one or two identifiers (numeric or “DESI”) with optional range syntax.  

• FAC1, FAC2, FAC3  
  – Multiplicative safety factors for results along up to three orthogonal directions.  
  – Often used to apply partial‐safety factors to stresses, forces or displacements.

• DIF1, DIF2, DIF3  
  – Thresholds or offsets added to the result in each of up to three directions.  
  – Useful to compute “exceedance” or margins relative to limits.

• DIRE  
  – Direction selector:  
 • X_ (1), Y_ (2), Z_ (3) for single axes  
 • XY (1+2), XZ (1+3), YZ (2+3) for planar components  
 • XYZ or ALL for the full vector magnitude.

• NMAT  
  – Index of a nonlinear material law (TALPA/ASE).  
  – Picks the first law by default if left blank.

• REF  
  – Reference “material” to restrict multi‐material composites to a single matching classification.  
  – When blank, all materials of the same type are considered if _MID/_MAX/etc. is used.

• Description  
  – Free text describing the effect of the record.  

2. Suffixes for Material‐Wise Aggregation  
When requesting beam‐bond or volume/area‐element results across multiple materials (composites), append:  
• _MID – arithmetic mean  
• _MAX / _MIN – maximum or minimum  
• _AMX / _AMN – absolute maximum or minimum  
• _LST – last recorded value  
• _SUM – summed value (only for bond forces)

If no suffix is given, only the first material or first nonlinear law is used.

3. Material‐Law Literals  
A comprehensive list of standardized concrete laws (EC2, DIN, SIA, BS, ACI, JIS, GBJ, SNIP, CSA, NZS, etc.) enables easy selection of national or specialized codes. E.g., EC_C, DNLC, AIHC, GBHC, SN_C, etc.

4. Cross–Load-Case Comparisons (KIND)  
• KIND TMAX / TMIN – envelopes max/min over a range of LCs (e.g. 1001 to 1010).  
• KIND DIF / QUOT – difference or ratio between two LCs or design cases.  
• Multidirectional comparisons use vector norms or scalar products as appropriate.

5. Time‐History (HYDRA)  
• HYDRA stores all echo‐step results under a single LC. Use parameter T to interpolate between time points.

6. Usage Examples  
– Envelope of support force, positive extremes:  
 LC 1001 ; LC 1010 KIND TMAX COLO C13 1001 C14 −1 ; NODE SZ  
– Minima, negative extremes:  
 …AND LC 1001 ; LC 1010 KIND TMIN COLO C13 −1 C14 1001 ; NODE SZ  
– Difference between service (DESI 2) and ultimate (DESI 1):  
 LC DESI 2 ; LC DESI 1 KIND DIF QUAD ASLH

This table underpins all load-case–linked extractions, filtering by direction, material, safety factors and inter‐case comparisons, ensuring consistent, reproducible results in post‐processing and design checks.

sections: 3.36 LC – Selection of a Load Case

content:
The excerpted input‐table defines two fields—KIND and TITL—that control, respectively, how load‐case results are compared and how they are labeled in the legend.  It appears as part of the LC record in AQUA/AQB commands (see also LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT) and uses a four-column layout: Item, Description, Unit and Default.  

1.  Item = KIND  
    •  Purpose: Specifies the type of comparison or aggregation to perform when two load cases (LC) or a range of load cases are involved.  If omitted, no comparison is done.  
    •  Description: “Kind of comparison of results.”  Internally the field is treated as a literal (Unit = LIT).  
    •  Default: “–” (no comparison).  
    •  Valid values:  
       – “–”  
          No comparison—results for the specified LC are displayed unchanged.  
       – AMX  
          Absolute maximum of two specified LCs.  Compares magnitudes and returns the larger absolute value.  
       – MAX  
          Maximum of two specified LCs (sign preserved).  
       – MIN  
          Minimum of two specified LCs (sign preserved).  
       – DIF  
          Difference between two specified LCs (LC1 – LC2).  
       – DIV  
          Division of two specified LCs (LC1 ÷ LC2).  
       – ADD  
          Sum of two specified LCs.  
       – TAMX  
          Absolute maximum over a range of LCs.  
       – TMAX  
          Maximum over a range of LCs.  
       – TMIN  
          Minimum over a range of LCs.  
       – TADD  
          Sum over a range of LCs.  
    •  Notes:  
       – When directional quantities (e.g. displacements, forces) are compared, global direction components are used.  For DIV the scalar value is used; for multiplication of two vector quantities, the scalar (dot) product is formed and the resulting direction calculated from the normalized product vector.  
       – To create envelopes of extremes across nonlinear analyses or design sequences, the KIND record is combined with two LC lines (e.g. LC 1001 ; LC 1010 KIND TMAX for the positive envelope, then KIND TMIN for the negative).  

2.  Item = TITL  
    •  Purpose: Defines the text that appears in the legend for the load case.  
    •  Description: “Designation of the load case in the legend (default as in the database).”  
    •  Unit: Literal up to 24 characters (LIT24).  
    •  Default: “*” (uses the database’s stored name for that load case).  
    •  Usage:  
       – When a custom or more descriptive name is required in the output legend, specify TITL followed by the text string.  
       – If omitted or “*” is used, the program fetches and displays the standard name stored in the LC database.  

Together, KIND and TITL give users fine‐grained control over how multiple load-case results are combined (maxima, minima, sums, differences, etc.) and how they are annotated in plots or tables.  They are typically specified immediately after the LC numbers in an AQUA input deck, for example:  
  LC 1001 ; LC 1010 KIND TMAX COLO C13 1001 C14 -1 ; NODE SZ  
or  
  LC DESI 2 ; LC DESI 1 KIND DIF QUAD ASLH TITL “Service–Ultimate Difference”

content:
The input of a load case or a design load case has an effect at the representation of all results which are stored in reference to the load case.. Reinforcements, design stresses from the program BEMESS and beam stresses from the pro- gram AQB are represented with the input of the design load case. All other load case–wisely stored results are addressed by NO..
 The program HYDRA stores all intermediate results (ECHO STEP) of a transient calculation with the same load case number. The selection of specific time values has to occur with the parameter T. The results are interpolated linearly, if T lies between two available time values.
 In the case of composite materials (beams) the results for the different materials are available with the same load case number or design case number. A specific material can be selected with MAT. If MAT is not input, the material first found is used. All materials are used if _MID, _MAX, _MIN, _AMX, _AMN, _LST and _SUM (for beam bond force only) are input. Only the materials of the same type and classification are used if a reference material in item REF is input.
 In the case of nonlinear material laws (area and volume elements from program TALPA / ASE) the results for the different material laws are available with the same load case number. A specific material law can be selected with NMAT. If NMAT is not input, the material law first found is used.
 Literals of several concrete laws:
 EC_C EC2 standard Concrete (C)
 ECLC EC2 Light weight Concrete (LC)
 ECCE EC2 elastic no tension Concrete (CE)
 ECDA EC2 deformation A Concrete
 ECDB EC2 deformation B Concrete
