Below is a structured, human‐readable description of the DSGN table and its fields. It explains what each parameter does, which values are allowed, what units apply, and what defaults are used. This text can be indexed in your RAG vector store to help users understand and query representation settings.  
   
1.  Table Context  
    •  The DSGN record governs how results (forces, moments, displacements, etc.) are drawn in post-processing: arrowheads, line segments, vector lengths, offsets, and so on.  
    •  It works together with other schema records (e.g. ARRO, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT).  
    •  See also the technical notes at the end (footnotes 1 and 2 below).  

2.  Fields of the DSGN Record  

    2.1  TYPE  (no units, default = ALL)  
         –  Defines which kinds of representations will be shown. Only the first TYPE designator in a sequence is used; subsequent values in the same input line are ignored.  
         –  Allowed literals:  
            •  ALL – draw every available representation (vectors, lines, areas)  
            •  SING – only draw single/vector (arrow) symbols  
            •  LINE – only line-shaped (no area fill) symbols  
            •  AREA – only area-shaped (filled or shaded) symbols  

    2.2  DTYP  (no units, default = LT)  
         –  Determines the orientation (direction) of the drawn symbol.  
         –  Can be a named axis, a gravity/reference direction, or a local vs. global axis.  
         –  Literals include:  
            •  X, Y, Z – Local element axes (x, y, z)  
            •  XX, YY, ZZ – Global coordinates X, Y, Z  
            •  URIC – Default local direction (as defined by the element’s local system)  
            •  EG – Gravity load direction (global downward)  
            •  BX, BY – Horizontal and vertical relative to the picture plane  
            •  PP, PQ, EP, EQ – Perpendicular variants for line-elements (right-hand side PP, then PQ; upwards EP, then EQ)  
            •  NM – “Normal” orientation: for line elements this equals PP; otherwise equals BX  

    2.3  LENG  (no units, default = –)  
         –  If specified, forces all symbols to this fixed length, independent of data magnitude.  
         –  Overrides both LMAX and LMIN.  

    2.4  LMAX  (cm, default = 10)  
         –  Maximum length allowed for drawn symbols.  
         –  Prevents very large result values from overrunning the plot.  
         –  If a vector would exceed LMAX, its line-style is switched to LFRB (footnote 2).  

    2.5  LMIN  (cm, default = 0)  
         –  Minimum symbol length. Ensures very small result values remain visible.  

    2.6  DIST  (cm or unitless “–”, default = 0)  
         –  Offset distance from the element’s start point.  
         –  Works like the SCH2 record’s DX/DY/DZ offsets, but applies along the element.  

    2.7  DISX, DISY  (– / no default)  
         –  Define the direction (as a 3D vector or DTYP literal) in which the DIST offset is applied.  
         –  DISX corresponds to the X-component of the offset direction; DISY to the Y-component.  
         –  Together with a third optional coordinate (DZ), you can build an arbitrary offset vector.  

3.  Footnotes / Special Notes  

    1.  Each result type (stress, deflection, force arrows, etc.) has a default “useful” drawing direction. DTYP lets you override it.  
    2.  If your result values vary greatly, setting LMAX ensures the largest arrows don’t clutter the view. Exceeding arrows are drawn with line style LFRB. LMIN makes the smallest arrows legible. Specifying LENG forces every arrow to the same length.  

See also ARRO, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT for related graphical‐control records.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the input table (DSGN sub-record) that controls various aspects of how load-vector representations are drawn in the RAG-vector store.  This table assumes you are already familiar with the related records ARRO, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT (which supply the geometry and result values); DSGN merely tunes the graphical look and feel.

1. Table structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the mnemonic code for the parameter.  
     – Description: what the parameter does, including any special rules or references to other records.  
     – Unit: the unit of measurement or “LIT” for literal values.  
     – Default: the value assumed when the item is omitted.  

2. Cross-references  
   • GFRB’s colour key uses the same palette as record COLO.  
   • TABS takes the same literal‐direction format as SCH2 DTYP.  
   • LFRB works together with LMAX (from the main representation record) to mark truncated arrows.  

3. Items  

  • DISZ  
    – Description: (no description supplied)  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: “–” (unused or reserved)  
    – Notes: This slot exists in the schema but carries no documented effect in the current release.  

  • GFRB  
    – Description: Colour of the “zero‐point” reference line (the baseline of the arrow when the result value is zero).  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 8001  
    – Details: Supply an integer colour key per the COLO record. If omitted, colour 8001 is used.  

  • LFRB  
    – Description: Line-type for arrow segments that have been cut off because they exceed the maximum length LMAX.  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 4  
    – Details: When a vector’s computed length (based on result magnitude) would overshoot the picture boundary, it is truncated at LMAX and drawn with this line type.  

  • EXCE  
    – Description: Factor controlling the display of load eccentrics (offsets).  
      * EXCE > 0: always draw eccentric arrows  
      * EXCE = 0: never draw them  
      * EXCE < 0: draw only if the load direction differs from the eccentricity direction  
    – Unit: –  
    – Default: 1.0  
    – Details: A multiplicative factor applied internally; by default (1.0) all eccentrics are shown.  

  • TABS  
    – Description: Type of the “distance‐at‐start” annotation (the little offset arrow or marker at the foot of the load). Uses the same syntax as SCH2 DTYP.  
    – Unit: LIT  
    – Default: “–” (none)  
    – Details: You can specify X, Y, Z, XX, YY, ZZ, EG, BX, BY, PP, PQ, EP, EQ, NM – exactly as you would for DTYP on a SCH2 record – to choose how the starting‐point arrow aligns.  

  • ADD  
    – Description: obsolete  
    – Unit:  
    – Default:  
    – Details: This field remains only for backwards compatibility; it has no effect in new drawings.  

4. How it all fits together  
   – The primary representation parameters (TYPE, DTYP, LENG, LMAX, LMIN, DIST, DVAR, DISX, DISY) define what arrows/vectors get drawn and in which direction, and how long.  
   – DSGN’s fields fine-tune visual styling: base‐line colour (GFRB), cut‐off style (LFRB), eccentric arrow logic (EXCE), and optional start‐offset markers (TABS).  
   – If you omit any DSGN items, the defaults above are used, ensuring consistent appearance across diagrams without extra input.

See also: ARRO, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT

A maximum length can be defined with LMAX in order prevented that large representations reach over the picture edge in the case of very different values. The rep- resentation is marked at such points with an other line type LFRB. A minimum value of the length LMIN can be input in order to make also very small representations more clearly. This table defines the parameters you can use to control how vectors (for example, load arrows or result‐direction arrows) are drawn in different types of graphical representations (single‐vector, line‐shaped, area‐shaped).  Each row (Item) names one input parameter; the Description column tells you what it does; Unit tells you the expected units or literal type; Default gives the value used if you don’t override it.

1. TYPE (LIT, default = ALL)  
   – Selects which kinds of representations the input applies to:  
     • ALL: all representation types  
     • SING: only single/vector symbols  
     • LINE: only line‐shaped results (e.g. bending‐moment diagrams)  
     • AREA: only area‐shaped results (e.g. surface‐load fields)

2. KIND (LIT, default = STAN)  
   – Defines the arrow‐head “style” for the primary direction in the view.  
   – STAN invokes a built-in shape (differs by result type).  
   – Or supply your own four‐letter literal.  The four letters code:  
     1st char – arrow‐head shape (underscore for none; O open arrow; P solid arrow; I transverse line; J/L/M/N for half‐page symbols; etc.)  
     2nd char – multiple‐head count (_, 2, 3, 4)  
     3rd char – extra transverse‐line count behind or at the end (_; 1, 2, 3; E–H for end‐lines)  
     4th char – bit‐pattern (0–9, A–Z) selecting insertion point (begin/end/center), rotated direction, two‐sided heads, separate pos/neg heads, etc.

3. KIN2 / KIN3 (LIT, defaults = KIND)  
   – Exactly like KIND, but control the arrow‐head style for the 2nd and 3rd vector directions in a 3D result.

4. LENG (cm/–, defaults = –0.2 for TYPE SING/AREA; –1.2 otherwise)  
   – Arrow‐head length:  
     • > 0 ⇒ absolute length in cm  
     • < 0 ⇒ fraction of vector length (for single/area) or spacing of direction vectors (for line plots)

5. WIDE (cm/–, defaults = –0.15 for TYPE SING/AREA; –0.8 otherwise)  
   – Arrow‐head width, same conventions as LENG.

6. DOUB (cm/–, default = –0.33)  
   – For multiple‐head arrows (when 2nd char of KIND>1), this is the distance from one head to the next:  
     • > 0 in cm  
     • < 0 as factor of LENG

7. CROS (cm/–, default = –0.25)  
   – Distance of any transverse‐line markers (the small crossbars you can add behind the head or at the shaft).

8. UKIN (LIT)  
   – When TYPE = SING is viewed “from above,” a single‐vector collapses to a point.  UKIN lets you draw a distinct top‐view symbol instead.  Give a three‐letter literal where:  
     1st char – symbol shape (_ none; + addition‐sign; C cross; S star; K polygon; Q square; R lozenge; V force‐vector special; M moment symbol)  
     2nd char – multiplicity (_, 2, 3)  
     3rd char – filled or not (_, filled)

9. FKIN (LIT)  
   – For TYPE = LINE only: controls whether the result “fill” is drawn with complete arrows or just discrete heads.  Supply another four-letter code, for example:  
     • C…: complete drawing of arrow tails plus heads  
     • …T: draw some heads at intervals (using FDIL spacing)  
     • …S: like T, but apply offset at the start  
     • …H: always print heads even if only half‐vector distance is available  
     • …L: place arrows in the middle of lines only when their direction is parallel to the line (otherwise draw them rectangular to the line)

Additional global inputs (not in this excerpt) let you set:  
• ARRO: overall arrow‐spacing or scaling (positive = cm, negative = factor of arrow length)  
• a “beginning” offset (positive = cm, negative = factor of FDIL)  
• default load‐arrow styles for line‐filling vs. area‐corner arrows.

By combining these parameters—TYPE to pick where it applies; KIND/KIN2/KIN3 to select head shapes and multiplicity; LENG, WIDE to size them; DOUB, CROS to space additional elements; UKIN to override single‐vector top‐view; FKIN to adjust line‐fill—you gain full control over how vector and load graphics appear in your RAG visuals.

The input “ARRO” table governs how RAG’s vector‐arrow representations are to be drawn in both line and area (surface) result plots.  It defines numerical defaults and three distinct four‐ or three‐character “literal” codes (KIND, FKIN, UKIN/UKI2/UKI3) that fully specify arrow‐head style, multiplicity, ancillary strokes, insertion‐point behavior and—in the special case of top‐view single‐vector symbols—shape and filling.  Below is a breakdown of each part of the table:

1. Numerical Defaults  
   • “>0” and “<0” columns  
     – “>0” entry gives the default positive‐load arrow spacing (in centimeters) or, if negative, as a fraction of the overall arrow‐length parameter LENG.  
     – “<0” entry gives the default negative‐load arrow offset (in centimeters) or, if negative, as a fraction of FDIL (the distance between repeated arrow heads in long vectors).  
   • These defaults are used when no explicit FKIN or KIND directives override them.

2. KIND (4‐letter code for load arrows)  
   Used for both line‐type and area‐type (corner) load arrows.  Its four positions each carry a very specific meaning—unused positions are underscored “_”:

   Position 1: Arrow‐head shape  
     • “_” no head  
     • I, J, K … transverse/barred line (full‐ or half‐page, left/right)  
     • O open arrow  
     • P closed (outline) arrow  
     • Q filled (solid) arrow  
     • L, M, N, R, S, T half‐page variants  

   Position 2: Head multiplicity  
     • “_” single head  
     • 2 double head  
     • 3 triple head  
     • 4 quadruple head  

   Position 3: Extra transverse lines  
     • “_” none  
     • 1–3 that many lines immediately behind the head  
     • E–H 1–4 lines at the vector’s tail end  

   Position 4: Bit‐pattern flags (0–9, A–Z → decimal 0–37)  
     Flags add (by bit) the following behaviors:  
       – +1 rotate head direction  
       – +2 heads on both ends  
       – +4 insert‐point at arrow center  
       – +8 separate heads for positive vs. negative loads  
       – +16 insert‐point at arrow start  
       – (value 0 means default end insertion)

3. UKIN / UKI2 / UKI3 (3‐letter code for single‐vector top views)  
   When TYPE=SING in a top‐view, vectors collapse to a symbol.  The three positions are:

   Position 1: Symbol shape  
     • “_” point  
     • + addition sign  
     • C cross  
     • S star  
     • K polygon  
     • Q square  
     • R lozenge  
     • V force out‐of‐plane (× or □ depending on direction)  
     • M moment  

   Position 2: Multiplicity  
     • “_” single  
     • 2 double  
     • 3 triple  

   Position 3: Fill  
     • “_” outline only  
     • (any other char) filled  

4. FKIN (4‐letter code for line‐representation fill with arrows)  
   Controls whether, and how, arrows are drawn along lines (e.g. beam shear diagrams).  Common flags:

   • C: complete arrows (tail + head at every FDIL interval)  
   • T: place arrows at regular FDIL intervals  
   • S: “T” plus offset at start, obeying FDIS rules  
   • H: even if only half‐vector space is available, still draw heads  
   • L: center the arrows on the line if the load direction is parallel to the line (or view direction); without L, heads sit perpendicular to the line  

Usage Workflow:  
 1. The RAG‐loader reads ARRO’s >0/<0 defaults.  
 2. If a KIND literal is supplied in the load record, its four sub‐fields override the shape, multiplicity, strokes and insertion‐point behavior.  
 3. For single, out‐of‐plane vectors, UKIN (or variants) governs the top‐view symbol.  
 4. When drawing forces/moments along lines, FKIN syntax determines head placement and density.  

Together, these parameters let users finely control arrow‐based result plots—selecting open vs. closed heads, single vs. multi‐headed arrows, decorative transverse strokes, where heads are anchored, and how collapsing “point” vectors are symbolized in plan (top) view.

The table under consideration defines a set of formatting parameters for arrow-based result visualizations (e.g. forces, moments) in line or single-vector representations.  Each row lists

•  Item – the parameter name used in the control deck  
•  Description – what aspect of the arrow (“head,” “spacing,” “fill,” etc.) it governs  
•  Unit – the physical or unitless measure expected  
•  Default – the value assumed when the parameter is omitted  

Below is a detailed, row-by-row description of each parameter:

1.  UKIN (LIT, default “*”)  
    – Kind of arrow‐head symbol used in the view for single vectors (TYPE SING).  
    – If STAN (standard) is off for the general KIND setting, you may supply a three‐letter literal (e.g. “Q2E”) to override the default arrow style.  

2.  UKI2 (LIT, default = UKIN)  
    – Arrow‐head kind for the second vector direction when multiple directions are shown (analogous to KIND).  

3.  UKI3 (LIT, default = UKIN)  
    – Arrow‐head kind for the third vector direction.  

4.  UPRO (–, default = 1.0)  
    – Ratio of top‐view symbol size (measured across its diagonals) to the actual vector length.  
    – Affects how large a “point,” “square,” “star,” etc. appears relative to the arrow length.  

5.  UWID (–, default = 1.0)  
    – Aspect ratio (length‐to‐width) of the top‐view symbol.  
    – Controls elongation of shapes chosen via UKIN/UKI2/UKI3 when seen in plan.  

6.  UDIS (cm/–, default = –0.15)  
    – Separation between multiple top‐view symbols (for double/triple‐headed arrows).  
    – If >0: an absolute spacing in cm (max 1/3 of symbol size).  
    – If <0: a fractional spacing relative to symbol size.  

7.  FKIN (LIT, default “*”)  
    – Filling style for line-type representations (TYPE LINE).  
    – STAN/WING: default fill behavior.  
    – NO: disables fill.  
    – Or supply a four-letter literal to define exactly which arrow segments and heads to draw (see main KIND definitions).  

8.  FDIC (cm, default = 0.25)  
    – Lateral offset (perpendicular to the vector direction) for drawing auxiliary direction vectors.  
    – Ensures that multiple arrowheads or mid-span “filling” arrows don’t all overlap on the centerline.  

9.  FDIL (cm/–, default = –1.5)  
    – Longitudinal spacing between successive arrow heads along a line.  
    – If >0: absolute distance in cm.  
    – If <0: interpreted as a multiple of the arrow-head length (LENG).  

10. FDIS (cm/–, default = –0.5)  
    – Shift offset for arrow-head placement near the start of a vector (for complex filling rules).  
    – If >0: absolute in cm.  
    – If <0: relative to FDIL (entering the same factor convention).  

General notes:  
– Positive values in any “cm/–” column are treated as absolute lengths in centimeters. Negative values denote relative factors (fractions or multiples of a reference dimension such as LENG, FDIL, or symbol size).  
– Literal parameters (UKIN, FKIN, etc.) accept alphabetic sequences where each position encodes a discrete visual feature (arrow‐head shape, multiplicity, transverse lines, bit‐pattern flags for dual‐headed arrows, rotation, etc.). Unused positions must be filled with “_.”  
– For top-view single vectors (TYPE SING) that collapse to a point, UKIN/UKI2/UKI3 govern the plan-symbol form (point, cross, polygon, lozenge, etc.), multiplicity, and fill.  
– See also related table sections (DSGN, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT, and ARRO) for complementary parameters on global styles, beam fractures, area results, isolation elements, and sectional loading.

See also: DSGN, STRU, LOAD, NODE, BEAM, QUAD, ISOL, SECT

The table defines the “LIST” record—a set of output‐control items used when GRAPHIC (or RESULTVIEWER) prints or exports result lists (e.g. via DLST or DLCT in QUAD/BEAM drawings).  Only currently valid and selected elements (by SELE, GRP, BOX or SEL records) appear in these lists.  Depending on whether you mix lists with real graphics on the same page or generate standalone reports (PLB or ERG files), the LIST settings determine which headers, subtitles and other annotations are printed.  

Structure of the table:  
• Four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—list every adjustable sub‐item of the LIST record.  
• Items of type LIT expect literal values (NO, YES, FULL, or custom text).  Other items are either bit‐patterns or are obsolete.  

Items in detail:  
1.  HEAD (unit = LIT; default = YES)  
   • Controls printing of the main result title.  
   • “NO” suppress headers entirely.  
   • “YES” print header only when a new picture/page begins or when the result type changes.  
   • “FULL” always print, regardless of context.  

2.  DATE (LIT; default = NO)  
   • When YES, prints the date on the list head.  

3.  DB (LIT; default = NO)  
   • Print database name if set to YES.  

4.  SYST (LIT; default = NO)  
   • Print the kind of system.  

5.  LCS (LIT; default = YES)  
   • List the loadcases.  

6.  SELE, ELEM, FACT, DIFF, MINV, RANG, TOTA (all obsolete)  
   • These sub‐items are no longer active; no unit or default applies.  

7.  CHEA (LIT; default = YES)  
   • Print column titles (headings of result columns).  

8.  SHEA (LIT; default = YES)  
   • Print subtitles for the current result.  Accepts the same literals as HEAD (NO, YES, FULL).  

9.  ADDT (LIT; default = “*”)  
   • Selects the kind of additional control to apply:  
      – LC for load‐case–specific listing  
      – SEL for selection listing (obsolete)  

10.  ADDV (unitless; default = +3)  
   • Bit‐pattern controlling which extra details appear in the list:  
     • For ADDT=LC:  
        +1 include “kind of load case” column  
        +2 include “action type” column  
     • For ADDT=SEL (if used):  
        +1 show selection designation  
        +2 list groups  
        +4 list BOXes  
        +8 list individual selected elements  

Usage notes (from additional context):  
- Before printing/exporting in GRAPHIC, you must set DLST or DLCT in the drawing orders (QUAD/BEAM).  
- Only currently selected items (SELE, GRP, BOX, SEL) are reported.  
- Lists may be sent to the LST file via GRAPHIC’s “File→Export values list” command.  
- If mixing lists and graphics, LIST’s DIST and margin items (MRGL, MRGR, MRGU, MRGD) control spacing.  
- Standalone list reports appear in the PLB file (ASE‐style chapter).  If “No PLB reports” is enabled in WPS (during WING input calculation), they go to the ERG ASCII file instead.

The input table (“LIST”) is a parameter table used by several structural‐graphics and post‐processing modules (GRAPHIC, RESULTVIEWER, WPS, etc.) to control the formatting, content and destination of printed lists of finite‐element results.  Below is a breakdown of its overall structure and the semantics of each field.

1. Overall Schema  
   •  Columns:  
     – Parameter: the literal name of the LIST field.  
     – Description: what this field controls in the output.  
     – Allowed Values: the set of permissible inputs (e.g. NO/YES/FULL, numeric).  
     – Default/Behavior: how the program behaves if the field is omitted or set to a particular literal.  
     – Affected Output: which file(s) or viewing mode(s) this parameter influences (LST‐file, PLB, ERG, on‐screen graphics).

   •  Rows: one per LIST parameter.  In total there are 12–14 parameters, each toggling a different aspect of the list‐printing process.

2. Key Parameters and Their Roles  
   1. HEAD  
      – Controls printing of list header lines (column titles, record IDs, etc.).  
      – Values: NO (suppress always), YES (prints only when data change or when AND=TRUE), FULL (always prints headers per layer).  
      – Default: depends on module; typically YES.  
      – Affects: LST and PLB output.

   2. DATE, DB, SYST, LCS, CHEA  
      – Each toggles inclusion of a standard head‐line item:  
         • DATE: time stamp of data.  
         • DB: database identifier.  
         • SYST: system or solution identifier.  
         • LCS: local coordinate system label.  
         • CHEA: check code or chemical flag.  
      – Values: NO (suppress) or YES (include).  
      – HEAD=NO will suppress all regardless of these flags.

   3. AND  
      – Logical “glue” for HEAD/DATE/… items: when AND=YES, headers are printed only if something has changed since the last layer; when AND=NO, headers obey only the individual literals.  
      – Values: YES/NO.  
      – Interacts with HEAD and FULL to reduce repetitive header printing in multi‐layer diagrams.

   4. DIST  
      – “Distance” (line spacing) when lists are overlaid on graphical views.  
      – Numeric (e.g. mm or points).  
      – Applied only in mixed pages (graphics + lists).

   5. MRGL, MRGR, MRGU, MRGD  
      – Page margins (Left, Right, Up, Down) for lists that are painted alongside graphics.  
      – Numeric (length units).  
      – Ignored when pure ASCII lists are sent to PLB or ERG.

3. File‐Destination Behavior  
   •  LST file export: when using GRAPHIC→File→”Export values list,” the LIST table’s settings determine which parameters appear, how often headers repeat, and margin placement if the list is drawn.  
   •  PLB file: if mixed with real graphics, LIST margins and DIST are honored; otherwise, lists get their own chapter, formatted like ASE static reports.  
   •  ERG (ASCII) file: produced only if “No PLB reports” is toggled in WPS, in which case all lists bypass PLB and go to ERG in plain text.

4. Selection and Filtering  
   •  Only elements currently selected by SELE, GRP, BOX or SEL records are listed.  
   •  When a structural representation type (DLST/DLCT) is active (e.g. via QUAD or BEAM drawing orders), the LIST table ensures that nodes and elements are enumerated in the same sequence as the graphical cut‐sections.

5. Usage Notes  
   – A “0” input to numeric fields (DIST, margins) can be interpreted as “no limit” or default spacing, depending on the module.  
   – FULL is most often used in debugging or very detailed layer‐by‐layer printouts, whereas NO/YES are used in routine batch runs to minimize redundant headers and save paper.  
   – Consistency across modules: although some programs ignore DIST/MRG*, all respect HEAD/DATE/… for controlling whether any list header lines are printed at all.

In summary, the LIST table defines a compact, 5-column by ~12-row control matrix that drives whether, how often and where the program prints textual result lists—either interspersed with graphics (honoring distance and margin settings) or as standalone ASCII tables in the LST/PLB/ERG files.

The table under discussion defines the set of parameters (items) available in the LIST record of the GRAPHIC module (or RESULTVIEWER) to control how result–lists are laid out, which columns appear, and how they are paged or printed.  It is organized into four columns:  

1. “Item”  
   – The mnemonic name of the control parameter you set in the LIST record.  

2. “Description”  
   – A brief explanation of what each parameter does.  For the special case of SUPP (suppress outputs), each bit of the integer value toggles a particular column or block of data on or off.  

3. “Unit”  
   – The physical unit or “–” if unitless.  Margins are in cm, spacing and counts are unitless.  

4. “Default”  
   – The default setting applied if you do not override it in your input.  

Detailed breakdown of each item:  

• SUPP  
  • Type: integer bit-pattern  
  • Function: suppresses individual output columns or blocks in the printed list.  
  • Bits and their meanings:  
    +1   → omit the “LC” column  
    +2   → omit the “Title” column  
    +4   → omit the “Edges” output  
    +8   → omit the “Areas” output  
    +16  → omit the “Material” output  
    +32  → omit the “Coordinate” output  
    +64  → omit the “local Direction” results  
    +128 → omit the “global Direction” results  
  • Unit: – (unitless integer)  
  • Default: +1+64+128 (i.e. suppress LC column, local Direction, and global Direction by default)  

• DIST  
  • Type: real number  
  • Function: sets the factor of line spacing when lists are “painted” together with real graphics on the same page.  A larger value increases the vertical gap between list lines.  
  • Unit: – (unitless multiplier)  
  • Default: 0.4  

• MRGL, MRGR, MRGU, MRGD  
  • Type: real numbers  
  • Function: define page margins around the list when it is mixed with graphics:  
     MRGL = left margin  
     MRGR = right margin  
     MRGU = top margin  
     MRGD = bottom margin  
  • Unit: cm  
  • Default: 0.5 cm for each side  

• LINE  
  • Type: integer  
  • Function: maximum number of lines per list page.  A setting of 0 means “no limit,” so the list will continue on the same page or chapter unless graphic pagination intervenes.  
  • Unit: – (unitless count)  
  • Default: 0 (no limit)  

How these interact with the overall LIST record (longer description from context):  
- HEAD, DATE, DB, SYST, LCS and CHEA control the printing of various header lines.  You may suppress all headers by setting them to NO, force them always by FULL, or allow them to appear only when associated layers change (YES).  
- When “painting” lists alongside real graphics, DIST and the four MRG* margins dictate precise positioning.  Otherwise the list is placed in its own chapter in the PLB file (or ERG text file if “No PLB reports” was enabled in WPS).  
- Records DLST or DLCT must be active in the drawing orders (e.g. QUAD, BEAM) to trigger the list export in RESULTVIEWER mode.  

Together, these LIST parameters give you fine control over which data fields appear in your printed or exported lists, how they are spaced, and how they coexist with graphical output—key for clear documentation of structural analysis results.

The table defines the input fields (Items) that control how structural elements and their annotations are represented in the output. It has four columns:  
• Item – the parameter name  
• Description – what it does and any literal codes it accepts  
• Unit – data type (mostly LIT for literal codes)  
• Default – the default value if you omit the field  

1. NUME (Unit=LIT, Default=–)  
  – Controls the overall element representation in the drawing. You supply one or more literal codes from a predefined list (see also: AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO, STRU, line, SCHH).  
  • DSGN: set only input values, no actual drawing  
  • NO: omit any drawing of the structure  
  • …plus additional codes to toggle display of axes, labels, supports, etc.  

2. NUMN (Unit=LIT, Default=–)  
  – When NUME is active, NUMN selects which element type it applies to (e.g. BEAM, QUAD, BRIC) or defines a specific node‐representation variant.  

3. OFFE, OFFN (Unit=LIT, Default=–)  
  – These two fields are now obsolete. Use the SCH2 OFFS record instead to shift element offsets.  

4. MARK (Unit=LIT, Default=–)  
  – Obsolete. Use COL2 C4 to control marker symbols and colours.  

5. MFIX (Unit=LIT, Default=–)  
  – Obsolete. Use COL2 C5 to define fixed‐support symbol styles.  

6. FACS (Unit=–, Default=1.0)  
  – “Factor for cross‐section contours.” When beam cross‐sections are drawn with full geometry (from AQUA), FACS scales them relative to the system scale.  

7. OPTI (Unit=LIT, Default=LONG)  
  – A multi‐code field for various representation options; codes may be combined in a single string.  
  • NO: clear all options  
  • PART: generate one picture per cutting‐pattern area  
  • WARP: orient the material’s warp direction upward in pattern views  
  • LONG: use full (long) axis text instead of short IDs  
  • PLON: use full placement text instead of IDs  

8. FILL (Unit=LIT, Default=NO)  
  – Determines fill‐type for elements, number backgrounds or cut areas. Accepted codes:  
  • NO: no fill, use simple outline colours  
  • VARC: no fill, variable outline colours based on value sign  
  • AREA: fill areas with variable colour shading  
  • VERT: for line‐representations, hatch perpendicular to baseline  
  • PARA: for line‐representations, hatch parallel to baseline  

Use these fields in your RAG‐store input to precisely control which structural components are drawn, how cross‐sections are scaled, which textual labels appear, and how fills or hatches are applied.

The input table is essentially the definition and parameter‐listing for the “STRU” record in a structural‐analysis/drawing program. It groups dozens of liter­als (fields) into functional blocks, specifies their units or default values, and—in some cases—enumerates permissible codes. Below is a structured walkthrough of its main sections:

1. General Annotation and Layout  
   • SCHH: Text size for annotation (dimension: cm/LT; default 0.16).  
   • NO/YES/“_”/>0: Flags controlling whether element designations appear, and if so whether the size is given explicitly in cm or uses defaults.  

2. Contour Generation (BCON, WCON)  
   • BCON: Which element‐edge types to test when building the outline. Default = “WING.”  
   • WCON: Further filters on edges (default “WING”) or a 4-letter literal.  
   • Edge‐type codes:  
     – M: intersection of ≥3 edges (e.g. T-profile)  
     – D: step in plate thickness  
     – K: local coordinate change  
     – G: omit globally uniform support symbols  
     – AGLA: geometric angle of a surface break  
   • FROM/TO/INC: Specify numeric ranges for numbering (defaults = smallest/largest/1.0).  

3. Hinting (HINT)  
   • Length unit = LT (grd, –/LT, cm).  
   • Default hint length = 0.0005 (DEFA).  
   • Hint color drawn via COLO record.  

4. Element‐Type Selection (STRU NUME)  
   A single code applies to all element types unless overridden by NUMN. A “*” in the right‐hand column flags types that can be individually selected.  
   – DSLN: design line elements  
   – BEAM (B), SPRI (S), TRUS (T), CABL (C), TUBE (P), QUAD (Q), BRIC (V), BOUN (R)  
   – EDGE nodal sequences, tendons (QTEN, BTEN, DTEN), external sections (SIR), points (GPT), lines (GLN), areas (GAR), volumes (GVO)  

5. Cross‐Section / Material Properties  
   For each element type the table may expose:  
   • GMRN: reinforcement material number  
   • AY, AZ: shear‐deformation areas (m²)  
   • YSMP, ZSMP: coordinates of shear center (m)  
   • AGAM: mass per length (kg/m)  
   • Plastic ultimate forces (design values, with safety-factors): NPL, VYPL, VZPL, MTPL, MYPL, MZPL (kN, kNm); plastic centers YSPC/ZSPC (mm)  
   • Plastic characteristic forces (no safety factor): NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD (kN, kNm)  
   • EIZE: elastic bending stiffness EIz (kNm²)  

6. Subsection: BEAM Sections and Elements  
   – XOUT: output cross‐section code  
   – EZMI/EZMA: position of duct axis relative to Z-max/Z-min  
   – NUMK for piles and bore profiles (BORE, BORA, BORT, BORL)  

7. Spring (NUMN SPRI)  
   – DP: damping constant (kNm/rad/m²)  
   – TSYR: area-related yield load (kN·sec/m, kNm/m²)  

8. Boundary Elements (NUMN BOUN)  
   – RDT: bedding stiffness in cross-local direction (kNm/m)  

9. Quad Elements (NUMN QUAD)  
   – ALFA: thermal expansion coefficient  
   – K1CS, K1TS, K1DI, K1MA, K1DA, K1TE, K1AN: Mohr-Coulomb and fracture parameters  
   – K2FS: friction angle for nonlinear behavior  
   – CUT: count of 3D cutting pattern areas  
   – CP2C, CP2S, CP2W: definitions for 2D cutting‐pattern contour and structure (with warp dir.)  

10. Reinforcement Definitions  
    – PRTP, PRST, PRGR, PRDF: reinforcement type, subtype, grading, definition  
    – MII, MIS: 3rd-layer disks and shear reinforcement (cm²/m², cm²/m)  
    – MAU*, COVU/L: maximum areas of upper/lower reinf. (cm²/m, mm)  
    – HRUQ/I, SGU*, SGL*: relative distances and stress limits (mm, MPa)  
    – WK2/3, SG1–3, SGA: reinforcement spacing and stress limits in principal directions  

11. Towers, Section Cuts (NUMN TOWR, QSEC, GSEC)  
    – ENO: cut number  

12. Additional Notes and Flags  
    • Cross‐section contours may be drawn instead of numbers (if imported from AQUA), optionally scaled by FACS.  
    • Local twisting (TWAR): difference between max/min node eccentricity to fitted incline.  
    • Fault‐plane parameters shown along meridian or descent angles.  
    • Beam hinges (BEAL) syntax: ‘h,n:i’  
    • Inverse shear resistances (WT, WVY, WVZ, WT2) used to avoid infinite-values.  
    • Foreground/background designation colors: COLO, COLB, FILL, FS, BS, BI, FI rules.  
    • Contour determination for QUAD/BRIC: edges classified as free, supported or fixed by BCON/WCON codes (ALL, FREE, PP, –PP, MM, –MM, PM, –PM, PF, etc.).  

By grouping fields into these thematic blocks, the table fully specifies how “STRU” controls both graphic‐output and calculation‐related parameters for all supported finite‐element types.

The table presented defines four configurable items within the STRU-SCHH record, each controlling how structural results are graphically represented.  For each item the table lists  
 •  the mnemonic (Item),  
 •  its purpose or detailed interpretation (Description),  
 •  the physical or logical unit (Unit), and  
 •  the default setting (Default).  

1.  ANGL  
 –  Description  
  “Maximum angle difference for contour buckling of a volume structure.”  
  •  If set to 0 grad, every change of geometry along adjacent element faces produces a separate contour line.  
  •  If set to 90 grad, no geometry break is considered—in effect all faces merge into a single contour.  
 –  Unit: grad (gradient, i.e. degrees‐scaled).  
 –  Default: 5 grad  

2.  REPR  
 –  Description  
  Selects the type of graphical representation for element‐based results.  The field accepts a literal (LIT) from the list below:  
  •  DSTR  –  Structure representation (wireframe or outline)  
  •  DTXT  –  Text labels at computed positions  
  •  DVEC  –  Vector plot (arrows showing magnitude and direction)  
  •  DLIN  –  Line plot (e.g. contour lines or isolines)  
  •  DARE  –  Area fill plot (color‐shaded regions)  
  •  DISO  –  Isoline representation  
  •  DCUT  –  Cutting line representation (sections)  
  •  DEDG  –  Distribution of values along a nodal sequence (edge‐based plots)  
  •  DREP  –  General “smart” choice: selects DVEC, DLIN or DARE automatically based on the element type and result field  
  •  DLST  –  Text list (data in tabular form)  
  •  DLCT  –  Text list of cut values (values at section cuts)  
  •  DLED  – Text list of distribution along nodal sequence  
 –  Unit: LIT (literal selection)  
 –  Default: *  (asterisk indicates that the program chooses a representation according to context)  

3.  BRIR  
 –  Description: obsolete (no longer in active use).  
 –  Unit: –  
 –  Default: –  

4.  UNIT  
 –  Description  
  Defines how numeric result values are scaled into a graphical length for representation purposes (for example, arrow length in a vector plot or bar length in a line plot).  Acceptable entries:  
  •  DEFA  –  Default scaling.  The largest graphic element will be approximately 2 cm long in the chosen output units.  
  •  LFAC  –  Use custom factor FACS when a length unit is defined.  
  •  LAST  –  Match the last used engineering unit from previous input of the same type.  
  •  > 0  –  A positive numeric value indicates which magnitude of the result field corresponds to exactly 1 cm of graphical length.  
  •  < 0  –  A negative numeric value indicates the approximate maximum length (in cm) of the largest result magnitude (rounded to a convenient engineering number).  
  •  < –1000  –  A special negative code invokes the default factor DEFA.  For example, –1002.5 yields a factor of 2.5.  
 –  Unit: –/cm/LT (the first “–” means no intrinsic physical unit; “cm” is the output graphic‐space length; “LT” denotes length‐type of the field).  
 –  Default: DEFA  

See also related commands and tables under AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO for naming and default‐value conventions; refer to record STRU line SCHH for background on “no‐designation” versus “designation,” text‐size scaling, and multi‐color foreground/background combinations.

The input “table’’ is in fact the definition of the STRU record used by the AQUA‐family of structural programs. It spans many pages and groups, but can be broken down into the following major blocks:

1. Header fields for drawing and designation  
   • SCHH – text size (unit cm/LT, default 0.16)  
   • NO/YES flags – suppress or enable designation text  
   • “_” and “>0” – switch to print designation in cm when > 0  
   • FROM / TO / INC – range and increment for numbering cross‐sections  
   • HINT – length hint for cut elements (uses COLO C20 colour record)

2. Contour generation parameters  
   • BCON – selects which element edge types to consider when building the graphic outline  
   • WCON – refines BCON via a 4-letter code or defaults (“DEFA” or “WING”)  
   • M, D, K – special contour lines: M for multi-edge (T-profiles), D for thickness steps, K where local coordinate system changes  
   • G – suppress global support symbols  
   • AGLA – geometric break angle in a volume surface

3. Structural element type codes (STRU NUME)  
   A table mapping literal names to single‐letter codes (marked “*” if user-selectable):  
   • DSLN – design elements  
   • BEAM (B), SPRI (S), TRUS (T), CABL (C), TUBE (P), QUAD (Q), BRIC (V), BOUN (R)  
   • EDGE sequences, tendons (QTEN, BTEN, DTEN), external sections (SIR), points (GPT X), lines (GLN L), areas (GAR A), volumes (GVO O)

4. System values for each element type (STRU NUMN)  
   a) General cross-section and reinforcement:  
     – GMRN: material number of reinforcement  
     – AY, AZ (shear areas), YSMP, ZSMP (shear centre coordinates), AGAM (mass/length)  
   b) Plastic ultimate forces (design values include safety factor):  
     – NPL, VYPL, VZPL, MTPL, MYPL, MZPL; plastic centre: YSPC, ZSPC  
   c) Plastic ultimate forces (characteristic, no safety factor):  
     – NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD  
   d) Elastic bending stiffness:  
     – EIZE (E·Iz)  

   e) Beam section outputs:  
     – XOUT (toggle), EZMI / EZMA (duct axis positions, m)  

   f) Special element sub‐types:  
     – Piles & bore profiles (NUMK): B, R, A, T, L  
     – Springs (NUMN SPRI): DP (damping const, kN·s/m), TSYR (yield load area)  
     – Boundary elements (NUMN BOUN): RDT (bedding stiffness)  
     – QUAD elements (NUMN QUAD): ALFA (thermal coeff), K1CS (cohesion), K1TS (strength), K1DI (dilatation), K1MA/DA/TE/AN (angles & fracture energy)—and secondary K2FS (friction), plus cutting patterns CP2C, CP2S, CP2W  
   g) Reinforcement definitions:  
     – PRTP, PRST (type/subtype), PRGR (grading), PRDF (definition)  
     – MII, MIS (3rd layer disks, shear bars), MAU* / MAUH / MAUQ / MAUI (upper rebars), COVU/COVL (cover), HRUQ/HRUI (relative distances), SG* (steel stress limits), WK2/WK3 (bar diameters), SGA/SG1/SG2/SG3 (stress limits)  

5. Additional system values  
   • NUMN TOWR – tower properties  
   • NUMN QSEC / GSEC – cuts through areas or volumes (ENO = cut number)  

6. Auxiliary notes and defaults  
   – STRU NUMN can also request full cross-section contours instead of numbers (if imported from AQUA); optional scale factor FACS  
   – TWAR – local twisting definition  
   – Fault‐plane orientation for QUAD/BRIC elements (meridian & descent angles)  
   – BEAL – beam hinges notation (‘h,law:i’)  
   – Inverse shear resistances (WT, WVY, WVZ, WT2) used in stress calc  
   – Colour and fill for designations (foreground via COLO / FS / FI, background via COLB / BS / BI, delete underlying)  
   – Final contour rules: any edge of QUAD/BRIC elements sharing a support is drawn unless filtered by BCON/WCON. Literals include ALL, FREE, PP, MM, PF, PM, MF, PMF, etc., to combine free, supported, fixed edges in various ways.

See also: AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO for related record definitions used in drawing annotations, defaults and arrow symbols.

1. FULL

   – Applicability: ALL element classes—beams (B), springs (S), truss bars (T), cables (C), tubes (P), quadrilateral shells (Q), brick/volume elements (V), boundary elements (R), nodal-sequence types (N), design/tendon elements (D) and external points/lines (E).

The input “table” is not a simple two-column listing but rather a flattened, annotated specification of a structural‐graphics record (record STRU) and its associated literals, defaults, units and element‐type‐specific parameters. It serves as the schema for a RAG-style vector store, defining everything from printed labelling and colour codes to geometry‐ and load-related properties for beams, shells, springs, boundary elements, etc. Below is a guided tour of its main sections:

1. General header and print/label controls  
   • SCHH, cm/LT, NO/YES, Designation, Text size, COLO/C20, FILL, DEFA, FS, FI, BI – these control whether a numbering or designation is printed, in what size, in which foreground/background colour, and with which fill pattern. Defaults (DEFA) are provided for each.

2. Contour-generation flags  
   • BCON and WCON define which element edges should generate the visible contour—literal options include ALL, FREE, PP, MM, PM, MF and negations (–PP, –MM, etc.).  
   • Additional flags (M, D, K, G, AGLA) specify special contour lines: multi-edge corners (M), thickness steps (D), local-coordinate breaks (K), globally-unsupported symbols (G), volume-surface angle breaks (AGLA).

3. Numbering range and hinting  
   • FROM/TO/INC define the first, last and increment of numbers drawn. Default is “smallest/largest from database” with step 1.  
   • HINT and LT record the “hint length” to draw for cut elements.

4. Element-type list (literal DSLN)  
   A master key maps shorthand codes to types—e.g.  
     – BEAM (B), SPRI (S), TRUS (T), CABL (C), TUBE (P), QUAD (Q), BRIC (V), BOUN (R)  
     – EDGE sequences (QTEN, BTEN, DTEN), external sections (SIR), points (GPT), lines (GLN), areas (GAR), volumes (GVO).  
   A “*” marks cases where a subspecialization (NUMN=…) can override the default NUME value.

5. System values per element type  
   For each type (controlled by NUMN or NUMK), a table of numeric parameters appears. For beams (NUMN=BEAM), for example:  
     – Cross–sectional shear areas AY, AZ (m²); shear-centre offsets YSMP, ZSMP (m); mass per length AGAM (kg/m)  
     – Fully plastic ultimate loads and moments (NPL, VYPL, VZPL, MTPL, MYPL, MZPL) in kN or kNm  
     – Plastic centres YSPC, ZSPC (mm)  
     – Characteristic (unfactored) values NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD (kN, kNm)  
     – Elastic bending stiffness EIZE in kNm²  
   Similar blocks follow for SPRI, BOUN, QUAD, GSEC, QSEC and special piles/bore profiles.

6. Reinforcement prescriptions (for plates/shells)  
   • PRTP, PRST, PRGR, PRDF define types and grading of reinforcement.  
   • Area densities MII, MIS, MAU*, MAUH, MAUQ, MAUI (cm²/m to cm²/m²), cover COVU/COVL (mm), layer offsets HRU* (mm).  
   • Steel stress limits SG*, SGL*, WK2/3 (mm) and global limits SGA, SG1–3 (MPa).

7. Special drawing and deformation flags  
   • Cross-section contours can be drawn (XOUT, FACS) or shown as numbers.  
   • Local twisting (TWAR) is computed as the eccentricity range of nodes to an inclined reference.  
   • Fault‐plane parameters (meridian/descent angles) control how cracks in QUAD or BRIC surfaces are visualized.  
   • Beam hinges (BEAL) use syntax ‘h,n:i’ to distinguish normal and implicit hinges.

8. Final summary table of top-level STRU literals  
   A four-column key shows for each literal (AXIS, MESH, GVO, GAR) its “X L A O” flags (–/–, * or blank) and its dimension (none in these cases).

Throughout, DEFA marks default values, “–” blanks, “*” selection possibilities. Units are explicitly noted (m, mm, kN/m², MPa, etc.), and every literal has an explicit “meaning” column. The fragment under scrutiny is the “Literal–Meaning–Applicability” lookup table used in the STRU record (and by extension in the structural‐drawing modules of a typical FE-pre/post-processor).  It defines every possible “literal” keyword (column 1) you can ask the program to print as a designation on element drawings, gives a human‐readable “Meaning” (column 2), specifies for which element classes each applies (column 3), and finally states its “Dim.” (column 4), i.e. its physical or unit‐less dimension.  

1.  Columns  
   •  Literal  
      –  A short all‐caps code you use in the input deck (e.g. ENO, GRP, COOR, SNO).  
   •  Meaning  
      –  A concise description of what gets printed (for example “Element numbers” or “Local x direction”).  
   •  Applicability (B S T C P Q V R N D E)  
      –  Eleven single-letter flags, each corresponding to an element family:  
         * B = BEAM elements  
         * S = SPRI (springs)  
         * T = TRUS (trusses)  
         * C = CABL (cables)  
         * P = TUBE (tubes/pipes)  
         * Q = QUAD (plane elements)  
         * V = BRIC (volume elements)  
         * R = BOUN (boundary elements)  
         * N = QTEN (quad tendon)  
         * D = BTEN/DTEN (beam or design tendons)  
         * E = SIR (external beam section)  
      –  A “*” in a column means that literal may be printed on that type of element; a “–” means it may not.  
   •  Dim.  
      –  Indicates whether the printed value carries a unit (for instance “m” or “mm”) or is simply “–” (unit-less ID).  

2.  Representative Rows  
   •  ENO  
      –  Meaning: Element numbers  
      –  Applies to all 11 families (all “*”)  
      –  Dim.: – (no physical unit)  
   •  GRP / GRPL  
      –  Group number / Group designation  
      –  Also universal across all element types  
   •  DOMA  
      –  Domain numbers (e.g. subdomain or analysis group)  
      –  Applies to all except tendon types (N, D)  
   •  INTE  
      –  Internally counted element numbers (different from ENO if you have user versus system numbering)  
   •  COOR, COOX, COOY, COOZ  
      –  Global (COOR) or local (COOX/COOY/COOZ) coordinate system IDs  
      –  Only valid where orientation matters (beams, tendons, springs, boundary elements, SIR)  
   •  SNO / SNOL  
      –  Cross‐section numbers and their designations (only on section‐aware elements: beams, springs, trusses, cables, tendons, SIR)  
   •  CSCA  
      –  First construction stage of cross section (same applicability as SNO)  

3.  How it fits into STRU  
   •  STRU is the record that controls which labels get plotted next to each structural element in graphic output and how they look (font, size, colour, background fill, etc.).  
   •  These “literals” are combined in the input (for example STRU NUMN=ENO,SNO,GRP) to request that element number, section number and group number be displayed.  
   •  Preceding context in the manual (BCON, WCON, COLO, SCHH, etc.) defines line-type, contour criteria, colour settings and so on; this table simply enumerates the textual identifiers you can output on or beside elements.  

4.  Why it matters in a RAG/vector-store context  
   •  When you index documentation or build a retrieval system for structural-drawing DSLs, this table is a prime reference for:  
      –  Recognizing valid literal tokens in queries or input decks  
      –  Mapping user‐friendly names (“element number”) to their code (“ENO”)  
      –  Knowing which element classes you can legally attach each label to  
      –  Automatically validating or enriching user inputs (e.g. warning if someone tries to print COOX on a brick element)

   – In each cell, a “*” means that this property is available (applicable) for that element type; a “–” means it is not.  
4. Dim.  
   – The physical unit associated with the property (for example kNm, kNm², mm, kN/m³, kN/m²).

The table is divided into logical groups by blank rows and bold headings:

Group 1: Fully Plastic Ultimate Forces (Design Value, Safety Factor Included)  
  • MYPD – Fully plastic bending moment My (kNm)  
  • MZPD – Fully plastic bending moment Mz (kNm)  
  • MBPD – Fully plastic warping moment (kNm²)  
  • M2PD – Fully plastic secondary torsional moment (kNm)  
  • YSPD – Plastic center y (mm)  
  • ZSPD – Plastic center z (mm)  

  In this group, for instance, “MYPD” is available for B, P, Q, V, and E (stars under those columns) but not for S, T, C, R, N, D.

Group 2: Elastic Stiffnesses of Gross Section  
  • EA  – Axial stiffness EA (kN/m³)  
  • GAY – Elastic shear stiffness Gy (kN/m²)  
  • GAZ – Elastic shear stiffness Gz (kN/m²)  
  • GIT – Elastic shear due to torsional moment GIt (kNm²)  
  • EIY – Elastic bending stiffness EI y (kNm²)  
  • EIZ – Elastic bending stiffness EI z (kNm²)  

  Here, EA and EIY/EIZ typically appear for B, T, C, P, Q, V, E, while the shear/torsion terms have a narrower applicability set.

Group 3: Elastic Stiffnesses of Effective Section  
  • EAE  – Effective axial stiffness EA (kN/m³)  
  • EIYE – Effective bending stiffness EI y (kNm²)  
  • EIZE – Effective bending stiffness EI z (kNm²)  

  These mirror the gross‐section stiffnesses but account for effective (e.g., cracked) section properties. Their applicability pattern often matches the gross values.

Key observations:  
– A star in the “B” column denotes the property is defined for BEAM elements; a dash means it is not.  
– The grouping and headings signal whether the values include material safety factors (design value) or are purely elastic parameters.  
– Units in “Dim.” are critical for downstream processing or dimensional checks in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store.  

Overall, this table enables automatic retrieval of section‐related stiffness and strength parameters across different element types by matching the literal code and checking applicability flags.

The input “table” is not a conventional row-and-column data table but rather a comprehensive dictionary of STRU-record fields (literals) used to control graphical output, element selection and property reporting in a structural-analysis/RAG environment.  It can be broken down into the following functional groups:

1. General Output and Designation Controls  
   • Text size (cm/LT), foreground/background colours (via COLO/COLB/FILL), fill modes (FS/BS/FI/BI), designation on/off (NO/YES), designation size (>0 in cm).  
   • Hints for cut elements (HINT record, unit LT).  
   • Default values (DEFA) for many parameters when no explicit input is given.

2. Contour Generation (BCON / WCON)  
   • BCON selects which plane/volume element edges to test; WCON refines by support/displacement type.  
   • Literal codes M, D, K, G define special contour lines:  
     – M: T–profiles or multi-edge joins  
     – D: thickness steps  
     – K: local coordinate changes  
     – G: suppress globally uniform support symbols  
   • AGLA: geometric break angle in surface volume  
   • Numeric ranges for numbering: FROM/TO/INC (default to full database range).

3. Element-Type Selection (NUME / NUMN / NUMK)  
   • NUME: master selector for all element types unless overridden by NUMN.  
   • NUMN lists individual families:  
     – DSLN: design elements  
     – BEAM, SPRI, TRUS, CABL, TUBE, QUAD, BRIC, BOUN, EDGE, QTEN, BTEN, DTEN, SIR, GPT, GLN, GAR, GVO, etc.  
   • NUMK refines BEAM-type to piles and bore profiles: BORE, BORA, BORT, BORL.

4. Section and Structural Property Records  
   • Cross-section warping and shear: AY/AZ (shear areas), YSMP/ZSMP (shear centre offsets).  
   • Mass and weight: AGAM (mass per length).  
   • Plastic capacities (with safety factors): NPL, VYPL, VZPL, MTPL, MYPL, MZPL; plastic centres YSPC/ZSPC.  
   • Characteristic capacities (no safety factor): NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD.  
   • Elastic stiffness: EIZE (bending stiffness E·Iz).

5. Beam-Section System Values (NUMN BEAM, DSLN)  
   • XOUT: flag to output full section geometry instead of section number.  
   • EZMI/EZMA: duct-axis offset to Z-max and Z-min (m).

6. Spring, Boundary, Quad and Bric System Values  
   • SPRI: DP (damping constant), TSYR (yield load per area).  
   • BOUN: RDT (boundary bedding stiffness).  
   • QUAD: ALFA (thermal expansion), cohesion K1CS, tensile strength K1TS, dilatation K1DI, angles K1MA/K1DA, fracture energy K1TE, direction K1AN; nonlinear crevice parameters K2FS, CUT.  
   • After ASE cuts: CP2C/CP2S/CP2W for 2D cutting patterns.

7. Reinforcement Definitions  
   • PRTP/PRST/PRGR/PRDF: types and subtypes of reinforcement.  
   • Layer densities: MII (3rd layer), MIS (shear reinforcement).  
   • Max reinforcement: MAU/MAUH/MAUQ/MAUI (upper layers), SGUH/SGUQ/SGUI, SGL/H/Q for stresses.  
   • Covers: COVU/COVL; relative distances HRUQ/HRUI.  
   • WK2/WK3: secondary directions; SGA, SG1/2/3: steel stress limits.

8. Towers and Section Cuts  
   • TOWR system values (NUMN TOWR).  
   • QSEC/GSEC: ENO (cut number).

9. Additional Graphic and Geometric Options  
   • FACS: scaling factor for beam-section contours.  
   • TWAR: local twisting of deformed shape.  
   • Fault-plane display in QUAD/BRIC.  
   • Beam hinges (BEAL): “h,n:i” syntax.  
   • Shear resistance uses inverse values (WT, WVY, WVZ, WT2).  
   • Colour/fill interplay for designations (SCHH plus BACX/BACY/BMIN/BMAX).

10. Subtable of Beam-Section Modifiers  
   A final mini-table lists X-literals for beam-section output:  
   • XS: section distance from beam start (m)  
   • XSPR: as percent of length  
   • XSN0/XOUT/XVOU/XBEN/XCOM/XEND/XFMB/XFCB/XMS/XCS/XPLA: flags for showing section numbers, vouts, bending/compression faces, main/cross shear, plate design; all dimensionless.

This organized dictionary enables automated parsing and vectorizing of structural data for rapid-access generation (RAG), ensuring every drawing detail—from section numbering through contour edges, material capacities, and reinforcement schedules—is fully specified by literal keys, defaults and units.

The excerpted table is drawn from the STRU-record documentation of a finite-element or CAD/graphic pre- and post-processor. It defines a handful of special “literals” (flags) that can be passed to the beam-section input (NUMN for BEAM elements, DSLN) to alter how cross-sections behave, are drawn or are interpreted internally. All of the entries share the same dimension (none; indicated by “–”).  

1.  Table Structure  
    •  Column 1 (“Literal”): the exact keyword or code that a user inputs.  
    •  Column 2 (“Meaning”): an English description of what that literal does.  
    •  Column 3 (“Dim.”): dimensional unit associated with the literal’s value. In this particular fragment every entry is “–,” meaning it is purely a flag or switch rather than a physical quantity.  

2.  Rows and Their Semantics  
    •  XVI1  
       – Literal:  “XVI1”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is virtual I – normal stiffness is zero (e.g. load trains).”  
       – Use case:  suppresses axial stiffness but keeps other stiffness terms non-zero. Ideal for modeling purely geometric chains or load-only elements.  

    •  XVI2  
       – Literal:  “XVI2”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is virtual II – all stiffness values are zero (e.g. load trains).”  
       – Use case:  completely “ghosts” the section mechanically; carries loads or coordinates but exerts no reaction forces.  

    •  XVI3  
       – Literal:  “XVI3”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is virtual III.”  
       – Usually implies a third variant of zero-stiffness behavior, perhaps preserving a subset of inertial properties.  

    •  XVI4  
       – Literal:  “XVI4”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is virtual IV.”  
       – A fourth variant of “virtual” section with its own specialized zero- or reduced-stiffness profile.  

    •  XINT  
       – Literal:  “XINT”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is interpolated.”  
       – Automatically generates a cross-section geometry by interpolating between two existing section definitions.  

    •  XCON  
       – Literal:  “XCON”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section is an enforced end of a continuous beam.”  
       – Marks a section boundary that prevents continuity across adjacent elements, even if they share the same section number.  

    •  XWRK  
       – Literal:  “XWRK”  
       – Meaning:  “Beam section with nonlinear work flow.”  
       – Activates a user-defined stress-strain or moment-curvature relationship rather than linear elasticity.  

    •  BIT1  
       – Literal:  “BIT1”  
       – Meaning:  “Internal bitcode I.”  
       – Reserved for the program’s own bookkeeping—no direct user semantics.  

    •  BIT2  
       – Literal:  “BIT2”  
       – Meaning:  “Internal bitcode II.”  
       – Same as BIT1: used internally to toggle low-level routines or data‐structure flags.  

3.  How It Fits into the Larger Context  
    •  These flags are one part of dozens of “literal” parameters (e.g. BCON, WCON, SCHH, DEFA, etc.) that control everything from contour generation to color-coding, numbering and the selection of element edges for boundary drawing.  
    •  In practice, a user might specify NUMN=XVI1 to zero out axial stiffness on a particular beam segment, or NUMN=XINT to have the software interpolate intermediate sections along the span.  
    •  The existence of BIT1 and BIT2 show that some literals are purely for internal program logic and not intended to be manipulated by end users.  

By capturing each literal’s name, its precise effect and the fact that none carry physical units, this description can be indexed in a RAG-style vector store to help an end-user or API automatically retrieve the correct flag when they need to adjust beam section behavior in STRU records.

The displayed table is one of several “System Value” tables associated with STRU NUMN records in a structural‐graphics context (for example, defining beam elements, tendons or ducts when generating contours, numbering and hatch fills).  In essence, it maps short “literals” (parameter names) to their full English meaning and the physical dimension (unit) in which they appear.  Below is a structured description of its layout, content and intended use:

1. Table Structure  
   • Three columns:  
     – Literal: a short, uppercase code used in input files or scripts.  
     – Meaning: a concise English description of what that code controls or specifies.  
     – Dim.: the unit or dimension associated with that parameter; if the field shows “–”, the parameter is dimensionless.  
   • Twenty rows, each defining one distinct parameter.

2. Logical Groupings of Literals  
   A. Construction and Material Identifiers  
     • BEN0  – “Numbers of beam elements / design elements” (–)  
     • ICS1  – “Construction stage number for placing” (–)  
     • ICS2  – “Construction stage number for grouting” (–)  
     • ICS3  – “Construction stage number for removing” (–)  
     • MATC  – “Numbers of materials of cross section on beam tendon” (–)  
     • MTCL  – “Designation of materials of cross section on beam tendon” (–)  
   These codes are used, for example, to tag which beam elements are active in a given construction stage, or which material property set applies to the tendon’s sheath and grout.

   B. Cross‐Section and Crack‐Width Parameters  
     • UT    – “Effective periphery for crack width” (mm)  
     • AH    – “Area of duct” (cm²)  
     • AT    – “Relative area for crack width” (m²)  
     • DIAM  – “Total diameter” (mm)  
     • TEMP  – “Temperature” (°C)  
     • REDF  – “Reduction factor within transmission length” (–)  
   These parameters describe the geometry of ducts or tendons and factors used in crack‐width calculations and prestress force transmission.

   C. Tendon Geometry and Profile Gradients  
     • ETSY  – “Eccentricity of duct axis to tendon axis in local y” (m)  
     • ETSZ  – “Eccentricity of duct axis to tendon axis in local z” (m)  
     • GDY   – “Gradient dy/dx of tendon” (–)  
     • GDZ   – “Gradient dz/dx of tendon” (–)  
   These four parameters define how the tendon or duct deviates from the beam centroidal axis in both transverse directions, plus the slope of its profile along the beam.

   D. Local Coordinates of Tendon and Duct Axes  
     • EXZY  – “Position of tendon axis in local y (related to origin of cross section)” (m)  
     • EXZZ  – “Position of tendon axis in local z (related to origin of cross section)” (m)  
     • EXSY  – “Position of duct axis in local y (related to origin of cross section)” (m)  
     • EXSZ  – “Position of duct axis in local z (related to origin of cross section)” (m)  
   These four values pinpoint the exact location of the tendon’s centroid (EXZY, EXZZ) versus the duct’s centerline (EXSY, EXSZ) within the local cross‐section coordinate system.

3. Usage Context  
   • In a RAG (Retrieval–Augmented Generation) vector store scenario, each row becomes a short knowledge node: “If user queries for ‘EXSZ’, retrieve: axis position of duct in local z, unit = m.”  
   • Together with other STRU tables (e.g. for QUAD, BRIC elements, prescribed reinforcement, etc.), they form a complete dictionary of all numeric input codes that drive the CAD/analysis program’s structural‐drawing output.  
   • The hyphen (“–”) in the Dim. column signals no unit conversion is needed (pure indices or counters).

By cataloging each literal, its clear meaning and units, the table ensures unambiguous interpretation of all beam–tendon parameters when generating drawings, computing crack widths, or assembling structural‐graphics commands.

The input table defines a set of “literals” (parameter names) used to specify system values for pile-type beam elements and associated bore profiles. It is intended for use in a CAD/FEA environment (e.g. within a NUMK record) where the engineer must supply soil–pile interaction properties, geometric positioning, and identification codes. Below is a structured description of its contents, column by column, followed by a synopsis of each group of parameters.

1. Overall Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Literal: the code that the user types in (up to four letters).  
     – Meaning: a short English description of what the literal represents.  
     – B, R, A, T, L: five flag columns indicating applicability to different element/profile types  
       • B = pile elements (BEAM)  
       • R = all bore profiles (BORE)  
       • A = bore profiles with axial bedding (BORA)  
       • T = bore profiles with transverse bedding (BORT)  
       • L = bore profiles with layered bedding (BORL)  
       A star (*) in any of these columns means that the literal is valid for that type.  
     – Dim.: the physical dimension or unit of the parameter (e.g. m, kN/m², kN).

2. Identification and Designation Codes  
   • BPNO – Bore Profile Numbers (no unit)  
   • BPNL – Bore Profile Designations (text label, no unit)  
   • COOX – Direction of the bore profile (no unit)  
   • XYZ – Combined position and direction (no unit)

3. Geometric Coordinates  
   • X, Y, Z – Cartesian coordinates of each bore profile layer, each measured in meters.  
     These three separate literals allow the user to specify the 3D location of soil layers along the pile.

4. Soil–Pile Bedding and Stiffness Moduli (kN/m²)  
   • CAB – Axial pile bedding (vertical stiffness)  
   • CQB – Basic transverse pile modulus at 0° (local +Z axis)  
   • CQBQ – Basic transverse pile modulus at 90° (local +Y axis)  
   • CQBN – Basic transverse pile modulus at 180° (local –Z axis)  
   • CQBY – Basic transverse pile modulus at 270° (local –Y axis)  
   • CQBE – Circular (isotropic) distribution of the basic transverse pile modulus  

   These six parameters define the Winkler‐type stiffness foundation for lateral and axial load transfer between soil and pile.

5. Soil Resistance and Loading Parameters  
   • PMAX – Maximum compression resistance (kN/m)  
   • PA – Cohesive loading (kN/m)  
   • PCOH – Cohesion constant (kN/m)  
   • TANR – Soil–pile friction angle (dimensionless, in degrees)  
   • TAND – Soil–pile dilatancy angle (dimensionless)  
   • KSIG – Pressure coefficient (dimensionless)  
   • MAXP – Maximum vertical force at pile toe (kN)

   These entries control the plastic‐limit or “ultimate” interaction capacity of the soil layers, including adhesion, friction, dilation, and toe resistance.

6. Applicability Flags  
   • Every literal is marked with stars under the five flag columns to show which element or profile variants support that parameter. For example, all pile‐related parameters (CAB, CQB series, PMAX, etc.) carry a star in the B column, indicating they apply to BEAM elements designated as piles. Bore­profile codes (BPNO, BPNL, COOX, XYZ) carry stars across R, A, T, L, since they are common to all bore-profile variants.

7. Usage Notes  
   • The table is used in conjunction with the NUMK record in a structural input file.  
   • Unstarred flag entries mean the parameter is ignored or inappropriate for that class.  
   • Consistent units must be observed: lengths in meters, stiffness in kN/m² or kN/m, angles dimensionless (interpreted as degrees), and forces in kN.

By providing this mapping of literal codes to meanings, types, and units, the table ensures that engineers can systematically define the soil-pile interaction properties for both beam-type piles and assorted bore-profile models within the simulation or drafting software.

Context notes:

The excerpted table is part of the “System Values of the Spring Elements (STRU NUMN SPRI)” section in a structural-analysis input reference. It defines the input literals you use whenever you assign properties to a spring element. Each row consists of three fields—Literal, Meaning, and Dim.—and together they control how the program interprets the mechanical and material characteristics of springs. Below is a breakdown of the table’s content:

1. Columns  
   • Literal: the code you type in the input record (e.g. SCP).  
   • Meaning: the full description of the quantity.  
   • Dim.: the physical units expected.

2. Rows / Literals  

   1. WL  
      – Meaning: Number of work law  
      – Dim.: – (unitless index into constitutive laws)

   2. RMAT  
      – Meaning: Reference material  
      – Dim.: – (unitless identifier of a material data set)

   3. AREA  
      – Meaning: Reference area  
      – Dim.: m² (used to normalize area-related constants)

   4. SCP  
      – Meaning: Axial spring constant  
      – Dim.: kN/m (linear stiffness in the spring’s axial direction)

   5. SCPR  
      – Meaning: Area related axial spring constant  
      – Dim.: kN/m³ (axial stiffness divided by AREA, for mesh-independent input)

   6. SCQ  
      – Meaning: Lateral spring constant  
      – Dim.: kN/m (stiffness in the transverse direction)

   7. SCQR  
      – Meaning: Area related lateral spring constant  
      – Dim.: kN/m³ (lateral stiffness per unit area)

   8. SCM  
      – Meaning: Rotational spring constant  
      – Dim.: kNm/rad (torsional stiffness around the spring’s axis)

   9. SCMR  
      – Meaning: Area related rotational spring constant  
      – Dim.: kNm/rad/m (torsional stiffness normalized by AREA)

   10. SPRE  
       – Meaning: Prestress of axial spring  
       – Dim.: kN (initial axial force applied before load steps)

   11. TSPR  
       – Meaning: Prestress of rotational spring  
       – Dim.: kNm (initial torque applied before loading)

   12. DP  
       – Meaning: Damping constant  
       – Dim.: kN·sec/m (viscous damping coefficient opposing axial motion)

3. How It Fits Into STRU Input  
   • You combine these literals under the record name SPRI when defining a spring element in the STRU module.  
   • WL and RMAT select the constitutive law and material properties.  
   • AREA, SCP, SCQ, SCM (and their “R” variants) govern stiffness scaling and normalization, which is especially useful for varying mesh densities.  
   • SPRE and TSPR let you impose an initial force or moment—commonly used to model pre-tensioned cables or torsion springs.  
   • DP captures energy dissipation through viscous damping.  

4. See Also  
   • AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO – other STRU record families that handle loads (AND), deformations (DEFO), design checks (DSGN), and arrow annotations (ARRO).

In practice, a minimal SPRI definition might look like:

  SPRI, WL=1, RMAT=3, AREA=0.0025, SCP=10000, SCQ=5000, SCM=200, SPRE=50, DP=5

   • Number of entries (rows): 4  

2. Context and Usage  
   • These four literals appear when STRU’s NUMN field equals BOUN, i.e. when defining boundary‐element (R) properties.  
   • They govern damping characteristics and local orientation for boundary support elements in static or dynamic analyses.  
   • The “Dim.” column indicates the engineering units employed; a dash “–” means dimensionless.

3. Column Definitions  
   A. Literal  
      – A short, uppercase code (2–4 characters) by which the program internally refers to each parameter.  
   B. Meaning  
      – A concise English description explaining what physical quantity or setting the literal controls.  
   C. Dim.  
      – The unit of measure for the quantity in question, in SI conventions enhanced by kN or m as required.

4. Row‐by‐Row Details  
   1) DT  
      – Meaning: Lateral damping constant  
      – Dim.: kN·sec / m  
      – Description:  Defines the viscous damping coefficient opposing motion parallel to the local support plane.  Used in dynamic or modal‐damping contexts.  
   2) DM  
      – Meaning: Rotational damping constant  
      – Dim.: kN·sec * m  
      – Description:  Specifies the moment-proportional damping resisting rotation about the local hinge or support axis.  Input in torque‐seconds per radian.  
   3) COOM  
      – Meaning: Moment direction  
      – Dim.: – (dimensionless)  
      – Description:  A flag or index that establishes which coordinate or local axis the damping moment (DM) refers to.  Often an integer 1–3 mapping to X, Y or Z rotation.  
   4) COOY  
      – Meaning: Lateral direction  
      – Dim.: – (dimensionless)  
      – Description:  A code indicating the local axis along which the lateral damping constant (DT) applies.  Again typically 1–3 to select local X, Y or Z translation.

   • When a boundary element (for example a spring or support) is defined, the user may want to include energy‐dissipating effects or orient those effects relative to the global or local coordinate system.

   • Treat “Literal,” “Meaning” and “Dim.” as separate fields for efficient retrieval.  
   • Index each row by its Literal (DT, DM, COOM, COOY) and tag with the parent context “System Values of the Boundary Elements.”  
   • Include unit conversions or look-up tables as part of the metadata to support dynamic queries (e.g., convert kN·sec/m to N·sec/m if needed).
