The input “table” is not a conventional two‐dimensional spreadsheet but rather a consolidated reference listing of record items, literals and default definitions used by a structural modeling and drawing program. It comprises several logical sections, each defining a group of parameters or options that control how elements, contours, reinforcements and graphic designations are handled. Below is a structured description of its contents:

1. General Text and Designation Controls  
   • SCHH / Text size of a type: expressed in cm per drawing unit (default 0.16).  
   • NO / YES flags: control whether an item is “No designation” (NO) or has a “Designation” (YES).  
   • When YES, designation is printed in cm (designation > 0).  
   • FROM / TO / INC: range and increment of numbering to be drawn; defaults take database limits.  
   • HINT: length used to “hint” cut‐elements in selection (unit LT, default 1.0).  

2. Contour Definition (BCON / WCON)  
   • BCON sets which element edge types are candidates for contouring; WCON further refines by support status or user‐defined 4-character literals.  
   • Contour‐line styles:  
     M = T-profile junctions,  
     D = thickness steps,  
     K = coordinate‐system changes,  
     G = no global support symbols.  
   • AGLA: geometric angle of surface break.  

3. Element‐Type Groups (STRU NUME and NUMN)  
   • DSLN (Design elements) enumerates the codes for:  
     – BEAM (B), SPRI spring (S), TRUS truss (T), CABL cable (C), TUBE/prism (P), QUAD planes (Q), BRIC volumes (V), BOUN boundary (R), EDGE nodal sequences, tendon types, structural points, lines, areas, volumes.  
   • NUMN selects which group’s system values follow.  

4. Cross‐Section and Material Parameters  
   (applicable across all element types unless a more specific NUMN literal is entered)  
   – AY, AZ: shear‐deformation areas (m²)  
   – YSMP, ZSMP: shear‐centre ordinates (m)  
   – AGAM: mass per length (kg/m)  

5. Plastic Ultimate Forces (design and characteristic values)  
   • Maximum (with safety factors):  
     NPL (axial), VYPL, VZPL (shears), MTPL (torsion), MYPL, MZPL (bending) in kN or kNm, plus plastic centre YSPC/ZSPC (mm).  
   • Minimum (characteristic): NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD in same units.  

6. Section and Element‐Specific System Values  
   • BEAM sections (NUMN = BEAM): XOUT output flag, EZMI/EZMA duct‐axis offsets (m).  
   • Piles and bore profiles (NUMK): BORE, BORA, BORT, BORL.  
   • SPRI springs (NUMN = SPRI): DP damping constant (kNm/rad/m²), TSYR yield area (kN·s/m).  
   • BOUN boundary elements: RDT boundary bedding stiffness (kNm/m).  
   • QUAD plate elements (NUMN = QUAD): thermal, cohesion, strength, friction angles, fracture energy, directions, plus nonlinear parameters, cutting‐pattern definitions (CP2C, CP2S, CP2W) and prescribed reinforcement definitions (PRTP, PRST, PRGR, PRDF).  

7. Prescribed Reinforcement Quantities and Limits  
   • MII, MIS: reinforcement area per unit (third layer disks, shear reinforcement).  
   • MAU*, MAUH, MAUQ, MAUI: maximum upper plate/shell reinforcement (principal, transverse, 3rd-layer).  
   • COVU, COVL: cover thickness to upper/lower reinforcement (mm).  
   • HRU*, HRUI, etc.: relative distances of layers (mm).  
   • WK*, WKH, WKQ, WKI: total and directional reinforcement disk diameters (mm).  
   • SG* and SGA: steel stress limits (MPa) for each layer and direction.  

8. Tower Elements and Section Cuts  
   • NUMN = TOWR for tower‐specific values (not expanded).  
   • QSEC/GSEC: ENO cut‐through area/volume element number.  

9. Graphic Representation Options  
   • FILL and colour records (COLO for foreground, COLB for background) with flags FS, FI, BS, BI for variable‐dependent or sign‐dependent colouring.  
   • BACX, BACY, BMIN, BMAX define fill‐rectangle extents in record SCH2.  

10. Contour Determination Logic  
   • BCON/WCON combinations select which edges (free, supported, fixed, fully fixed) generate contour lines.  
   • Possible literals: ALL, FREE, PP, MM, PM, F, PF, MF, PF etc., with “–” prefixes to invert selection.  

11. Miscellaneous Definitions  
   • TWAR: local twisting in deformed structures.  
   • BEAL: beam hinge notation “h,n:i” for normal/implicit hinges.  
   • Inverse shear resistances (WT, WVY, WVZ, WT2) used to avoid infinite values at zero shear‐stress points.  
   • Material fault‐plane orientation rules for QUAD/BRIC elements based on meridian/descent angles.  

In summary, the table is a master dictionary of all input literals, their meanings, units and default behaviors, organized by element class and function (geometry, material properties, reinforcement, graphic output and contour rules). It serves as the central schema for both data entry and the automated generation of structural drawings and analyses.

This table appears in the context of the STRU record group (see also AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO) of a structural‐analysis input deck. It defines two distinct sets of “literals” (parameter codes), each with a short descriptive text and a physical dimension. These codes are then available to downstream modules (e.g. post-processing graphics, report routines) whenever STRU-type elements reference them.

1. Columns  
   • Literal  
     – A short alphanumeric code used in the STRU record (and in related NUMN or NUME subrecords) to identify a specific property.  
   • Meaning  
     – Human‐readable description of what physical property the literal stands for.  
   • Dim.  
     – The units in which the value must be supplied.

2. Section A: Stress Limits of Prescribed Reinforcement Layers  
   This block lists stress‐limit parameters (in MPa) that apply to the reinforcement layers specified for plate or shell elements. The values defined here typically drive design checks, crack control, or yield‐limit verifications in reinforced concrete shells and plates.  
   • SGLI  
     – Lower 3rd reinforcement layer (plates/shells)  
     – MPa  
   • SG  
     – Total reinforcement (combined all layers)  
     – MPa  
   • SGH  
     – Principal (main) reinforcement layer  
     – MPa  
   • SGQ  
     – Transverse reinforcement layer  
     – MPa  
   • SGI  
     – 3rd (tertiary) reinforcement layer (disks)  
     – MPa  

   Usage note: If multiple reinforcement layers are defined (via PRTP, PRST, PRGR, etc.), these S G-literals establish the allowable stresses for each layer or combination. They are typically read when performing “reinforcement‐related” limit‐state checks.

3. Section B: Stiffness in Fixed Halfspace Levels  
   This second block defines the elastic stiffness (in MPa) of a supporting halfspace (e.g., soil or rock) at discrete depth levels below its surface. These values are used by boundary‐element or soil‐structure‐interaction elements (BOUN, QSEC, GSEC) to interpolate or assign stiffness properties at different depths.  
   Code nomenclature: “SH” = Stiffness Halfspace, numeric suffix = depth (in meters).  
   All entries carry MPa units.  
   • SH0   – Stiffness at the halfspace surface (z = 0 m)  
   • SH1   – Stiffness at z = 1 m below surface  
   • SH2   – Stiffness at z = 2 m below surface  
   • SH3   – Stiffness at z = 3 m below surface  
   • SH5   – Stiffness at z = 5 m below surface  
   • SH10  – Stiffness at z = 10 m below surface  
   • SH15  – Stiffness at z = 15 m below surface  
   • SH20  – Stiffness at z = 20 m below surface  
   • SH30  – Stiffness at z = 30 m below surface  

   Usage note: A BOUN element reading these entries can interpolate stiffness continuously or apply layerwise constant values to simulate stratified ground. These stiffnesses interact with inverse‐shear resistance parameters (WT, WVY, WVZ) when calculating soil response.

4. How It Fits Into the RAG Vector Store  
   – Each literal serves as a metadata key for model parameters.  
   – The “Meaning” field provides the natural-language description to be indexed for semantic search.  
   – The “Dim.” field ensures correct unit conversions in downstream RAG pipelines.  
   – See also related STRU-record tables: element edge‐definition (BCON/WCON), section output controls (XOUT, FACS), and other NUMN/NUME blocks (BEAM, SPRI, QUAD).

The input table is the definition of the STRU record for a structural‐drawing module. It is organized into a sequence of literal fields, grouped by functional blocks, each field having:

 ‑ A four‐character “Literal” code  
 ‑ A “Meaning” or description  
 ‑ A “Dim.” column giving its unit or “–” if dimensionless  
 ‑ Default values (often “DEFA” or a numeric default)  
 ‑ In some blocks an asterisk in the right‐hand column marks whether the parameter may be changed for different element types  

Below is a high‐level tour of its main sections:

1. Text and Designation Settings (SCHH block)  
   • Text size (cm per drawing unit) – default 0.16 cm/LT  
   • NO/YES flag: whether to draw an item designation  
   • If YES: a positive numeric designation (in cm)  

2. Contour Generation Definitions (BCON / WCON)  
   • BCON selects which element‐edge “types” are tested for drawing the external contour (default “ALL”).  
   • WCON refines that by selecting edges that also satisfy support/displacement criteria (e.g. “FREE,” “PP,” “MM,” “F,” “PMF,” etc.).  
   • Special 1–letter literals (M, D, K, G) override defaults to pick contours around T‐profiles, thickness steps, coordinate‐system changes or suppress global support symbols.  

3. Supported Element Types (DSLN listing)  
   • Maps text codes to element families: BEAM (B), SPRI (S), TRUS (T), CABL (C), TUBE (P), QUAD (Q), BRIC (V), BOUN (R), EDGE sequences, tendons, points, lines, areas, volumes, etc.  

4. System Values for Element Types  
   a. Material/Reinforcement number (GMRN)  
   b. Cross‐sectional properties:  
     – AY, AZ (shear areas)  
     – YSMP, ZSMP (shear‐centre offsets)  
     – AGAM (mass per length)  
   c. Fully plastic ultimate forces and moments (factored):  
     – NPL, VYPL, VZPL, MTPL, MYPL, MZPL  
     – Plastic centers YSPC, ZSPC  
   d. Characteristic (unfactored) plastic capacities: NPD, VYPD, VZPD, MTPD  
   e. Elastic bending stiffness (EIZE)  

5. Beam‐Section Output (for NUMN = BEAM)  
   • XOUT = output contour flag  
   • EZMI/EZMA = duct‐axis positions to section top/bottom (m)  

6. Piles and Bore Profiles (NUMK block)  
   • BEAM (piles), BORE (all profiles), BORA (axial bedding), BORT (transverse), BORL (layered)  

7. Spring Elements (NUMN = SPRI)  
   • DP = damping constant (kN·s/m)  
   • TSYR = area‐related yield load (kN·m²)  

8. Boundary Elements (NUMN = BOUN)  
   • RDT = boundary‐bedding stiffness per direction (kN·m⁻¹)  

9. Quad Elements (NUMN = QUAD)  
   • Thermal expansion (ALFA), cohesion (K1CS), strength (K1TS), dilatation‐angle (K1DI), meridian (K1MA), descent (K1DA), fracture energy (K1TE), direction (K1AN)  
   • Secondary plane friction angle (K2FS), cut‐pattern counts (CUT)  

10. Two‐Dimensional Cutting Patterns (post‐ASE):  
   • CP2C = contour; CP2S = structure; CP2W = structure with warp direction  

11. Prescribed Reinforcements  
   • PRTP/PRST = reinforcement type/subtype  
   • PRGR = grading; PRDF = definition style  
   • MII, MIS = 3rd‐layer disk area and shear reinforcement  
   • Maximum reinforcement areas MAU, MAUH, MAUQ, MAUI (cm²/m); cover COVU/COVL (mm); relative distance HRUQ/HRUI (mm)  
   • Stress limits SGUH, SGUQ, SGUI, SGL, SGLH, SGLQ (MPa); bar diameters WK2, WK3; multi‐direction stresses SGA, SG1, SG2, SG3 (MPa)  

12. Tower Data (NUMN = TOWR)  
   • ENO (tower ID), NAME, AREA representation, ZLEV (elevation), HLEV (height), VOLU (volume repr.)  

13. Section/Volume Cuts (NUMN = QSEC/GSEC)  
   • ENO = cut number  

14. Colouring and Fill Options (related SCH2/COLO/FILL records)  
   • Fore/background colours for designation, positive/negative value schemes (FS, BS), variable fill flags (FI, BI)  
   • Background fill deletes underlying graphics over the area defined by BACX, BACY, BMIN, BMAX

The table under consideration defines the output variables for “storey‐level” results in a structural analysis or building model.  It consists of three columns—Literal, Meaning, and Dim.—and enumerates a set of standardized fields (literals) that describe geometry, mass properties and global stiffness characteristics of each floor or “storey.”  Below is a narrative breakdown of the table’s structure and content:

1. General Structure  
   •  Literal: the short code or field name used in data files or software output.  
   •  Meaning: a human‐readable description of what that field represents.  
   •  Dim.: the physical dimension or unit for numeric values; “–” indicates a unitless or ordinal identifier.

2. Identification Fields  
   •  ENO (–): “Storey level number.”  A sequential integer that uniquely identifies each storey in the model.  
   •  NAME (–): “Designation of storey level.”  A text label or code chosen by the user—e.g. “L1,” “Roof,” “Mezzanine.”  
   •  TOWR (–): “Tower.”  A grouping identifier for buildings with multiple towers or substructures; supports multi‐tower models.

3. Area Representation  
   •  AREA (–): “Area representation of storey level.”  Possibly a code or reference to a polygon/shape record that defines the plan‐area footprint.

4. Elevation & Height  
   •  ZLEV (m): “Storey elevation (upwards positive).”  The vertical coordinate of the storey datum above a reference plane (often ground level or sea‐level).  
   •  HLEV (m): “Storey height.”  The inter‐storey height measured between this level and the one immediately below.

5. Plan Extents  
   •  XMIN, XMAX (m): “Storey extensions Xmin/Xmax.”  The minimum and maximum X‐coordinates of the storey’s plan projection.  
   •  YMIN, YMAX (m): “Storey extensions Ymin/Ymax.”  The minimum and maximum Y‐coordinates.

6. Centres of Mass & Rigidity  
   •  XM, YM, ZM (m): “Coordinates of centre of mass X/Y/Z.”  The 3D coordinates of the storey’s mass centroid.  
   •  X, Y, Z (m): “Coordinates of centre of rigidity X/Y/Z.”  The 3D location where lateral stiffness is concentrated—used for torsion checks in seismic design.

7. Mass Properties  
   •  MASS (t): “Storey mass.”  Total mass lumped at the level, expressed in tonnes (t).  
   •  RMAS (t·m²): “Rotational mass moment of inertia about Z.”  The second moment of mass about the vertical axis, crucial for torsional response.

8. Global Rigidity  
   •  STFX (kN/m): “Storey rigidity in global X.”  The lateral stiffness of that floor in the global X‐direction; derived from summed element stiffnesses.  
   •  STFY (kN/m): “Storey rigidity in global Y.”  Likewise, the lateral stiffness in global Y.

Usage & Context for RAG Vector Store  
–  Each row corresponds to one storey element; the ENO field serves as a primary key for retrieval.  
–  All numeric fields (e.g. ZLEV, MASS, STFX) can be normalized and embedded into a vector space for similarity search—useful when comparing storey stiffness distributions across buildings.  
–  Text fields (NAME, TOWR) enrich embeddings with semantic context, enabling retrieval by tower name or level designation.  
–  The plan‐extent fields (XMIN…YMAX) allow spatial queries, e.g. finding storeys whose footprints exceed a given bounding box.  
–  Centre‐of‐mass and centre‐of‐rigidity coordinates support advanced queries: “Show me storeys where the mass‐rigidity offset exceeds 0.5 m,” helpful for torsion‐sensitive designs.  
–  Moment of inertia (RMAS) and mass (MASS) can be used to rank storeys by dynamic characteristics, supporting time‐history analysis retrieval tasks.

In summary, this table is a compact, standardized schema for storing and querying key geometric, mass, and stiffness attributes of individual storeys in a multi‐story structural model. When loaded into a RAG‐enabled vector database, it supports both precise numeric queries and semantically enriched retrievals based on textual identifiers.

The input “STRU” table is a configuration-and-output specification used by the AQUA/GRAPHIC family of RAG-enabled structural analysis and drawing modules.  It controls everything from font‐sizes and designation styles to which element edges generate contour lines, which element-type parameters to report, and how to colour or hint cut elements.  Below is a structured, human-readable breakdown of its main sections and fields:

1. General Text and Designation Settings  
   • Text size (cm/LT): 0.16  
   • NO / YES: suppress or enable automatic numbering  
   • “_” : forces no designation  
   • >0 : forces designation in cm (overrules default)  
   • SCHH (line): controls size of designation area and interplay of foreground/background colours  
     – COLO/COLB/FILL records set text and fill colours (single, positive/negative, or variable)  
     – BACX, BACY, BMIN, BMAX (in SCH2) define background bbox  

2. Contour-Generation Logic (BCON / WCON)  
   These two parameters define which plane‐ or volume-element edges appear in outlines.  You choose  
   – BCON: base set of edge types to test (“ALL”, “FREE”, “PP”, “MM”, “PF”, etc.)  
   – WCON: additional properties an edge must have (fixed, supported, free, mixed)  
   – M, D, K, G variants add special contour styles (T-profiles, steps, local coords, no support symbols)  
   – AGLA: geometric angle threshold  
   – FROM / TO / INC: numeric ranges for printed counts  
   – HINT: dashed hint for cut elements  

3. Element-Type Selection (STRU NUME and NUMN)  
   • NUME chooses global element families; “*” marks optional overrides via NUMN.  
   • DSLN – design lines  
   • BEAM, SPRI, TRUS, CABL, TUBE, QUAD, BRIC, BOUN, EDGE, QTEN, BTEN, DTEN, SIR, GPT, GLN, GAR, GVO  
   • NUMN refines by section type (e.g. BEAM piles vs bore profiles), spring laws, boundary fixities, quad volumetrics, etc.  

4. System Values for Element-Type Parameters  
   Each element family reports a standard suite of geometric, mass, and capacity data.  Asterisks denote applicability.  
   – GMRN: reinforcement material number  
   – AY, AZ: shear‐deformation areas (m²)  
   – YSMP, ZSMP: shear‐centre offsets (m)  
   – AGAM: mass per length (kg/m)  
   – Plastic capacities (with and without safety factors): NPL/NPD, VYPL/VYPD, VZPL/VZPD, MTPL/MTPD, MYPL, MZPL  
   – Plastic centres YSPC, ZSPC (mm)  
   – Elastic bending stiffness EIZE (kNm²)  

5. Section and Profile Definitions  
   • XOUT: draw full cross-section contours instead of section numbers (scale by FACS)  
   • EZMI/EZMA: duct axis positions to section top/bottom (m)  
   • Piles and bore profiles (BEAM/BORE/BORA/BORT/BORL)  

6. Special Families  
   – SPRI (springs): DP (damping), TSYR (yield area)  
   – BOUN (boundary): RDT (local bedding stiffness)  
   – QUAD (2D solids): ALFA (thermal α), K1CS (cohesion), K1TS (strength), K1DI/K1MA/K1DA (angles), K1TE (fracture energy), two-plane non-linear K2FS, CUT pattern counts/contours/structures; CP2C/S/W  
   – Reinforcement definitions: PRTP, PRST, PRGR, PRDF; areas per layer MII, MIS; maxima MAU*, covers COV*, relative spacings HRU*, stresses SG*, bar spacings WK*; steel limits SGA, SG1/2/3  
   – TOWR: tower-related data  
   – QSEC/GSEC: cuts through areas or volumes (ENO: cut number)  

7. Cross-Section Rendering and Twisting  
   – Local twisting (TWAR): eccentricity range about an incline  
   – Fault-plane display for QUAD/BRIC based on meridian/descent angles  
   – Beam-hinges (BEAL): “h,n:i” notation for normal vs implicit hinges  
   – Inverse shear resistances (WT, WVY, WVZ, WT2) for finite stress calculation

The table shown is the definition of the “structural‐point” literals for the STRU record in the RAG/GRAPHIC data model.  It maps each three‐ to five‐character code (Literal) to the meaning of the field and, where appropriate, its physical dimension.  These fields are used whenever node or point data are requested—for example in listings, plots or graphical output—and can be combined with other STRU‐related records (see AND, DEFO, DSGN, ARRO).  

1.  Identifier and numbering fields  
   •  NNO   – Node number (no unit)  
   •  INTE  – Internally counted node number (no unit)  
   •  NEX   – Explicitly defined node number or point number (no unit)  
   •  NGEO  – Node identification number (no unit)  
   •  NNO, INTE and NEX let the program distinguish between the user’s point IDs, the internal indexing, and any remapped numbering.  

2.  Support and coupling information  
   •  FIX   – Numbers of the supported (fixed) nodes (no unit)  
   •  FIXB  – Bit pattern of the nodal support (no unit)  
   •  COUP  – Numbers of the coupled nodes (no unit)  
   These fields convey boundary conditions and multi‐point constraints.  

3.  Patch identification  
   •  PATC  – Node patch identification (no unit)  
   •  PATG  – Node patch plus identification number (no unit)  
   Patches may group nodes for graphical highlighting or processing.  

4.  Cartesian coordinates (global final state)  
   •  X     – X‐coordinate of the node (final state) [m]  
   •  Y     – Y‐coordinate of the node (final state) [m]  
   •  Z     – Z‐coordinate of the node (final state) [m]  
   •  GZ    – Geodetic height (elevation) [m]  

5.  Coordinates for incremental launching or special loadcase  
   •  LCX   – X‐coordinate for a loadcase/construction stage [m]  
   •  LCY   – Y‐coordinate for a loadcase/construction stage [m]  
   •  LCZ   – Z‐coordinate for a loadcase/construction stage [m]  
   These allow output of node positions at intermediate states (e.g. during incremental bridge launching).  

6.  Local coordinate system orientation  
   •  COOR  – Coordinate system index of the structural points (no unit)  
   •  COOX  – Local x‐direction code of the structural points (no unit)  
   •  COOY  – Local y‐direction code of the structural points (no unit)  
   •  COOZ  – Local z‐direction code of the structural points (no unit)  

Usage notes:  
-  When STRU NUMN is set to this literal set, all node‐related queries will return the above columns.  
-  To draw deformed shapes or to color‐code support conditions, these codes can be combined with SCHH (color/line), BCON/WCON (contour determination) and other STRU‐series settings.  
-  For full context, see related records AND (loads), DEFO (deformations), DSGN (design results), ARRO (arrow symbols).  
-  Units are only shown where a physical dimension applies; otherwise the field is dimensionless.

The image shows a three-part reference table that defines shorthand literals for node‐related data in a structural model.  Each part is headed by its scope, and all share the same three columns:  

• Literal – the short code used in input or output records  
• Meaning – a brief text description of what the code represents  
• Dim. – the physical dimension or units of the quantity  

Below is a structured breakdown of each section:

1.  General QUAD/BRIC Node Identifiers  
    • C00Z  
       – Local z direction of the structural points  
       – Dim.: “–” (no unit; it is a direction index)  
    • T  
       – Thickness of the QUAD element nodes  
       – Dim.: m  
    • QCOR  
       – Coordinate system of the QUAD element nodes  
       – Dim.: –  
    • QCOX, QCOY, QCOZ  
       – Local x, y, z directions of the QUAD element nodes  
       – Dim.: –  
    • QKN  
       – Internally counted numbers of the QUAD element nodes  
       – Dim.: –  
    • BKN  
       – Internally counted numbers of the BRIC element nodes  
       – Dim.: –  
    • PHAN  
       – HASE pile node number  
       – Dim.: –  

2.  Non-Persistent Nodal Masses  
    (These masses are defined for loading or transient analyses but not carried over persistently.)  
    • MNT  
       – Transversal nodal masses  
       – Dim.: t (metric tons)  
    • MNTX, MNTY, MNTZ  
       – Transversal nodal masses in global X, Y, Z directions  
       – Dim.: t  
    • MNR  
       – Rotatory nodal masses  
       – Dim.: tm (t·m, rotary inertia)  
    • MNRX, MNRY, MNRZ  
       – Rotatory nodal masses about global X, Y, Z  
       – Dim.: tm  

3.  Working Nodal Masses  
    (These are the masses actively used in dynamic or modal calculations.)  
    • MET  
       – Transversal nodal masses  
       – Dim.: t  
    • METX, METY, METZ  
       – Transversal nodal masses in global X, Y, Z directions  
       – Dim.: t  
    • MER  
       – Rotatory nodal masses  
       – Dim.: tm  
    • MERX, MERY, MERZ  
       – Rotatory nodal masses about global X, Y, Z  
       – Dim.: tm  

Key observations:  
– The first block does not carry a sub-heading label but deals exclusively with node geometry, orientation, and internal numbering for QUAD and BRIC elements (and piles via PHAN).  
– The second and third blocks are explicitly labeled “Non persistent nodal masses” and “Working nodal masses” respectively.  They parallel each other in structure: each lists the total transversal mass (MNT or MET), its components in X/Y/Z, the total rotary mass (MNR or MER), and rotary components about each global axis.  
– Dimensional conventions are consistent: masses in tons (t), and rotary inertias in ton‐meters (tm).  
– Literal codes are typically four characters (e.g. QCOX) or three (e.g. MNT), making them easy to reference in a structured input file or vector store schema.

Below is a descriptive summary of the two related tables governing the “LOAD” command and its graphical representation options.  This text can be used to populate a RAG vector store for retrieval and indexing.

1.  LOAD-Selection Parameters  
Columns: Item, Description, Unit, Default  
•  TYPE  
   – Defines which loads to display.  Options: ALL (every load), LT (load type), BEAM, LILO, ALAL (area loads), ALVL (volume loads), LOST (parts of loads not fully used on elements).  
   – Default: ALL  
•  LT  
   – Further refines TYPE by literal load‐type codes.  
   – Default: NO (show only used loads) or YES (show origin loads) depending on LOST setting.  
•  SHOW UNUSED LOADS  
   – YES / NO toggle. When YES, loads that have no element assignment still appear in the graphics.  

2.  Available Load Types  
Columns: Type code, Loading direction or projection, Dimensions  
•  ALL  
   – All loads regardless of type; dimension placeholder “*”  
•  PG  
   – Gravity direction (global Z)  
   – kN, kN/m, kN/m²  
•  PPP  
   – All global projections (X, Y, Z summed)  
   – kN, kN/m, kN/m²  
•  PXP / PYP / PZP  
   – Part-global projection in X, Y, or Z  
   – kN, kN/m, kN/m²  
•  PXY, PXZ, PYZ  
   – In-plane loads on the specified plane  
   – kN, kN/m, kN/m²  
•  WXX, WYY, WZZ  
   – Part-global displacements in X, Y, or Z  
   – mm  
•  D*, D, DX, DY  
   – Rotations (all or local directions)  
   – mrad  
•  PRSZ  
   – Pressure in local Z  
   – kN, kN/m, kN/m²  
•  TEMP, T, DT, DTXY, DT*, DTY, DTZ  
   – Temperature fields (absolute, uniform changes, differences)  
   – degrees  
•  PMXI, PMYI, PMZI  
   – Local bending moments around axes X, Y, Z  
   – kNm  
•  PVI, PVYI, PVZI  
   – Internal prestress shear forces in local X, Y, Z  
   – kN  
•  IN  
   – Influence area forces  
   – kN/m  

Notes on dead-load visualization: special TYPE codes DL, DLX, DLY, DLZ represent dead load factors computed by the ASE program.

3.  Graphical Representation Settings  
Columns: Item, Description, Unit, Default  
•  UNIT  
   – Scale factor for all load‐arrow lengths; refer to STRU record  
   – Unitless multiplier (“*”)  
•  SCHH  
   – Text height for load labels; see STRU record  
   – cm  
•  ALIG  
   – Obsolete (superseded by DSGN DIST)  
•  NIVE  
   – Obsolete  
•  ND  
   – Number of decimal places in labels; controlled via SCHH ND  
•  FACS  
   – Factor applied to eccentricities when drawing load lines  
   – Default: 1.0  
•  SING (Point‐Load Representation)  
   – TCOM: sums components into one resultant (default)  
   – VECT: draw each nodal load as a separate vector  
   – AVEC: as VECT but without sign arrows  
•  LIN (Line‐Load Representation)  
   – EMPT: no filling  
   – ARRO: arrows along the loaded line (default)  
   – PLAN: hatch perpendicular to the element  
   – PLAP: like PLAN but with line‐style filling  

4.  Additional Behavior and Notes  
•  GTYP selector chooses which processing stage to display:  
   – ELEM: loads assigned to actual elements or nodes  
   – INP: user-defined “input” loads (no arrows for local directions)  
   – LVEC: nodal resultant loads used in the finite‐element solver

The input table is a comprehensive catalogue of “load” types used in a structural‐analysis or finite‐element context. It defines each load code, provides a human‐readable description of what that code represents (direction, projection, or physical quantity), and specifies the applicable units or dimensions. The table is organized into three primary columns:

  • Type  
  • Loading (description)  
  • Dimension (units)  

Below is a structured breakdown of the table’s content and key groupings:

1.  General “P” (Force) Loads  
    – Codes beginning with “P” denote various force or load projections and directions.  
    –   P*  “All loads (forces)” – summarizes every force type.  
    –   P   “All local directions” – total in element‐local axes.  
    –   PX, PY, PZ  “Part local x/y/z” – components in each local axis.  
    –   PP  “All global directions” – sum in global coordinate axes.  
    –   PXX, PYY, PZZ  “Part global X/Y/Z” – component in each global axis.  
    –   PG  “In gravity direction” – typically vertical load.  
    –   PPP, PXP, PYP, PZP  “Global projections” – all or part projected onto global axes.  
    –   PXY, PXZ, PYZ  “Load in XY/XZ/YZ plane” – planar components.  
    Dimension for all these is kN, kN/m, or kN/m² as appropriate for point, line, or surface loads.

2.  “W” Displacement or Deflection  
    –   WXX, WYY, WZZ  “Part global X/Y/Z” – deflection or displacement in mm along each global axis.

3.  “D” Rotations  
    –   D*  “All rotations” – rotation about all axes, unit mrad.  
    –   D   “All local directions” – total in element‐local frame, mrad.  
    –   DX, DY  “Part local x/y” – component rotations, mrad.

4.  Temperature‐related Loads  
    –   TEMP  “All temperatures” – absolute temperature, degrees.  
    –   T  “Maximum absolute temperature.”  
    –   DT  “Uniform temperature change.”  
    –   DTXY  “Uniform temperature change QUAD” – specialized for quadrilateral elements.  
    –   DT*  “All temperature differences.”  
    –   DTY, DTZ  “Temperature difference in local y/z.”  
    All dimensioned in temperature units (e.g. °).  

5.  Pressure and Prestress  
    –   PRSZ  “Pressure in local z” – in kN, kN/m, kN/m² on an element face.  
    –   PMXI, PMYI, PMZI  “Moment in local x/y/z” – internal bending moments, kNm.  
    –   PVI, PVYI, PVZI  “Internal prestress (shear forces) in local directions,” kN.  

6.  Influence Areas  
    –   IN  “Influence area (forces)” – load per length kN/m, used for line loads derived from area influences.

7.  Dead Load Factors (post‐ASE calculation)  
    –   DL  “Dead weight” – total dead‐load factor applied, kN, kN/m, kN/m².  
    –   DLX, DLY, DLZ  “Part global X/Y/Z” – dead‐load factors by global axis, same units.

Key Notes from Additional Context  
  • TYPE: default selection “LT ALL” shows all load types. Variants (“ALAL”, “ALVL”, etc.) let you display only area or volume loads.  
  • LOST: can hide loads not fully applied to elements (default NO, switchable to YES).  
  • GTYP: controls processing stage of loads—e.g. GTYP ELEM shows only loads actually assigned to elements/nodes; GTYP INP shows user‐defined “input loads” without projection arrows; GTYP LVEC reveals nodal load vectors used by the solver.  
  • Visualization rules: free and line loads draw in load direction; element‐area loads (ELLO) draw normal to surface. Projections on QUAD elements use global axes by default.  
  • Legend placement can be controlled by LEGX/LEGY (explicit insertion point) or STAN (default to right/above).  
  • Overlapping loads may be offset if verification (SCHH REVI) and SEPA YES are enabled.

     • Free loads (BLLO) always in global axes, regardless of element‐local axes.  
  – Legend positioning:  
     • Using LEGX, LEGY places the legend at a specified insertion point.  
     • Using STAN aligns it along the right or top border by default.  
  – Overlap handling:  
     • If SCHH REVI is enabled and SEPA = YES, overlapping load symbols are offset slightly in the opposite direction to avoid coincidence.  

In sum, this table is a master key for:  
  a) selecting which load or result types to fetch,  
  b) interpreting their abbreviations,  
  c) knowing their physical units, and  
  d) controlling how they are filtered and represented in the graphics/legend of the RAG tool.

Every entry consists of:

 3.  Dimension

Detailed breakdown:

1. Influence–Area of Normal Forces (Type “IN…”)  
   • INX  
     – Loading: n-xx  
     – Dimension: kN/m  
     – Represents the influence‐area result for the normal force acting in the local x-direction per unit length.  
   • INY  
     – Loading: n-yy  
     – Dimension: kN/m  
     – Normal force component in the local y-direction per unit length.  
   • INXY  
     – Loading: n-xy  
     – Dimension: kN/m  
     – The shear‐coupling normal force component in the plane (interaction of x and y), per unit length.

2. Influence–Area of Bending Moments (Type “IM…”)  
   • IMX  
     – Loading: m-xx  
     – Dimension: kNm/m  
     – Bending moment about the local x-axis, distributed per unit length.  
   • IMY  
     – Loading: m-yy  
     – Dimension: kNm/m  
     – Bending moment about the local y-axis, per unit length.  
   • IMXY  
     – Loading: m-xy  
     – Dimension: kNm/m  
     – Twist or coupling bending moment in the xy plane, per unit length.

3. Influence–Area of Shear Forces (Type “IV…”)  
   • IVX  
     – Loading: v-x  
     – Dimension: kN/m  
     – Shear force component in the local x-direction per unit length.  
   • IVY  
     – Loading: v-y  
     – Dimension: kN/m  
     – Shear force component in the local y-direction per unit length.

(Note: In some renderings a row “IV” appears simply as the group header “Influence area (shear forces)” with dimension kN/m; the actual directional results are IVX and IVY.)

Key observations and context:

- “Influence area” here refers to the distributed (per-unit-length) result derived from nodal loads or projected element loads over a plate or shell element.  
- The directional sub‐codes (X, Y, XY) correspond to the local coordinate axes of the element: X typically aligned with one edge, Y with the orthogonal edge, and XY indicating cross‐coupling terms.  
- Units:  
   • Normal and shear forces use kilonewtons per meter (kN/m).  
   • Bending moments use kilonewton-meters per meter (kNm/m), effectively a moment per unit length.  
- This table forms part of a larger schema of load‐type definitions (see also: AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO) that drive both visualization and extraction of results in the RAG vector store or related finite‐element pre/post-processors.  
- By selecting one of these “TYPE” codes in a report or graphic output record, the user can isolate and display the corresponding influence distribution—for example, plotting color‐contours of IMY to see how the bending moment about the y-axis varies across a slab.  
- Each code is matched internally to the solver’s output arrays; consistency in code naming ensures that scripting or automated extraction routines can query results unambiguously.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the “NODE” input table, organized by columns (items), their roles, inter-dependencies and the special literals applicable to nodal loads and boundary forces. Where relevant, cross-references to records such as AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, STRU, SCH2, LOAD, BEAM and GRAPHIC are noted.

1. General Purpose  
   • Defines how nodal values (displacements, rotations, forces, moments) are represented in graphic output.  
   • Only reference nodes are handled here; their numeric IDs, kinematic constraints and applied loads are plotted.  
   • Vectors (forces/moments) use single or double arrow tips (ARRO). If the vector is near-perpendicular to the viewing plane, four-corner symbols (cross/rectangle) mark its foot.  

2. Key Columns (Items)  
   – TYPE  
     • Literal code indicating the quantity to display at the node.  
     • Drawn using DSGN; strings set input values only—no automatic drawing.  
     • See record STRU for plotting node numbers.  
   – DSGN  
     • Determines graphic attributes (line style, symbol type).  
     • Does not render non-DSGN items.  
     • For arrows or status lines use ARRO settings.  
   – UNIT  
     • Scaling factor for vector length.  
     • Default: cm/LT. For relative scales, use cm/%. A zero value suspends plotting.  
     • “STRU UNI2” may supply a second-type scale.  
   – SCHH  
     • Text height for labels.  
     • If SCHH ND is specified, it also controls number of decimal points.  
   – UMIN, UMAX, LMAX  
     • Upper/lower limits for automatic scaling (obsolete UMIN/UMAX replaced by SCH2 MIN/… and DSGN LMAX).  
   – OFFS  
     • Text offset along the vector, measured  
       >0 in cm from start of vector  
       <0 in % of vector length  
   – DTYP  
     • Direction code for arrow or status-line representation (see ARRO, DSGN DTYP).  
   – ND (Decimal places)  
     • Overrides SCHH ND for numeric formatting.  
   – SUME (obsolete), TOTA  
     • Sum of line distributions (see GRAPHIC TOTA PAIR/GENE).  
   – STAT  
     • Frequency of symbol repetition along boundaries (record BEAM STAT).  
   – FILL  
     • Fill style for symbols (record STRU FILL).  

3. Valid TYPE Literals and Their Dimensions  
   – Geometric / displacement:  
     • GH   ­– Geodetic height (m)  
     • UL   – Displacement local 3-vector (mm)  
     • UXL, UYL, UZL – Component displacements in local X, Y, Z (mm)  
     • R    – Global rotation vector magnitude (mrad)  
     • RX, RY – Rotation about global X, Y (mrad)  
   – Constraint forces & boundary loads:  
     • CFZ – Constraint force component Z (kN)  
     • TEZ – Total boundary force global Z (kN/m)  
     • TEMN, TEMX, TEMY, TEMZ – Boundary moments about local longitudinal or global axes (kNm/m)  
     • REMX – Residual moment X (kNm) – e.g. post-eigen or dynamic analysis  
   – After specialized analyses:  
     • Eigen, earthquake (DYNA), vibration time-step (ASE), non-linear (TALPA, ASE)  

4. Local vs. Global Directions  
   • Local axes (L) only available if node connects to a structural element.  
   • Boundary forces along edges show either normal (S) or tangent (T) components for curved/skew edges in 3D. The first T-direction aligns to the normal of the first QUAD element at the node. Use STRU COOR/COOX/COOY/COOZ BOUN to verify.  

5. Irregular vs. Regular Distributions  
   • Irregular edge loads (EDGE, EM, etc.) come directly from FE results.  
   • To enforce a uniform line distribution (for wall load design), use  
     – Literals EXD, EYD, EZD, END, ESD, ETD, EMD  
     – GRAPHIC input TOTA TRAP for EX, EY, EZ, EN, ES, ET, EM.  
   • GRAPHIC will compute and draw a trapezoidal distribution whose total and centroid match the original irregular loads. Optionally, only the resultant and centroid line can be displayed (TOTA PAIR or GENE).  

6. Nodal Sequence Representation (REPR DEDG)  
   • Single nodal forces, spring forces or constraint reactions can be distributed along a user-defined node sequence (EDGE).  
   • Each segment is used once; only like-directed forces are combined. A continuous arrow/status-line run is drawn over all connecting lines for that direction.  

See also records AND, LC (load cases), DSGN (graphic design), ARRO (arrow styles) for complete customization of vector plotting at nodes.

The table defines five control keywords for the graphical representation of line‐based forces, moments and couplings in a structural model. Each keyword is a literal (LIT) entry in the input deck and ties into other record definitions (STRU, SCH2, DSGN, ARRO, etc.) to govern how loads are summed, averaged, annotated and which nodes participate.  

1. REPR  
   • Purpose: Selects the “type of representation” for the line loads or coupling forces.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “*” (inherits whatever STRU REPR has been set to)  
   • Notes: Under the hood, this parameter simply passes its value to the STRU REPR record, where valid options (e.g. ARRO, status‐line, vector tip, rectangle) are defined.  

2. UOFF  
   • Purpose: Vertical offset of textual designations in the plan (top) view.  
   • Unit: – / LIT (uses the same syntax as SCH2 OFFS: positive numbers shift up; negative can be percent‐based)  
   • Default: +4  
   • Notes: Exactly equivalent to record SCH2 OFFS. A higher UOFF moves the annotation farther from the load line, reducing clutter when many lines run in parallel.  

3. TOTA  
   • Purpose: Determines how the “sum” or resultant of a line‐distributed force/moment is treated graphically.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: “–” (no special sum handling; draw the original line‐by‐line distribution)  
   • Options:  
     – CONS: Collapse the distribution to a constant (uniform) line whose total equals the original.  
     – TRAP: Show a trapezoidal (linearly varying) average that preserves the total and centroid.  
     – PAIR: Draw a couple of forces at the positive and negative extremities to represent the same resultant.  
     – GENE: Insert a single resultant vector at the calculated centroid point.  
     – MOM: As GENE but also draw a moment arm equal to (distance – length/2), highlighting the rotational effect.  
   • Context: GRAPHIC enforces three conditions before averaging: nonzero sum, associable distribution, and an essentially straight base line. Otherwise the raw line is shown.  

4. TOTT  
   • Purpose: Selects which textual components of the sum to display.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: DEFA  
   • Options:  
     – DEFA: Show all – total, length, distance.  
     – V: Only the resultant magnitude.  
     – L: Only the length of the load line.  
     – A: Only the distance (centroid location) along the line.  
   • Placement: By default the text block is centered on the area under the trapezoid (centre of gravity). Adding an “M” option (e.g. DEFA M) moves it to the midpoint of the line, matching the MOM convention.  

5. SELN  
   • Purpose: Chooses which nodes participate when distributing or coupling nodal loads along lines (REPR DEDG).  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: ALL  
   • Options:  
     – ALL: Use every node in the sequence.  
     – N1: Only “dependent” nodes (nodes at free ends or supports).  
     – N2: Only “reference” nodes (master nodes to which quantities are assigned; see group N2 description).  
   • Notes: If N2 is selected, forces and moments live in the node objects themselves; boundary‐force status lines follow the local DTYP setting, and vector arrows/types derive from ARRO.

• LC – separation by load case  
• DSGN – designation position and text literal controls  
• ARRO – arrow style and vector tip definitions

The table at hand defines a small but important subset of node‐based rotation result types used in the RAG‐vector‐store schema. It lists seven “Literal” codes, each of which is a shorthand tag for a particular rotation quantity. These tags appear in the TYPE column of a node‐result record and drive both data retrieval and graphical representation of rotations in post‐processing. Below is a structured breakdown of the table’s contents and how it fits into the broader RAG/GRAPHIC framework.

1. Columns  
   • Literal  
     – A short alphanumeric code used in input and output records to identify which rotation result is being referenced.  
   • Meaning  
     – A clear, human‐readable description of what physical quantity the code stands for.  
   • Dim.  
     – The unit of measure for that quantity; in this case, all entries share the same unit, milliradians (mrad).

2. Row‐by‐Row Description  
   – RZ  
     • Meaning: Rotational component about the global Z‐axis.  
     • Usage: Used when one needs to extract or visualize twisting of a node around the Z‐direction in global coordinates.  
   – RXY  
     • Meaning: Rotation vector composed of global X and Y components.  
     • Usage: Provides a two‐dimensional resultant vector in the global XY‐plane, combining rotations about X and about Y into a single vector entity.  
   – RV  
     • Meaning: Resultant rotation as a vector.  
     • Usage: Computes the magnitude and direction of the full three‐component rotation (about X, Y, Z) and represents it as one vector in space.  
   – RL  
     • Meaning: Rotations about local components.  
     • Usage: A generalized tag for all local‐axis rotations; vectors are drawn in the node’s local coordinate system. Available only when the node is attached to a structural element that defines local axes.  
   – RXL  
     • Meaning: Rotational component about the local X‐axis.  
     • Usage: Used to isolate twisting about the element‐defined local X direction.  
   – RYL  
     • Meaning: Rotational component about the local Y‐axis.  
     • Usage: Isolates bending or twist about local Y.  
   – RZL  
     • Meaning: Rotational component about the local Z‐axis.  
     • Usage: Captures warping or out‐of‐plane rotation about local Z.

3. Contextual Integration  
   • These Literals are passed to the record LOAD (for nodal loads) or to GRAPHIC when rendering results. GRAPHIC relies on the record ARRO to determine arrow style (single or double tip) and on the record STRU for text appearance.  
   • UNIT (cm/LT) and SCHH (text height) settings from the STRU record affect scaling and labeling of these rotation vectors on the plot.  
   • For global‐axis rotations (RZ, RXY, RV) the coordinate frame is fixed in the model’s principal axes; for local‐axis rotations (RL, RXL, RYL, RZL) the coordinate frame follows the element orientation.  
   • When a three‐dimensional representation is generated (e.g., for girders in GIRD systems), these vectors help the engineer quickly see where and how a structure twists under load or vibration.  

4. Why This Matters in a RAG Vector Store  
   • Having concise literal codes enables efficient storage and lookup of multiple result types in a compressed index.  
   • When users query the vector store for rotation results, they can specify “TYPE=RZL” or “TYPE=RV” and retrieve both numeric data and the pre‐scaled graphical vectors for display.  
   • Consistent units (mrad) simplify post‐processing scripts, ensuring that all rotation quantities can be plotted on a uniform scale.

In summary, this table is a focused glossary of rotation‐related TYPE literals, their semantic meaning, and their unit. It underpins how rotational behavior at nodes is both stored in the RAG database and rendered in subsequent graphic outputs.

The input is a three-column reference table that defines the literal TYPE-codes you can request in nodal and boundary result output (record LOAD or STRU) and how they are rendered (with DSGN, ARRO, UNIT, SCH2, etc.).  It is structured as follows:

1. Columns  
   • Literal: the code you specify as TYPE.  
   • Meaning: a short English description of what the code produces (e.g. which component of displacement, rotation, force or moment).  
   • Dim.: the physical units associated with that quantity (mm, m, kN, kNm/m, mrad, etc.).

2. Major code groups  
   A. Displacement in global components (prefix O)  
     – OUX, OUY, OUZ: individual X, Y, Z global displacements (mm)  
     – OUV: resultant displacement vector in global XYZ (mm)  
   B. Displacement in local components (prefix OUL; also OUXL, OUYL, OUZL)  
     – Only available if the node is attached to a structural element; local axes come from STRU COOR/COOX/…  
   C. Rotation in global (OR, ORX, ORY, ORZ; ORV, ORXY variants)  
     – ORV: resultant rotation vector of global components (mrad)  
   D. Rotation in local (ORL, ORXL, ORYL, ORZL)  
   E. Kinematic constraint forces & moments (prefix KINE or CF)  
     – CF, CFX, CFY, CFZ (kN) – Component constraint forces.  
     – CFMN, CFMX, CFMY, CFMZ (kNm) – Component constraint moments.  
   F. Boundary forces and moments (prefix TE and TEM)  
     – TEZ: total boundary force in global Z per unit length (kN/m)  
     – TEMX, TEMY, TEMZ: boundary moments about global axes (kNm/m)  
     – TEMN: moment about the boundary’s local longitudinal direction (kNm/m)  
   G. Residuals after dynamic or non-linear runs (REMX, REMY, REMZ)  
     – e.g. REMX: residual moment component X (kNm)

3. Rendering and context parameters  
   • UNIT: scales the vector lengths (e.g. cm per unit). SCH2 UNIT2 may define a second scaling.  
   • SCH2 MIN/MAX and DSGN LMAX: govern automatic clipping of vector lengths above/below thresholds.  
   • OFFS: text offset along the vector; positive in cm, negative as percent of vector length.  
   • DTYP: arrowhead style and orientation; see record ARRO for single/double arrow tips and icons for vectors perpendicular to view.  
   • ND (decimal places) and STAT (frequency of labels) come from SCHH or BEAM STAT.  
   • FILL: fill style of arrowheads or vector ends (record STRU FILL).

4. Special considerations  
   • Local directions for curved/skew boundaries align to the first adjacent QUAD element’s normal.  
   • Irregular boundary-load distributions can be converted to regular ones (EXD, END, etc.) or summarized via TOTA TRAP.  
   • A linearly variable (trapezoidal) distribution is automatically computed by GRAPHIC when the total sum ≠ 0, the distribution is “associative,” and its base direction is stable.  
   • You can replace line distributions with their total and centroid positions (TOTA PAIR or GENE), and GRAPHIC will draw a single resultant vector with offset controlled by SCH2 FMVY.  
   • REPR DEDG allows distributing nodal forces or spring forces along nodal sequences in the manner of boundary loads, grouping only like-directed components.

This table is your master key for specifying exactly which result component appears in the node‐output, how it is scaled, drawn, and labeled when constructing your RAG‐backed result‐visualization workflows.

The table is a comprehensive legend of “literals” used in GRAPHIC/RAG output for nodal‐ and boundary‐related vector quantities.  Each literal is a three‐ to five‐letter code, followed by an English description (“Meaning”) and the physical unit (“Dim.”).  For clarity, the literals fall into five functional groups:

1. Kinematic‐Constraint Forces and Moments  
   • CFV – Resultant kinematic constraint force as a vector  (kN)  
   • CFXY – Kinematic constraint force in X and Y as a vector  (kN)  
   • CM – Kinematic constraint moments in components  (kNm)  
   • CMX, CMY, CMZ – Component of kinematic constraint moment about global X, Y or Z  (kNm)  
   • CMV – Resultant kinematic constraint moment as a vector  (kNm)  
   • CMXY – Kinematic constraint moment in X and Y as a vector  (kNm)  
   • CMB – Kinematic constraint warping moment  (kNm)  

2. Boundary‐Force and Boundary‐Moment Distributions  
   • BOUN – All boundary forces and moments in global components  (kN m, kN/m)  
   • E – Boundary forces in global components  (kN/m)  
   • EX, EY, EZ – Boundary force components in global X, Y or Z  (kN/m)  
   • EN, ES, ET – Boundary force in longitudinal (N), transverse S or transverse T directions  (kN/m)  
   • EXY – Boundary force in transverse direction in the global XY plane  (kN/m)  
   • EM – Boundary moments in global components  (kNm/m)  

   Average (regularized) boundary quantities:  
   • EXD, EYD, EZD – Average boundary force components global X, Y or Z  (kN/m)  
   • END, ESD, ETD – Average boundary force in longitudinal N, transverse S or T  (kN/m)  
   • EXYD – Average boundary force in transverse dir. in XY plane  (kN/m)  
   • EMD – Average boundary moment  (kNm/m)  

3. Totals of Boundary Forces and Moments from Database  
   • TEX, TEY, TEZ – Total of boundary force global X, Y or Z  (kN/m)  
   • TEN, TES, TET – Total of boundary force in longitudinal N, transverse S or T  (kN/m)  
   • TEXY – Total of boundary force in the XY plane  (kN/m)  
   • TEM, TEMN, TEMX, TEMY, TEMZ – Total of boundary moment global and component moments  (kNm/m)  

4. Dynamic or Vibration Loads (Post‐processing Literals)  
   After eigenmode, earthquake (DYNA), time‐step vibration (ASE) or nonlinear (TALPA, ASE) runs:  
   • QF – Resultant nodal load vector  (kN)  
   • QFX, QFY, QFZ – Nodal load vector components in global X, Y, Z  (kN)  
   • QM – Resultant nodal moment vector  (kNm)  
   • QMX, QMY, QMZ – Nodal moment components about global X, Y, Z  (kNm)  

5. Earthquake/Vibration Reaction Forces and Moments  
   • FQ – Resultant reaction force vector  (kN)  
   • FQX, FQY, FQZ – Reaction force components  (kN)  
   • FM – Resultant reaction moment vector  (kNm)  
   • FMX, FMY, FMZ – Reaction moment components  (kNm)  

Key usage notes (drawn from the extended context):
– “CFV”‐type quantities use the record LOAD for nodal loads; plotting styles (vector arrow, cross/rectangle) are governed by the ARRO record.  
– Boundary forces (E, EX, EY, …) can be represented continuously along element edges or as average trapezoidal distributions (EXD, EYD, …) if required for wall‐load procedures.  Totals and centroids can be printed via TOTA PAIR or GENE.  
– Local and global directional options (DTYP, STRU COOR/COOX/COOY/COOZ BOUN) permit skew or curved boundary force decomposition into N/S/T or XYZ components.  
– All “sum” (TOTAL) items require non‐zero net loads and largely uniform direction along the base line to compute a single resultant and centroid in GRAPHIC’s line representation.

The table defines the set of “storey‐level” result identifiers used in a RAG (Result Analysis Graphic) vector‐store context. Each row associates  
1. A Literal (the keyword you specify in the input deck)  
2. Its Meaning (what physical quantity is being reported)  
3. Its Dim(ension) or unit  

These identifiers appear when you draw storey‐level forces, moments, displacements or drifts in the program’s graphic output (GRAPHIC). They can be filtered by load case (record LC), labeled or formatted via record DSGN, scaled with UNIT, and plotted with structural annotation records (STRU, SCHH, etc.). Arrow styles (single/double tip, perpendicular‐to‐plane) follow record ARRO.  

1.   Forces and Moments of Storey Levels  
     • S_PT: Resulting base shear in the XY‐plane (kN)  
     • S_PX: Base shear in global X (kN)  
     • S_PY: Base shear in global Y (kN)  
     • S_PZ: Total vertical force at and above the storey (kN)  
     • S_MX: Moment about global X (kNm)  
     • S_MY: Moment about global Y (kNm)  
     • S_MZ: Moment about global Z (kNm)  
     – These vectors are drawn at each storey level. You control arrow direction (DTYP) and scale (UNIT). If the force vector lies near‐perpendicular to the viewing plane, ARRO switches from arrowheads to a cross or rectangle.  

2.   Displacements of Storey Levels  
     • S_UT: Resulting average storey displacement in the XY‐plane (mm)  
     • S_UX: Displacement in global X (mm)  
     • S_UY: Displacement in global Y (mm)  
     • S_UZ: Displacement in global Z (mm)  
     • S_RZ: Storey rotation in the XY‐plane (mrad)  
     – These are plotted with “vector” or “rigid‐body” symbols. The record STRU controls text placement and COOR defines local coordinates if needed.  

3.   Inter‐Storey Drift  
     • S_DT: Resulting inter‐storey drift in the XY‐plane (mm)  
     • S_DX: Inter‐storey drift in global X (mm)  
     • S_DY: Inter‐storey drift in global Y (mm)  
     • SADX: Maximum inter‐storey drift in X (mm)  
     • SADY: Maximum inter‐storey drift in Y (mm)  
     • S_DR: Inter‐storey rotation in the XY‐plane (mrad)  
     – Drifts may be shown as line‐distributed results along columns or as resultant arrows. When representing them as a trapezoidal distribution (TOTA TRAP), GRAPHIC computes the total and centroid and can plot a representative line (TOTA PAIR or GENE).  

Contextual Notes from the Additional Text:  
- Only reference nodes N2 are used for node‐based results; storey outputs bypass nodal numbers but obey the same styling rules (STRU, SCH2, etc.).  
- DSGN only sets input values (literal keywords, numeric parameters); drawing attributes (line type, arrow tip) are defined by dedicated records (ARRO for arrows, STRU/FILL for fills, SCHH for text height).  
- Units (UNIT) and scaling factors apply globally or can be overridden per result type (UNI2 for second scaling). Obsolete items UMIN/UMAX/UMA2 are superseded by SCH2 MIN/LMAX in new setups.  

See also:  
- AND (combine multiple result channels)  
- LC (select load case)  
- DSGN (input‐only designations)  
- ARRO (arrow styling)

The table before you is a concise mapping of short “literals” (codes) to their full physical meanings and associated dimensions. It would typically be used in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) context to help a graphics or post-processing engine translate terse output flags into human-readable labels and correct SI units when rendering velocity and angular-velocity vectors. Below is a breakdown of its structure, content and implied usage:

1. Overall Structure  
   • Three columns:  
     – Literal: the code you’ll actually see in the output file.  
     – Meaning: a brief English description of the quantity.  
     – Dim.: the physical dimension or unit (always SI here).  
   • Twelve rows, grouped conceptually into two blocks:  
     a. Translational velocities (codes beginning with “V”)  
     b. Angular velocities (codes beginning with “VA”)

2. Block A – Translational Velocities  
   Rows 1–6 cover all the standard velocity outputs:  
   Literal  
     • V    → “Velocities in components”: implies a 3-component vector (VX, VY, VZ).  
     • VX   → velocity in the global X direction.  
     • VY   → velocity in the global Y direction.  
     • VZ   → velocity in the global Z direction.  
     • VV   → “Resultant velocity as vector”: the scalar magnitude |v| = sqrt(VX² + VY² + VZ²).  
     • VXY  → “Velocity X and Y as vector”: planar magnitude sqrt(VX² + VY²), omitting Z.  
   Dim.: all six share the dimension “m/sec.”

3. Block B – Angular Velocities  
   Rows 7–12 define the rotational analogues, with units “1/sec” (radians per second):  
   Literal  
     • VA    → “Angular velocity in components”: full triplet (VAX, VAY, VAZ).  
     • VAX   → component about global X-axis.  
     • VAY   → component about global Y-axis.  
     • VAZ   → component about global Z-axis.  
     • VAV   → “Resultant angular velocity as vector”: |ω| = sqrt(VAX² + VAY² + VAZ²).  
     • VAXY  → “Angular velocity X and Y as vector”: planar resultant sqrt(VAX² + VAY²).

4. Interpretation and Use in Graphics or Tables  
   • When the program’s result file tags a data column with “VX,” your RAG agent should label it “Velocity component X” and know the values are in m/sec.  
   • If it sees “VAV,” it should treat the numbers as magnitudes of the 3D angular-velocity vector and attach “1/sec” to axes or legends.  
   • The “VV” and “VXY,” “VAV” and “VAXY” codes enable quick plotting of either full 3-D magnitudes or planar projections without recomputing on the client side.  

5. Contextual Fit  
   • In a broader schema—where other tables define forces, moments, displacements, etc.—this velocity table slots in under the TYPE definitions for nodal or element results.  
   • Upstream records (e.g. STRU, LOAD, DSGN, ARRO) determine how and where these quantities are drawn; downstream modules read this mapping to generate axis labels, tooltips or legend entries consistently.  

6. Key Patterns to Leverage in a RAG-Vector Store  
   • Prefix “V” always refers to translational motion; “VA” to rotational.  
   • Suffixes X, Y, Z designate orthogonal components; “V…V” indicates a resultant magnitude; “V…XY” is the planar subset.  
   • Uniform unit patterns simplify downstream formatting: one group in m/sec, the other in 1/sec.  

By capturing this metadata in your vector store, you ensure that any automated retrieval of “VX” or “VAV” carries along not only the numeric values but also the correct human-readable descriptions and units for rendering, reporting or further annotation.

The table in question defines a set of “literals” (short names) that you can use in a node‐output or result‐output command to request various dynamic quantities (velocities, accelerations, angular terms, etc.) in a finite‐element post-processing system. It has three columns:

 1. Literal  
 2. Meaning  
 3. Dimension (“Dim.”)  

Here is a structured description of each column and how it fits into the workflow of a RAG-style vector store or a graphics‐driven postprocessor:

1.  Literal  
    •  A fixed two- or three-character code you type in the input deck (for example, after a “TYPE=” keyword) to specify which physical quantity you want to extract or plot.  
    •  These codes appear in records such as NOD (nodal output), BOUN (boundary output), or in a DSGN (designation) record that assembles values for drawing.  
    •  Examples in this portion of the table include VT, A, AX, AY, AZ, AV, AXY, AA, AAX, AAY, AAZ, AAV, AAXY, AT, etc.

2.  Meaning  
    •  A short English description of the physical quantity corresponding to each literal.  
    •  Helps you confirm that you’re requesting the correct result.  
    •  For instance:  
      – “VT” stands for “Twist velocity”  
      – “A” is “Acceleration in components”  
      – “AX” is “Acceleration component X,” and so on.  
      – “AV” denotes the “Resultant acceleration as a vector.”  
      – “AA” is “Angular acceleration in components”  
      – “AAV” is “Resultant angular acceleration as vector,” etc.  

3.  Dim.  
    •  The units in which the postprocessor will print or scale the chosen quantity.  
    •  Typical units:  
      – Linear acceleration “m/sec²”  
      – Angular acceleration “1/sec²”  
      – Twist velocity or twist acceleration “1/msec” or “1/msec²”  
    •  These dimension tags ensure that the vector‐store or graphic routines (AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO) apply correct scaling (UNIT, SCHH, OFFS, DTYP, etc.) when drawing arrows or placing text.

Context & Usage Notes  
•  You would combine these literals with other control parameters:  
   – LC (load case) to pick which load or time step you want,  
   – AND to turn on nodal result components,  
   – ARRO to choose if vectors get single or double arrowheads,  
   – DSGN to funnel literal values into the drawing engine (it does not itself render graphics).  
•  UNIT and SCH2 or STRU records then define how large arrow lengths are (cm per unit), text height, number of decimal places (ND), and positional offsets (OFFS).  
•  In dynamic or earthquake analyses (DYNA, ASE, TALPA), you will frequently request accelerations (A, AX, AY, AZ, AV), angular accelerations (AA, AAX, etc.) or twist terms (VT, AT) to check the nodal response.  
•  In a RAG vector store, each literal serves as a key under which the numerical data are indexed. Queries can then efficiently fetch, say, all “AX” fields for visualization or further processing.

The table under review defines a set of “literals” used in nodal result reporting, broken into two main families—incremental results (prefixed “I”) and residual results (prefixed “R”).  Each row associates a short code (Literal) with a human-readable description (Meaning) and a physical unit (Dim.).  In the context of a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, these codes can serve as vector embedding keys or tags that link to more detailed documentation (e.g. record DSGN, LOAD or STRU), and they dovetail with related input items such as AND, LC, ARRO and scaling or formatting records (UNIT, SCHH, SCH2, etc.).

1. Incremental Results (prefix “I”)  
   • IU: “Incremental displacement in components” (mm)  
   • IUX: “Incremental displacement component X” (mm)  
   • IUY: “Incremental displacement component Y” (mm)  
   • IUZ: “Incremental displacement component Z” (mm)  
   • IUV: “Resultant incremental displacement as vector” (mm)  
   • IUXY: “Incremental displacement X and Y as vector” (mm)  

   • IR: “Incremental rotation in components” (mrad)  
   • IRX: “Incremental rotation component X” (mrad)  
   • IRY: “Incremental rotation component Y” (mrad)  
   • IRZ: “Incremental rotation component Z” (mrad)  
   • IRV: “Resultant incremental rotation as vector” (mrad)  
   • IRXY: “Incremental rotation X and Y as vector” (mrad)  

   These “I-” values typically appear in transient, eigen-form or incremental‐load analyses (e.g. ASE time‐step, DYNA earthquake or TALPA non-linear runs).  They can be toggled on/off with TYPE=I* and formatted by SCHH for text height, ND for decimals, UNIT for scaling, etc.

2. Residual Results (prefix “R”)  
   • RE: “Residual forces in components” (kN)  
   • REX: “Residual force component X” (kN)  
   • REY: “Residual force component Y” (kN)  
   • REZ: “Residual force component Z” (kN)  
   • REV: “Resultant residual force as vector” (kN)  
   • REXY: “Residual force X and Y as vector” (kN)  

   • REM: “Residual moments in components” (kNm)  
   • REMX: “Residual moment component X” (kNm)  
   • (…and so on, following the same pattern)  

   Residual values quantify unbalanced loads or moments at nodes after equilibrium checks.  They are often used to flag convergence issues or to drive automatic load correction.  As with incremental types, display parameters (DTYP direction, OFFS text offset, FILL style on vectors/arrows) are controlled by corresponding STRU, ARRO or DSGN records.

Integration Notes for RAG Vector Store  
- Each literal can be stored as an embedding “key” with associated metadata fields:  
    • “full-name” = Meaning  
    • “unit” = Dim.  
    • “category” = {Incremental, Residual}  
    • “related_records” = {LOAD, STRU, DSGN, SCHH, ARRO, …}  
- Queries like “list all vector-type outputs in mm” or “show only residual moments” map directly to prefixes (“IUV,” “REMX,” …) and units.  
- For multi­dimensional tagging, prefix and suffix patterns (e.g. I*Z, *XY) can be used to filter subsets via simple wildcard queries in the vector store.

See also: AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO for how these literals interact with other graphical and configuration records.

Below is a structured, detailed description of the four‐row input table.  This table defines the literal codes you can use in the TYPE field when requesting residual‐moment results in a GRAPHIC or RAG vector output.  It shows which component or combination of components will be plotted, and all quantities share the same unit of kNm.

1. Table structure  
   – Number of columns: 3  
     • Literal  
     • Meaning  
     • Dim. (unit)  
   – Number of rows: 4 (one entry per available residual‐moment option)  

2. Column breakdown  
   a. Literal  
      • This is the keyword you supply to the TYPE parameter of your input record (for example, TYPE=REMY).  
      • It selects which residual‐moment quantity to extract and display.  
   b. Meaning  
      • A short English description of exactly what moment the literal refers to.  
      • Links the code to a physical quantity (component around a given axis or a resultant).  
   c. Dim.  
      • The dimension (unit) in which the result is given: kNm (kilonewton‐meter).  
      • All four options use the same unit.  

3. Row‐by‐row entries  
   1) REMY  
      – Meaning: “Residual moment component Y”  
      – Dim.: kNm  
      – Use case: Plot the unbalanced or residual bending moment about the global Y-axis at a node or along a boundary after load‐case or dynamic calculations.  
   2) REMZ  
      – Meaning: “Residual moment component Z”  
      – Dim.: kNm  
      – Use case: Plot the residual moment about the global Z-axis. Often needed in 3D models to check torsional imbalance about Z.  
   3) RMXY  
      – Meaning: “Resultant residual moment as vector”  
      – Dim.: kNm  
      – Use case: Compute and display the vector sum of the residual moments in the global X and Y directions. GRAPHIC will draw an arrow whose magnitude and orientation represent that resultant in the XY-plane.  
   4) REMV  
      – Meaning: “Residual moment X and Y as vector”  
      – Dim.: kNm  
      – Use case: Similar to RMXY, this literal also causes GRAPHIC to generate a two‐component vector (X and Y) showing both moment components side by side or combined, depending on your arrow‐style settings (see ARRO).  

4. How to apply in a RAG/vector‐graphic setup  
   – In the input deck, under your desired record (e.g. RECORD=LOAD or RECORD=STRUC), set TYPE to one of the above literals to specify which residual moment to visualize.  
   – UNIT is by default kNm for these items, so you do not need to override scaling unless you want enlarged arrows (via UNIT or UNI2).  
   – You can control arrow style and direction with the ARRO record (single vs. double tip, projection plane, etc.).  
   – Text labels (showing numerical values) follow the SCHH or SCH2 settings for height, format (ND), and offset (OFFS).  

5. Cross‐references  
   – See ARRO ‒ for vector arrow styling and projection rules.  
   – See SCH2 or SCHH ‒ for text‐formatting parameters (number of decimals, offsets).  
   – DSGN only sets input values; it does not draw graphics.  
   – LC or AND can be used if you need to combine residual moments from multiple load cases or apply logical filters.

 Average Line Representations and Resultants
 The calculation of a regular line distribution or their resultant occurs with these conditions:
 • The total sum of the line representation must be unequal to 0.
 • The line representation must associate.
 • The direction of the basic line of the line representation may not change essentially (Oth- erwise the components which act in different directions are added in the case of the mo- ments.)
 Then GRAPHIC determines a linearly variable distribution (trapezium) whose sum and centre of gravity is equal to the initial values.
 Instead of the line representation the sum of this and the position of the centre of gravity can be printed with the input of TOTA PAIR or GENE. GRAPHIC shows a line from the total to the line. The length depends on the vertical distance of texts (offset) (record SCH2 FMVY).
 Representation at nodal sequences (REPR DEDG)
 Certain single nodal forces, forces at kinematic constraints or spring forces can be dis- tributed along a nodal sequence (EDGE) similiar to the boundary forces. Each connecting line between two nodes is used exactly once, even if more than one nodal sequence was defined at this line. Only forces with the same direction are be summarized.

The input table is part of the BEAM record definition in the RAG‐vector store.  It specifies which result quantities can be drawn on beam‐type elements (beams, trusses, cables, springs, piles or external SIR‐sections), under what conditions, and in which units.  The table is organized roughly into five columns:

1. Element‐type availability  
   • Columns headed D, B, P, C, I indicate whether the quantity is stored for  
     – D: design elements  
     – B: beam elements  
     – P: pile elements  
     – C: truss & cable elements  
     – I: external beam sections (program SIR/AQB)  
   • Each cell may contain  
     – “*” meaning generally available  
     – “–” meaning not available  
     – “1”, “2” or “3” meaning only stored by STAR2/AQB, ASE or COMPOSITE, respectively  

2. STYP code  
   – A short literal (e.g. HNS, EN, SPZ, SGMA, ULN, ASU9, PTZ, etc.)  

3. Quantity name  
   – A brief description of the result quantity (e.g. “Hinge reaction N”, “Axial force N”, “Spring force in global Z”, “Maximum design stress in tendon”, “Utilisation level Vy”, “Stirrup reinforcement layer 9”, “Lateral bedding forces in local z”, etc.)  

4. Detailed descriptor  
   – Extended text that clarifies whether the quantity is a total displacement (m), rotation (rad), force (kN), stress (MPa), reinforcement area (cm²/m), bedding pressure (kN/m²), utilization ratio (–), cross‐section class, bond force per length (kN/m), von Mises stress (N/mm²), etc.  

5. Units  
   – The physical unit in which the quantity is to be represented (m, rad, kN, kNm, kN/m, kN/m², MPa, N/mm², cm²/m, – for dimensionless).  

Key groups of STYP codes include:  
 • Hinge reactions (HNS, HVYS, HVZS, HMTS, HMYS, HMZS, HNT, HMZ2–HMZ3, HMY4)  
 • Spring results (SPY, SPZ, SPM, ASP, ASPV, ASPX, ASPY)  
 • Prestressing tendon design stresses (SGMA, SGMI, SGPM, SGSW)  
 • Internal forces and moments (EN, EVY, EVZ, ULN, ULVY, ULVZ, ULMT, ULMY, ULMZ, ULMB, ULM2)  
 • Bond and dowel shear (BOND, BNDO)  
 • Stress point results (SDPT, SZPT, STPT, SVPT, SPCP)  
 • Cross‐section classification and checks (CSCL, CPCL, CECL, CCHK)  
 • Utilisation levels and decisive design ratios (TCF, SCCB, SCBN, ASU*, AST*)  
 • Bedding pressures in soil‐structure interaction (PT, PTY, PTZ)  

Additional notes and context:  
 • Only one element type (D, B, P, C or I) can be edited per BEAM record.  If TYPE admits only one STYP, STYP is fixed.  
 • UNIT controls the graphic scaling of lengths; ROPT, R, P choose constant‐value text alignment.  
 • DTYP selects representation direction (local y/z or global X/Y/Z, or special cases like influence lines).  
 • SCHH and STAT control text height and the number of status‐line designations.  
 • When shear or rotation derivatives are available at beam sections, cubic‐parabola “engineering lines” are drawn; their maxima are generated internally but not stored for superposition or design.  
 • For composite cross sections, a material number (LC MAT) must be specified for SIGU…SIGV; stress‐point data can be read from AQUA.  
 • Internal creep‐shrinkage stresses (MT1 series) are added to N…MT1 if present.  

See also the records AND, LC, DSGN and ARRO for load‐case control, design parameter selection and arrow‐style options.
