This record is used in GRAPHIC/WING to fine-tune the appearance of status lines, labels and curves when you plot internal forces, displacements, slopes, influence lines, etc.  Only one element type (TYPE/STYP) can be active per BEAM record; all other parameters then apply to that single type.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown of the table you provided:

1. STAT  
   • Description: Selects which intermediate values get text designations.  
     – MAX: label only the global maxima and values at beam ends  
     – END: include maxima and all end‐section values  
     – ALL: also at every beam‐cut location  
     – INTE: also at other intermediate positions  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: MAX  

2. MIN, MIN2, OFFS (obsolete)  
   • These three parameters are now superseded by SCH2 records—MIN… and FMVX/FMYY—so they no longer accept new input.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: * (available in legacy files but ignored)  

3. ND  
   • Description: Number of decimal places to print behind the comma. Controlled by SCHH ND.  
   • Unit: – / LIT  
   • Default: * (inherits from global settings)  

4. FILL  
   • Description: Fill style of the status‐line or area under the curve. For valid fill patterns see the STRU record’s FILL parameter.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NO (no fill)  

5. REPR  
   • Description: Representation type—e.g. linear (DLIN), smoothed spline, stepped line, etc. See STRU REPR for options.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: DLIN  

6. STAL  
   • Description: Controls whether intermediate lines themselves (not just their labels) are drawn. Uses the same keywords as STAT.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: END  

7. OFFZ  
   • Description: Vertical offset of text labels relative to the baseline of the curve or status line.  
     – EDGE: at the baseline  
     – MIDD: mid‐height of the stroke (default)  
     – REPE: at the top end of each segment  
     – ABOV: above the entire curve  
     – BELO: below the baseline  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: MIDD  

8. NCRV  
   • Description: Maximum number (1…10) of extra curvature (second derivative) evaluation points to plot for moment or displacement splines.  
     – 0 suppresses the added extremes and uses the raw database values only.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: ‑10  

Usage notes from the context text:

- When shear (derivative of moment) or rotation (derivative of displacement) is available at beam sections, GRAPHIC/WING draws a cubic parabola to represent the continuous distribution. Additional “maximum” points may be generated internally; these are not saved back to the database or used in further superpositions or design checks.
- STAT and STAL interact: you can choose to draw only the extreme or also every cut, and separately choose whether to show the line itself.
- ND and SCHH control numeric precision; SCHH also affects text height (SCHH TEXT).
- FILL, REPR and OFFZ reference STRU settings: BEAM merely passes these through to the plotting engine.
- The BEAM record sits alongside STRU (structure elements) and LOAD (point/element loads) and is conditional on element TYPE/STYP. Only one element type’s results can be active per BEAM record.

This table is the core of the BEAM‐record in our RAG‐vector store.  It defines every “TYPE” of result that can be plotted on beam, truss, cable or spring elements, gives a human‐readable description, the engineering unit, and indicates for which element classes the result exists.  In addition, the table ties into related controls (STYP, DSGN, UNIT, STRU, SCHH, DTYP, ROPT) described elsewhere.

1. Column Layout  
‐ Columns D, B, P, C, I  
 • D = Design elements  
 • B = Beam elements  
 • P = Pile elements  
 • C = Truss & Cable elements  
 • I = External beam sections (from SIR/AQB)  
 Each cell holds one of:  
  “*” = generally available  
  “–” = not available  
  “1” = only stored by STAR2/AQB  
  “2” = only by ASE  
  “3” = only by COMPOSITE  
‐ TYPE  
 The literal code used in the BEAM record to request this result.  
‐ Description  
 Full name of the result (e.g. “Shear force Vy”, “Maximum design stress in tendon”).  
‐ Unit  
 Physical dimension for plotting (m, rad, kN, kN/m, MPa, N/mm², cm²/m, etc.).

2. Key Functional Groups in the Table  
‐ Hinge reactions & total displacements/rotations  
 HNS, HVYS, HVZS, HMTS, HMYS, HMZS (global N, Vy, Vz forces and Mₜ, My, Mz moments; units m or rad)  
 Also plastic hinge displacement (HNT) and performance indices (HMZ2, HMY3, HMZ3, HMY4).  
‐ Spring results  
 SPY, SPZ (global Y/Z forces), SPM (moments), and area‐related forces ASP, ASPV, ASPX, ASPY (kN/m²).  
‐ Tendon design stresses (QUAD elements)  
 SGMA (max), SGMI (min), SGPM (permanent), SGSW (stress range) – all in MPa.  
 “Loss of prestress” if available.  
‐ Internal forces & moments in beams/trusses  
 EN (axial), EVY (shear Vy), BOND (bond force), BNDO (shear in dowels) – kN, kN/m.  
‐ Section stress points (SPT)  
 SDPT (min), SZPT (max), STPT (shear), SVPT (von Mises), SPCP (principal compression) – N/mm².  
‐ Cross‐section classes & checks (COMPOSITE only)  
 CSCL, CPCL, CECL (class elastic/plastic), CCHK (check flag).  
‐ Utilisation indices  
 TCF (total), SCCB (cross‐section resistance), SCBN (buckling), ULN, ULVY, ULVZ (force util.),  
 ULMT, ULMY, ULMZ, ULMB, ULM2 (moment/torsion util.).  
‐ Reinforcement requirements (per cut length, cm²/m)  
 Stirrups: ASU9–ASUF (layers 9–15), tension bars AST, AST0–AST9, ASTA.  
 FASU = design error indicator.  
‐ Bedding forces under piles/slabs  
 PT, PTY, PTZ (lateral bedding in global/ local axes; kN/m²).  
‐ (Beyond snippet) Stresses SIGU, SIGL, SIGD, SIGZ (uniaxial + total section extremes), energies ENER/PIEZ.

3. How to Read “Availability” Flags  
– “*” means you can request that TYPE for the given element class in BEAM.  
– “–” means it won’t plot (data not stored).  
– Numeric codes 1/2/3 signal special storage routines (STAR2/AQB, ASE, COMPOSITE).

4. Usage Notes  
• Only one element type (D, B, P, C, I) can be chosen in a single BEAM record.  
• If a TYPE supports exactly one STYP, STYP is set automatically.  
• UNIT scales vectors/diagrams; STRU toggles numbering; SCHH controls text‐height labels.  
• DTYP can override default local‐axis (Y/Z) or global representation directions (e.g. for influence lines or U.S. moment conventions).  
• Certain max‐value curves (e.g. cubic parabolas for shear or rotations) are drawn but not saved for superposition or design.  
• For composite sections you must supply LC MAT to select the material in multiplestate results (SIGU–SIGV).

In sum, this table is your master map from TYPE codes to engineering quantities, units, and their applicability across element families when generating graphical status lines in RAG.

  • MT2, MT1

  – The “implicit hinge reaction nonlinear” set (HALL, HN, HVY, HVZ, HMT, HMY, HMZ) all dimensioned “0 / 00” to indicate they are non-dimensional or require special interpretation in the nonlinear (plastic) solution.  
  – The corresponding linear elastic hinge reactions (HNL, HVYL, HVZL, HMTL, HMYL, HMZL) expressed in kN or kNm.  
  – Finally the total displacement or rotation at the hinge (HNS, HVYS, HVZS, HMTS, HMYS, HMZS) with units in meters or radians.

  • HNT, HMZ2, HMY3, HMZ3, HMY4, etc.  
    – Performance indices by category (2nd, 3rd, 4th) for hinge moments.  
  • SPY, SPZ, SPM, ASP…  
    – Spring forces and moments in global Y/Z or per unit area.  
  • SGMA, SGMI, SGPM, SGSW  
    – Tendon design stresses (maximum, minimum, permanent, range) in prestressed elements.  
  • PT, PTY, PTZ

The table is part of the BEAM record definition in a structural‐analysis/vector‐graphics system. It enumerates result types (literals) that can be drawn for various element categories, supplies a human‐readable meaning for each literal, and gives the physical dimension (unit) of the quantity.

1. Column Layout  
   • D, B, P, C, T, I – flags indicating availability by element type  
     – D: design elements  
     – B: beam elements  
     – P: pile elements  
     – C: truss & cable elements  
     – T: all spring elements  
     – I: external beam sections (from SIR/AQB)  
     A “*” means generally available, “–” not available, “1,2,3” means available only in specific programs (STAR2/AQB, ASE, COMPOSITE).  
   • Literal – short code used in the BEAM record to request that quantity  
   • Meaning – full description of the quantity plotted on the beam axis  
   • Dim. – physical unit (kN, kNm, %, N/mm², 1/m, cm²/m, etc.)

2. Result Groups  
   a) Internal Forces & Moments (flags “1 1 – – – *”)  
     • EVZ – shear force Vz (kN)  
     • EMT – torsional moment Mt (kNm)  
     • EMY – bending moment My (principal bending, kNm)  
     • EMZ – bending moment Mz (transverse bending, kNm)  

   b) Non-linear Stiffnesses (same flags)  
     • EA, GAY, GAZ – axial and shear stiffnesses (%)  
     • GIT – torsional stiffness (%)  
     • EIY, EIZ – bending stiffnesses (%)  

   c) Plastic Deformations  
     • KPX – plastic strain x (%)  
     • KPY, KPZ – plastic curvature y/z (1/m)  

   d) Design & Stress Quantities  
     • SIGD – minimum stress (N/mm²)  
     • SIGZ – maximum stress (N/mm²)  
     • STAU – shear stress, SVPT/v.Mises stress, SPC/principal compression, SPT/principal tension (all N/mm²)  
     • SIGU – uniaxial top stress; SIGL – uniaxial bottom stress (for prestressed concrete)  
     • SIGW – stress in welds; DECO – decompression stress; FACV – shear reduction factor (–)  
     • SWMT, SWSM – sway stresses of normal and shear stress (N/mm²)  
     • BOND – bond force per length across material interfaces (kN/m)  

3. Reinforcement & Bedding  
   • ASU9–ASUF – stirrup reinforcement layers 9–15 (cm²/m)  
   • AST, AST0–ASTA – torsion longitudinal and stirrup layers 0–10 (cm²/m)  
   • PT, PTY, PTZ – lateral bedding forces (kN/m²), only in ASE (flag “2”)

   – Only one element type may be selected per BEAM record. If an element has only one STYP, that STYP is implied.

The table is part of the BEAM-record definition in a structural-analysis RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store. It defines which result “literals” (i.e. named output quantities) can be requested, for which element types they exist, what they mean, and in what units they’re reported. Below is a breakdown of its structure, columns and how to interpret it in the context of a BEAM record:

1. Column headers (applicability flags):
   • D = Design elements  
   • B = Beam elements  
   • P = Pile elements  
   • C = Truss & cable elements  
   • T = (All) spring elements  
   • I = External beam sections (from program SIR/AQB)  
   In each flag-column you will find one of:  
     –   means “value not available”  
     *   means “generally available”  
     1,2,3 indicate “only stored by program STAR2/AQB (1), ASE (2), or COMPOSITE (3)”

2. Literal column:  
   The short code or “literal” you will pass to the BEAM record (e.g. CSGC, SWVT, AS2, ASU0).

3. Meaning column:  
   A human-readable description of the quantity. For example:  
     CSGC → Utilisation level of common materials (except concrete), longitudinal compression  
     SWVT → Shear‐wall vertical reinforcement (total)  
     AS2  → Reinforcement in layer 2 (above)

4. Dimension column (Dim.):  
   The units in which the quantity is reported, e.g. “cm²”, “cm²/m”, “m”, “–” (dimensionless).

5. Table groupings:  
   a) “CSG…” group (uniaxial stresses & utilizations):  
      • CSGC, CSGT, CSHE, CSGV  
   b) “SW…” group (Shear‐wall design):  
      • SWVT, SWST, SWL1, SWL2, SWL3, SWS1–SWS3, SWWA, SWWB  
   c) “AS…” group (Reinforcements across multiple layers):  
      • AS  (total), AS0…AS9 (individual layers)  
   d) “ASU…” subset (Stirrups per cut part, up to layer 9 and beyond):  
      • ASU, ASU0…ASU9, ASUA…ASUF, etc.

6. Interpretation of flags and availability:  
   – A “*” under B for literal AS2 means you can request AS2 for beam elements.  
   – A “–” under C for AS2 means it doesn’t apply to truss/cable elements.  
   – A “3” under D for CSCL (Cross‐section class) means this property is only stored if you run COMPOSITE.

7. Usage in BEAM record:  
   • Specify TYPE = BEAM, STYP = the element subtype if needed.  
   • Use UNIT to scale lengths/forces (e.g. cm, kN, N/mm²).  
   • Use DTYP to choose representation direction (local y/z or global X/Y/Z).  
   • SCHH controls text height for status-line annotations.  
   • Only one TYPE can be active per BEAM record; STYP is auto-set if only one choice exists.

8. Contextual notes:  
   – The “CSG…” stresses relate to prestressed/post-tensioned design.  
   – “SW…” group covers shear‐wall reinforcement quantities in total and by zone.  
   – “AS…” and “ASU…” groups cover longitudinal and stirrup reinforcement layers, respectively.  
   – If a value is known only in certain programs (STAR2, ASE, COMPOSITE), flags 1–3 appear.  
   – These quantities appear when you plot status lines (BEAM draws the structural lines plus optional annotations).

 The stresses SIGU and SIGL are uniaxial stresses (e.g. for prestressed concrete) according to the ratio M/W for the external fibres which were determined by the program AQB. On the other hand SIGD and SIGZ are minimum and maximum stresses in the total cross section. The normal stresses for truss elements and cables are represented with SIGU.
 The bond force BOND is calculated from the difference of longitudinal forces per material be- tween the beam sections. If more than one material exists the total can be calculated (LC MAT _SUM REF...).
 ENER and PIEZ are drawn in the global Z direction with reference to the minimum Z coordinate. In this cases the geometric scale is the default for UNIT.
 Representation
 Representation
 Logical defaults are prescribed for the representation directions of all values. The usual values are represented along the local y or z axis. Influence lines are drawn with their components in the global coordinate directions. In special cases (for example the line of vision is equal to a local axis, but also for moment diagram in USA) all other types of representation can be selected by using DTYP.

The usual values are represented along the local y or z axis. Influence lines are drawn with their components in the global coordinate directions. In special cases (for example the line of vision is equal to a local axis, but also for moment diagram in USA) all other types of representation can be selected by using DTYP..
 The values are represented always with their real dimension also in the skew directions.
 Additional designations are represented at the status lines, if SCHH is not zero. The amount of the designations can be controlled with STAT. No designations occur, if the distance of the beam sections becomes smaller than the text height and the check of the text is not activated (record SCHH REVI).
 If shear forces (derivatives of moments) are known in beam sections, a cubic parabola is drawn to create an engineering line. In this case maximum values may be calculated. The user has to check these maximum values if the loads include line moments, because high-order moment lines are generated then. Or more nodes or beam sections have to be defined. A warning is printed.
 Attention: These (maximum) values are generated internally in GRAPHIC/WING. They are not saved in the database and are not provided for superpositioning and design calculation.
 Beam displacements
 If rotations (derivatives of displacements) are known in beam sections, a cubic parabola is drawn to create an engineering line. In this case maximum values may be calculated. The user has to check these maximum values because these cubic parabola results from the displacements formulation of Finite Elements Method (solution of minimum of deformations energy) and each loading (e.g. line loads) requires a high-order line. Or more nodes or beam sections have to be defined. A warning is printed.
 Attention: These (maximum) values are generated internally in GRAPHIC/WING. They are not saved in the database and are not provided for superpositioning and design calculation.
 Beam loading
 The loading is represented with its defined distribution considering the load factors, the gravity loading, the moments due to the eccentric loading and the generated loads.
 Point loads are drawn as vectors with UNI2.
 Composite cross sections
 A material number (record LC MAT) for SIGU to SIGV must be specified for composite cross sections. The results can be saved in the database also with a stress point defined in the program AQUA. Then the designation (literal) of this stress point can be input for MAT.

Point loads are drawn as vectors with UNI2.. Composite cross sections. A material number (record LC MAT) for SIGU to SIGV must be specified for composite cross sections. The results can be saved in the database also with a stress point defined in the program AQUA. Then the designation (literal) of this stress point can be input for MAT..
 Internal forces and moments
 The internal forces and moments of inherent stresses of the cross section from creep and shrinkage are added to the internal forces and moments N...MT1, if they are available in this load case.

This table specifies the input‐data fields (keywords) and allowed values for plotting quadrilateral (QUAD) and brick (BRIC) finite‐element results in the SOFiSTiK/WING graphics module. It serves as a reference for a RAG vector store: each row is an “Item,” with a brief “Description,” its “Type” (data type or enumeration), and—for many entries—a unit or pointer to another control record.

1. General Plotting Keywords  
   • TYPE  
     – Selects what result quantity you want to plot (stresses, forces, displacements, reinforcement demands, error estimates, etc.).  
     – The table sketches dozens of valid TYPE‐literals, grouped by analysis program (ASE, TALPA, BEMESS, HYDRA, etc.). Each literal is accompanied by a short meaning and its dimension (e.g. “SXU Upper membrane stress in x,” kN/m²).  
   • DSGN  
     – If set, only the input values are passed through; nothing is actually drawn.  
   • UNIT  
     – Scaling factor for lengths of vector or tensor glyphs (see STRUCT record).  
   • SCHH  
     – Text height (pointer to STRUCT record SCHH).  
   • MIN / MINT  
     – Obsolete minimum‐value thresholds; superseded by SCH2 MIN1, MIN2.  
   • STYP  
     – Selects the sampling or display point for each element:  
       · ELEM (value at element center)  
       · QUAD (identical to ELEM for QUAD elements)  
       · NODE (nodal extrapolation of Gauss‐point values)  
       · GAUS (the four corner‐adjacent Gauss points)  
       · E2N (average nodal values from element centers)  
       · G2N (average nodal values from Gauss points)  
       · ERIN (error estimate at element center)  
       · EE2N (average nodal error estimates)  
       · BRIC / BRIK (centers and nodes for 3D brick elements)  
   • ND  
     – Number of decimal places in the output text (see SCHH ND).

2. Fill, Line and Annotation Control  
   • FILL (fill pattern or area‐filling for contours; see STRU FILL)  
   • LT (line type for cuts, isolines, outlines)  
   • NO (item‐number suppression flag)  
   • REVI, DIST (now obsolete: replaced by SCHH REVI and SCH2 BACX/BACY)  
   • A (text string for perimeter reinforcement labels; used when plotting reinforcement).

3. TYPE Literals by Analysis Module  
   – ASE / TALPA / FEABENCH (plate‐bending/shear results, principal stresses, cut‐directions, bedding stresses, displacements).  
   – Non‐linear ASE (damage variables, crack openings, hardening/damage parameters).  
   – TALPA (3D principal stresses, plane stresses).  
   – BEMESS (decompression strains, reinforcement areas by layer and design check variables, crack‐widths, stress ranges).  
   – HYDRA / DOLFYN and HASE (hydraulic or special element results).  

4. Representation Modes  
   • REPR DVEC / DARE / DREP / DTXT: Tensile/compression symbols, flow‐velocity vectors, principal stress vectors, tensor glyphs.  
   • REPR DISO: Isolines within each element (hyperbola‐based interpolation), with uphill text labeling, interval control via DTXT/CDIS.  
   • REPR DCUT: Section‐cuts through QUAD elements, with option to draw status lines or filled areas, transform results into cut‐normal (N) and tangential (T) directions, weld‐seam stress approximations.  
   • Special flags for plasticized areas (FLIE), reinforcement mats (ASUM/ASLM), isolines or cuts of reinforcement, minimum‐value clipping in cuts and isolines.

Cross‐references at the top (“See also: AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, ISOL, SECT”) point to related record types controlling appearance of arrows, isolines, section cuts, etc. Together, this table defines the complete input “vocabulary” for graphically representing a wide range of finite‐element results on QUAD and BRIC elements in SOFiSTiK.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The table shown is an excerpt from the SOFiSTiK/WING manual and defines a group of graphical‐output control items for area (QUAD) results.  It would typically appear under a “STRU” (structure) or “NODE” record section in an input deck.  Below is a structured breakdown suitable for a RAG‐style vector store ingestion:

1.  Table Structure  
    •  Four columns:  
       –  Item (literal name)  
       –  Description (what the item controls)  
       –  Unit (if any; often “LIT” for literal keyword or a physical unit)  
       –  Default (the default value when the item is omitted)  
    •  Eleven rows, each defining one control item.

2.  Row‐by‐Row Detail  
    1.  DANG  
        •  Description: Marked obsolete; kept for backward compatibility.  
        •  Unit: “–” (none)  
        •  Default: “*”  

    2.  LEGX  
        •  Description: Obsolete; users should instead set SCH2 FMVX.  
        •  Unit: “–”  
        •  Default: “*”  

    3.  LEGY  
        •  Description: Obsolete; users should instead set SCH2 FMVY.  
        •  Unit: “–”  
        •  Default: “*”  

    4.  REPR  
        •  Description: Selects the type of graphical representation for areas (contours, cuts, filled areas, etc.).  Values are literal keywords defined under record STRU REPR (e.g. DARE, DCUT, DISO).  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: DARE  

    5.  AVER  
        •  Description: Controls averaging of node‐wise results on group boundaries (visible as contour lines).  
            –  NO: do not average across element boundaries (results may jump)  
            –  YES: average them for a smooth transition  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: NO  

    6.  TOTA  
        •  Description: If line (cut) representations are summed, this item switches the summing on or off.  Links to NODE TOTA.  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: – (none)  

    7.  OFFZ  
        •  Description: Offset of text labels for line/cut representations.  Semantically equivalent to BEAM OFFZ.  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: MIDD  

    8.  CDIS  
        •  Description: Distance (in cm) between successive text labels when area representations (e.g. filled contours) are annotated.  
        •  Unit: cm  
        •  Default: 2.0  

    9.  COMT  
        •  Description: When REPR DTXT (distributed texts) is active, determines whether identical texts within one area are collapsed to a single summary label.  
            –  YES: summarise identical strings  
            –  NO: show every occurrence  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: NO  

   10.  TOTT  
        •  Description: Specifies which text strings appear in sum annotations (NODE TOTT defines the actual text content).  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: DEFA  

   11.  PUNT  
        •  Description: Controls which parts of the punching‐force output are printed when REPR PUNC/ASPS is chosen.  
            –  DEFA: all texts (default)  
            –  N: node number only  
            –  V: force value only  
            –  B: eccentricity factor ß only  
        •  Unit: LIT  
        •  Default: DEFA  

3.  Contextual Cross‐References  
    •  “See also” records: AND (annotations), LC (loadcases), DSGN (design), ARRO (arrows), ISOL (isolines), SECT (sections), QUAD (element‐type specifics).  
    •  Many of these keywords interact with STYP (selection of centre, node, Gauss, error‐estimate values) and TYPE (which result quantity to plot).  
    •  The items above fine‐tune how texts, offsets and averaging behave once the underlying result data (e.g. stresses, displacements) have been calculated by ASE, TALPA, FEABENCH, BEMESS, etc.

This description captures all relevant table fields, their semantics, default settings and how they fit into the broader SOFiSTiK/WING graphics workflow.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
This table is one of the central lookup‐lists for QUAD‐element result types in SOFiSTiK/WING. It defines the short “Literal” codes you place in a TYPE field to extract specific bending, membrane or shear result components. Three columns appear:

1. Literal  
   • The exact keyword you enter (e.g. HM, MI, NXY).  
2. Meaning  
   • A concise English description of what that code represents (e.g. “Principal moments, magnitude and direction,” “Membrane shear force in local xy”).  
3. Dim.  
   • The physical unit in which the value is returned (e.g. kNm/m for bending, kN/m for membrane, plain kN/m for shear).

The table is logically broken into four major blocks, separated by blank lines and sub-headings:

– BENDING-MOMENT RESULTS  
  • HM: principal bending moment (magnitude & direction) – kNm/m  
  • MI / MII: principal moment I / II – kNm/m  
  • BM: local bending moments – kNm/m  
  • MX / MY: bending about x or y axes – kNm/m  
  • MXY: twisting moment in the local xy‐plane – kNm/m

– BENDING AT A DEFINED CUT  
  (Only available if you first define a cut with DCUT or equivalent.)  
  • MN: bending moment along the cut – kNm/m  
  • MT: bending moment perpendicular to the cut – kNm/m  
  • MNT: twisting moment at the cut – kNm/m

– MEMBRANE-FORCE RESULTS  
  • HN: principal membrane forces (magnitude & direction) – kN/m  
  • NI / NII: principal membrane force I / II – kN/m  
  • N: membrane force vector in the local plane – kN/m  
  • NX / NY: components in x or y – kN/m  
  • NXY: membrane shear force in xy – kN/m  
  • IN1 (first invariant) = 0.5·(NX+NY) – kN/m  
  • IN2 (second invariant) = NX·NY – NXY² – kN/m

– MEMBRANE FORCES AT A CUT  
  (Again, requires a cut definition.)  
  • NN: membrane force in cut direction – kN/m  
  • NT: perpendicular to cut – kN/m  
  • NNT: shear at the cut – kN/m

– SHEAR-FORCE RESULTS  
  • VR: principal shear (signed) – kN/m  
  • BV: local shear (signed) – kN/m  
  • VX / VY: components in x or y (signed) – kN/m  
  • AVR: principal shear (absolute) – kN/m

How to use:  
– In your WING or GRAPHIC input, set ETYP QUAD and then TYPE to one of these Literals.  
– STYP controls where in the element the value is sampled (centre, nodes, Gauss points, averaged).  
– SCH2 or SCHH records let you scale, label or filter by minimum values.  
– FILL, LC, ISOL and SECT settings govern the graphical rendering (isolines, cuts, fill areas).  

See also the broader context keywords AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, ISOL and SECT for layering, legend controls, design checks, arrow/vector styles, isolines and sectional plots.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The table is a small excerpt from the SOFiSTiK result‐literal catalog.  In SOFiSTiK’s graphics and reporting modules you pick a “TYPE” (what result field to show) by specifying its literal code; this table tells you what each code stands for and the physical dimension it carries.  Upstream in the input you would control the display location with STYP (e.g. QUAD centre, Gauss point, NODE), the overall TYPE with these literals, the scaling with UNIT, and the drawing style with DSGN, FILL, etc.

This particular section is split into two logical groups:

1. Bedding stresses and forces (PT-, PR-, PEFF)  
   • PTX, PTY, PTZ  
     – “Tangential bedding stress in global X, Y, Z”  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
     – These are the soil‐structure contact (Winkler spring) shear stresses resolved in the global axes.  
   • PTT  
     – “Total of tangential bedding stresses (after ASE, DYNA), without direction”  
     – kN/m²  
     – Summation of PTX, PTY, PTZ magnitudes for dynamic or static analyses.  
   • PR  
     – “Resulting bedding values”  
     – kN  
     – The net spring (bedding) force vector magnitude at an element or node.  
   • PTR  
     – “Resulting tangential bedding”  
     – kN  
     – The shear (tangent) component of the bedding force.  
   • PEFF  
     – “Effective bedding (= Bedding stress/settlement)”  
     – kN/m³  
     – For soil springs: ratio of contact pressure to corresponding deflection, used in p–y curves.

2. Displacements of QUAD elements (U-)  
   • U  
     – “Vector of displacements of the QUAD nodes”  
     – m  
     – The full 3D displacement vector.  
   • UX, UY, UZ (alias W)  
     – “Displacement global X, Y, Z of the QUAD nodes”  
     – m  
     – Individual components in the global coordinate system.  
   • UXYZ  
     – “Components of displacements of the QUAD nodes in local directions”  
     – m  
     – Used when you want local‐axis results rather than global.  
   • UUX, UUY, UUZ  
     – “Displacement local x, local y, local z of the QUAD nodes”  
     – m  
     – Breakdown of UXYZ into each local direction.  
   • UUXY  
     – “Displacement of the xy plane of QUAD element”  
     – m  
     – In‐plane shear displacement measure.  
   • UUN  
     – “Displacement in cut direction”  
     – m  
     – Used in cut‐plotting routines (REPR DCUT) where N is along the cut line.  
   • UUT  
     – “Displacement perpendicular to the cut”  
     – m  
     – Complementary to UUN, for through‐thickness or out‐of‐plane motion.

How you use it in practice:  
• In your SCHH (structure text) record you set TYPE=PTX (for example), UNIT=… (to scale the result), STYP=NODE or QUAD, and DSGN (e.g. vector arrow, isolines, etc.).  
• For bedding stresses you’d choose fill patterns or contour plots (REPR DISO), for displacements you might draw vectors (REPR DVEC).  
• The broader context listing in your question shows the full universe of TYPE literals (stresses, strains, reinforcements, error estimates, principal values, etc.).  This little table is just one slice—covering soil springs and basic nodal/element displacements for QUAD shells.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The QUAD record in SOFiSTiK/WING controls how results over four‐node (and eight‐node volume) finite elements are selected, sampled, scaled and drawn. It is one of several graphic‐output records (see also: AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, ISOL, SECT). Below is a structured breakdown of its inputs and the typology of available result fields (“TYPE”) you can request.

1. Core Input Items  
• TYPE  – Specifies which result quantity to display (see “TYPE Literals” below).  
• DSGN  – If set, reads input values only; no graphical primitives are drawn.  
• UNIT  – Scaling factor for lengths/vectors in the plot (see record STRU).  
• SCHH  – Text height for annotations (see record STRU).  
• MIN, MINT  – (Obsolete) Lower display threshold; use SCH2 MIN… instead.  
• STYP  – Sampling location of the result field:  
 – ELEM / QUAD  Centre of 2D quadrilateral element  
 – BRIC  Centre of 3D brick element  
 – NODE / BRIK  Nodal values for quad/brick  
 – GAUS  Gauss‐point values (corner points of QUAD; eight points for BRIC)  
 – FULL  Both nodal + element‐centre values  
 – E2N  Extrapolate element‐centre values to nodes and average  
 – G2N  Average Gauss‐point values at nodes  
 – ERIN  Error estimate at element centre  
 – EE2N  Extrapolate & average element‐centre error to nodes  
• ND  – Number of decimal places in printed values (see record SCHH ND).  
• FILL, LT, REVI, DIST  – Fill‐pattern, line‐type, revision filter and offset (see STRU/FILL, SCH2).  
• A  – Text override for perimeter reinforcement annotation.  

2. TYPE Literals by Analysis Module  
A) ASE / TALPA (linear plate shell)  
 • ABV, AVX, AVY  Absolute shear forces in local x/y (kN/m)  
 • After cut definition: VN (normal shear), VT (transverse shear), P (bedding stress, kN/m²)  
 • PT  Tangential bedding stresses (with direction)  
 • UUT  Displacement normal to cut (m)  
 • TXYU  Upper membrane shear σxy (kN/m²)  
 • IS1U, IS2U  First/second invariants of top‐surface stress (kN/m²)  
 • SNU, STU  Top‐surface stress in/cross to cut (kN/m²)  

B) ASE (non‐linear plate shell)  
 • S2LN, S2LX, S2LY, S2LT  Bottom non‐linear stresses & shear (kN/m²)  
 • S2U, S21U, S22U  Top non‐linear principal stresses + directions  
 • CRA1–3, TCR1–3  Hardening/damage variables (unitless)  
 • CCR1–2  Crack openings (mm)  
 • SIGT  Max concrete tension in layers (kN/m²)  

C) TALPA (axisymmetric & 3D shells)  
 • HS3D, S3D1–3  3D principal stresses (kN/m²)  
 • HS, SI  Plane‐stress principal values (kN/m²)  

D) BEMESS (tendon & reinforcement design)  
 • DCSM  Max decompression strain in tendon direction (‰)  
 • ABU*, AWU*, AWL*  Area of required reinforcement layers (upper/lower, cm²/m)  
 • DC*, DCV  Design check ratios & stirrups (unitless)  
 • WK1–3  Crack width layers (mm)  
 • SRMA, SRUM, SRU1–2  Stress ranges in reinforcement (N/mm²)  
 • CTAN, CTAT  Shear stresses in cut directions (N/mm²)  

E) Punching & weld‐seam stresses  
 • PUNC, ASPS  Punching result visuals (uses COLO C13/C14)  
 • SWNU, SWNL, SWNM, S3NU, S3NL, S3NM  Weld‐seam normal & shear stresses post‐cut  

3. Sampling & Averaging (STYP)  
Quadrilateral elements: 5 Gauss points (4 near corners + centre).  
Brick elements: up to 8 Gauss points + centre.  
WING can:  
 – Extrapolate Gauss values to nodes (G2N)  
 – Extrapolate element‐centre values to nodes (E2N)  
 – Compute nodal error from element‐centre error estimates (EE2N)  

4. Representation Modes  
• As vectors/tensors (REPR DVEC, DARE, DREP, DTXT): real‐size lines drawn in projected directions for flow, membrane forces, strains, etc.; negative values get caps.  
• Isolines (REPR DISO): hyperbola‐based interpolation within each element; text placed “uphill”; controlled with SCHH, DTXT, CDIS.  
• Cuts (REPR DCUT): 1D slices through QUAD mesh; status lines or filled areas; local N/T transforms for cut‐aligned stresses.  
• Fill areas and hatch patterns: via FILL/LT.  

5. Additional Notes  
• Many inputs have been deprecated in favour of SCH2 or SCHH variants.  
• Reinforcement mats (ASUM/ASLM) and transverse meshes (ASUR/ASLR) require consistent element orientation.  
• For non‐linear plastic‐area plots (TYPE FLIE), set FROM = 0 to isolate yielded zones.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The input table is a concise, three-column lookup that maps SOFiSTiK “TYPE” literals (result‐field identifiers) to their human‐readable definitions and physical dimensions. It appears in the context of weld‐seam stress and principal‐shear stress results, especially “after a cut definition,” and supplements the more comprehensive lists of TYPE codes found elsewhere in the documentation (see “See also: AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, ISOL, SECT,” etc.). 

1. Table Structure  
   • Column 1 “Literal”  
     – The code or keyword used in the SOFiSTiK input to request this particular result.  
   • Column 2 “Meaning”  
     – A brief description of what is being calculated or reported. Where appropriate, the underlying formula is shown.  
   • Column 3 “Dim.”  
     – The physical units or unit‐system annotation for the result (e.g. kN/m², N/A±M/W).  

2. Rows and Their Definitions  
   1. SWNL  
      • Meaning: Lower equivalent stress in the weld, combining normal and shear contributions on the lower surface of a weld seam.  
      • Formula:  
         SWNL = √(STL² + TTM² + SNTL²)  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (using N/A + M/W, i.e. normal force per area plus bending moment per width)  
   2. SWNM  
      • Meaning: Equivalent stress in the weld on the middle plane, considering only the N/A component (no bending moment).  
      • Formula:  
         SWNM = √(STM² + TTM² + SNTM²)  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A only)  
   3. S3NU (after a cut definition)  
      • Meaning: Upper equivalent stress weld as per EN 1993-1-8, combining normal σ⊥ and shear τ⊥, τ‖:  
         √(σ⊥² + 3·(τ⊥² + τ‖²))  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A – M/W, i.e. difference of normal and bending‐moment contributions)  
   4. S3NL  
      • Meaning: Lower equivalent stress weld, same formula with sign convention for positive bending:  
         √(STL² + 3·(TTM² + SNTL²))  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A + M/W)  
   5. S3NM  
      • Meaning: Equivalent stress weld on the middle plane, including three‐times shear terms but excluding bending:  
         √(STM² + 3·(TTM² + SNTM²))  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A only)  
   6. HTAU  
      • Meaning: Principal shear stress τ_xy-max (the maximum membrane shear stress in the slab).  
      • Formula:  
         = √((0.5·(SY − SX))² + TXY²)  
      • Dimension: kN/m²  
   7. HTUU  
      • Meaning: Upper principal shear stress (combining normal and bending contributions).  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A – M/W)  
   8. HTUL  
      • Meaning: Lower principal shear stress (normal plus bending, lower surface).  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A – M/W)  
   9. HTUM  
      • Meaning: Principal shear stress on the middle plane (no bending component).  
      • Dimension: kN/m² (N/A only)  

3. Context and Usage Notes  
   – These TYPE codes apply specifically to weld‐seam stress results in cut definitions, where “N/A” refers to normal force per unit area and “M/W” to bending moment per unit width.  
   – The upper (U) and lower (L) suffixes refer to the top and bottom faces of the weld or plate; “M” indicates the mid‐plane.  
   – These entries are part of a larger schema that defines dozens of possible TYPE literals for planar stresses, bending moments, shear forces, displacements, reinforcement demands and more.  
   – In practice, the user selects one of these literals in a DRAW or RECORD input to extract and visualize the corresponding stress field on cuts or isolines.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The snippet you’ve provided is a small extract from a much larger “TYPE‐Literal” table used in SOFiSTiK/WING to map short code words (“literals”) to physical quantities, their descriptions and units. In a RAG‐ready data model you would store each row as an object with fields {literal, description, unit, category}, possibly also linking it back to higher‐level groups (e.g. “Principal Stresses”, “Slab Shear Stresses”, etc.). Below is a detailed breakdown of the excerpt:

1. Table structure  
   • Columns  
     – literal: the short code used in input files and graphics commands  
     – meaning: a concise English description of the physical quantity  
     – dim.: the unit or dimension in which it is expressed (e.g. kN/m², kN/m)  
   • Row grouping  
     – Groups are visually separated by blank lines and often have an implied heading (not shown here) corresponding to the calculation context (e.g. “Principal stresses with N/A±M/W,” “Slab shear stresses,” “Middle shear stresses”).

2. Group 1 – Principal stresses (N/A±M/W)  
   • SPT  
     – meaning: Maximum principal tensile stress  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • SPTX  
     – meaning: Principal tensile stress in local x  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • SPTY  
     – meaning: Principal tensile stress in local y  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • SPC  
     – meaning: Maximum principal compressive stress  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • SPCX  
     – meaning: Principal compressive stress in local x  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • SPCY  
     – meaning: Principal compressive stress in local y  
     – unit: kN/m²  

3. Group 2 – Linear principal slab shear stress (1.5·V/(b·h))  
   • SSIG  
     – meaning: Shear stress (considered with sign)  
     – unit: kN/m²  
   • ASSG  
     – meaning: Absolute shear stress  
     – unit: kN/m²  

4. Group 3 – Middle shear stress with V/A  
   • HTM  
     – meaning: Shear stress from principal shear force (with sign)  
     – unit: kN/m  
   • NTM  
     – meaning: Shear stress from shear forces in local directions (sign)  
     – unit: kN/m  
   • TXM  
     – meaning: Shear stress from shear force in local x (with sign)  
     – unit: kN/m  
   • TYM  
     – meaning: Shear stress from shear force in local y (with sign)  
     – unit: kN/m  

5. Notes for RAG ingestion  
   – literal → primary key/identifier  
   – meaning → descriptive text for retrieval and summarization  
   – unit  → normalized field for unit‐based filtering  
   – category (implicit) → “Principal Stress,” “Slab Shear,” or “Middle Shear”  
   – blank‐line separators → signal new sub‐group (could be stored as a “group” attribute)  

By structuring each row into a JSON/YAML/document entry with these fields, your vector store can answer queries like “Which TYPE codes measure principal tensile stress?” or “List all shear‐stress codes in kN/m.”

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The excerpted table is a fragment of the SOFiSTiK‐WING “TYPE” dictionary used to drive post‐processing of quadrilateral plate‐bending results (programs ASE/TALPA with N/A ± M/W output). It associates each short literal (column 1) with

• a human-readable Meaning (column 2)  
• its physical Dimension or Unit (column 3)

and is normally combined with other record inputs (e.g. STYP, SCHH, SCH2) for cuts, isolines, fill areas, reinforcements, etc.

1. Shear forces in global/local directions (edge forces in kN/m)  
 • AHTM – “Shear stress from principal shear force (absolute)”  
 • ANTM – “Shear stress from absolute shear forces in local directions”  
 • ATXM – “Shear stress from shear force |v-x|”  
 • ATYM – “Shear stress from shear force |v-y|”  

2. Shear forces after a cut definition (edge forces in kN/m)  
 • TNM – “Shear stress in cut direction”  
 • TTM – “Shear stress perpendicular to the cut”  

3. Membrane stresses in the middle of the plate (N/A) (units kN/m²)  
 – these are the classic plane stresses without bending contributions, evaluated at the centroid of the element:  
 • HSM – “Plane principal stresses”  
 • SIM – “Plane principal stress I”  
 • SIIM – “Plane principal stress II”  
 • NSM – “Stresses in local directions”  
 • SXM – “Stress in local x”  
 • SYM – “Stress in local y”  
 • TXYM – “Membrane shear stress in xy plane”  
 • IS1M – “Stress mean value (1st invariant)” = 0.5·(SXM + SYM)  
 • IS2M – “Stress deviator (2nd invariant)” = SXM·SYM – TXYM²  

4. Additional stresses after a cut (N/A) (kN/m²)  
 • SNM – “Stress in cut direction”  
 • STM – “Stress perpendicular to the cut”  
 • SNTM – “Membrane shear stress nt at the cut”  

5. Upper‐surface stresses (N/A – M/W) (units kN/m²)  
 – bending contributions added algebraically, evaluated at the top fiber:  
 • HSU – “Upper plane principal stresses”  
 • SIU – “Upper plane stress I”  
 • SIIU – “Upper plane stress II”  
 • NSU – “Upper stresses in local directions”  
 • SXU – “Upper stress in local x”  
 • SYU – “Upper stress in local y”  

(If continued, one would find the corresponding “lower” stresses (e.g. HSL, SII L, NSL, etc.), plus combined invariants, principal angles, and shear‐stress components in cut directions.)

Contextual notes from the larger schema:

– STYP specifies where results are sampled (centre of QUAD, Gauss points, nodes, averaged node values from Gauss points or element-centre values, BRIC volume analogue).  
– DSGN, UNIT, SCHH, SCH2 records govern drawing scale, text height, decimal precision, min/max value clipping and fill patterns.  
– REPR settings (DVEC, DISO, DCUT, etc.) control whether values are drawn as vectors/tensors, isolines, cuts or filled patterns.  
– After non‐linear analyses (ASE, TALPA nonlinear, BEMESS, HYDRA/DOLFYN) entirely different TYPE literals (e.g. S2U, CRA1, DCSM, AWU, DCV, etc.) appear.  

This table fragment is critical for any RAG‐vector indexing of SOFiSTiK results: each code yields a specific numeric field, a geometry (QUAD or BRIC element location), and a unit, enabling downstream search, comparison and visualization workflows.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The input table is the master definition for how SOFiSTiK‐generated result quantities are handled, formatted and plotted in a RAG (record–action–graphics) vector store.  It defines the valid “literals” you can request, their meaning, units, where they are sampled (nodes, element centres, Gauss points, etc.), and how they are represented graphically.  Below is a structured overview of its contents:

1.  Column Definitions  
    •  QUAD Item – the keyword or literal that identifies a result field (e.g. SXU, VT, ABU).  
    •  Description – human‐readable meaning of that literal.  
    •  TYPE – the type of result (stresses, shear forces, displacements, reinforcement design, etc.).  
    •  DSGN – flag indicating whether this record only “sets” values (no drawing) or actually controls output.  
    •  UNIT – physical unit or scale factor (e.g. kN/m², cm²/m, mm).  
    •  STRU / SCHH / SCH2 – references to other control records that govern text height, decimal precision, minimum thresholds, etc.  
    •  STYP – sampling location/type:  
       – ELEM / QUAD / BRIC  : centre of element (2D or 3D)  
       – NODE / BRIK        : element’s nodes  
       – GAUS               : raw Gauss‐point values  
       – E2N / G2N          : nodal values averaged from centres or Gauss points  
       – ERIN / EE2N        : error estimates at element centres or averaged to nodes  
    •  ND – number of decimals after the comma (linked to SCHH ND).

2.  General Plotting Options  
    •  FILL, LT, NO           : fill‐pattern, line‐type, “no plot” switch (via STRU FILL).  
    •  REVI, DIST (obsolete)  : legacy revision or B‐coordinate control (replaced by SCHH / SCH2).  
    •  A                      : annotation text for reinforcement perimeters.  

3.  QUAD TYPE Literals by Analysis Module  
    A.  ASE / TALPA / FEABENCH (plate and slab analyses)  
       – ABV, AVX, AVY   : shear forces in local directions (kN/m)  
       – After “cut” definitions:  
         • VN, VT        : shear force normal and tangential to the cut (kN/m)  
         • P             : bedding pressure (kN/m² or kN/m)  
         • PT            : tangential bedding (kN/m², directional)  
         • UUT           : out‐of‐plane displacement (m)  

    B.  Linear stress results (ASE / TALPA)  
       – TXYU, IS1U, IS2U : upper‐side xy shear, mean stress, deviator (kN/m²)  
       – After cut: SNU (normal), STU (tangential) stress on the cut plane (kN/m²)  

    C.  Non‐linear stresses (ASE)  
       – S2LN, S2LX, S2LY, S2LT : bottom‐side non‐linear stresses in local x,y, xy (kN/m²)  
       – S2U, S21U, S22U        : top‐side principal stresses and directions  
       – Damage/hardening/crack results: CRA1–3, TCR1–3, CCR1–2 (– or mm)  
       – SIGT                   : maximum concrete tension (kN/m²)  

    D.  TALPA (axisymmetric / 3D)  
       – HS3D, S3D1–3 : 3D principal stresses (kN/m²)  
       – HS, SI       : plane principal stresses without σ-z  

    E.  BEMESS (tendon/bond and reinforcement design)  
       – DCSM       : max decompression strain (‰)  
       – ABU…, AWU…: reinforcement areas in top (ABU) or bottom (AWL) mats and layers (cm²/m)  
       – DC…, DCH…: disk counts for design checks (–)  
       – WK1–3      : crack‐width checks in layers (mm)  
       – SRMA, SRU1–2: stress‐range in reinforcement (N/mm²)  
       – CTAN, CTAT : shear stresses of section in cut and tangential directions (N/mm²)  

4.  Sampling Location Details  
    •  QUAD elements use five Gauss points; “centre” is Gauss‐point 5.  
    •  NODE values come from extrapolation/averaging of element Gauss points.  
    •  E2N/G2N allow user‐forced averaging when node values are missing or to smooth results.  
    •  BRIC (volume) elements have up to eight Gauss points; “BRIC” = centre, “BRIK” = nodal.

5.  Graphic Representation Modes  
    •  REPR DVEC, DARE, DREP, DTXT – control drawing as vectors/tensors, arrows or text.  
    •  Vector/Tensor:  
       – HM, NS, EPSU, S2U, etc. draw a line of real‐world length in projected view.  
       – FL, PA, Q draw flow‐velocity vectors.  
       – All other single‐valued types draw isolines, cuts or shaded areas.  
    •  Error‐estimate overlay: STYP ERIN can plot error bars for selected types.  
    •  Punching shear: PUNC, ASPS use special colours (C4, C13, C14) and compare min thresholds (SCH2 MIN1).  
    •  Isolines (REPR DISO): hyperbolic interpolation per element, uphill text orientation, label density via SCHH / CDIS, optional min cutoff.  
    •  Cuts (REPR DCUT): QUAD‐element slices along user‐defined lines, status lines or filled areas, directional results (N/T components), weld‐seam stress approximations (SWNU, SWNL, S3NM, etc.).

In practice, you reference a QUAD record to request a specific result (e.g. TYPE=SXU, STYP=GAUS, UNIT=kN/m²) and control its display via the associated STRU/SCHH/SCH2 settings.  The table thus centralizes all valid result literals, their context, sampling locations and graphical rules for the RAG‐based output.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The snippet you provided is a three-column lookup table defining a set of “TYPE” literals (here all strain‐related quantities) that can be requested from the SOFiSTiK/WING postprocessor after a finite‐element run.  Below is a breakdown of its structure, content and how it ties into the broader context:

1. Table Structure  
   - Column 1 “Literal”: the short code you pass into the TYPE field (e.g. ENU, EXU, …).  
   - Column 2 “Meaning”: an English description of what physical quantity that code refers to.  
   - Column 3 “Dim.”: the unit or dimension in which the quantity is reported; here all strains are in “0/00” (per mille).  

2. Logical Groupings  
   The entries are grouped in blocks, each block representing a family of strain measures:  
   A. Total (Membrane) Strains  
     • ENU – Total top‐surface normal strain ε<sub>xx</sub> on the top face  
     • EXU – Total top‐surface normal strain in local x‐direction  
     • EYU – Total top‐surface normal strain in local y‐direction  
     • EXYU – Total top‐surface shear strain γ<sub>xy</sub>  

     • ENL – Total bottom‐surface normal strain  
     • EXL – Total bottom‐surface normal strain in local x  
     • EYL – Total bottom‐surface normal strain in local y  
     • EXYL – Total bottom‐surface shear strain γ<sub>xy</sub>  

   B. Principal Strains  
     • EPSU – Total top‐surface principal strain magnitude  
     • EIU – Top‐surface principal strain in principal direction I  
     • EIIU – Top‐surface principal strain in principal direction II  
     • EPSL – Total bottom‐surface principal strain  
     • EIL – Bottom‐surface principal strain direction I  
     • EIIL – Bottom‐surface principal strain direction II  

   C. Equivalent Strains  
     • EVU – Total top‐surface equivalent (von Mises) strain  
     • EVL – Total bottom‐surface equivalent strain  

3. Contextual Usage  
   - These literals apply when you specify TYPE=<literal> in the DRAW / CUT / ISO command after a *linear* calculation (programs ASE or TALPA, system PESS).  
   - By choosing STYP you also decide where values are sampled: at element centres (QUAD), at Gauss points (GAUS), extrapolated to nodes (NODE), or averaged (E2N, G2N, EE2N).  
   - All these strain results share the common unit “0/00” reflecting engineering strain in per-mille.  

4. How this Helps in a RAG Vector Store  
   - As you build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) knowledge base, each row becomes a small document or knowledge snippet:  
     • “ENU → Total top strain, units 0/00”  
     • “EPSU → Total top principal strain, direction I, units 0/00”  
     … and so on.  
   - You can index by “literal” or by “meaning” keywords (“top strain,” “principal,” “shear,” etc.) to allow natural‐language queries such as “show me top principal strains” or “list all bottom-surface shear strains.”  

In summary, this table is a compact mapping of strain result codes to their descriptions and units.  Its structured grouping (total vs. principal vs. equivalent, top vs. bottom, global vs. local) and uniform units make it straightforward to encode as metadata entries in a RAG vector store for automated lookup, filtering and contextualization in code or interactive GUIs.

content:
This table is an excerpt from the SOFiSTiK/Q U A D-TYPE catalogue, defining a range of post-processing result quantities (“literals”) that can be requested for quadrilateral plate or shell elements—particularly after cut definitions or non-linear analyses. Each row gives the code, its physical meaning, and its unit/dimension (Dim.). Below is a structured description of the entries shown:

1. Total Strains at Top and Bottom (in cut analyses)  
   • EPNU – Total top surface strain in the cut (direction N)  
   • EPTU – Total top surface strain perpendicular to the cut (direction T)  
   • EPNL – Total bottom surface strain in the cut direction  
   • EPTL – Total bottom surface strain perpendicular to the cut  
   All four are reported in permille (0/00), i.e. in “‰”.

2. Concrete and Reinforcement Strains (permille)  
   • ECON – Maximum concrete compression strain  
   • EREC – Minimum averaged reinforcement strain (includes pre-strains from temperature and creep per the material law)  
   • ERET – Maximum averaged reinforcement strain (same inclusion of temperature/creep effects)  
   • EPSR – Maximum local reinforcement strain in the crack  

3. Non-linear Reinforcement Stresses (kN/m²)  
   • SMU  – Non-linear top-layer reinforcement stress  
   • SML  – Non-linear bottom-layer reinforcement stress  
   • SMUM – Non-linear top-layer maximum reinforcement stress  
   • SMLM – Non-linear bottom-layer maximum reinforcement stress  

4. Averaged Steel Strains (permille)  
   • EPSC – Minimum averaged steel strain (accounts for (pre)strains from temperature and applied strain loads)  
   • EPST – Maximum averaged steel strain (same inclusions)  

5. Wrinkle (Local Buckling) Compression Strains (permille)  
   • WRK1 – Wrinkle compression strain in the first principal direction (shown orthogonal to compression)  
   • WRK2 – Wrinkle compression strain in the second principal direction  

6. Layered Material Results  
   Strains (permille)  
     • FLSD – Minimum strain in a layered material (compression)  
     • FLSZ – Maximum strain in a layered material (tension)  
   Stresses (kN/m²)  
     • FLYC – Maximum compressive stress of the layered material  
     • FLYT – Maximum tensile stress of the layered material  

7. Non-linear Plate Stresses at Top Surface (kN/m²)  
   • S2UN – Principal non-linear top stress (scalar resultant)  
   • S2UX – Non-linear top stress in local x-direction  
   • S2UY – Non-linear top stress in local y-direction  
   • S2UT – Non-linear top shear stress (xy-component)  

Usage Notes:  
– These TYPE-literals are selected via the RECORD TYPE entry when defining a QUAD post-processing (e.g. for cuts, isolines or filling).  
– Strains are always in “permille” (0/00), while stresses use surface loads (kN/m²).  
– Many of these results (cut-direction strains, reinforcement stresses, layered material parameters) are only meaningful in conjunction with a cut definition (DTYP) or non-linear analysis (ASE/TALPA).  
– The user can control the location of output (centre, nodes, Gauss points) via STYP settings.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The snippet you’ve shown is a small “lookup” table used by SOFiSTiK/WING’s post-processing to interpret the various stress‐output codes (literals) for QUAD (plate) elements after a linear FE analysis.  Here is a breakdown of its structure and purpose:

1. Table Structure  
   - Column 1 (Literal)  
     • A short alphanumeric code that the user may specify as TYPE=… in a DRAW or GRAPHIC record.  
   - Column 2 (Meaning)  
     • A concise English description of the physical quantity that code represents.  
   - Column 3 (Dim.)  
     • The engineering units in which the result is reported (here: kN/m²).

2. Scope and Context  
   • Applies to plate/quadrilateral elements (ETYP = QUAD) in a *linear* stress analysis (programs ASE, TALPA, etc.).  
   • These are the “standard” stress resultants or stresses available at element interiors or (by extrapolation) at nodes.  
   • If one is making cut‐line plots (REPR DCUT), a separate set of codes (SN, ST, SNT) becomes valid, representing stresses resolved into the cut‐line (normal, transverse, shear).

3. Literal Codes and Their Meanings  
   A. Plane Principal Stresses and Invariants  
     • SII  
       – Plane principal stress II (i.e. the smaller of the two in‐plane principal stresses), *excluding* the σ-z component.  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • IS1  
       – First invariant (mean stress) = (SX + SY)/2  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • IS2  
       – Second invariant (deviatoric stress measure) = SX∙SY − (TXY)²  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • SIGV  
       – Equivalent (von Mises) stress in the plate  
       – Units: kN/m²  

   B. Direct and Shear Stresses in Local Axes  
     • NS  
       – Stresses resolved in the local element axes; a generic tag, often further specified by SX, SY, SZ.  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • SX, SY, SZ  
       – Normal stress components along the element’s local x, y, and z axes respectively.  
       – Units: kN/m² each  
     • TXY  
       – In‐plane (membrane) shear stress in the x–y plane of the plate.  
       – Units: kN/m²  

   C. Cut‐line Specific Codes (after defining a cut–plane)  
     • SN  
       – Normal stress *along* the cut direction (i.e. resolved component perpendicular to the cut‐plane normal).  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • ST  
       – Stress *perpendicular* to the cut direction (i.e. normal to the cut‐plane but in the plate).  
       – Units: kN/m²  
     • SNT  
       – Membrane shear stress *at* the cut, in the plane of the element but tangential to the cut‐line.  
       – Units: kN/m²  

4. How It Is Used in Practice  
   – In your SCHH/SCH2 or similar plot‐control records you would set TYPE=SX or TYPE=TXY, etc., to extract exactly that stress field.  
   – If you then specify an isoline plot (REPR DISO) or a cut plot (REPR DCUT), GRAPHIC knows how to interpolate nodal values from element Gauss‐point results and draw the appropriate contour or section.  
   – Units are always reported in force per area (kN/m²), consistent across all these stress‐type literals.

In essence, the table is the decoder ring by which the post-processor knows “when you ask for TYPE=IS2, go compute or fetch the (σₓσᵧ – τₓᵧ²) field and label it ‘Stress deviator (2nd invariant)’ in kN/m².”

All entries in this snippet share the same dimension (“cm²/m”), i.e. area of steel per meter, which is the conventional unit for reinforcement ratios in slab or plate design.  

— Group 1: Lower reinforcement (standard)  
  • ABL  – Lower reinforcement  
  • ABLH – Lower principal reinforcement  
  • ABLQ – Lower transverse reinforcement  
  • ABLI – Lower 3rd reinforcement layer  
  • ABLM – Lower maximum reinforcement  

These five literals give the basic lower‐face (tension side) steel requirements in bending design, broken down by principal, transverse and tertiary layers, plus an overall maximum.  

— Group 2: Info reinforcement for bending design only  
  • AB   – Total reinforcement disks  
  • ABH  – Principal reinforcement disks  
  • ABQ  – Transverse reinforcement disks  
  • ABI  – 3rd reinforcement layer disks  
  • ABM  – Maximum reinforcement disks  

Here “disks” means discrete steel layers or “bars per unit width.” These are informational outputs used in the bending design module (for checking or printing), not for shear or non‐linear checks.  

— Group 3: Upper reinforcement if increased due to shear  
  • AIU   – Upper reinforcement  
  • AIUH  – Upper principal reinforcement  
  • AIUQ  – Upper transverse reinforcement  
  • AIUI  – Upper 3rd reinforcement layer  
  • AIUM  – Upper maximum reinforcement  

When shear alone governs the required steel on the tension side, these literals give the adjusted (upper) layer areas.  

— Group 4: Lower reinforcement if increased due to shear  
  • AIL   – Lower reinforcement  
  • AILH  – Lower principal reinforcement  
  • AILQ  – Lower transverse reinforcement  
  • AILI  – Lower 3rd reinforcement layer  
  • AILM  – Lower maximum reinforcement  

Analogous to Group 3 but on the lower face when shear requirements drive the design.  

— Group 5: Total reinforcement disks if increased due to shear  
  • AI   – Total reinforcement disks  
  • AIH  – Principal reinforcement disks  
  • AIQ  – Transverse reinforcement disks  
  • AII  – 3rd reinforcement layer disks  
  • AIL   (note: likely a typo in the source; if present this duplicates “lower” layer)  
  • …  

These “AI-” entries report the discrete steel layers (“disks”) needed when shear controls, broken down by orientation and layer.  

All five groups use a uniform unit of “cm²/m,” reflecting that SOFiSTiK reports steel area per meter width for slabs and plates. In practice:

- The “ABL…” and “AL…” entries feed into bending‐check prints (record DSGN, TYPE ASU/ASL).
- The “AB…” and “AI…” entries are informational prints or checks for shear‐controlled reinforcement (record LOAD/SCHH).
- When combined with TYPE = ASUM/ASLM, they allow automating reinforcement mat layouts.

Looking up these literals in the RAG vector store enables retrieval of both the semantic meaning (“upper principal shear reinforcement”) and the numeric scale (“steel area in cm² per meter”), ensuring any vector‐based query about reinforcement demand or graphical annotation can be unambiguously resolved.

This table defines a set of three related groups of “literals”—short alphanumeric codes—that SOFiSTiK/WING uses to label, extract and display stress- and crack-width results.  Each literal has a precise meaning and a physical unit (“Dim.”).  The three groups are:

1. “After a stress calculation according to theory of elasticity”  
   • SMIU: Upper minimum stresses (N/mm²)  
   • SMAU: Upper maximum stresses (N/mm²)  
   • SMIL: Lower minimum stresses (N/mm²)  
   • SMAL: Lower maximum stresses (N/mm²)  
   • TAUM: Minimum shear stresses (N/mm²)  
   • VSMA: Maximum von Mises stress (N/mm²)  
   • VSMU: Upper von Mises stress (N/mm²)  
   • VSML: Lower von Mises stress (N/mm²)  

   Explanation: These eight codes correspond to the principal tensile/compressive stresses and shear stresses at the top (“upper”) and bottom (“lower”) fibers of plate or shell elements.  The von Mises entries track the yield criterion extremes.

2. “Stress ranges of material (e.g. steel)”  
   • SDU: Upper stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDL: Lower stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDUI: Upper minimum stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDLI: Lower minimum stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDUA: Upper maximum stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDLA: Lower maximum stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDPU: Upper permanent (residual) stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  
   • SDPL: Lower permanent (residual) stress in the direction of the stress range (N/mm²)  

   Explanation: These eight codes are used primarily in fatigue or cyclic-loading checks, where one needs to know the alternating and mean stresses, the extremes of each cycle (upper/lower), and any permanent set.

3. “After a strain calculation (SLS)”  
   • WKUM: Maximum top crack‐width design (mm)  
   • WKU1: Top crack‐width design, 1st reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKU2: Top crack‐width design, 2nd reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKU3: Top crack‐width design, 3rd reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKLM: Maximum bottom crack‐width design (mm)  
   • WKL1: Bottom crack‐width design, 1st reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKL2: Bottom crack‐width design, 2nd reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKL3: Bottom crack‐width design, 3rd reinforcement layer (mm)  
   • WKM: Maximum crack‐width design for reinforcement “disks” (mm)  
   • WK1: Crack‐width design, 1st “disk” layer (mm)  
   • WK2: Crack‐width design, 2nd “disk” layer (mm)  
   • WK3: Crack‐width design, 3rd “disk” layer (mm)  

   Explanation:  These codes arise in serviceability‐limit‐state (SLS) checks for crack control in reinforced concrete.  They distinguish crack widths at top vs. bottom reinforcement layers, and also per discrete “disk” (sectional) reinforcement elements.

General structure of the table:  
- Column 1 “Literal” is the short code used in SCHH/SCH2 record entries (e.g. for cuts, isolines or text).  
- Column 2 “Meaning” gives a human-readable description.  
- Column 3 “Dim.” specifies the physical unit: N/mm² for stresses, mm for crack widths.

Context and usage hints (from the larger manual text):  
• These literals plug into the TYPE field of DRAW records (e.g. QUAD items for plate elements).  
• STYP selects where the values come from (element centre, Gauss points, nodes, or averaged).  
• Once the TYPE literal is set, GRAPHIC and WING know how to fetch the proper post-processing result and draw it—whether as a tensor, vector, isoline, cut diagram, or fill plot.  
• Stress ranges (SD*) are particularly important in fatigue assessments; crack widths (WK*) control serviceability checks under quasi‐static or repeated loads.

   • When only a subset of depths is available, interpolation routines in the analysis software will estimate missing values—however, explicit definition at more depths improves accuracy.  
   • All stiffness entries must share the same unit (MPa) to avoid scaling errors in downstream computations (e.g., finite-element stiffness matrices, subgrade reaction models).

By codifying these six stiffness parameters, the table enables a clear, unambiguous exchange of depth-dependent modulus data between geotechnical modelers, RAG vector databases, and analysis engines.

sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
The input table is a concise mapping of SOFiSTiK output‐record literals to their human‐readable meanings and physical dimensions. It comprises three columns:

 1. Literal  
    – The short alphanumeric code used internally in SOFiSTiK data files and record definitions.  
 2. Meaning  
    – A brief description of what physical quantity the literal represents.  
 3. Dim.  
    – The unit or dimension associated with that quantity.

Below is a grouped breakdown of the 28 entries in the table:

1. Temperature  
   • TEMP  
     – Temperature  
     – Unit: K (Kelvin)  
   • TMPK  
     – Temperature  
     – Unit: °C (Celsius)  

2. Hydraulic Potential & Pressure  
   • H  
     – Hydraulic potential  
     – Unit: m (meters)  
   • HF  
     – Hydraulic potential with free surface  
     – Unit: m  
   • PH  
     – Piezometric height  
     – Unit: m  
   • PRES  
     – Pressure  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
   • PREX  
     – Resulting pressure on area in global X-direction  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
   • PREY  
     – Resulting pressure on area in global Y-direction  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
   • PREZ  
     – Resulting pressure on area in global Z-direction  
     – Unit: kN/m²  
   • PS  
     – Pressure of steam saturation (function of temperature)  
     – Unit: Pa (Pascal)  

3. Nodal Fluid Velocities (from DOLFYN)  
   – These entries refer specifically to fluid velocities computed at mesh nodes by the DOLFYN solver.  
   • NFL  
     – Fluid velocity magnitude in nodes  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • NFLK  
     – Fluid velocity vector components in nodes  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • NFLX, NFLY, NFLZ  
     – Fluid velocity in the X, Y, Z components (respectively)  
     – Unit: m/s  

4. Fluid Velocities (from HYDRA)  
   – Hydrodynamic solver output of velocity fields (volume‐based rather than strictly nodal).  
   • FL  
     – Fluid velocity magnitude  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • FLK0  
     – Fluid velocity vector components  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • FLX, FLY, FLZ  
     – X, Y, Z components of fluid velocity  
     – Unit: m/s  

5. Particle Velocities  
   – Output from particle‐tracking or Lagrangian models.  
   • PA  
     – Particle velocity magnitude  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • PAK0  
     – Particle velocity vector components  
     – Unit: m/s  
   • PAX, PAY, PAZ  
     – Particle velocity in X, Y, Z directions  
     – Unit: m/s  

6. Heat Flux  
   • HT  
     – Heat flux magnitude  
     – Unit: m/s (interpreted here as flux per length; in practice often W/m²)  
   • HTK0  
     – Heat flux vector components  
     – Unit: m/s  

Key observations:  
- The “K0” or “LK” suffix generally implies the full vector of components, whereas the plain literal or single‐letter suffix (X, Y, Z) denotes a scalar component in a specific global direction.  
- The table covers both nodal (“NFL…”) and element‐based (“FL…”) velocity outputs, as well as temperature, pressure, and heat‐flux results.  
- All quantities are expressed in SI‐derived units, facilitating automated parsing, unit conversion, and consistent RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) indexing.

content:
The fragment shown is a lookup table used by SOFiSTiK (and its WING/G RAPHIC post-processor) to map short “literals” or codes to their full names (“Meaning”) and to the physical units or dimensions in which they are reported. In a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store context, this table serves as metadata, enabling automatic systems to recognize and interpret simulation‐output fields, group them by category, and display or filter them correctly. Below is a structured description of its key aspects:

1. Table Structure  
   • Column “Literal”: A unique short code used in input or result files to identify a specific field.  
   • Column “Meaning”: A concise English description of what the code represents in terms of physical quantity or simulation result.  
   • Column “Dim.” (Dimension): The units in which the quantity is measured, using standard SI or derived units.

2. Categories of Variables  
   The entries in the table can be grouped into several physical or application domains:  
   A. Heat Flux Components  
     – HTX: Heat flux in X direction (m/sec)  
     – HTY: Heat flux in Y direction (m/sec)  
     – HTZ: Heat flux in Z direction (m/sec)  
   B. Flow Quantities  
     – Q: Volumetric flow rate (l/sec)  
     – QN: Flow quantities at nodal points (l/sec)  
     – TK: Transmissivity (m²/sec), dependent on load case  
   C. Thermal Energy and Flux  
     – HEAT: Heat quantities at nodes (W)  
     – TOHT: Total flux (W)  
   D. Phase or Material State  
     – LFR: Liquid fraction (–)  
     – MUET: Turbulent viscosity (kN·sec/m²)  
     – TE: Turbulent kinetic energy (m²/sec²)  
     – TDN: Turbulent dissipation rate (m²/sec³)  
   E. Boundary and Ageing Metrics  
     – HOPT: Boundary‐layer thickness or similar boundary metric (m)  
     – AGE: Effective age (h)  
     – HDGR: Degree of hydration (–)  
   F. Smoke and Gas Concentration  
     – SMOK: Smoke concentration (g/m³)

3. Usage Context and Postprocessing  
   – After a thermal or flow analysis run (e.g., with HYDRA, DOLFYN, or coupled ASE/TALPA solvers), these codes appear in result files.  
   – In G RAPHIC, the user selects one of these literal codes via the record TYPE to request plotting. The record STYP then determines whether to show values at element centers, nodes, Gauss points, or averaged values.  
   – The “Dim.” column ensures that axis labels, legends, and color‐bar annotations display correct SI units. Automated scripts can use this mapping to populate chart metadata and to convert units if needed.  

4. Integration into a Vector Store  
   – Each literal record becomes a document or embedding in the vector store, containing its code, meaning, and dimension.  
   – Upstream applications (chatbots, dashboards) can query “What does MUET stand for?” or “Show me smoke concentration results in kg/m³,” and the RAG pipeline retrieves this table entry to answer or to trigger unit conversions.  
   – By storing the full text of the “Meaning” field and its “Dim.” alongside the code, downstream components can generate human-readable legends, tooltips, and automated report sections without hard-coding dozens of individual mappings.

In summary, the input table is a canonical dictionary linking simulation‐result keywords (literals) to their semantic definitions and physical units, covering fluxes, flow rates, turbulence quantities, ageing metrics, and concentration values. It is an essential piece of metadata for any automated postprocessing or QA workflow that ingests SOFiSTiK thermal and hydraulic outputs.

content:
The figure presents a schematic overview of how a planar “cut” is defined through a generic quadrilateral or polygonal element when preparing a section or “slice” for stress, shear‐force or reinforcement representation.  At its base is an irregular six-sided polygon (drawn in simple straight segments) that represents the outline of a finite‐element plate or shell—this is the element through which the cut will pass.  

Superimposed on that polygon is a long straight line, drawn horizontally, which denotes the actual section line (“cut line”).  At the left extremity of that line sits a small open circle, identified by the adjacent legend text “Starting point.”  At the right extremity of the same line the word “End” is placed.  Thus the line conveys both the geometrical position of the cut and the parametric direction (from Start → End) used to traverse the element.  

About midway along the cut line, just to the right of where it intersects the polygon, an L-shaped tick mark is drawn.  One arm of the L is collinear with the main cut line and the other arm is perpendicular to it.  A leader line points to this L-shaped symbol, with the label “Section line.”  Implicit in this mark is the convention that the longer arm indicates the tangent to the cut (the “N” or normal direction along the cut), and the shorter arm indicates the transverse or in-plane “T” direction (perpendicular to the cut).  In many SOFiSTiK or WING graphics contexts, these directions are used to decompose stresses and shear forces into components along (N) and across (T) the cutting plane.  

Below the entire assembly is the caption text “Figure 3.11: Directions of the cut.”  No numerical scales or coordinate axes are shown—this is purely a schematic.  The style is minimal: black linework on white background, consistent with technical‐drawing conventions for reinforcement and result cuts.  

Taken together, the diagram communicates:  
• How to position a cut through an arbitrary plate element.  
• Which end of the cut is the parametric “start” versus the “end.”  
• How to identify the local “along‐cut” (N) direction and the “across‐cut” (T) direction for resolving stress and shear results in subsequent plotting routines (e.g., when specifying DTYP, STYP or cut‐related TYPE entries in an analysis graphic).

 The quadrilateral elements in SOFiSTiK includes five Gauss points. Four points are located near the corners and one point in the middle of element.

metadata.sections: 3.44 QUAD – Single Results of QUAD Elements

content:
Four points are located near the corners and one point in the middle of element.. The point in the middle corresponds to the value ’Centre of QUAD elements’ (STYP QUAD). For some non-linear results, it is possible to printout with ’Gauss points’ (STYP GAUS) the values of the four Gauss points which are located near the corners..
 In order to get a smoothed distribution of these values of the four Gauss points which are lo- cated near the corners, WING is able to calculate an averaged value of all Gauss points in the node which is important for cuts or isolines. This value is called ’Averaging node values, read from Gauss points’ (STYP G2N).
 The programs for the analysis (eg. ASE) calculate the nodal values using an extrapolation of the values of the four Gauss points into the nodes and average them about all adjacent ele- ments. In WING it is value ’Nodes of QUAD elements’ (STYP NODE).
 Sometimes the programs do not determine values in the nodes, e.g. in the case of a superpo- sition only for ’ETYP QUAD’ in program MAXIMA and missing input ’ETYP QNOD’ for values in the nodes although these nodal values are necessary for the graphical presentation of isolines or cuts. In such cases it makes sense to calculate temporarily the nodal values of the ’Centre of QUAD elements’ by shifting the value of the centre into the nodes. Subsequently, this value is averaged about all adjacent elements. This value is called ’Averaging node values, read from element centre’ (STYP E2N).
 The programs of the analysis are able to calculate error estimates in the centre of the elements. These values are the ’Error estimates in centre’ (STYP ERIN).
 However, since no error estimates are calculated in the nodes by the programs during analy- sis, WING can determine them similarly to the STYP E2N. This corresponds to the ’averaging node values, read from error estimates’ (STYP EE2N).
 The volume elements are correspondingly used, however, they can have up to eight Gauss points.
 The point in the middle of the volume element corresponds to the value ’Centre of BRIC ele- ments’ (STYP BRIC).
