content:
An input for a minimum value (record SCH2 item MIN1) which should be represented is compared with the support reaction.. Representation at Isolines (REPR DISO). The isolines are calculated one element at a time from the nodal values and drawn. The isolines are defined within each element with a hyperbola. The lines are straight, if the part of the hyperbola is small..
 The designation of the isolines occurs in such a way that the text is readable so called uphill. A designation must be input explicitly with SCHH, if more than 50 isoline values are active.
 The isolines may be designated in intervals (DTXT). GRAPHIC searches for favourable posi- tions within subareas whose size has to be defined via CDIS. The program does not search for closed lines to designate the isolines. CDIS acts only to the designation of the isolines with the same value. An overwriting can not be prevented always in the case of a different level.
 The TYPE FLIE is only possible after a non-linear calculation (programs TALPA, ASE-IV). Usu- ally then the item FROM should be input with zero. In this case only the plasticized areas are represented.
 The types ASUM and ASLM are suitable for reinforcement drawings, if reinforcement mats should be used. For reinforcement mats with transverse reinforcement it is helpful to designate the elements with QUAD ASUR and ASLR additionally, if the transverse reinforcements is larger than 20 percent.
 A reinforcement representation as isolines or in cuts is only reasonable, if the positioning of the reinforcement (direction) is equal in all used elements.
 Either the values of the nodes are directly available or the values are determined from the element values. This may be controlled with an input for STYP.
 Representation at Cuts (REPR DCUT)
 All active DRAW elements with an input for DTYP are cut with the structure (only QUAD elements). The results are represented as status lines along the cuts. The status lines can be marked and/or generated as areas. If only one fill pattern was defined, the colours C13 and C14 and this fill pattern are used.
 Some values can be transformed into the directions of the cut. In this case N is the direction of the cutting line and T is the direction in the element plane perpendicular to the cut.
 After a cut definition, weld seam stresses are also available (TYPE SWNU, SWNL, SWNM, S3NU, S3NL, S3NM).

content:
Some values can be transformed into the directions of the cut. In this case N is the direction of the cutting line and T is the direction in the element plane perpendicular to the cut.. After a cut definition, weld seam stresses are also available (TYPE SWNU, SWNL, SWNM, S3NU, S3NL, S3NM)..
 As GRAPHIC does not know the exact geometry of the weld seam, the required values are approximated from the plate on which the cut lies. The following assumptions are made:
 • Thickness of weld seam = Thickness of the cut plate (area A = t ∗ 1m)
 σ⊥ = Normal stress in the plate that acts perpendicular to the cut (perpendicular to the weld seam)
 •
 τ∥ = Shear stress that lies in the plane of the plate, acting in the direction of the cut
 τ⊥ = Shear stress resulting from the shear forces V and Vy, acting in the cutting direction
 GRAPHIC calculates the stresses of the QUAD elements (plate) via N/A±M/W. In this context, middle (TYPE SWNM, S3NM) means that only the part N/A (slab centre) is used.

content:
The provided table defines a set of parameters (Items) for configuring isoline (contour) generation in a graphics or mapping system. Each row specifies the parameter name, a brief description, the expected unit or literal type, and its default value. Cross‐references (“see record …”) point to other table entries or records (for example, FILL ISOL FROM, STRU, QUAD) that further detail permitted values or behaviors. Below is a structured, field-by-field explanation suitable for indexing in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store:

1. Item: TYPE  
   • Description: Identifies which “type” of isoline or dataset is to be drawn. When set via the DSGN command, it merely assigns input values without rendering. For additional literal options, refer to the QUAD record under TYPE.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal)  
   • Default: * (wildcard/any)

2. Item: FROM  
   • Description: Lower bound of the isoline range. In practice, you must consult FILL ISOL FROM to see how this interacts with fill‐type logic.  
   • Unit: * (unitless or as defined in associated record)  
   • Default: *

3. Item: TO  
   • Description: Upper bound of the isoline range. See FILL ISOL TO for precise interpretation.  
   • Unit: *  
   • Default: *

4. Item: INC  
   • Description: Increment or step between isolines. Detailed behavior is in FILL ISOL INC.  
   • Unit: *  
   • Default: *

5. Item: SCHH  
   • Description: Text height used when labeling isolines.  For further text‐style parameters, see the STRU record.  
   • Unit: cm/LIT (centimeters or literal size units)  
   • Default: H6 (a predefined height category)

6. Item: STYP  
   • Description: Graphic element type or symbol used at isoline vertices or markers.  See QUAD STYP for allowable literal values.  
   • Unit: LIT  
   • Default: NODE

7. Item: CINC  
   • Description: Controls how often a numerical designation (label) is placed:  
      – If CINC < 0, label every |CINC|-th isoline.  
      – If CINC > 0, increase the label value by CINC in the units of TYPE.  
   • Unit: *  
   • Default: –1 (every line is labeled)

8. Item: CDIS  
   • Description: Minimum distance (in cm) allowed between two identical labels to avoid overlap, and also dictates how many decimal places are shown in the designation.  
   • Unit: cm  
   • Default: 5.0

9. Item: ND  
   • Description: Number of decimal places (digits) to display in each label. For default ties to text height, see SCHH’s ND setting in the STRU record.  
   • Unit: –/LIT (numeric count or literal)  
   • Default: * (inherit or auto)

10. Item: FILL  
    • Description: Specifies whether and how the areas between isolines are shaded or colored.  For fill‐style options and patterns, see the STRU FILL record.  
    • Unit: LIT  
    • Default: NO (no fill)

11. Item: AVER  
    • Description: If set to YES, the system will compute and apply an average value over group or block boundaries rather than using raw data points.  See QUAD AVER for more options.  
    • Unit: LIT  
    • Default: NO

Cross-References and Context:  
• AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, QUAD, SECT – These are other record families in the overall schema that define command syntax, literal sets, design conventions, arrow styles, quadrilateral attributes and sectional views respectively. “ISOL” is the specific record for isoline settings; the above table entries may inherit or override defaults from those higher-level records.  
• STRU – Often defines structural or styling defaults that can be overridden here (e.g. text height, fill patterns).  
• FILL ISOL FROM/TO/INC – Specialized fill logic for range and increment, distinct from general INC or FILL commands.

The table under review defines a single configuration parameter, EXTR, which governs how extreme numerical values are marked in a visual representation (often a graph or “picture”). Below is a structured breakdown of its contents and implications:

1. Column Definitions  
   • Item  
     – A short alphanumeric code identifying the parameter. In this case, “EXTR.”  
   • Description  
     – A human-readable explanation of what the parameter controls, followed by a list of possible literal values (enumerations) and their semantics.  
   • Unit  
     – Indicates the data type or category of the parameter’s value. Here it’s “LIT,” denoting a literal or string identifier.  
   • Default  
     – Specifies which enumeration is used if the user does not override the setting. The default here is “LOCA.”

2. EXTR Parameter Purpose  
   “Designation of extreme values” means that, when rendering a dataset visually, certain nodes or points can be flagged to highlight either global extremes (absolute minima or maxima) or local extremes (relative to neighboring points). This helps end users quickly spot key peaks or troughs in the data.

3. Enumeration Values (under Description)  
   • NO  
     – No designation; the system will not highlight any special points.  
   • GLOB  
     – Global extremes only. Both the single smallest and the single largest value across the entire dataset (“the picture”) are marked.  
   • GMAX  
     – Only the single largest point in the entire dataset is marked.  
   • LOCA  
     – Local extremes. Every node that is either a local minimum or local maximum—i.e., smaller or larger than all of its immediate neighbors—is marked.  
   • LMAX  
     – Only local maxima. Nodes that exceed all of their immediate neighbors are highlighted; local minima are ignored.

4. Default Behavior  
   When EXTR is not explicitly set, it defaults to LOCA. This choice suggests that, in typical usage, highlighting every local peak and valley provides the most informative overview of data trends.

5. Cross-References (“See also”)

   • AND – logical conjunction settings  
   • LC – line‐cap or local‐contrast definitions  
   • DSGN – design or styling parameters  
   • ARRO – arrow or vector‐direction controls  
   • QUAD – quadrant‐based partitioning  
   • SECT – sectional annotations or slices  
   • ISOL – isolation or contour settings

The table defines three literal‐type options—AVER, TOTA and TOTT—that control how post-processing results are averaged, summed and annotated when drawing contour lines or cut-lines in a finite‐element model. All three entries share the same data type (“Unit” = LIT, meaning a literal flag) but differ in their default values and in the specific STRU/NODE records they reference.

1. AVER  
   • Purpose: Governs whether nodal results on boundary elements (which become visible as contour lines when you use record STRU WCON) are averaged across shared nodes, or left as raw “jumps.”  
   • Behavior:  
     – NO  : Do not average. The plot will show discontinuous jumps in the result at element boundaries.  
     – YES : Average the results at each node so that the contour is smooth across elements.  
   • Unit = LIT  
   • Default = NEIN  (German for “no”; the system will, by default, not perform averaging.)  
   • Cross-reference: record STRU WCON defines which group boundaries are drawn as contour lines.

2. TOTA  
   • Purpose: Controls the summation (total) of the line representation when you display “cuts” through the model. A cut is a user-defined line along which results are collected and plotted.  
   • Behavior: Since this is a literal flag, specifying TOTA toggles on the summation mode for cut-line results.  
   • Unit = LIT  
   • Default = –  (dash indicates no preset default; you must explicitly turn it on if you want total values.)  
   • Cross-reference: see record NODE TOTA, which actually collects and sums the data points along the cut.

3. TOTT  
   • Purpose: Determines whether textual annotations of the sums (calculated by TOTA) are placed in the graphical output. In other words, if you have summed values along a cut, TOTT controls whether those total values are actually printed as text on the display.  
   • Behavior: As a literal, it can be enabled or disabled.  
   • Unit = LIT  
   • Default = DEFA  (an abbreviation for “default on,” meaning annotation is shown unless you explicitly turn it off.)  
   • Cross-reference: see record NODE TOTT, which handles placement and formatting of the sum labels.

Contextual Notes:  
• All three literals belong to the STRU family of plotting records (the same group that includes AND, LC, DSGN, ARRO, ISOL, SECT, etc.), but they specifically tie into WCON (for contours) and NODE (for cut-line operations).  
• These controls do not alter analysis results—they only affect how those results are visually represented in the post-processing GUI or printed output.  
• Since they are “LIT” or literal flags, the command syntax typically looks like “AVER=YES,” “TOTA=ON,” or “TOTT=OFF,” depending on the system’s accepted keywords.  
• By default, averaging is off (NEIN), summation is off (no default), and sum annotations are on (DEFA), which reflects a philosophy of showing raw element behavior unless the engineer explicitly requests smoothing or aggregated labels.

  • NFLK  – Component‐wise fluid velocities in nodes, unit: m/sec  
  • NFLX/X, NFLY/Y, NFLZ/Z  – Velocity components along X, Y and Z, unit: m/sec  

3. Fluid Velocity (from HYDRA)  
  • FL   – Magnitude of fluid velocity at nodes, unit: m/sec  
  • FLK0 – Component‐wise fluid velocities, unit: m/sec  
  • FLX, FLY, FLZ – Velocity components along X, Y and Z, unit: m/sec  

4. Particle Velocity  
  • PA   – Magnitude of particle velocity, unit: m/sec  
  • PAK0 – Component‐wise particle velocities, unit: m/sec  
  • PAX, PAY, PAZ – Velocity components along X, Y and Z, unit: m/sec  

5. Heat Flux  
  • HT   – Total heat flux magnitude, unit: W/m²  
  • HTK0 – Component‐wise heat flux, unit: W/m²  
  • HTX, HTY, HTZ – Heat flux components along X, Y and Z, unit: W/m²  

6. Flow & Heat Quantities  
  • Q    – Total flow rate through an element, unit: l/sec  
  • QN   – Nodal flow rates, unit: l/sec  
  • HEAT – Nodal heat quantities, unit: W  

7. Material/Medium Property  
  • TK   – Transmissivity (dependent on load case H–Z and hydraulic conductivity), unit: m²/sec  

How to Read and Apply  
– When you see, for example, “NFLY” in a result file, you know it refers to the Y-component of fluid velocity computed by DOLFYN.  
– Plotting records (STRU, LOAD) will look up this literal, apply any scaling (UNIT record), set text height (SCHH) or decimal precision (ND), and render arrows, isolines or color maps according to the chosen REPR style.  
– Obsolete codes (e.g. SCH2 MIN) have been replaced by newer records—refer to the STRU chapter for up-to-date formatting parameters.  

By indexing each physical variable with a clear literal, meaning and unit, the table provides an unambiguous key for automated processing, plotting and post-processing scripts in a RAG-style vector store.

The table is a concise mapping of short alphanumeric “literals” to their engineering meanings and associated units. It is organized into three thematic blocks—basic reinforcement quantities (AS series), decisive design checks (DC series), and stress‐range outputs following an SLS (Serviceability Limit State) strain calculation (SR series). Each row associates a literal code (column “Literal”) with a human‐readable description (“Meaning”) and a dimensional unit (“Dim.”). Below is a breakdown of its structure and contents:

1. Reinforcement Quantities (AS, AS1–AS3)
   • AS   – Total reinforcement in three orthogonal directions; Dim.: cm²/m  
   • AS1  – Reinforcement in the 1st (principal) direction; Dim.: cm²/m  
   • AS2  – Reinforcement in the 2nd direction; Dim.: cm²/m  
   • AS3  – Reinforcement in the 3rd direction; Dim.: cm²/m  
   Notes: These values typically come from the design output of RC (reinforced concrete) elements.  “cm²/m” indicates area of steel per unit length.

2. Decisive Design Check (DC, DC1–DC3)
   • Legend heading: “Decisive design check”  
   • DC   – Overall reinforcement requirement in three directions (no unit; left blank “–” because it may represent a nondimensional check factor or flag)  
   • DC1  – Check value for reinforcement in 1st direction; Dim.: –  
   • DC2  – Check for second direction; Dim.: –  
   • DC3  – Check for third direction; Dim.: –  
   Notes: These DC values often represent utilization ratios or design‐go/no‐go indicators. The absence of a physical unit suggests a ratio or Boolean count.

3. Post‐SLS Strain Calculation Outputs (SRM, SR, SR1–SR3, CPM, SDTM)
   • Heading: “After a strain calculation (SLS):”  
   • SRM  – Maximum stress range across all directions; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • SR   – Stress range aggregated over three directions; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • SR1  – Stress range in the 1st direction; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • SR2  – Stress range in the 2nd direction; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • SR3  – Stress range in the 3rd direction; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • CPM  – Maximum design concrete pressure under SLS conditions; Dim.: N/mm²  
   • SDTM – Maximum skew principal tensile stress for design; Dim.: N/mm²  
   Notes: N/mm² is equivalent to MPa. These entries are typically used to verify crack widths, fatigue, or serviceability limits in concrete or composite structures.

General Observations:
• The “Literal” column provides a compact code for automated data querying or vector‐based indexing.  
• The “Meaning” column delivers the full label, ideal for rendering in reports or GUI legends.  
• The “Dim.” column ensures any consumer of these values understands whether they are dealing with an area density (cm²/m), a dimensionless check, or a stress in N/mm².  
• Group headings (not listed as separate literals) clarify the context in which each block of codes is generated—e.g., reinforcement summary, design‐check flags, or SLS stress‐range results.

Use in a RAG Vector Store:
– Each row can be represented as a separate document embedding (Literal + Meaning + Dim).  
– Group context (AS vs. DC vs. SR) can be encoded via metadata tags (e.g., “type: reinforcement,” “type: design_check,” “type: SLS_output”).  
– Queries against this vector store can quickly resolve a mysterious code (e.g., “What does SR2 mean?”) to its full description and unit.

The table is a concise “data‐dictionary” summary for the INTE control record, which governs interactive drawing and printing parameters in the system.  It defines:

1.  Four columns  
    •  Item  
    •  Description  
    •  Unit  
    •  Default  

2.  Two major row-blocks  
    •  The first—row “SET”—lists all the logical switch-groups.  
    •  The second—rows “PAR1 … PAR9” and “PA10 … PA27”—indicates parameter slots whose exact meaning depends on which SET is active.

Below is how to read and index the table for a RAG vector store:

— Column “Item”  
  •  SET  
     –  This is the controlling index: its integer value (0, 1, …, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 101, 102, 103) selects one of the major switch‐groups described in the “Description” field.  
  •  PAR1 … PAR9, PA10 … PA27  
     –  These are generic parameter positions.  Their semantic “slot” (color index, tolerance threshold, text size, etc.) is determined by which SET number has been chosen.

— Column “Description”  
  •  For SET: a bullet list of all supported SET values and their high-level purpose:  
     –  0: “Current” interactive session values (sheet, picture, layer)  
     –  1…7: various interactive switches (highlighting, 2D/3D mode, grid presentation, reference‐point request, etc.)  
     –  8: properties of the current GRAPHIC printer (sheet dimensions, print borders)  
     –  9: numeric precision / decimal‐place rules for displayed values  
     –  11: QUAD‐cut properties (line group, color, distance to edge, cut‐adjustment modes, etc.)  
     –  12: cutting‐pattern (geodetic lines) properties  
     –  13: additional line properties (group, color, margin)  
     –  14: additional text properties (group, color, background, direction, height, width, alignment, units)  
     –  15: axis properties (group, color, background, text direction, height, width, alignment)  
     –  101: tolerances for line-value label placement (height vs. width thresholds, text displacement rules)  
     –  102: further tolerances for line representation (value‐difference limits, break‐angle, minimum distance for projection, step criteria)  
     –  103: tolerances for area representation (value‐difference limits, isoline gradient limits, minimal element area, normal‐direction uniformity)  

  •  For PAR1…PAR9 and PA10…PA27: a single generic note—“Switch of different meaning according to the input for SET”—indicating that you must look back at the SET description to decode each parameter’s exact role.

— Column “Unit”  
  •  For SET: “–” (no physical unit applies)  
  •  For PAR… / PA…: “*” (meaning “varies by parameter; see SET‐specific documentation”)

— Column “Default”  
  •  For SET: “–”  
  •  For PAR… / PA…: “*” (defaults are parameter‐specific and listed in the detailed record text)

How to index this in your RAG store:

•  Store “SET” as a discrete property with allowed values {0,1,2,…,7,8,9,11,12,13,14,15,101,102,103}.  
•  For each SET value, maintain a sub-document that enumerates its PAR/PA parameters (PAR1…PARn), their descriptions, units, and defaults.  
•  Use the generic table row for PAR1…PAR9; PA10…PA27 as an umbrella entry pointing to the detailed definitions under each SET.  

This schema lets you quickly retrieve, for any given SET (e.g. SET=14), the list of active parameter slots (PAR1…PA11) and look up their precise meanings, units, and default values.

The input table is a structured, two‐dimensional grid of integer identifiers laid out in 5 rows and 8 columns.  It appears to serve as a simple map of element or node numbers in a uniform block discretization (for example, a finite‐element mesh or a BRIC representation), where the table cells encode a three‐digit ID whose hundreds place tracks the row (layer) and whose units place tracks the column (position) within that layer.

1. Overall Dimensions and Headings  
   • Columns: 8 total, headed (left to right) by the numbers “8 7 6 5 4 3 2 1.”  
   • Rows: 5 total, implicitly numbered (from top to bottom) 1 through 5 (though the table itself does not explicitly print row numbers, we infer 5 horizontal strips).  

2. Cell‐Value Pattern  
   • Each cell’s value = (row index) × 100 + (column heading).  
     – Row 1 yields values in the range 101–108, row 2 yields 201–208, …, up to row 5 → 501–508.  
     – Because the columns are labeled in descending order (8 on the left through 1 on the right), the leftmost entry in row r is r*100 + 8, and the rightmost is r*100 + 1.  
   • Example entries:  
     – Top‐left corner (row 1, column 8) = 108  
     – Top‐right corner (row 1, column 1) = 101  
     – Bottom‐left corner (row 5, column 8) = 508  
     – Bottom‐right corner (row 5, column 1) = 501  

3. Spatial Interpretation  
   • Think of “row” as a Y‐coordinate (layers 1…5) and “column heading” as an X‐coordinate (positions 8…1).  
   • This yields a regular 5×8 grid with unit spacing, where each cell holds a unique identifier combining its (X,Y) position.  
   • Such a layout is common when defining surface elements or volume elements on a BRIC block: the hundreds digit denotes the layer number (e.g. depth or vertical slice), while the final digit denotes the position along the horizontal axis.

4. Use in RAG (Retrieval‐Augmented Generation) Vector Store  
   • Each cell can be converted into a vector record with fields:  
     – “row_index”: integer 1–5  
     – “column_index”: integer 1–8 (inverted if you preserve the header ordering)  
     – “element_id”: the three‐digit value from the table  
     – Optionally, “x_coord” and “y_coord” if you want physical positions  
   • These vector records allow fine‐grained retrieval by location, row/column pattern, or specific element ID.  
   • One might also add metadata for “layer stress data” or “surface‐cut flags” if using this grid in the context of BRIC cuts, isolines (ISOL), or section definitions (SECT) as described in the surrounding SOFiMSHA setup.

5. Pattern Regularity  
   • The table is fully regular—no gaps or irregular numbering.  
   • This simplicity makes automatic parsing trivial: for row r = 1…5, column c = 8…1, compute id = 100·r + c.

In summary, the table is a concise 5×8 matrix enumerating a grid of element numbers in a block, with a straightforward arithmetic rule generating each identifier. This structure is ideally suited for building a RAG‐backed vector store where each cell’s spatial coordinates and ID become searchable, retrievable records.

Representation at the surface
 Results can be represented at the BRIC surface, that is at all visible outer areas, as long as no BRIC cuts are defined. An explicit definition of QUAD elements in the program SOFiMSHA is not necessary for the output. If the records ISOL or SECT are used, the literal BRIC must be input for STYP. Then also the results of the volume elements are read from the database (and not the available QUAD results). A three-dimensional observer point of view is selected with the input
 VIEW STAN 1 1 NEGZ
 for a better representation.
 A picture with the structure is generated for the check: which elements are in the surface.
 STRU NUME 1 NUMN 0
 If now a BRIC cut is defined with the records MOVE and DRAW, the cutting area is used as the represented area and not the BRIC surface. The cutting area is determined with the MOVE- DRAW line and the line of vision input with DTYP. If the cutting area cuts the edge of a volume element, the result in the intersection point is interpolated linearly from the beginning node or end node of this edge.
 Further cuts can be defined through the generated cutting areas for the evaluation with the record SECT. For the cutting definitions attention is to be paid, that the line of vision of this cuts is defined perpendicular (in the normal direction) to the BRIC cutting area. The definition of the cut should occur now after the input of the BRIC cut, because perhaps a later input deletes the BRIC cut (the first MOVE after a drawing deletes all additional elements of the current group).
 In the record BRIC the user has the possibility to input plane principal stresses (two directions) instead of three-dimensional stresses (three directions). In this case the third direction is equal to zero. This output is only reasonable, if the cutting areas are defined parallel to the principal axes and correspond with the correct TYPE.
